Prakash Raj announces Sept 1 march over deletions in Karnataka SIR, slams EC: ‘Why put voters in so much trouble?’
Announcing the “Election Commission Chalo” campaign in Bengaluru on September 1, Raj said civil society groups would march against SIR of electoral rolls.
Actor-filmmaker Prakash Raj on Tuesday announced a protest march in Karnataka over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in the state.
Announcing the “Election Commission Chalo” campaign in Bengaluru on September 1, Raj said civil society organisations would march against the SIR of electoral rolls and raised concerns over its alleged flaws, ANI news agency reported.
Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar too said the exercise had “thrown up alarming numbers”, with over 1.08 crore voters marked as ASDDO (Absent, Shifted, Dead, Duplicate, and Others).
This cane after the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) on Monday published the Draft Electoral Roll following the Special Intensive Revision (SIR)-2026 exercise. CEC Kumar lauded the cooperation of voters in the exercise, which he said had earned SIR earn recognition from other countries as well.
Also Read | Karnataka's draft SIR rolls released, over 27% voters face cut
Raj says groups plan to move courts, Shivakumar seeks extension of timeline
Prakash Raj, while addressing a press conference in Bengaluru, said that civil society groups also planned to move the courts to seek a stay on the SIR exercise in Karnataka. “For how many years will a voter of this country, a citizen, have to run after the courts? Why are you putting every voter in this country through so much trouble?” he said. Raj said that Karnataka had another two years left for polls, adding the exercise was “not urgent.”
The actor further questioned the process of selection of members of the Election Commission, calling it “undemocratic.”
“With two members from the ruling party and only one from the opposition, where is the democracy in that? Furthermore, the government decided in Parliament to grant judicial immunity to the Election Commission, ensuring that no case can be filed against any officer for the rest of their lives,” he said, according to ANI.
CM Shivakumar, earlier on Tuesday, said 43 lakh people were set to receive notices over logical discrepancies, and sought an extension of timeline for the exercise. “Extend the period for claims and objections, so genuine voters excluded from the draft roll have adequate time to file claims,” Shivakumar said in a post on X. He further asked for an extension for voters facing notices for logical discrepancies and absence of a link to the 2002 roll.
The Karnataka CM urged increasing the number of EROs and DEOs to handle the claims, objections and applications and “prevent errors and unfair exclusions.” “Mobility, poverty, lack of documentation or lack of information must not become reasons for disenfranchisement,” he said.
What did CEC Gyanesh Kumar say?
Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar said the SIR exercise needs “guts.” Speaking about the exercise at the second regional conference on “Electoral Literacy Clubs (ELC 2.0) and ECINET”, organised by the ECI in Lucknow, CEC Kumar said conducting SIR “requires not only guts on the part of the Election Commission but also the cooperation of the voters.”
“That is precisely why, today, others look to the Election Commission of India, learning from it and praising it, wishing they could or resolving that they will do the same in their own countries,” ANI cited him as saying. The CEC said elections in India are held strictly as per the Constitution of India, law and instructions issued by ECI and “conducted transparently under the concurrent audit of political parties, candidates or their representatives at all stages.”

Who replaces Salah as Africa's Premier League king?
- Published
Six years ago Liverpool were heading into the new Premier League season as defending champions after African superstars Mohamed Salah and Sadio Mane had fired the Reds to a first title in three decades.
Mane's time at Anfield ended in 2022 and now the reign of Egyptian King Salah has also drawn to a close following his move to Trabzonspor in Turkey.
Salah's stats during his nine Premier League seasons with Liverpool are astonishing: 308 games, 191 goals and 93 assists.
The 34-year-old departed Merseyside as the fourth-highest scorer in the competition's history.
A tough act to follow? You bet.
BBC Sport Africa looks at some of those vying to take Salah's place as the continent's star name in the biggest league in the world.
Antoine Semenyo (Manchester City)
The leading candidate, Semenyo's rise to the top has been remarkable - not least because he has certainly done it the hard way.
The Ghana forward was rejected by Arsenal, Tottenham and Crystal Palace as a teenager and did not make his Premier League debut until February 2023.
Three years later, Manchester City decided his energy, power and eye for goal made him worth £65m.
A player who takes his Christian faith seriously, City and Ghana fans will hope Semenyo's move to a Premier League giant will see him start to rival Salah's numbers.
The 26-year-old enjoyed his best league season in terms of goals last time out, finding the net 17 times, even if that tally left him a fair way behind team-mate Erling Haaland and Brentford's Igor Thiago.
If he can continue his seemingly inexorable improvement, this season could see Semenyo become one of football's biggest names.
- From non-league to the World Cup - the Semenyo story 
  - Published23 June
Omar Marmoush (Manchester City)
If there truly is to be a new 'Egyptian King', Marmoush is the only possible heir.
The problem is this Pharaoh has spent most of his time playing second fiddle to top viking Haaland.
The 27-year-old has made 22 Premier League starts in the season and a half since his move from Frankfurt and found the net only three times in the league in 2025-26.
Marmoush scored a double against Atletico Madrid in his first pre-season outing, taking a chance to impress new Manchester City head coach Enzo Maresca.
However, his chance to shine could come away from Etihad Stadium - with Tottenham in talks to sign him.
Bryan Mbeumo (Manchester United)
Now firmly established as one of the Premier League's best forwards, the Cameroonian racked up a combined 27 goal involvements in his final league season for Brentford before moving to Manchester United for £65m.
Mbeumo, 27, only managed 14 goal involvements in his first Premier League campaign at Old Trafford, but he finished strongly after returning from the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) as United regained some of their old swagger under Michael Carrick.
Having missed out on the World Cup, will a summer off allow him to hit the ground running?
Ismaila Sarr (Crystal Palace)
Sarr has been linked with a move to join Mbeumo at Old Trafford and it's not hard to see why.
The Senegal forward will be coming into the new season on a high, having equalled African legend Roger Milla's record tally of four goals at a single World Cup.
The 28-year-old also enjoyed a stellar campaign with Palace last season, scoring a career-high 21 goals in all competitions as he fired the Eagles to glory in the Uefa Conference League.
Outsiders looking to challenge
While Sarr was thriving at the World Cup, Mohammed Kudus was probably watching on with envy.
A long-term hamstring issue denied him a place in the Ghana squad and the 26-year-old will hope injury problems are finally behind him as he looks to secure a starting place in Roberto de Zerbi's Tottenham rebuild.
Kudus undoubtedly has the talent, but showing his trickery and invention on a consistent basis has been the issue.
Everton's Iliman Ndiaye is perhaps the candidate with the real wow factor. Only City's Jeremy Doku completed more dribbles in the Premier League last season.
After a second World Cup campaign, Saudi side Al-Hilal have shown interest, while Manchester United and Arsenal have also been linked.
Would a move to a Champions League team give the man Toffees fans call Skilliman the platform he needs to show his magical twinkling feet can turn tricks into silverware?
At Newcastle United, a knee injury resulted in Yoane Wissa missing the first half of last season as well as Afcon.
But he scored three goals for DR Congo at the World Cup and will surely be a key figure for Newcastle as they look to rebuild.
And could the new king be a defender?
Benjamin Fredrick has just signed a four-year deal and been promoted to Brentford's first-team squad.
That rarest of things - a player signed by a Premier League side direct from Nigeria - he was enjoying a successful loan in Belgium last season and was due to be one of the Super Eagles' starting centre-backs at Afcon until suffering a knee injury on the eve of the tournament.
Bees boss Keith Andrews sees "a lot of potential" in the 21-year-old.
A new arrival...?
Of course, when Salah first arrived in the Premier League, signing for Chelsea from Basel in 2014, very few people knew who he was.
The same could now be said for fellow wideman Zadok Yohanna, who cost Brighton £21.5m in June.
Like Salah, the pacy Nigerian is a left-footer who plays off the right.
Newcastle's £43m signing Bazoumana Traore operates on the opposite flank, and the Ivorian has already been winning praise for his pre-season performances.
Coventry City's new midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi made his mark in the collective consciousness with some high-class performances for Ghana at the World Cup, scoring the late winner against Panama.
The Sky Blues paid a club record £23m for the 20-year-old.
Or could Salah's replacement still be waiting in the wings?
Another World Cup star, Morocco's Ayyoub Bouaddi, looks to be on his way to Manchester City, with the 10-time league winners in negotiations with Lille for the central midfielder who oozed a classy confidence in the Atlas Lions' opener against Brazil despite only being 18.
Or will Victor Osimhen finally land in England, having been constantly linked with a move over the years?
The 27-year-old striker, beloved in Nigeria, already has the profile and hit 29 goals in all competitions last year.
With Salah having moved to Turkey, Osimhen swapping Galatasaray for the Premier League would go some way to filling the hole for African fans.

If you're tight on space or just want a more aesthetically pleasing machine, the best air purifier for home depends on your needs.
If you live in a small apartment like me, you may need to have a multifunctional air purifier for a practical reason: space. These compact, dual-purpose machines are useful if you are tight on square footage or don't want to shell out the money for two separate appliances. Or maybe you're aesthetically driven and want something that looks cool in your space rather than a clunky, large air purifier that can be an eyesore.
Regardless of the reason, these multiuse air purifiers look good, save space, and combine appliances into a single, energy-efficient device.
Check out our other home air quality guides, including the Best Fans, Best Space Heaters, Best Humidifiers, Best Dehumidifiers, and Best Window ACs.

Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Fan
This Dreo offers 99.97 percent HEPA filtration and an air quality sensor. You can control it with a remote, the Dreo app, Google Home, and Amazon Alexa. Best of all, the fan and purifier can operate independently, in case you need just one or the other or want to extend the filter lifespan (replacements run around $40). The 12-month warranty isn’t the greatest, but the device has been trouble-free for nearly two years in our long-term tests. If you're in the market for a fan and purifier in one, this model is definitely worth a look. —Kat Merck

Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Heater
Blueair’s small-room model is a little under 2 feet tall and has built-in heating and cooling. Blueair’s app is easy to use, and I preferred it rather than the actual control panel. The panel did not always illuminate when pressed, making the buttons difficult to use. The app also has more options, like controlling the oscillation speed and angle. Blueair uses both mechanical HEPA filtration and electrostatic technology to capture pollutants in the air. Its CARB certification is listed as electronic, unlike HEPA-only air purifiers that are listed as mechanical.
The ComfortPure 3-in-1 also has an air quality index indicator light that responds to the purifier's built-in sensor to measure particulate matter (PM) 2.5. The easy-to-miss sliver of light glows blue for excellent, green for good, yellow for moderate, orange for polluted, and red for very polluted. It has a control panel lock and filter change indicator light. I also appreciate the cloth handle that makes moving the Blueair easy. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Vacuum
The Eye-Vac Air combines an air purifier with a touchless vacuum. Sweep debris up to the stationary unit, and it'll suck it up. It has two sets of HEPA and activated carbon filters pulling in air from both sides of the purifier. Its filter placement lets you position the Eye-Vac flush against the wall, which is especially useful in kitchen settings. The air filter can clean the air effectively, achieving five air exchanges per hour in a 120-square-foot space. While the large control panel is easy to read, the air purifier and vacuum offer only two options: manual or automatic. Indicator lights show when the bagless vacuum canister is full and when the air purifier filters need replacing. There are three fan speeds, but there are no color-coded indicator lights that correspond to air quality. Instead, three blue bars indicate the fan setting. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Best Air Purifier That Doubles as Art
After testing a dozen or so air purifiers in my tiny apartment, I realized what an eyesore they can be. This air purifier doubles as art and, at the very least, a conversation piece. With such little space, I generally want my tech to be multifunctional, or at the very least look good. When my mom visited, she thought the MinusA2 was an art TV or a monitor with an art background, until it auto-engaged and ran on high after the Canadian wildfire smoke reached New York this summer. This air purifier comes in several artwork styles, including Monet's Water Lilies and Van Gogh's Starry Night, and can be easily hung flush against the wall by removing the bottom stand and using the included mounting bracket.
You can also customize the six-layer filter system inside, with options for a pet allergy-specific filter (which I opted for), germ defense for viruses and bacteria, a charcoal-enhanced odor remover, and a toxin absorber that reduces formaldehyde, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and harmful chemicals. Along with the custom filter, there is a reusable, washable prefilter; a medium filter for pollen and mold; a HEPA filter; an activated carbon filter for odor control; and a negative ion generator. The filters should last up to two years on average if the unit runs for 12 hours a day and is cleaned regularly. I didn't love that it doesn't have wheels or a handle, but it can be easily mounted if you'd rather display it off the floor. It was also super quiet, even on the highest fan speeds. With the remote or the buttons on the unit, you can change fan speeds or pick settings like auto, sleep, or pollen mode. On the front, there's also an odor sensor and light indicating air quality.

Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Sunrise Alarm Clock
The Mini Restful is part of Blueair’s Sleep Collection, and is nearly the smallest air purifier I’ve tested. Blueair claims the Mini Restful can effectively clean the air at the CDC-recommended five air changes an hour in a 140-square-foot space, but only at its highest setting. My sound level meter registered 60 dB—around the sound of a conversation. No one is sleeping with that noise—the Mini Restful is only quiet on its lowest setting. The sunrise alarm clock feature was easy to program through Blueair’s app, and it has nine sounds to choose from, like Midnight Rain, Happy Rise, and Mantra Breeze. I set the alarm to Nordic Flow, a blend of light harp strings and birds chirping. The alarm is designed to begin the subtle sunrise light anywhere from 15 minutes to 30 minutes before the selected wake-up alarm time. I set the alarm to 5 am and was woken by the light at 4:45 am. Even after moving it to my hallway, I could still wake up successfully to the pleasant sounds of Nordic Flow. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Pet Bed
The PetAir is part of the growing market of pet-focused air purifiers. It has a Pet Mode that quiets the fan speed and reduces the air-cleaning capacity when it senses an animal friend is lying on the unit. It has a prefilter that collects pet hair, a high-efficiency H13 HEPA filter, and an activated carbon filter to capture VOCs and odors. There’s even a storage space for toys. It's only about 10 inches high and sits at ground level, so if you’re looking for a pet-specific air purifier, then this fan/airflow placement might be ideal. It can effectively clean the air with the recommended five air exchanges per hour in a 260-square-foot room. However, for general air purification, I prefer taller models as they seem to react more quickly to pollutants throughout a room, like those created by cooking. As for my two testers, I could not get either cat to lie on the bed successfully, but I did collect cat hair in the prefilter. I also wish the PetAir had a built-in heated pet bed, as I am sure my cats would have used it for warmth. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

I was excited to try this air purifier/side table hybrid complete with a mood light and phone charger. At first I wanted to place it next to my bed, but as I read the fine print, I saw the SwitchBot Air Purifier Table needs 12 inches of clearance on three sides. Air purifiers, especially cylindrical models, need unobstructed airflow. The SwitchBot Air Purifier Table allows for one side to be 1 inch away from a wall, but not curtains. Those kinds of placement restrictions keep the air purifier from being a side table. If you don’t mind a small table that can stand against the wall, then the air purifier table might work for a small entryway or bathroom. It has both a HEPA filter and an activated carbon filter to remove odor and VOCs. And while the SwitchBot table can exchange the air in a 260-square-foot room at five times an hour, that would be at its highest, loudest setting. The ideal size for the SwitchBot would be more like a 100-square-foot space, such as a mud room, entryway, or bathroom. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Why Choose a Multiuse Air Purifier?
Small-apartment dwellers need a multipurpose air purifier for a practical reason: space. These compact appliances handle two or more tasks to maximize efficiency, while possibly saving you money too. They also reduce cords, the need for outlets, and storage space when the machine is not in use during off-seasons. Or maybe you're more aesthetically driven and want something that looks cool in the space rather than a clunky, large air purifier.
How I Tested
I tested each model for nearly a month, moving it around my house to test in different locations: when cooking on my unventilated gas stove, under my living room window that draws in a lot of building and exhaust fumes, and outside my cat's litter box. I measured whether and when the air purifier auto-engages, and how long it takes to return to clean air quality. I also used an air quality monitor to check for pollutants and the purifiers' efficacy, and a decibel monitor app on my phone to measure noise level when the appliance is on high. I also tested each setting, paying special attention to the multipurpose features and whether they were actually useful or just gimmicky. When another tester reviews a machine, they use the same metrics.
What I Look For in a Dual-Purpose Air Purifier
One of the main things I considered when testing was whether the extra features were actually useful. Each recommendation on the list has been deemed successful in both air purification and its other marketed “dual-purpose” function. I also considered size and purification ability—that's why the fun terrarium isn't a top pick; while it's super cute, it's not as effective as an air purifier.

- SEGA officially showed the first look at Crazy Taxi World Tour’s multiplayer gameplay at Gamescom ONL 2026.
- The trailer shows players competing with each other in what looks like the Pickup Race mode.
- Crazy Taxi World Tour is officially scheduled to release in 2027.
Crazy Taxi World Tour is confirmed to be hitting the streets in 2027 as SEGA showcases the first multiplayer look of the game at Gamescom ONL 2026. The new multiplayer trailer features multiple taxis racing through the city as SEGA prepares for a closed network test next month.
The new Crazy Taxi World Tour multiplayer first-look trailer shows a new Pickup Race mode. In this multiplayer mode, up to six players race against time across the open map to drop off as many passengers as possible, with the highest cash earner winning.
Earlier, the first look at Crazy Taxi World Tour confirmed that Alex was making a return to the arcade racing series along with Gena, Joe, B.D., and Gus. The latest Gamescom trailer featured Bad Religion’s “Ten in 2010” track, which means that we might be getting songs from the original Crazy Taxi in the upcoming World Tour installment.
Right now, players can sign up for the Crazy Taxi World Tour closed network test until August 31 before the closed network test kicks off on September 11, 2026. SEGA will select a small group of players for the test, so only a handful of players get a chance to play the game before its official release.
Eligible players will be able to participate in two multiplayer modes: Pickup Race and Cops n Cabbies. The test will bring 2 maps, 4 characters, 6 cars, and many more tune-up options for your crazy taxi. On a side note, the closed network test will not feature a single-player story mode.
The full game will offer much more than multiplayer and will also include a story campaign starring Axel, who travels across the globe while running his taxi business in Crazy Taxi World Tour.
This was SEGA’s only showcase at Gamescom ONL 2026, and we did not get to see anything about Stranger Than Heaven tonight. However, fans can still enjoy a chaotic look at Crazy Taxi World Tour and look forward to playing it with friends in multiplayer on Xbox Series X|S, PS5, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2 as it releases in 2027.

New Zealand's tour of South Africa: All Blacks come from behind to beat Lions 41-35 after huge scare in tour match
New Zealand fight back from 18 points down to beat the Lions and remain unbeaten on their tour of South Africa, who they beat in the first Test of their three-match series - watch the second Test live on Sky Sports Action and Sky Sports + from 4.55pm on Saturday
Tuesday 25 August 2026 23:20, UK
New Zealand fought back from an 18-point deficit in the second half to beat the Lions 41-35 and avoid a shock defeat at Ellis Park on Tuesday.
It means that the All Blacks have swept all four provincial teams to remain undefeated on their six-week, eight-match tour of South Africa, on top of beating the Springboks 33-16 in the first Test at the weekend.
New Zealand fielded only three players from that Saturday Test victory over South Africa on the same ground and involved five injury replacements summoned on tour - including one who arrived on Monday - as well as giving a debut to prop Saula Ma'u.

Their defence struggled and missed 19 tackles over the course of the contest that saw them trail 14-0 after seven minutes.
They were still behind at half-time and 35-17 behind in the 47th minute, as the Lions threatened to become the first South African provincial side to beat New Zealand since Orange Free State, now known as the Cheetahs, in 1976.
But like the Stormers, Sharks and Bulls who the All Blacks had already beaten, the Lions are out of season and not match fit.
Having not played since May 30 in the United Rugby Championship quarter-finals, New Zealand eventually came storming back in the last 30 minutes with four successive tries.
Rieko Ioane scored two of them, flanker Ethan Blackadder went over for a second time to earn the All Blacks the lead for the first time in the 62nd minute, while a second too by winger Emoni Narawa in the 79th finally settled the touring side's nerves.
"The Lions came out hissing," Blackadder said. "But we stayed composed and found a way in the end. They were quality tonight."
Blackadder - whose father Todd was on the last traditional tour in 1996 - was one of the New Zealand standouts along with inside center Timoci Tavatavanawai, Narawa, and fly-half Richie Mo'unga, back from Japan and in a black jersey for the first time since the 2023 World Cup final.
All Blacks coach Dave Rennie thought Blackadder was phenomenal. "He's got a massive engine and was everywhere," he said.
Blackadder's Test prospects also improved after Anton Segner was ruled out of the rest of the tour.
Segner was a late withdrawal from the first Test reserves due to an ankle injury that's needed two surgeries. The injury was assessed as acute inflammatory arthritis and he won't be replaced in the squad.
Mo'unga, like New Zealand, got better as the game got older, but he and Beauden Barrett could convert only three of the team's seven tries.
On the other hand, Chris Smith, at home, converted all five of the Lions tries and hit the post with a long penalty.

Premier League new boys Coventry survived an EFL Cup second-round scare at League One Plymouth before easing through 4-2 at Home Park.
City had showed their class by racing into a 2-0 lead within five minutes courtesy of goals from Taiwo Awoniyi and Jack Rudoni but Argyle fought back to level nine minutes into the second half thanks to debutant Danny Irow and Xavier Amaechi.
Second-half substitute Ephron Mason-Clark scored City's third goal within five minutes of his 62nd-minute introduction before Victor Torp wrapped things up with a 78th-minute penalty.
Awoniyi fired City ahead on three minutes, picking his spot after a brilliant flick-on by Caleb Yirenkyi.

Yirenkyi's sublime pass on the spin from skipper Liam Kitching's through ball set striker Awoniyi on his way to goal and he had time to pick his spot to beat home goalkeeper James Storer with a side foot finish.
Within two minutes City increased their lead following a lightning break down the right. Awoniyi set Rudoni racing on his way to goal and he made no mistake, again beating Storer with a clinical finish, this time from the edge of the box.
Jake Bidwell came close to making it 3-0 on the 18th minute, heading just past the post from Joel Latibeaudiere's pinpoint cross to the far post.
Argyle responded in the 21st minute through Irow, who cut in from the left and beat Latibeaudiere, before sending a low shot past City keeper Daniel Bentley into the far corner.
Midfielder Harvey White had sent Irow - who has just joined Plymouth on loan from Tottenham - away down the left with a superb pass from his own half after spotting the winger out wide.
The unmarked Awoniyi could have doubled his tally on 27 minutes but headed wide from six yards from Latibeaudiere's deep cross.
Striker Will Evans' effort flew off the foot of Bentley and on to a post in the 31st minute after the keeper had failed to hold White's long-range effort.
Argyle restored parity on 54 minutes when half-time sub Amaechi won the ball from City defender Kitching and raced into the box before beating Bentley with a thumping low drive into the corner.
Tatsuhiro Sakamoto volleyed just over from Mason-Clark's cross in the 65th minute before the latter restored City's lead in the 67th minute from close range, turning in Torp's thumping cross.
Torp gave Coventry some breathing space by converting a penalty following a foul by sub Joe Edwards on Brandon Thomas-Asante, who could have increased City's lead in stoppage time but hammered his volley over from the edge of the six-yard box.
The managers...
Plymouth's Tom Cleverley:
"It was an entertaining cup tie. It was never in our plan to conceded two goals in the first four minutes.
"We showed a lot of resilience in pre-season, defensive records are what you can build results on so we need to be strong defensively.
"The reaction to that, losing two goals so early, was excellent. I couldn't be happier with the players.
"I thought all four debutants were good. Oli Irow gives us something different. He wants to take players on, good pace and he's direct.
"I thought Tyreeq Bakinson look assured and Joe Mwaro was excellent on his debut. It's a night he will never forget against top opposition and James Storer in goal.
"Then you bring on Xavier Amaechi and he looked sharp, motivated. There were a lot of good performances out there.
"This is what you want from cup ties, I have got a healthy headache ahead of Saturday's league game against Bradford.
"We have lost a game which I never want to do but we are in a healthier place. I thought as a team we showed more personality. We took the hand brake off."
Coventry's Frank Lampard:
"You have always got to enjoy a win but at this point it is also looking at performance and individual and collective performances.
"We made a lot of changes and so for me it's good to have a look at players that we didn't start at the weekend (Friday) and are pushing for places.
"I expected it to be difficult, it's not an easy place to come. It was a great start to the game, two really good goals, high quality goals.
"Exactly what we want running through back lines and just showing good capacity to run and good combination stuff as well.
"Maybe we relaxed or something but we didn't put our foot down. When you get teams in that situation you should go and put your foot properly down and we didn't.
"In an early round in the cup it can happen. Big mistakes for the goals, we must be honest about that, and then a good reaction to win the game pretty well.
"Ephron is a big player for us so it was good to see him looking strong. He wants to get better all the time.
"But of course a win is a big deal because it's a nice feeling to take back on the bus for four hours."

The Trump administration plans to revoke up to 200,000 business and tourism visas held by people who've sought asylum in the U.S., AP first reported on Monday.
Why it matters: It would be the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history and would likely trigger legal challenges.
What they're saying: "We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told AP.
He wouldn't say how many visas might be revoked, adding, "as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."
Representatives for the State Department and the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.
Last year, the administration began "continuous vetting" of more than 55 million U.S. visa holders for potential violations that could lead to revocation or deportation.

Iran-US war latest: US responds to Iranian video threatening to assassinate Trump’s son Barron
Tehran insists Strait of Hormuz is still closed despite ‘understanding’ with Oman
The US secret service says it is aware of an Iranian state television video discussing an alleged plot to assassinate Donald Trump’s youngest son, Barron Trump, 20.
The three-minute video claims Barron is being monitored and that there’s a $10m bounty for his killing.
“The US Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees. Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence,” secret service spokesperson Nate Herring said in an email to Reuters.
Trump previously said he was “number one on the kill list for Iran”.
Meanwhile, Iran said the Strait of Hormuz remained closed despite Tehran agreeing on a temporary transit route through the key waterway with Oman.
“The understanding between Iran and Oman does not mean the opening of the Strait of Hormuz,” deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said.
The statement came as Trump threatened to launch new strikes on a nuclear site as well as Iranian military ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Bessent and Bahrain’s finance minister discuss Iran sanctions
US treasury secretary Scott Bessent spoke about Iran sanctions with Bahrain’s finance minister Sheikh Salman bin Khalifa Al Khalifa, stressing that “Iran must not be permitted to threaten international commerce or use the Strait of Hormuz as leverage against the global economy”.
He also emphasised “the importance of sustained financial pressure on Iran’s remaining economic lifelines” and said that “the US will hold the regime’s financial enablers accountable”.
In a post on X, the treasury department said: “He also emphasised the importance of sustained financial pressure on Iran’s remaining economic lifelines and underscored that the United States will hold the regime’s financial enablers accountable.
“Secretary Bessent also welcomed Bahrain’s longstanding partnership and its continued commitment to safeguarding the integrity of the international financial system. The two officials agreed on the importance of continued coordination between the United States, Bahrain, GCC partners, and the broader international community to combat illicit finance and strengthen economic security.”

Editorial: America’s might has failed in Iran – an ‘economic D-Day’ is also unlikely to succeed
If the best way to get Iran to bend to America’s will is the imposition of unprecedented financial sanctions – an “economic D-Day” – then the obvious question arises: what was the point, in Trump-speak, of bombing the hell out of them, destroying their antiquated conventional forces and threatening the death of a “whole civilisation”?
Indeed, anyone might wonder why, six months ago, the US joined in Israel’s campaign against its implacable enemy in the first place, given that, before that strategic blunder, the Strait of Hormuz was open to shipping, the supply of oil and natural gas was normal, and the whole world was looking forward to some economic growth for a change.

US sanctions four India-based companies and three Indians over involvement in Iran’s petroleum and petrochemical trade
The US has sanctioned four India-based companies and three Indian nationals over their alleged involvement in Iran’s petroleum and petrochemical trade.
The targeted firms are accused of importing or facilitating the import of Iranian petroleum products worth tens of millions of dollars, with one company allegedly involved in imports worth about $69m.
The sanctions are part of the US’s wider effort to cut off Iran’s oil revenues, with Washington targeting around 60 Iran-linked individuals, entities and vessels.
The move comes as the US threatens further penalties against countries continuing to trade with Iran, although it has so far stopped short of imposing secondary sanctions on countries themselves.
A tanker is hit and disabled off Oman's eastern coast
A strike on an oil tanker on Monday night off Oman's coast disabled the ship's engine, the British military's United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organisation reported.
It said all crew were reported safe.
There were no immediate reports of any environmental impact.
Iran periodically fires at vessels attempting to transit the strait to enforce its control of the waterway, though there was no immediate claim for Monday's attack.
The U.S. has also fired on vessels while imposing a blockade of Iranian ports.
Temporary route agreed with Oman doesn’t mean reopening Hormuz, Iranian deputy foreign minister says
Iran says it has agreed with Oman on establishing a temporary 11km-wide transit route through the Strait of Hormuz, with the entry point and part of the exit route passing through Iranian territorial waters.
However, deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said the arrangement “does not mean opening the Strait of Hormuz”.
“We agreed with Oman that the entry route to the Strait of Hormuz will be through our territorial waters, and part of the exit route will also be through our territorial waters,” Gharibabadi said.
He said activating the route would “mean closing the southern route in the strait”, which the US had opened “under pressure from Oman”, arguing that the move violated Article 5 of the two countries’ memorandum of understanding aimed at ending the war.
Iran says Iraq can play ‘decisive role’ in shaping new regional order
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has reportedly said Iraq could play a “decisive role” in shaping a new regional order, particularly in the Gulf, as US forces prepare to withdraw from Iraq.
Speaking to the president of Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council, Faiq Zaidan, Ghalibaf described the moment as “historic” for both countries.
“A new regional order is being created. The situation is sensitive and historic for Iran and Iraq. The fact that the American coalition forces are going to withdraw from Iraq is a historic honour for the Iraqi government and people,” Ghalibaf told Zaidan, according to Iran’s Tasnim news agency.
He said the US started its war against Iran with “the intention of overthrowing the Islamic Republic and expanding American hegemony in West Asia and the Islamic world”.
He said Iran’s resistance “clearly defeated” US war goals.“America lost the military and political war against Iran, and it will also fail in economic measures,” Ghalibaf told Zaidan.
Trump ‘grossly profiting’ from ‘illegal’ war on Iran, US senator says
US senator Chris Van Hollen has accused Donald Trump of personally profiting from the “illegal” war with Iran, citing a Democratic report that found the president’s oil and gas holdings may have gained up to $15.5m this year.
Van Hollen alleged that Trump had turned the White House into a “pay-to-play casino” and was “grossly profiting off of a senseless war”, while claiming Trump had “pocketed over a billion dollars” since returning to office.
He later wrote on X: “While prices are going up for Americans, things couldn’t be going better for his stock portfolio.”
“Trump continues to profit off Americans’ pain – including the senseless war he started in Iran.“Pure corruption.”
China warns about US sanctions threat disrupting its cooperation with Iran
China has warned that expanded US sanctions targeting entities and individuals linked to Iran, including some based in China, “should not disrupt” or “undermine” its cooperation with Tehran.
Foreign ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said China-Iran cooperation has complied with international law.
China is one of Iran’s biggest trading partners and buys most of the country’s oil exports.
The warning came after the US treasury department announced sanctions on nearly 60 Iran-linked entities on Monday, including several in China, although it stopped short of imposing secondary sanctions on countries trading with Iran.

I have skinny wrists. So skinny, in fact, that during the craze from the late 1990s to early 2010s, when watch cases started to tip over 48 mm, it became hard to find pieces that suited those of us not blessed (or cursed) with Schwarzenegger-sized forearms. Thankfully, watch case sizes have calmed down considerably since then, and now it's easy to find smaller models, particularly around that 38- to 40-mm Goldilocks zone.
This brings us neatly to Omega's latest collection of Speedmasters, all of which come in that ideal 38-mm size. The seven references in new color variations have been tweaked to improve the existing 38-mm Speedy collection. The most notable improvement? The oval subdials have been banished in favor of proper rounded versions seen on the Moonwatch. They have also been overhauled in Moonwatch style and are now thicker with the essential Dot-Over-Ninety.
Across the new collection, two self-winding movements power the pieces. The Caliber 3330 powers the six references with date functions, including a $11,700 “cappuccino” style version with an ivory-color main dial, contrasting brown PVD-coated subdials, a stainless steel case, and an 18K Sedna gold bezel.
It's the seventh Black Dial reference with no date that's the pick of the bunch, however, powered by the Caliber 3332. Omega positions the $6,500 watch as much more “closely aligned with the signature look of the Moonwatch,” which it certainly is, compared to the existing black 38-mm model with a date window and inferior bezel design.
The reduced sizing, clean, uncluttered black matte-finish varnished dial, Moonwatch-style five-link bracelet, and much-improved black aluminum bezel bring to mind the classic Speedmaster Reduced from the late 1980s. A friend of mine has a Reduced, and I have coveted it for years as, when I see it, it always looks the perfect size on the wrist.
Launched in 1988, the Speedmaster Reduced had an ideal 38.5-mm case size, rather than the 38 mm in this new model. Other subtle differences include the crown position on the Reduced, which is lower and visibly offset from the pushers, and the bezel doesn't have the Dot-Over-Ninety, either.
The biggest giveaway that this is not a faithful reissue of the Reduced is that the subdials are in different positions. On the Reduced, the layout was running seconds at 3, 12-hour totalizer at 6, and 30-minute totalizer at 9. On this 38 mm, it's reversed, with the 30-minute totalizer at 3, and running seconds at 9, just as on the larger Moonwatch.
So perhaps it's best to think of this enticingly sized new 38-mm black Speedy as a “mini Moonwatch,” as it shares more design cues with the iconic Speedmaster, even if its diminutive dimensions conjure up memories of the Reduced models from the ’80s. Either way, the 38-mm’s price makes it the cheapest black-dial “Moonwatch” Speedmaster now available, which is most welcome—and it's a rare thing indeed to be rewarded for having skinny wrists.

Indonesian streaming platform Vidio has partnered with ReelShort, the microdrama platform owned by Crazy Maple Studio, marking ReelShort’s first entry into the Indonesian market.
Hundreds of ReelShort titles will become available on Vidio starting Sept. 1.
The content will stream through a dedicated Short Drama tab, accessible to subscribers on Vidio’s TV Extra, Platinum, Platinum Extra and Ultimate packages. The catalog spans genres such as fantasy, family drama, romance and billionaire romance, told in episodes running 60-90 seconds. More than 200 titles will launch with Indonesian dubbing, with a wider slate available in Indonesian subtitles.
Beyond distribution, the deal includes a co-production slate between ReelShort and Indonesian production houses, with resulting series set to appear on both platforms. The partnership is also framed as a skills exchange, giving Indonesian creative talent exposure to ReelShort’s production pipeline. The agreement was brokered by AR Global Media Network.
Popular on Variety
The Vidio tie-up extends ReelShort’s Southeast Asian expansion after earlier partnerships in Thailand with AIS and in the Philippines with Globe. According to Media Partners Asia (MPA), ReelShort holds an estimated 29% share of global short-form drama revenue.
Vidio’s Short Drama section has existed on the platform since last year. Vidio closed the second quarter of 2026 with 5.8 million paying subscribers in Southeast Asia, the third-largest total in the region. MPA data cited identifies Indonesia as Asia-Pacific’s biggest market for short-form drama viewership, representing 39% of the region’s audience, while mobile ad company Mintegral has recorded quarterly growth of 50%-200% for short-form drama apps since the third quarter of 2023.
“Vidio continues to evolve alongside the changing ways Indonesians consume entertainment,” said Sutanto Hartono, CEO of Vidio. “As audiences increasingly look for content that fits seamlessly into their daily lives, we want to ensure they can find every type of entertainment they love on a single platform, from live sports, local originals, global entertainment to now, the rapidly growing format of short dramas. Our partnership with ReelShort not only responds to this emerging audience demand but also strengthens Vidio’s position as Indonesia’s most comprehensive entertainment platform, offering more choice, greater convenience, and an even richer viewing experience for our subscribers.”
Crazy Maple Studio founder and CEO Joey Jia called the deal a milestone for the company’s regional strategy, saying it reflects a shift in how audiences consume entertainment as microdramas move toward the mainstream. “Indonesia is one of the region’s most dynamic entertainment markets,” Jia said. “We see tremendous potential not only to expand access to our global catalogue, but also to create original stories for Indonesian audiences. Through our planned local productions with Vidio and Indonesian production partners, we look forward to combining ReelShort’s global experience in developing high-performing short-drama IP with local creative talent to build stories and franchises that resonate locally while reaching audiences across the region and beyond.”
Vidio’s move builds on its existing lead in Indonesia’s subscription video market. Per the MPA and AMPD Online Video Consumer Insights: Southeast Asia Q2 2026 report, Vidio holds the largest share of Indonesia’s SVOD subscriptions, at 20.7%.
MPA CEO and executive director Vivek Couto pointed to that scale as central to Vidio’s standing in a crowded field. “Indonesia is one of the most competitive streaming markets in Southeast Asia, with strong demand for both local and international content,” Couto said. “Vidio’s position as the platform with the largest share of SVOD subscriptions in Indonesia, at 20.7%, reflects its ability to build scale through a deep understanding of the local market, supported by strong local content and engagement across categories. This position also highlights the increasingly important role of local platforms in shaping the streaming landscape across Southeast Asia.”
Thousands of ReelShort episodes will be accessible on Vidio’s Short Drama tab starting Sept. 1.

Even though the World Cup is among the pinnacles of the sport, it is safe to say the timing of this edition was one of major inconvenience for the Indian men’s team. After the year it had endured, in which it was well short of matching up against top contenders, the World Cup only served to magnify the flaws already present in the set-up.
Without it, India would have gone into the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya as a hot favourite to retain the gold, which might have masked its deficiencies.
In the World Cup in Amstelveen, those flaws were laid bare. The manner of the capitulation in the must-win game against Argentina would have brought back nightmares of the 8-0 drubbing the South American side dished out in the Pro League earlier this year. Head coach Craig Fulton shouldered responsibility for the loss, but the repeated errors and indecision on the field must be shared by the players, too.
India came into the tournament as the world No. 8 side. It also played like one. This side expectedly beat lower-ranked sides Wales and Pakistan, but lost all three of its outings against higher-ranked opposition: England, Netherlands and Argentina. The only consistent thing about this team has been its inconsistency, managing a good half in just two of the four quarters across these matches.
The losses against these three nations highlighted how far behind India is when it comes to speed, physicality and technical ability. The ease with which some of the Argentine players beat their markers with skill and directness was in stark contrast to India, which struggled to break open opposition defences.
Fulton conceded that his players were struggling to form the connections needed to get into good scoring positions inside the circle. Among the top eight sides, India had scored the fewest field goals after five games. If not for Harmanpreet Singh’s dragflicks, which yielded six goals, this could have ended even worse.
With a seventh-eighth classification game to go, India has let in 16 goals in five matches, the most it has conceded in an edition since 2010. Yet, the class of 2026 is a significantly experienced group.
The performances of some of the seniors, including Amit Rohidas and Mandeep Singh, were underwhelming. Rohidas had an ordinary outing, while Mandeep, who is yet to score, has been on the periphery. Is there a road ahead for them beyond the Asian Games?
Manpreet Singh, approaching the latter half of his 30s, also had a mixed World Cup. Repeated injury concerns for Harmanpreet, who played the second-round matches with a back strain, will add to Fulton’s woes.
With the pressure mounting, Fulton will know that a gold medal at the Asian Games, which would also seal a Los Angeles Olympics berth in 2028, would offer him some breathing room. But he must act swiftly if India is to avoid slipping further away from the rest of the world.
Ray of hope
The same cannot be said for the women’s team, however. Expectations were low-key for a side that only began to take shape under the returning Sjoerd Marijne seven months ago.
But in a short period, progress can be measured in both results and performances, from a squad that included 11 tournament debutants. Put together in a tough group involving China and England, the world No. 9-ranked side pipped the latter to break into the top eight. With a fifth-sixth classification game to come, the women’s side is on track for its best World Cup finish since the inaugural edition in 1974.
After turbulent spells under Janneke Schopmann and Harendra Singh, Marijne has brought familiarity and much-needed belief that had previously been lacking. “The team’s environment has changed a lot. It’s a healthy environment where everyone can speak, everyone can laugh, and questions are asked for their improvement,” Savita Punia, the senior-most member of the team, told Sportstar.
India started with an impressive 2-2 draw against world No. 4 China, before holding England to a goalless draw. In the five matches it played, it lost just once, to three-time reigning champion Netherlands, which was made to work hard for its win.
Bichu Devi, who has stood up in Savita’s absence in recent times, continued her rise with another solid showing, adding a career highlight with the last-minute save against England that ensured India’s progress into the second round.
Several young players, including Sakshi Rana, Sunelita Toppo, Deepika and Ishika, impressed. But the lack of tournament experience also cost the side when Shilpi Dabas conceded a Penalty Stroke in the draw against China, and in the error-strewn performance in the goalless draw against Australia, which ended its semifinal hopes. The over-reliance on Navneet Kaur, India’s top-scorer, for goals ultimately caught up with it.
There will be plenty to learn from this exposure for Marijne’s transitional side, which will head into the Asiad hoping to upset China once again and go for gold.
The furore over the new kits died down as both teams started on a positive note in them. But the irony was hard to miss: in orange, India lost all three matches against teams wearing blue.

Trump’s nutrition advisor says kids should eat food fresh from the ground - like hot dogs
Dr. Ben Carson was promoting healthy school lunches that mean pupils ‘won’t have a craving for the unhealthy foods’
President Donald Trump’s nutrition adviser has said kids should eat food fresh from the ground, and then suggested hot dogs as an option.
During an event to promote nutritious school meals from local farmers on Monday, Dr. Ben Carson talked about teaching children where their food comes from and having them taste veggies straight from the soil.
“I remember not too many months ago, [Agriculture] Secretary [Brooke] Rollins and I went to a school, and we were giving the children whole milk. They were just so amazed. They said, ‘I didn’t know milk could taste this good!’
“And what if we introduced them to food fresh from the ground? Teaching them — making these relationships with the farmers so they learn about the soil. They learn about irrigation. They learn about the effect that it has on their crop,” Carson said.
Carson then listed some examples of food children could eat on these farms, with one processed meat catching the audience’s attention.
“They get an opportunity to eat a tomato fresh off the vine. It’s a different food than you get in the store, quite frankly. Fresh sweet corn and hot dogs,” Carson said to laughter. “But what a difference it makes when they can taste these things. They won’t have a craving for the unhealthy foods that are so prevalent in our society.”
Carson, a former neurosurgeon and an opponent of Trump during the 2016 presidential election, was sworn in as the national advisor for nutrition, health and housing at the Department of Agriculture last September. He also served as Trump’s Department of Housing and Urban Development secretary during his first presidential term.
His comment about feeding children hot dogs for a nutritious lunch is the latest flub from a Trump official attempting to carry out the goals of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, which scrutinizes ultra-processed foods.
In late July, Kennedy grossly underestimated ingredient costs while presenting a recipe on his cooking show, The Real Food Show, which is focused on healthy, affordable meals. Instead of calculating how much it costs to buy the whole ingredient, just the price of each serving of the ingredient needed for the recipe was shown.
As Washington Post columnist Monica Hesse noted in an article, “that kind of practical thinking is not helpful to a parent who has $20 in cash to get them to tomorrow’s paycheck.
“Safeway does not let you walk in, scoop some mayo out of a jar and pay one dollar at the cash register. You have to buy the whole thing.”
Rollins was also roasted earlier this year for suggesting Americans eat “a piece of chicken, a piece of broccoli, corn tortilla and one other thing” as a budget meal.
“‘You should eat prison meals’ prob not the best message,” Variety’s Chief Correspondent Marlow Stern wrote on X at the time.
Carson was at the Agriculture Department’s Washington, D.C. headquarters on Monday to support Rollins and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s new “Harvest to Hallways” initiative as part of the administration’s MAHA agenda.
The initiative will include a $50 million investment in school cafeterias, which, in part, will help pay for new equipment and up to $25 million in grants for schools to provide kids with locally grown foods.
These investments in healthy school lunches come at a time when a packed lunch for children costs more than $6, and Americans struggle to pay for their grocery bills.
While many school districts do offer some kind of cafeteria lunch for free, or at a reduced price, fewer children automatically qualify due to changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program made under the Trump administration.

In August 2026, social media users circulated an apparent Truth Social post from U.S. President Donald Trump in which he floats the idea of renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America.
A screenshot of the purported post circulated on X and Threads. Here's what Trump allegedly said, in full:
The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don't expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer. Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP
Trump did, in fact, make the above Truth Social post on Aug. 25, which can be viewed on his account (archived). The White House also shared the screenshot on X (archived). As such, we have rated this claim as true.
The president later shared a map of the area, with "Lake Ontario" crossed out and replaced with "Lake America."
Trump's social media posts about renaming Lake Ontario came after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from negotiations over tariffs amid a contentious trade war between the United States and Canada.
"When the Americans go to the negotiation table first with the right attitude towards our industries and a true partnership, of course we'll come to the negotiation table," Carney said. "But an attitude that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States … that's not something we're going to accept."
Snopes previously confirmed that Trump said he wanted to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, which he eventually followed through on via executive order.
As with the Gulf of Mexico, Trump is allowed to change Lake Ontario's name for official U.S. government use, but he can't dictate what other governments call it. Lake Ontario is a shared international waterway, and Canada and the United States jointly manage it through multiple agreements.

Hackers linked to Iran have been blamed for a cyber-attack that caused a British power plant to be temporarily shut down.
The incident involved a small-scale energy generator, according to the UK government and at no point was there there risk to the wider energy system.
However, it marks an apparent escalation in the threat posed by Iran after the UK said it had given permission for the US to launch “defensive” operations against Tehran from British bases.
The power plant was shut down for four days as a result of the attack last month, according to the Sunday Telegraph, which first reported it.
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This story refers to an incident impacting a small-scale energy generator, and at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system. The UK has a highly resilient energy system. We work closely with the energy sector to protect infrastructure and ensure the highest security standards.”
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which deals with attacks on critical infrastructure, is understood not to have received any reported outages from regulated operators of power stations.
Hostile states such as Russia, China and Iran are increasingly targeting systems behind the UK’s key services, according to a warning this year from Richard Horne, the NCSC’s chief executive.
The government said last month the UK was “ready to defend itself” after Iran’s military warned any bases being used by the US were “legitimate targets”.
The UK has allowed the US to launch so-called defensive operations from British bases hosting American planes since the start of its war on Iran but has refused to help in offensive operations. That policy has not been altered by the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, who was notified last week that a decision had been made to extend the agreement with the US.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said last month that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.
Iran has been accused for years of carrying out cyber-attacks on various countries, including in relation to a massive power outage in Turkey in 2015 and several possible breaches of Israeli government websites in 2022.
US government security agencies issued a warning earlier this year of cyber-attacks on critical infrastructure by hackers linked to the IRGC.
The US has alleged that an Iran-affiliated group known as “CyberAv3ngers” carried out a campaign against it in 2023 that compromised at least 75 devices in multiple infrastructure sectors.

The untold tragedy of three IAS aspirants who drowned to death in the basement of their coaching centre in New Delhi’s Old Rajinder Nagar, is a macabre reminder that anyone can drown, anywhere. Ironically, this grim but entirely preventable incident, which occurred due to callous negligence and lax regulations, took place two days after countries observed Drowning Prevention Day — a WHO led global event, held annually to raise awareness about this leading cause of death.
The world is drowning. Rising seas, maximum cities, spiralling poverty and risky livelihoods, 120 million forcibly displaced people, children who make perilous journeys to reach schools – all these conditions are colliding to make death by drowning a haunting and increasingly frequent occurrence. Studies have warned that in the not so distant future ravaged by cyclones, hurricanes, tsunamis and floods, our exposure to water will amplify manifold. Most at risk will be children under 10 and adolescents who already account for half of all drowning deaths.

Israel’s Netanyahu claims Iran tried to murder one of his sons
Netanyahu’s coalition is trailing in opinion polls two months before an October 27 general election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed that Iran tried to kill one of his sons.
However, he gave no details about when the alleged plot took place, which son was targeted or how close it came to being carried out.
Netanyahu's allegation underscores the heightened tensions since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began in February, during which Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other senior Iranian leaders were killed.
Netanyahu, whose coalition is trailing in opinion polls two months before an October 27 general election, made the claim in a telephone interview with Israel's Channel 14. He was responding to reports that one of Israel's security agencies had refused to provide protection for a political rival ahead of the nationwide vote.
"As for my sons. Here, I think there is something quite unbelievable, yes. Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to kill, to murder one of my sons," Netanyahu told the conservative channel known for its favourable coverage of the government.
"Iran tried to murder one of my sons, and therefore this security protection is not a luxury," he said, without providing any further details about the alleged plot or how close it came to being carried out.
It was not immediately clear which of his sons he was referring to. Netanyahu's elder son, Yair, lives in Miami.
Iran's mission at the United Nations in New York did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the accusation.
Netanyahu also said he had told the Shin Bet security agency chief David Zini that appropriate security should be provided for any prime ministerial candidate.
Israeli media had reported earlier that Zini declined to provide security for Gadi Eisenkot and told the country's election authority there was no plot to harm him.
Eisenkot's party is projected to win the largest number of seats in the election, although Israeli governments are usually formed through coalitions among multiple parties rather than by a single party winning a parliamentary majority outright.

Before sunrise, Shameema slips on her worn rubber sandals and checks the insulated box – the ice packs inside must maintain the crucial cold chain at between 2C and 8C (35.6-46.4F). She hoists the container on one shoulder and steps out into the dark.
Tanzeela follows with her own pack, after quickly retying the laces of her canvas shoes. Both women live in Pulwama, a district where summer temperatures climb to 37C. Their destination lies higher, out of the valley where asphalt turns to dirt track and then to a barely distinguishable footpath along the floor of the mountain pine forests.
Shameema, 45, has worked as a vaccinator for more than a decade, while Tanzeela, 28, joined the programme three years ago. They form part of India’s army of 2.5 million frontline health workers – the human machinery behind the world’s largest immunisation campaign.
Shameema estimates she has administered polio drops to more than 3,000 children during her years as a vaccinator. She remembers a boy in her village who limped with a deformed leg, the legacy of a polio infection before India had fully eradicated it. It is this memory that keeps her going.
“I saw that child struggle to walk to school,” Shameema says during a pause near a stream. “His mother held him on her back until he grew too heavy. [People in] these mountains need protection too – the children here deserve the same health as those in the cities.”
This morning, they are walking towards Namblan, a meadow ringed by pine trees where nearly 50 dhokas, the seasonal mud-and-stone homes of Gujjar and Bakarwal nomadic families, are scattered over the hillsides.
Even before the paved roads end, the electricity lines stop far below these settlements. Horses are the primary transport for the families who spend the summer months with their livestock in these highlands.
The women climb more than 12 miles (20km) with the heavy insulated cool boxes, which hold vials of the oral vaccines, ice packs and the thick paper registers that document the day.
Tanzeela has given polio drops to about 800 children since she joined the programme. She wears the same shoes she uses for farm work. The soles have worn thin, but they grip the rocky paths better than the sandals of some colleagues, she says. One fellow worker walks barefoot for parts of the trail.
“The payment is small and the paths are steep,” Tanzeela says. “I think about my own nephews when I climb. The drops take seconds, but they change a life for ever.”
Their compensation is 125 rupees a day – about £1 – from the state government for the two-day vaccination campaigns, which happen four to six times a year during the national immunisation drives that target all children under five.
India’s polio programme represents a triumph of planning, vigilance and human endurance. The country has been certified polio-free since 2014 – with the final confirmed case in January 2011 in West Bengal – largely thanks to a surveillance network of 60,000 health workers, who monitor 40,000 reporting sites for acute flaccid paralysis, the signature symptom of wild poliovirus.
The oral polio vaccine uses a live but weakened form of the virus developed by a Polish scientist, Albert Sabin, in the late 1950s. The two drops placed on a child’s tongue stimulate antibodies in the intestinal lining that destroy the virus before it can enter the bloodstream and attack the nervous system.
The same gut immunity reduces viral shedding in infected children, ending the chain of transmission in communities where clean water comes from streams and springs. The oral formula creates communal immunity, protecting whole clusters of children who share courtyards and water sources.
This biological shield proves especially vital in the disputed region of Indian-administered Kashmir, where 73% of the 14 million population live in rural areas, with hundreds of thousands of children under six living in far-flung villages and mountain settlements.
Seasonal migration routes take the Gujjar and Bakarwal pastoral communities of about 1.2 million people far from clinics and hospitals during the summer. Reaching them requires coordination between state health departments, local panchayats (village councils) and the frontline workers who know the mountain trails.
The national immunisation effort targets 27 million children under five, and up to 1.7 million vaccinators can be deployed during a single day of a national immunisation drive. Those workers staff 750,000 booths, then fan out with mobile teams into forests, deserts and urban slums.
The scale of this operation dwarfs most military logistics exercises. Insulated boxes travel by foot, bicycle, boat and bus, but in regions such as Kashmir, the final leg of this journey is always down to women travelling on foot.
The dhokas sit miles apart, sometimes separated by ravines and streams that swell with melted snow. A mother might walk two hours to meet the vaccinators halfway, her baby strapped to her back. The workers record these encounters in their paper registers, marking the child’s name, age and the date of the dose.
Shameema and Tanzeela know the terrain and the communities, and time their ascent to reach the first dhokas as the families finish their morning prayers.
“The families welcome us with tea and bread,” Shameema says. “They know the value of these drops. Some remember the days prior to full eradication, when children in neighbouring villages fell ill.”
India’s greatest public health victory still depends on these health workers willing to make such critical journeys for little reward, dedicated to maintaining the country’s protection against the devastating disease.
By late afternoon, the final dhoka receives the vaccinators. A child opens their mouth, gets two drops on their tongue, another name goes on the register and the insulated box is a bit lighter as the women begin their descent down the same tracks they climbed hours earlier. It will be dark by the time they reach home.

Researchers at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN), Hyderabad, have found that exposure to lead can significantly disrupt the natural waste-clearing and recycling system of nerve cells, providing fresh insight into how environmental factors may contribute to cellular changes associated with neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease.
Effects of lead and protein fragments associated with Alzheimer’s disease studied
The study examined the effects of lead and amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptides, protein fragments associated with Alzheimer’s disease, on human neuronal cells in the laboratory. Nerve cells rely on lysosomes, tiny structures within cells that act as a waste-disposal and recycling system. They break down damaged proteins and other unwanted cellular material, helping maintain cellular health and function.
Impact on structures that act as a waste-disposal and recycling system
The researchers found that exposure to either lead or amyloid-beta peptides individually impaired lysosomal function. However, combined exposure caused significantly greater disruption as it reduced cell survival, disturbed the acidic environment required for normal lysosomal function and damaged lysosomal structure.
In addition, lysosomal membranes became unstable and leaky, potentially allowing harmful enzymes to escape into the cell and cause further damage. According to the researchers, these findings suggest that environmental lead exposure may amplify the cellular stress associated with amyloid-beta and make nerve cells more vulnerable to injury.
ICMR-NIN’s Head of Cell Biology Suresh Challa, who led the research team, said, “Understanding these cellular changes can help us better understand how environmental exposures may influence neuronal health.” “The study highlights the importance of understanding the interaction between environmental pollutants and biological factors in maintaining brain health,” said ICMR-NIN director Bharati Kulkarni, according to a press release.
