Rajasthan Agriculture and Rural Development Minister Dr. Kirori Lal Meena has been admitted to the Medical ICU ward at Sawai Man Singh Hospital in Jaipur after testing positive for swine flu. The minister experienced fever and restlessness before testing positive for the H1N1 virus. Doctors at SMS Hospital confirmed that his health status is stable while placing him in the ICU due to breathing difficulties. The incident comes amid a rapid surge in swine flu cases across Rajasthan and the rest of the country.
Delhi Police have registered a case of abetment to suicide against unknown persons following the death by suicide of a thirty-one-year-old Master of Science physics student at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi campus. The police registration aligns with Supreme Court guidelines regarding student suicides within educational institutions, and an investigation remains underway. Meanwhile, campus protests have intensified as students demand one crore rupees in financial compensation for the family, the resignation of senior student affairs officials and the physics department head, alongside an independent probe into the incident. The institute announced a five-member external inquiry panel comprising a former state police chief and a senior psychiatry head to submit a report within two weeks, alongside measures such as an ombudsperson for grievances and mental health mentoring support. However, protesting students rejected the administration's response as inadequate and evasive, demanding immediate administrative accountability and continuing their demonstrations on campus.
The New York City Mayor has expressed opposition to a planned event featuring the RSS chief at Madison Square Garden on August 29. Addressing a news conference, the mayor stated that he does not support the rally, citing his vision of India as a pluralistic society and a secular republic. However, he noted that municipal authorities may not have the jurisdiction or legal power to cancel a privately organized gathering. The RSS chief arrived in the United States as part of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh's centenary year global outreach program, where he is scheduled to address members of the Indian diaspora at the iconic venue. The bulletin highlights that opposition to the visit has also been raised by US religious freedom officials and civil rights organizations calling for restrictions, while organizers continue preparations for the gathering.
A family suicide case in Andhra Pradesh involving Panchayat Raj Assistant Engineer K. Nooka Raju, his wife Meena, and their daughter Soujanya has drawn widespread attention following allegations of extortion, harassment, and forced conversion. The three jumped into the Godavari River on August 16, while Soujanya's 10-year-old son survived after being rescued by fishermen. Investigators recovered suicide notes written by Soujanya and Nooka Raju accusing rifle shooting coach Sheikh Sadiq Khan of subjecting the family to months of mental torture, financial pressure, and attempting forced conversion to Islam. Soujanya also alleged in her five-page letter that Khan poisoned her deceased husband, Kovvur Jagadeesh Reddy, monitored her continuously, and threatened to kidnap her son. Khan was arrested in Meerut on August 22 and brought back to Andhra Pradesh, where police registered FIRs under sections including abetment to suicide, extortion, and forced conversion.
During Operation Sindoor, an Indian loitering munition deployed to hunt Pakistani radar systems near Sargodha ran low on fuel and unintentionally struck Kirana Hills, a strategically sensitive nuclear hub. Satellite imagery of the complex showed smoke rising from the hilly area near underground storage bunkers, surface storage areas, and radar installations. The incident exposed vulnerabilities in sensitive Pakistani military infrastructure and raised questions regarding aerial defense capabilities over key strategic sites. In addition, military planners initially identified Skardu as a target during the escalation matrix, but adverse weather conditions prompted a shift to strike Bhoolari near Karachi, ensuring the final strike was delivered by Indian forces. Furthermore, approximately seventy to eighty percent of military platforms deployed across land, air, and naval domains are of Chinese origin. Original equipment manufacturer personnel from China were reportedly present to fulfill contractual obligations for servicing and maintaining these weapon systems during military operations.

The Atlantic announces Jessica Goldstein as SVP of events
Goldstein joins after leading events at NPR and the Skoll Foundation
The Atlantic has hired Jessica Goldstein as senior vice president of events, who will work in partnership with managing director for events Evan Smith to lead and produce the magazine’s robust live programs nationwide. She begins with The Atlantic in early September.
Jessica has spent her career telling stories through reporting and creating live experiences that resonate far beyond the stage. She spent eight years creating and leading NPR’s live cultural programming, including creating the Tiny Desk Contest, NPR’s annual search for new musical talent, and the How I Built This Summit. She most recently led the Skoll Foundation’s global convenings strategy and directed the Skoll World Forum.
At The Atlantic, she will work with Evan to lead one of the most influential and long-running events practices in media. The Atlantic convenes dozens of annual in-person and virtual events that reach thousands of people every year, anchored by its flagship event, The Atlantic Festival, which returns to New York City September 17–19, after being held for nearly two decades in Washington, D.C. The Atlantic is also under way with a new 50-state tour, The Atlantic Across America, that has already held events in 10 states, addressing some of the most complex issues of our time.
Below is Evan Smith’s announcement to staff:
I’m excited to let you know that we’ve hired the amazing Jessica Goldstein as our new senior vice president of events. As the second-in-command on our growing team, she’ll oversee the operations, planning, and execution of our robust public programs, working closely with our sales, marketing, design, and CSG colleagues to grow The Atlantic’s audience and revenue; shine a great, big light on our brand; and—most crucially—bring our journalists and our journalism to stages from coast to coast through The Atlantic Festival, The Atlantic Across America, The Atlantic Summits, and so much more.
Jessica comes to us most recently from the Skoll Foundation, where she was managing director of convenings, leading the organization’s global events strategy and directing the Skoll World Forum, a weeklong gathering of heads of state, social entrepreneurs, and civil-society partners. But it’s her reputation at NPR that really precedes her—and makes her the ideal hire in this moment. As senior director and executive producer of Events & Experiential, she spent eight years creating and leading NPR’s live programming, including the Tiny Desk Contest and the How I Built This Summit. Previously she was a senior supervising producer for NPR Music, a senior producer on the science desk, and a producer of audio documentaries known as NPR Radio Expeditions. A native of New York, Jessica is a graduate of the University of Wisconsin at Madison.
Jessica believes in the power of storytelling, of sharing ideas and sparking inspiration, which is precisely how we think about our work in the events space. There is no loftier task before us than getting people from divergent backgrounds—great minds who don’t think alike—in a room to listen and talk and continue the conversation after we’re gone. The Environment Ministry plans to abolish subsidies for solar panels under its financial aid program for facilitating the introduction of photovoltaic power generation systems, sources have said.
Behind the move are falling prices of solar panels. Subsidies will not be paid for solar panels to be newly purchased in fiscal 2027 and beyond while installation costs will remain eligible for the aid in principle, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Subsidies will also continue to be available for projects that are under way.
The ministry plans to shift its focus to the promotion of next-generation perovskite solar cells, key materials for which can be sourced domestically, as a part of efforts to strengthen industrial competitiveness. It is expected to request ¥28 billion in related funds under the government’s budget for fiscal 2027, which starts next April, roughly four times the amount under the fiscal 2026 budget.
Currently, the ministry provides businesses that install solar power generation equipment at places such as parking lots and farmland with subsidies at fixed amounts or at certain rates to help them cover purchase, installation and labor costs.
But many of the public comments sought for a review of the support program said that benefits of the aid for solar panels to domestic industries are limited.
China controls over 80% of the global market for conventional solar panels, and Japan relies on imports for most of its procurement for domestic supply.
Prices of conventional panels have fallen about 50% from their peak level due to mass production around the world.
Meanwhile, Japan ranks second in the world in the production of iodine, a key material for perovskite solar cells.
The government hopes that power generation by perovskite solar cells in 2040 will reach 20 gigawatts, equivalent to the output by 40 nuclear reactors.
As problems have been reported from many large-scale solar power projects, the ministry aims to promote renewable energy-based power generation systems that do not cause environmental damage, are less vulnerable to natural disasters and can better coexist with local communities.

Trump Plans to Buy Midterm Ads About His Own Record
Some Republicans welcome his involvement, but whether voters will is another question.
President Trump gathered his top political advisers in the Oval Office early this month to solve a problem of riches: how to spend his super PAC’s $400 million political war chest with fewer than 100 days to go before the midterm elections.
Republican strategists are concerned about Trump’s low approval ratings and voter anxiety about the economy. One person familiar with the Oval Office strategy meeting put it this way: “When the issues that you typically campaign on don’t move voters—or voters are pissed off at you about those issues—the question becomes: What do you campaign on?” Some GOP strategists favor focusing entirely on specific races in an effort to convince voters of the merits of individual candidates and local issues.
But Trump himself has rejected that approach. House and Senate Democrats, the president noted during the meeting, will make their fall campaigns a referendum on him. His advisers told him that the poor polling reflects the fact that the voting public still does not know about many of his accomplishments—the dozens of new stock-market highs, a decline in fentanyl deaths, the “sealed” southern border, the increase in domestic-manufacturing production.
The solution Trump settled on, according to three people familiar with the meeting, was to lean into the Democratic strategy of focusing on himself. The president ordered a series of television advertisements about his own record that will serve as a backdrop to the hundreds of individual House and Senate contests. Trump wanted what one person described to us as “environmental lift” ads—commercials that would focus on nationalizing the midterms broadly around his victories—and he suggested that the ad makers mine his own on-camera statements as building blocks. “Go look at the clips,” the president told his team, according to this person. “I cite accomplishments all the time.”
That decision has resulted in a Trump midterm-election ad blitz that is set to be rolled out soon from MAGA Inc., the main repository of Trump’s political fundraising, according to people familiar with the discussions, all of whom insisted on anonymity to describe internal conversations. Most of MAGA Inc.’s spending is still expected to go to targeted House and Senate races, for which the group has been establishing teams to review polling, voter modeling, and message testing. “We are going to unload the guns on both chambers real soon,” one of the people said. But another person told us that because Trump will inevitably be part of voters’ considerations, highlighting his achievements makes sense. “I think everybody does understand that the president and his agenda are on the ballot to some degree,” another person told us.
A spokesperson for MAGA Inc. told us that the group does not comment on internal deliberations or plans. Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, told us that Trump is committed to maintaining the Republican majorities in Congress. “President Trump is cleaning up Joe Biden’s mess,” she said in a statement. “There is a great story to tell because the United States of America has never been stronger than under his leadership.”
Trump’s decision to focus a portion of his spending on himself echoes President Biden’s decision in the fall of 2023 to launch a series of ads trumpeting his own legislative record, as he sought to increase his approval rating in advance of his reelection bid. But Trump is not on the ballot this fall, which presents new risks. A new strategy of touting Trump’s achievements could well backfire by aiding Democratic efforts to make each race about national issues at a time when Trump’s approval rating is at record lows. Yet given the midterm headwinds, Republicans may have little choice but to present their most effective communicator to voters.
The political climate—an economic election in which voters don’t feel that their life has gotten better, despite some positive indicators—is in many ways similar to what Democrats faced in 2010 and 2022, when the electorate blamed their party for the economic pain of the 2008 financial crisis and the coronavirus pandemic, respectively. But in other ways, the situation Trump faces is different. Polls show that voters aren’t just anxious about inflation; they are frustrated with Trump’s war of choice with Iran and concerned about government corruption. Before Trump’s first midterm election as president, in 2018, the Pew Research Center found that 51 percent of the country believed that the economy was doing well, including 13 percent who described the economy as excellent. By July of this year, only 22 percent felt that the economy was doing well, and only 3 percent described it as excellent. Trump’s economic approval rating hovered at about 50 percent in 2018 public polls. Most polls this year show that his standing has fallen into the 30s.
Republican political consultants have voiced concerns both publicly and privately in recent weeks about the triumphant tone of some of Trump’s economic messaging. Democrats see a familiar dilemma. “You’ve got to take voters from where they are to where you want to go, and the only way to do that is to not dismiss in any way what they know—and what I mean by that is, you can’t go in playing ‘It’s Christmas Time’ when that’s the last holiday they can afford,” Rahm Emanuel, who worked for the Obama and Biden administrations and is a potential contender in the 2028 presidential election, told us. “They’re going to put you on mute.”
In 2010, Barack Obama wrestled with this problem by alighting on a “car in the ditch” metaphor to explain why, after the 2008 financial crisis, the promised recovery still felt slow in coming. Yet even that formulation proved ineffective, Obama’s senior strategist David Axelrod told us. “We sort of abandoned it because what we found was even that was offensive to people, because it felt like we were trying to blame others,” he said. “What we learned very quickly is, you cannot jawbone people into feeling what they do not feel in their own lives, and Biden defied that to his own detriment.”
Trump has shown much more interest in hyperbole than in complicated metaphors, branding his second term in office as a new “Golden Age.” While stumping last Friday for Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina, Trump spoke glowingly about his second term. “You have record manufacturing and auto plants being built right now in the United States and in South Carolina,” he said. “We have the greatest economy in our history. Now, some people haven’t seen it yet, but they will.” Axelrod noted that Trump argued at the same rally that his own polling “should be at 100 percent on the economy.” “If you’re the average person out there, you’re seeing that and thinking What planet is he living on?” Axelrod said. “You have to acknowledge that people are struggling and this is a work in progress.”
David Winston, a Republican strategist who works with congressional leadership, told us that key to the midterms is whether voters, when they walk into a grocery store, feel that they can manage at least a little bit better than before Trump returned to office. “So Republicans need to be talking about what actions they took in terms of the economy to at least get things moving in the right direction, and what the outcome has been,” he said. “This is one where it can’t be a laundry list of 35 talking points. This has to be one or two key things.”
Trump’s advisers are hoping to drive home a discrete set of facts about his accomplishments over the past 19 months. The list is likely to include new tax breaks for certain workers and seniors, the stock market’s rise over the past two years, the military’s boat strikes purportedly targeting fentanyl, and his efforts to “seal” the U.S.-Mexico border, to name a few. Rather than distance himself from congressional elections—the preference of some Republican candidates in swing districts—Trump has argued that he can drive turnout in those races by making himself the center of the conversation. Next month, he will host the Republican Party for a two-day “midterm convention” rally in Dallas aimed at nationalizing the November races as a choice between extreme Democrats and Republican accomplishments. Trump has asked his supporters to treat November as though his name is on the ballot. “What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote. It’s so important,” Trump said on Friday in South Carolina. “Just say that I’m on the ballot one more time.”
In other, important ways, Trump is better positioned than either Obama or Biden were at this point in their midterm races. He has a massive cash advantage, thanks to his aggressive fundraising over the first year of his term that collected tens of millions from crypto companies, AI entrepreneurs, and traditional Republican donors. He also enjoys a sharply gerrymandered political map in the House that has created a new cushion of Republican-leaning seats after mid-cycle redistricting. And the Senate majority will be decided by races in Republican-leaning states such as Texas, Alaska, Ohio, and Iowa.
Trump’s advisers have not yet indicated to Republican consultants how much money the president will spend on the midterms, according to people familiar with the matter. But the merits of Trump inserting himself into the election may be less important to some Republicans than the fact that MAGA Inc. is starting to spend. Some in the party have worried for months that Trump might hoard his fundraising for the 2028 presidential-election cycle—or for something else entirely.
MAGA Inc. has begun work on a number of campaigns about specific House and Senate races for the fall. Much of that advertising is expected to feature negative attacks on Democratic candidates, the traditional role of independent super PACs. MAGA Inc. has commissioned polling and research, along with modeling in the targeted House and Senate races. It has also shared information with other independent groups, including the Senate Leadership Fund and the Congressional Leadership Fund, which are affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota and Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana.
In the early spring, Trump’s aides hoped to launch a disciplined sales pitch to voters focused on Trump’s accomplishments, only to have that effort largely derailed by the open-ended Iran conflict. Trump’s approval ratings have eroded further since then. Now is the president’s last chance for a do-over, and his team is projecting confidence that it can get it right. “Anybody that is saying we are headed for a shellacking absolutely can’t just read the numbers,” one of the people familiar with the Oval Office meeting told us. With early voting starting in the first weeks of October, Republicans are once again betting that more Trump is their best way to block Democratic hopes of a wave election.

No more full Vande Mataram in Karnataka: CM Shivakumar stands by Congress stance
DK Shivakumar said he will stick to Congress's decision to sing only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram at government and public programmes.
Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar on Wednesday said his government would adhere to the Congress’s decision to sing only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram, making it clear that he stood by the party’s position. Dismissing the singing of all six stanzas at an Independence Day event in Karnataka, Shivakumar said the decision was taken without his knowledge and maintained that the government would stick to singing only the first two stanzas.
"I believe in my party’s ideology. Whatever we have decided, I stand by that. I think without my knowledge, it might have happened in some corners, but in future and in any government programmes, we will stand by what we had decided earlier, the two stanzas," he said at the India Today Roundtable in Karnataka, when asked bout the full reddition during the Independence Day event.
The Congress Working Committee (CWC) last week reaffirmed its 1937 resolution that only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram should be sung at public and national gatherings. The decision came after the new Vande Mataram Bill mandated the singing of all stanzas of the national song, and amid a political row between the Congress and the BJP over its rendition.
Commenting on the politics of appeasement in Indian politics, Shivakumar said the Congress believes in diversity and accused the BJP of practising appeasement politics.
"This is a country of diverse communities. The BJP is pursuing appeasement politics, whereas we believe in taking every section of society along with us. That is what our ideology stands for," Shivakumar said in his first media interview after assuming office as the Chief Minister.

Vietnam’s business hub aims to phase out petrol and diesel transport from central areas by mid-2027, starting with buses and delivery fleets
Under the proposal, the city would pilot the LEZ from July 2027 in its core downtown area and the new Thu Thiem urban area, covering roughly 930 hectares (2,300 acres), Thanh Nien reported, citing city authorities.
From early 2029, the LEZ will expand to within the city’s Ring Road 2, an area that already restricts heavy trucks and sleeper buses from the inner city during certain hours.
The new timeline is later than a previous proposal, in which the implementation of the LEZ was set to begin early this year.
The revised plan adjusts the scope and some milestones to align with the launch of green transport infrastructure and give residents and businesses more time to switch vehicles.

A landslide at a huge waste dump in Guinea’s capital has killed 30 people, the government said on Sunday, after heavy rains overnight prompted it to collapse, engulfing nearby tents and shacks.
The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa.
The landslide took place at about 2am (3am UK time) in the Gbessia commune of Conakry, according to a government statement.
The death toll was 30, with six people seriously injured and 16 more lightly injured, the statement said.
Rescue workers were using excavators and other tools to clear the site of the landslide, which witnesses said was large enough to bury an apartment building along with more precarious dwellings.
One woman, Cire Diallo, told reporters at the scene that her five children were killed. “I have lost all my children. All I can do is put my trust in God,” she said.
Guinea holds the world’s largest bauxite reserves and richest untapped iron ore deposit at Simandou, where a massive mining project was launched in November. But the west African country has poor infrastructure and widespread poverty, with 3.7 million of its 15.1 million people living on less than $4.20 a day, according to a World Bank report published in April.
On Thursday Guinea’s minister of territorial administration, Djénabou Touré Camara, announced that the government was closing the landfill because it was unsafe and said the waste was to be relocated outside Conakry.
The prime minister, Amadou Oury Bah, visited the landfill on Sunday to assess the damage and supervise the response, the government statement said, adding that people should “remain calm, show solidarity, and strictly follow the instructions of rescue services and the competent authorities”.

Dolly Parton was one of country music's biggest superstars, but she wasn't always a millionaire.
Parton grew up in Sevierville, Tennessee, where she shared a two-room log cabin with her parents and 11 siblings.
She continued to call Tennessee home as her music career skyrocketed, though she upgraded to a 3,324-square-foot ranch in Brentwood, purchased in 1999. She shared the home with her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean, until his death in March 2025 at the age of 82.
Parton died on Tuesday at the age of 80. Her many accolades included inductions into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, the Living Legends Medal from the Library of Congress, the Kennedy Center Honors, a lifetime achievement award from the Recording Academy, and 10 Grammys.
Parton was also a philanthropist who gave away millions to support children's literacy and public health initiatives.
With ventures like the Dollywood theme park and a line of Duncan Hines cake mixes, Parton's net worth was an estimated $450 million as of June 2025, Forbes reported.
Here's how she made and spent her fortune.
Dolly Parton skyrocketed to country superstardom with songs like "Jolene" and "9 to 5."
Dolly Parton wrote her first song at age 5 and played her first show at Nashville's Grand Ole Opry at 13. She released her debut album, "Hello I'm Dolly," in 1967.
Forbes reported that a significant portion of Parton's fortune came from her music catalog, worth an estimated $120 million.
Parton released over 50 studio albums and achieved 26 No.1 hits on Billboard's Hot Country Songs chart. She also lent her songwriting talents to other artists, such as Whitney Houston's megahit "I Will Always Love You."
Parton owned nearly all of the publishing rights to her music through the company she founded.
When her contract with Combine Music expired in 1966, Parton founded her own publishing company with her uncle and then-manager Bill Owens, according to her official website.
This allowed her to maintain the publishing rights to almost all of her music and receive a publishing fee whenever one of her songs was played on the radio or used in film or TV, Forbes reported in 2021.
Her music catalog earned her between $6 million and $8 million in royalties every year.
Dollywood, her theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, was her biggest financial asset.
In 1986, Parton partnered with the existing Silver Dollar City theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, to remodel and rebrand it as Dollywood. She grew up less than 10 miles away, in Sevierville, Tennessee.
"I always thought that if I made it big or got successful at what I had started out to do, that I wanted to come back to my part of the country and do something great, something that would bring a lot of jobs into this area," Parton told the Associated Press in 2010. "Sure enough, I was lucky, and God was good to me and things happened good. We started the park and 25 years later, we're still at it."
The park spans 160 acres in the Great Smoky Mountains.
Parton had a 50% stake in the theme park, worth about $165 million, Forbes reported in 2021.
Dollywood remains the top tourist attraction in Tennessee with around 3 million visitors each year, according to CBS affiliate WVLT. A one-day adult ticket costs $94.99.
She also had shares in Dollywood's Splash Country water park, worth an estimated $20 million in 2021.
Opened in 2001, the 35-acre water park is located next to Dollywood. It operates seasonally, from May to September.
Parton also co-owned the DreamMore Resort and Spa with a stake worth $15 million.
The 20-acre hotel in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, features a shuttle to and from Dollywood and pieces of Dolly Parton memorabilia.
A chestnut "Dream Box" displayed in a glass case on the hotel's lower level contains a recording of "My Place In History," a song Parton wrote to be released on her 100th birthday in 2046.
In 2023, Parton opened her second hotel in Pigeon Forge, the HeartSong Lodge and Resort.
Her lines of housewares, Duncan Hines cake mixes, and "Doggy Parton" pet apparel provided additional revenue streams.
Parton's colorful collection of cookware and home decor is available at stores like Kohl's and JCPenney.
Her "Doggy Parton" pet gear, including bandanas, wigs, and toys, is available on Amazon, and a portion of sales support Willa B. Farms animal rescue.
After releasing two Duncan Hines cake mixes in 2022, the singer expanded the line to include mixes for corn bread, brownies, and biscuits along with her coconut- and banana-pudding cakes.
Parton reportedly purchased the Brentwood, Tennessee, home she shared with her husband, Carl Dean, for $400,000 in 1999.
The grounds of the 3,324-square-foot home include a tennis court, swimming pool, garden, and barns for livestock, the Daily Express reported.
In an interview published in the 2017 book "Dolly on Dolly," Parton said that she and Dean would take pictures of Southern mansions in Mississippi on their annual anniversary trip and note features they wanted to incorporate into their eventual dream home.
"I knew that house before it was built and I built it long before we could afford it 'cause I knew we'd be able to — someday," she wrote, according to an excerpt published in The New York Post. "I scouted all over Tennessee for a piece of land with hills in front and a stream around it.
The book continued: "It's got a bitty bridge, and I made sure it's just narrow enough so's no tour bus can git over it. Carl and me can walk around stark naked there and nobody'd see. We have chickens and cows and a vegetable garden. It's a quiet, homey place for me and the special people in my life."
It's a far cry from her roots: Parton grew up in a two-room log cabin with her parents and 11 siblings in Sevierville. The cabin had no electricity or running water, but Parton remembered her years there fondly in her 1973 song "My Tennessee Mountain Home."
Dollywood features a replica of her childhood home built by her brother, Bobby, and furnished by her mother, Avie Lee.
While she wore elaborate bedazzled outfits for public appearances and onstage performances, Parton was more frugal with her everyday clothes.
In a 2020 appearance on the Scandinavian talk show "Skavlan," Parton said she bought most of her clothes off the rack and didn't splurge on designer items.
"I really like to earn money, but I love to spend it, too. But I spend it on things that I feel like that's needed," she said. "I'm not the kind of person that will go out and spend like three or four thousand dollars on a coat or one outfit."
She added that the steep price tags on expensive items made her think of her parents, who "could have fed a family of 12 on what I would pay for a coat."
Parton was renowned for her generous charity work through The Dollywood Foundation, which she founded in 1988.
"I just give from my heart," she said in a speech while accepting the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy in 2022. "I never know what I'm going to do or why I'm gonna do it. I just see a need and if I can fill it, then I will."
The Dollywood Foundation's Imagination Library continues to give away around 3 million books to children each month.
Parton founded her Imagination Library in 1995, inspired by her father's struggles with literacy. The nonprofit sends free books to children from birth through age 5 each month.
"This actually started because my father could not read and write and I saw how crippling that could be," she told the Associated Press in 2022. "My dad was a very smart man. And I often wondered what he could have done had he been able to read and write."
She continued to invest in her hometown, funding a new medical center and scholarships for students in her old high school.
LeConte Medical Center opened in 2010 with the help of Parton's philanthropy and fundraising. She also funded its Dolly Parton Center for Women's Services and Dolly Parton Birthing Unit.
The Dollywood Foundation offers $15,000 scholarships to five high school seniors in Sevier County, Tennessee, and covers college tuition and books for its theme-park employees, CBS News reported.
Her $1 million gift to Vanderbilt University in 2020 proved integral to the development of Moderna's coronavirus vaccine.
A report in the New England Journal of Medicine on the development of the Moderna coronavirus vaccine acknowledged the Dolly Parton COVID-19 Research Fund among supporters of the research.
Parton qualified to get the vaccine she helped fund in Tennessee in early February 2021, but she said she wanted to wait "until some more people" got theirs.
"I don't want it to look like I'm jumping the line just because I donated money," she told the Associated Press. "I'm very funny about that."
In a video of her getting the vaccine in March 2021, Parton sang a rendition of her hit song "Jolene," changing the lyrics to "vaccine, vaccine," and encouraging everyone to get vaccinated as soon as possible.
In 2024, Parton donated a total of $2 million toward Hurricane Helene relief.
Hurricane Helene made landfall in Florida as a Category 4 storm on September 26, 2024, flooding neighborhoods and leaving over 1 million homes and businesses without power.
At an October 2024 press conference in Newport, Tennessee, Parton announced that she planned to donate $1 million from her personal fortune to help those impacted by Hurricane Helene and an additional $1 million through her businesses such as Dollywood and Dolly Parton's Stampede.
"I can't stand to see anyone hurting, so I wanted to do what I could to help after these terrible floods," she said.
She continued, "I hope we can all be a little bit of light in the world for our friends, our neighbors — even strangers — during this dark time they are experiencing."
After Parton's death was announced on Tuesday, President Donald Trump ordered flags flown at half-staff across the US.
Flying flags at half-staff to acknowledge a private citizen's death is a rare honor. Past honorees have included Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, Neil Armstrong, and Charlie Kirk.
"There has never been anyone like her, and never will," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

The Gun Lobby’s Most Cynical Move Yet
New data show how pro-gun groups target their political spending after fatal school shootings.
As a newspaper reporter, I covered my first school shooting in 2007 at Virginia Tech, where 32 students and faculty were murdered and 17 others were wounded. In one story, I recounted how Emily, a 19-year-old sophomore, was lying partially behind a desk on the floor of her French class while the shooter gunned down her teacher and nearly every student around her before shooting himself in the head. I can’t forget the image of Emily, shot twice herself, who pretended to be dead but surreptitiously grabbed a cellphone on the floor that another student had used to call 911 before he was shot. I listened many weeks later to a recording of the call. At first, she was too terrified to speak. All the police dispatcher could hear was the sound of her breath and the loud pop pop pop of gunfire all around her.
“I can’t talk,” she whispered, gasping for breath. “Please hurry.”
After the Virginia Tech massacre, I reported on many other school shootings, including Sandy Hook in 2012, when twenty 6- and 7-year-olds were shot to death in their first-grade classrooms and six staff members were killed. Attorney General Eric Holder, whom I covered at the time as The Washington Post’s Justice Department reporter, told me that walking through the bullet-riddled classrooms still caked with blood was the most difficult day of his professional life. He later cried openly when he saw the crime-scene photos of the children lying dead in their classrooms.
I wrote about so many school massacres that I lost count. After each one, I reached out to the National Rifle Association, the National Shooting Sports Foundation (the gun industry’s trade association), and other organizations that the nation’s gun lobby comprises for their response. They rarely commented beyond a statement offering thoughts and prayers to the victims and their families. I twice attended the world’s largest firearms trade show, held annually in Las Vegas for tens of thousands of gun makers, sellers, and other professionals but closed to the general public. There, too, leaders of the NRA, other advocates, and representatives of the multibillion-dollar gun industry would not comment on school shootings, except to reiterate their support for armed guards in schools and a government registry of mentally ill people, and to resist calls to strengthen background checks and restrict access to semi-automatic rifles such as the AR-15.
But the gun lobby had another response to school shootings behind the scenes—one I didn’t know about at the time. A study by Stanford University researchers this year found that after fatal school shootings, pro-gun political-action committees dramatically increased their contributions to their preferred U.S. House candidates in the districts where the shootings occurred, when those races were competitive. These shifts in spending were not observed after other incidents of mass gun violence or after nonfatal school shootings—only when children were killed in schools. Over the many years that I reported on gun violence, the gun lobby’s enormous campaign spending was no secret. But the Stanford study reveals how these groups targeted their money, raising their aggressive tactics to a new level.
In the first study of its kind, the authors analyzed 25 years of data, linking campaign-finance records to every fatal K–12 school shooting from 2000 to 2024. They then compared campaign contributions between the districts that did and did not have a school shooting. After school shootings where children died, pro-gun contributions to candidates in competitive congressional districts increased on average by more than 30 percent. And when the shooting occurred within two months of an election, contributions surged by 2,820 percent. “The data shows that the gun lobby saves its political firepower for the moments when public grief is greatest and lawmakers are under the most pressure to act,” Eric A. Baldwin, one of the authors, told me.
In November 2021, for example, a 15-year-old killed four students and injured seven other people at Oxford High School, in Michigan. The pro-gun PACs contributed $50,650 during the 2021–22 election cycle in the district where the high school was located, a 434 percent increase from the previous cycle and a 591 percent increase from an average of the previous five cycles, according to the Stanford researchers. In December 2013, a 17-year-old senior was killed at Arapahoe High School, in a suburb of Denver. Before the shooting, the pro-gun PAC contribution had been $1,000. Afterward, it soared to $49,470.
Gun-safety PACs also increased their spending in competitive districts after school shootings. But the pro-gun groups were by far the dominant spenders until 2018, the year of the Parkland shooting, which left 17 students and faculty dead at a high school in Florida; at that point, gun-safety groups began to significantly increase their spending, sometimes equaling or even surpassing the spending of the pro-gun groups.
The Stanford researchers did not find that increased spending by either side after fatal school shootings measurably affected which party actually won a competitive House election. (The districts that the study looked at represent only a subset of the gun lobby’s overall election spending.) Nevertheless, the study shows how pro-gun PACs work to undermine anti-gun feelings in communities suffering from the trauma of children being killed in schools.
In poll after poll for more than a decade, the majority of Americans have favored stricter gun laws. Most Americans specifically want a ban on weapons such as AR-15s, and also favor stricter background checks. That sentiment is particularly acute after a school shooting, when “public demand for reform is especially high,” according to the Stanford researchers. But, they write, the pro-gun spending surge means that “instead of yielding to constituent pressure, candidates are fortified to resist it and are empowered to reframe their opposition to reform as principled rather than unresponsive.”
Although the NRA’s power has been waning in recent years, it still spent $10 million in the 2024 election. Other pro-gun groups have emerged and are influencing national policy; together with the NRA, they spend about $14 million a year on lobbying. In response to lawsuits from a number of pro-gun entities, including Gun Owners of America, a federal judge in Texas recently found unconstitutional a 1934 federal law that placed strict requirements on anyone purchasing silencers, short-barreled rifles, and shotguns, among other firearms. The Justice Department did not immediately appeal the ruling.
In recent months, the Trump administration has announced new actions to make it easier for gun purchasers to avoid background checks when obtaining firearms. In April, then–Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Justice Department officials announced the rollback of gun regulations alongside leaders from the NRA, the National Shooting Sports Foundation, the National Association for Guns Rights, and Gun Owners of America. And House Republicans proposed a bill to cut nearly $300 million from the budget of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, the agency that enforces the nation’s gun laws.
The killing of America’s children and teenagers in their classrooms has become normalized. From a young age, our children and grandchildren are being taught vocabulary and math alongside lessons in how to hide when an “active shooter” storms their classrooms. The Stanford study is a compelling reminder of how far the gun lobby will go to block any efforts to protect our children.

Instagram is launching a new Reels-editing feature that automatically trims your video clips to focus on the highlights. The feature, called First Draft, is rolling out to Instagram’s iPhone app and provides a “starting point” that you can build upon with other edits, according to an announcement on Tuesday.
Instagram’s ‘First Draft’ trims your Reels clips for you
The Reels-editing feature automatically cuts out pauses across your clips.
An example shared by Instagram shows a user selecting multiple clips for a reel and then tapping the “First Draft” button. From there, Instagram analyzes the clips — each of which is more than a minute long — before trimming them down to eliminate pauses and showcase the most important parts. Instagram then combines the snippets into a reel that’s ready to edit and share.
It sounds similar to Adobe’s AI-powered Quick Cut feature, which automatically combines clips based on a prompt. But unlike Adobe’s feature, Instagram’s First Draft tool doesn’t use AI, according to Instagram spokesperson Nicole Rechtszaid.
Instagram says First Draft works with “multi-clip montages, talking-head videos, and day-in-the-life content.” You can find the feature by opening the camera app in Instagram, filming your video, and tapping the First Draft Button. You can also find it in your Reels gallery after selecting more than one clip.
Update, August 25th: Added confirmation that First Draft doesn’t use AI.

A day after 
Kriti Sanon
 responded to criticism over her outfit in a Raksha Bandhan advertisement, the jewellery brand behind the campaign has withdrawn the ad. The brand issued a statement saying it holds Indian culture, traditions and festivals in the highest regard.
For those not in the know, Kriti had addressed the backlash on August 25 through a note on Instagram. For the jewellery advertisement, the actor was dressed in an off-white outfit featuring a bralette-style blouse, a cape and a draped skirt. This outfit led to backlash about the kind of clothes one should wear for raksha bandhan.
In its statement shared on Instagram on Wednesday, the brand apologised if the campaign had unintentionally offended anyone and announced that it had been removed from all media platforms.
“If our recent advertisement has inadvertently hurt the sentiments of some segments of society, that was not our intent at all. Out of respect, we have withdrawn the said advertisement from all media. Wish you all the love & positivity this festive season!”
Kriti, meanwhile, had argued that festivals are defined by their emotions and traditions rather than clothing. Sharing her thoughts on the criticism, she wrote: “The essence of festivals is not in the clothes you wear, it is in the emotions and meaning you hold for the traditions. 
Rakshabandhan
 is a bond of protection. My sister and I tie rakhi to each other.”
She further explained how the festival is celebrated in her family, adding that the bond of protection is not limited to a brother-sister relationship.
“We know we can protect each other no less than a brother would have. We pray for each other’s health, happiness & long life. And for us, this prayer and promise extends to our dogs too! Afterall, they are family!"
She concluded her note by saying, "Also, when will we stop telling women what to wear?? Ethnic fashion has evolved over the years, but still a woman’s respect for her culture is measured with just her clothes!! Culture & Traditions are in her heart, not in her neckline!"
The ‘Cocktail 2’ actor also questioned the practice of judging a woman’s connection to her culture based on her clothing.

Buc-ee’s picked a fight with a tiny Ohio store over a beaver. Now an entire town is fighting back
Gas station giant Buc-ee’s has sparked a backlash in Ohio over one of its frequent trademark infringement lawsuits
Buc-ee’s says it is simply protecting its trademark.
The company said it discovered Beaver's Mini Mart after owner Vic Boparai registered the trade name in October. State records show the business incorporated as Hanes Road Carryout in 2017 before changing its name to Beaver's Mini Mart in January 2025.
Buc-ee’s said it repeatedly tried to contact Boparai after identifying what it considered a trademark conflict but received no response, eventually prompting the lawsuit.
According to state filings, the enterprise incorporated in 2017 under the name Hanes Road Carryout before changing its title to Beaver’s Mini Mart in January 2025—about four months after Buc-ee's broke ground on its Dayton-area site.
Buc-ee's stated that after identifying a brand conflict, it reached out to Boparai multiple times without receiving a response, leaving it with no option but to file suit.
Boparai has not publicly addressed the allegations but thanked supporters for rallying behind his business.
“We are overwhelmed by your support for our business and other small businesses everywhere,” he said.
The lawsuit is not Buc-ee’s first Ohio trademark fight.
In February, the company sued the owner of northern Ohio's Mickey Mart gas stations, arguing its cartoon moose mascot could be confused with Buc-ee’s beaver.
Mickey Mart's response was simple: “A moose is not a beaver.”
Buc-ee’s has previously pursued other businesses over animal-themed logos as part of what the company says are efforts to protect its valuable brand.
Back in Beavercreek, the controversy has become a community cause.
The City Council unanimously passed a resolution declaring the beaver a permanent part of the city's more than 200-year history, with local school mascot Bucky the Beaver attending the meeting.
Satirical images mocking the lawsuit have spread rapidly across social media. One viral graphic featured the Ohio State University football mascot, Brutus Buckeye, tackling the Buc-ee's beaver.
Community backing has also extended to financial support. A GoFundMe page aimed at helping Beaver's Mini Mart cover legal fees to avoid going out of business—a fate suffered by other small operations targeted by Buc-ee's—raised at least $69,000.
The mini mart also gave The Original Goodie Shop bakery in Upper Arlington permission to put its mascot on a specialty cookie, with $1 from each sale earmarked for legal expenses. Meanwhile, Beavercreek bakery Cake, Hope & Love began selling beaver-decorated cookies, encouraging residents to support local shops.
Several other businesses near Dayton—including a Lego retailer and a root beer shop—temporarily adapted their corporate logos to feature beavers in solidarity. Dozens of local companies in Beavercreek already include the town's name or the word beaver in their business titles.
Even Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, who attended the opening of the new Buc-ee's earlier this year, has criticized the lawsuit.
“It is Beavercreek, for heaven’s sake,” DeWine said, calling the legal action “absurd.”

In a world where trees are considered a hazard and hindrance to development, a village in Telangana is standing by the tree they loved and cherished for decades.
Residents of Pedda Thandrapadu, a village in Rajoli mandal of Jogulamba Gadwal district, have forged a united front against attempts to pull down a Peepal tree (Ficus religiosa) located inside the premises of a private property.
The villagers approached the authorities at Mandal level during recently held ‘Prajavani’ programme, and submitted a representation seeking protection of the Peepal tree at the village centre, which they claimed was encroached upon by illegal structures.
“There was a cement platform raised around the tree earlier, where people used to relax and conduct village meetings. But the platform was demolished later, and a compound wall was constructed enclosing the tree,” said a villager unwilling to be quoted.
Matters got worse when the property owner applied to the Forest Department seeking permission to fell the tree, calling it a hazard. Getting wind of the application, all the villagers banded together to object to it. They made representations to the police, the Forest Range Officer, the Mandal Revenue Officer, the Mandal Parishad Development Officer, the District Collector, and the National Green Tribunal, requesting them to stop the felling.
“The tree is a part of our lives. For generations, we have been using its ‘Paala Komma’ (sacred branch) in various rituals, such as weddings. We seek a comprehensive inquiry into how the tree was encroached upon,” the petitioners said, demanding that the Peepal be declared a ‘heritage tree.’
Kurva China Ramudu, an 85-year-old villager, vouches that he had witnessed the tree being planted during his childhood, which makes it easily about 70-75 years old.
Jangam Bhogeshwar Rao, the owner who applied for felling permission, said his parents bought the piece of land during the 1960s, which was later divided among the siblings.
“I got the platform demolished and constructed the compound wall around it because the platform was attracting drunkards and vagabonds. Villagers who are protesting now had helped me construct the wall. Now, an issue is being made out of it purely due to personal rivalries,” he alleged.
A government teacher, he says he is ready to even bear the cost of translocation if needed. However, the root mass of the tree would be so huge that it would pose a danger to the structural stability of the house if translocation is attempted.
Village Panchayat Secretary Durga Prasad, when sought his version, said there was no apparent dispute about the title of the land, and confirmed that the existing documents vouch it as private land. Panchayat has not taken any decision with regard to the tree felling, and no proposal for alternative land allocation to the owner is made.
Forest Range Officer Parvez Ahmed said permission has not yet been granted for felling of the tree, upon objections by the villagers.
“Peepal is an exempted species as per the rules. If it is in private land, all they have to do is to simply apply online and go ahead with felling. We usually do not object, but this is a special case where all the villagers except the family are objecting to the felling. So we are not permitting it,” he said.

Mondelez India, the maker of Bournvita and Cadbury products, has withdrawn health and nutritional claims flagged by India's food regulator, as the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) intensifies action against misleading advertisements and labelling practices.
The regulator said on Tuesday that several major food businesses had taken corrective measures after receiving notices over claims and labels that allegedly breached food safety rules.
Mondelez India Foods Pvt Ltd withdrew the claims and related advertisements from e-commerce platforms after FSSAI raised concerns over misleading health and nutrient-comparison claims linked to Bournvita.
The latest action adds to regulatory scrutiny of Bournvita, which faced questions in 2023 over its sugar content and nutritional marketing, particularly in advertisements aimed at children.
FSSAI said its action against Mondelez India followed findings of misleading health claims and nutrient-comparison claims.
Following the notice, the company "withdrawn the claims and advertisement from e-commerce platforms and ensured compliance."
The regulator did not provide further details of the specific Bournvita claims in its statement, but said the company had taken corrective action following its intervention.
The move comes as FSSAI steps up enforcement against food companies making claims that could give consumers an inaccurate impression about the nutritional qualities or composition of their products.
FSSAI said other businesses had also taken corrective measures after receiving notices.
Sapiens Labs has withdrawn misleading claims and advertisements, while Kerala-based Juza Foods has agreed to remove claims relating to immunity, stronger bones and comparative calcium content from its baby-food products.
In another case, Vichi Agro Products Pvt Ltd received a notice over an allegedly misleading trade name. FSSAI said Flipkart responded by confirming that the product had been delisted from its platform.
"Response from Flipkart was received, wherein the FBO mentioned that he has delisted the product from his platform," the regulator said.
Amway India has removed the term "100%" from its "100% Pure Coconut Oil" packaging and promotional material after FSSAI flagged the claim as misleading.
The company has also discontinued the term "Energy Drink" from its caffeinated XS product range. Amway said the revised packaging would be introduced from the next production cycle in August 2026.
"Amway India submitted a compliance response confirming that it has voluntarily removed the term '100%' from its product packaging and promotional materials in accordance with the FSSAI advisory and confirmed that old stock has been discontinued from sales channels," the regulator said.
Amway has sought permission to sell existing stock carrying the older "Energy Drink" artwork until the inventory is exhausted.
The latest actions form part of a wider FSSAI enforcement drive against misleading food advertisements, product claims and labelling violations.
The regulator said that "major food business operators (FBOs) have taken prompt corrective action" following notices issued by the authority.
More than 150 notices have reportedly been issued to food businesses as part of the campaign. Companies named in the regulatory action include Nestlé India, PepsiCo, Coca-Cola India, Abbott India, Red Bull India, Danone India, Monster Energy India, Ferrero India and Kenvue.
(With PTI inputs)

Trump Is Losing Touch With the Public
As the president spends less time with his base at rallies, his populist instincts are failing him.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
One of the few issues that unites voters and politicians of both parties right now is data centers. Three-quarters of Americans would oppose a data center being built near where they live, according to a new poll released last week by Heatmap Pro and Embold Research. The two leading lights of the left, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders, have sponsored a bill in Congress to create a temporary moratorium on new centers. They have an unlikely ally in archconservative Governor Greg Abbott of Texas, who said yesterday on ABC’s This Week that data-center companies “basically dug their own grave” and “got the backlash they deserve.”
Standing against this consensus is Donald Trump. The president remains a big booster of data centers. “Communities that don’t take a data center—they’re making a mistake,” he said Thursday during an interview with his on-again, off-again lackey Michael Cohen. “Data centers throw off tremendous amounts of jobs and money.”
This was no one-off. Trump had made several similar comments recently. “If I were the mayor of a town or the governor of a state and I had a chance to get a big plant in, an AI plant or a data center, I would absolutely want it, because the jobs are enormous and the money paid, the taxes paid, are just enormous,” Trump said last week—although he allowed that the sector could use “a little public-relations help.”
This puts Trump, the most successful demagogue in American political history, in the unusual position of misreading, and opposing, a populist groundswell. During his 2016 presidential campaign, Trump took many stands that were unpopular among establishment politicians. Some of these positions put him at odds not only with Democrats but also with most Republican elected officials. Trump broke with Republicans in claiming that he would protect social-welfare programs such as Medicare and Social Security, and he broke a bipartisan consensus by attacking free-trade agreements and promising protectionism. On these matters (as well as on his willingness to encourage and participate in gutter racism), Trump demonstrated that a big constituency existed for views that other politicians had deemed electoral liabilities.
Data centers’ political arc has been different. Initially, many officials seemed to back the centers, following exactly Trump’s logic: They offered jobs and tax benefits. But as public opinion turned—driven by a mix of backlash to AI in general, environmental concerns, worries about energy prices, and old-fashioned NIMBYism—politicians changed their view as well.
Why has Trump missed the shift? Presumably one reason is that he is surrounded by advisers and tech executives such as David Sacks and Larry Ellison, who are major boosters of and players in the industry. Tech companies invested heavily in Trump at the start of his second administration, lavishing him with gifts, including a gold-plated bauble and donations to projects such as his inauguration and his ballroom, and Trump has reciprocated by taking policy stances that benefit them. Trump may also be personally profiting from the AI boom; his financial disclosures show he’s become more of a tech investor.
Trump has always tended to adopt the latest thing he’s heard, no matter what it is. He has been willing to alienate corporate interests in the past—when he saw some political upside. But he is not hearing from voters who might alert him to how unpopular data centers are. Trump’s rallies and speeches once created a feedback loop in which he conveyed his message to voters and—crucially—they conveyed their thoughts to him. Now, as his energy sinks, his travel schedule gets lighter, and security makes events more challenging, Trump is getting out less.
Though his stump speeches dragged on for hours, Trump was carefully attuned to audience attention and what did and didn’t work. “You know, if it gets a little boring, if I see people starting to sort of, maybe thinking about leaving, I can sort of tell the audience, I just say, ‘We will build the wall!’ and they go nuts,” he told The New York Times in 2016. I think often about a speech Trump delivered in July 2022. It was billed as the launch of a new policy agenda, but as he read it, both Trump and his audience seemed bored. Then he ad-libbed a riff about trans athletes and the crowd came alive. Trump picked up on the shift and emphasized it; trans issues would become a central talking point for his 2024 campaign.
The president has always been susceptible to fake news and bad at filtering information, but rallies provided a gut check about his base, if not about the broader national reality. Now Trump isn’t even receiving that kind of information. One of his major conduits for information is Natalie Harp, a sycophantic aide who isn’t interested in exposing Trump to criticism. He could read public-opinion data, but as his own approval sinks, he has taken to saying (and may well believe) that polls are fake.
As his world shrinks, Trump’s populist touch has faded. Despite being elected twice on an antiwar platform, he’s launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran. As the Iran war has gotten bogged down, he’s been incapable of reading the public mood. He has dismissed voter frustration over rising fuel costs, saying “I don’t even think about” gas; he previously called affordability a “hoax.” In response to reports that American sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln were struggling with a long deployment, Trump said they hadn’t been deployed “nearly long enough.” And the collapse of trade talks with Canada on Friday threaten Republican prospects in border states including Michigan and Ohio.
Each of these cases represents a growing gap between Trump and his base, but none is as ironic as Trump’s stance on data centers. The AI facilities store terabytes of data, but the president can’t get access to the information about them that he needs.

The Trump Comedians Are Tired
By Will Gottsegen
In 2017, as Donald Trump was getting used to the White House furniture, Alec Baldwin was feeling exultant. His impersonation of the new president on Saturday Night Live had made him momentarily inescapable and given the comedy show its highest ratings in years. To capitalize on the momentum, Baldwin co-authored a book-length satirical memoir written from Trump’s perspective. Baldwin’s autobiography—which also came out that year and was excerpted as a cover story for Vanity Fair—noted that his take on the president “seemed to delight nearly everyone in the People’s Republic of Manhattan.” When he accepted an Emmy for his performance in the fall, he addressed Trump directly: “At long last, Mr. President, here is your Emmy.”
It was disorienting, then, to hear Baldwin declare, when I spoke with him earlier this summer, that this sort of comedy has become stale, boring, and useless. “None of it’s funny. I don’t find it funny anymore,” he told me. “There’s nothing left to say about Trump.”

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Good camera. Slightly improved design. IP68 water and dust resistance. Qi2 25W wireless charging. Slick AI features and software.
TIRED
Significantly weaker specs than other Pro models. Comparatively chunky. $100 more than last year’s 10 Pro Fold.
The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a predictably iterative improvement over last year’s foldable, with slight upgrades to performance and the camera, but it comes with an unwelcome $100 price bump. The IP68 rating for water and dust resistance and the Qi2 25W support for faster magnetic charging are standouts in a category where Google is lagging, but it has never been known for its hardware. Software is where the company excels, and some folks will appreciate the unrivaled AI-infused software features.
Google is good at elevating its devices beyond the spec sheet, but the 11 Pro Fold is perilously close to the Pixel 11 on paper, a phone that’s less than half its price. Beyond the big unfolding screen and customizable rear LEDs, little else justifies the “Pro” tag. With Samsung’s fresh Fold8 form factor and a folding iPhone on the horizon, I’m not convinced Google has done enough to make this the foldable you drop $1,900 on.
Devil in the Details
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold doesn’t look different from the 10 Pro Fold, but Google has shaved off a fraction of a millimeter and 19 grams. Sadly, the 11 Pro Fold is still heavier and thicker (239 grams and 10.1 mm) than Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold8 (201 grams and 9.7 mm), the Fold8 Ultra (215 grams and 8.9 mm), and the Honor Magic V6 (219 grams and 8.75 mm, not sold in the US). That makes it a little trickier to handle, though the horizontal camera bar means less rocking than Samsung’s phones when they lie flat.
The double-camera module has had a makeover, so it looks less chunky, and the back is matte-textured glass that feels lovely. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold scores an impressive IP68 rating for water and dust resistance. That compares favorably to Samsung’s IP48 ratings, which means both can survive shallow submersion, but Google’s phone is dust-tight, whereas Samsung’s phones are at risk from fine dust and sand.
Photograph: Simon Hill
It’s a shame the Fold is only available in two colors: Obsidian, the color of my review unit, looks more like a dark matte gray than black, while Olive Green has a shinier gold frame.
I’m not a fan of Google’s asymmetrical design. With the Pixel 11 Pro Fold closed, there’s a curved corner cutout, and when you open the phone, the two halves have slightly different thicknesses. All folding phones still have a detectable fold line in the middle of the screen when you open them, but Google’s is among the most noticeable. Some folks won’t notice or care, but I’m the kind of guy who goes upstairs to turn the light on so the downstairs switches aren’t misaligned.
The fingerprint sensor in the power button always bugs me when I switch to a folding phone, because I have to pick it up to touch it and unlock the screen, rather than pressing on the screen like most phones. You do have face unlock with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and it works well provided there’s ample light, but it still doesn’t work in a dark room, which is still annoying.
You get two lovely, sharp OLED displays in the Pixel 11 Pro Fold: an 8-inch main screen and a 6.5-inch cover screen. Both push peak brightness to 3,600 nits, remaining legible in direct sunlight, and boast a variable refresh rate up to 120 Hz. They’re smooth, with rich colors, and I have nothing to complain about beyond that crease.
Pro Pretender
I’m not convinced the 11 Pro Fold earns the “Pro” in its title. It does have the new HiLight feature, a group of color LEDs in the camera module’s flash that light up different colors based on who is calling, or swirl through the rainbow while you chat to Gemini. It’s neat, if a little underbaked. It’s handy if you put your phone face down when you’re working or trying to relax, but it’s a very minor feature.
All the Pixels get the new Tensor G6 processor, and the Fold has 16 GB of RAM paired with 256 GB, 512 GB, or 1 TB of storage. Switching from the Pixel 10 Pro XL, it was mostly smooth sailing. But it froze a couple of times in split-screen view in Gmail and after launching an app on the outer display, then unfolding the inner display.
The 11 Pro Fold actually has more in common with the regular Pixel 11, because it misses out on the high-end camera in its Pro siblings. Folding phones struggle to match flagships on camera specs because of form-factor limitations, and they must include two front-facing cameras (one for open and one for closed).
Photograph: Simon Hill
You get the same 48-megapixel main camera and 10.8-megapixel telephoto for 5X optical zoom as on the Pixel 11, but the Fold drops to a 10.5-megapixel ultrawide. The main camera is excellent in a wide range of scenarios, and I used the telephoto lens a lot. The 5X zoom produces sharp, detailed shots, though things get a little fuzzy if you push up to the maximum digital zoom capability at 30X. The ultrawide is a very obvious weak spot, producing relatively grainy images, though it doubles as a macro lens for decent, if slightly distorted, close-ups. The 10-megapixel front-facing cameras are passable for selfies.
The 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL cameras are superior across the board (50-MP main, 48-MP ultrawide, 48-MP telephoto, and 42-MP front-facing). They also boast instant Night Sight, 120X digital zoom, and better video capture. That said, I took some great shots with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold; its camera results compare favorably to other foldables, and a good telephoto is more useful than an ultrawide.
I like the new camera tricks: Camera Looks lets you define your preferred style, dictating contrast and colors; Magic Capture makes it easy to get video and photos from an event without focusing on the viewfinder; and Creator Suite will delight content creators with some useful tools, like a built-in teleprompter. You can even use Circle to Search in the camera app to get info on anything you circle without snapping a shot first.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, main camera
Unfortunately, there’s one significant area where the Fold looks amateur, and that’s battery life. The 4,806-mAh battery is smaller than the one in last year’s 10 Pro Fold (5,015 mAh). While that downgrade is mitigated by greater power efficiency in the new Tensor chip, Google suggests 24 hours for the 11 Pro Fold, compared to 30-plus for the other Pixel 11 models.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Compared to a folding phone with a silicon-carbon battery, like the Honor Magic V6, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold lacks stamina, but it shouldn’t be an issue for most folks. The battery lost 6 percent in an hour of video streaming, and an hour of casual gaming claimed 9 percent. It will get you through an average day easily, but when I pushed the Fold with a lot of photography and graphically demanding gaming, I had to engage the battery saver before bedtime.
There’s 30-watt wired charging, but you should definitely embrace Qi2 wireless charging with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold as it tops out at 25 watts and is so much more convenient. The magnets stick firmly and ensure perfect alignment. It’s nice to see Qi2 25W in a folding phone, since many competitors haven’t even adopted it in their regular flagships yet.
Software Save
I’m a big fan of Google’s Pixel-exclusive software features. Call Screen saves me from telemarketers daily; I use Now Playing often to add songs to my playlist, and several new features may just persuade you to board the Pixel train. My colleague Julian Chokkattu talked about Rambler in his Pixel 11 Pro review as a more conversational voice-to-text message-drafting tool. I also like that AI overviews pop up contextually to save you a step, offering a Calendar link when someone texts to suggest a meet-up, for example, though it does mean granting Gemini access.
But one of the most useful new features for the Fold is Bubbles. With this, you can keep a floating circular profile picture from an open chat and open or minimize it with a tap. It’s not a new idea (Facebook Chat Heads did it more than a decade ago), but it lets you get on with other things without leaving the chat, potentially floating above two apps in split-screen mode. It also minimizes to a bar at the bottom right when you’re using the main screen.
With folding phones, people always talk about the ability to watch movies and play games on a big screen, but their real strength is multitasking. Message apps can show the list and a preview simultaneously. You can read a café review and check the location on a map, or watch a movie while you skim your emails.
Photograph: Simon Hill
That said, many apps still aren’t optimized for folding phones, so they can look clownishly big or occasionally obscure buttons. As mentioned, I ran into freezing issues and had to restart apps more than once. Sometimes, when you switch from the cover display to the big screen, it fails to scale up, and you might get a prompt to restart the game for full-screen view, as I did with Bloons TD 6.
Foldable newcomers should also beware of the big black bars. You must rotate the opened Fold for maximum screen viewing, but virtually nothing is made for this weird, almost square aspect ratio. You get more room when browsing something like Netflix, but start a video and you’re not much better off than with a large flagship phone like the Pixel 11 Pro XL.
Games fare a little better, and the 11 Pro Fold is great for titles like Clash of Clans, point-and-click adventures like Machinarium, and tower defense games like Bloons TD 6. It’s also a good option for older games via emulators, but for anything too demanding, like Wuthering Waves or Genshin Impact, you can expect dropped frames galore.
The other reason I find myself unfurling the big screen is to read. For browsing the web, doomscrolling Reddit, or, best of all, reading an ebook, a folding phone is a big step up from a regular phone screen. Whether it’s worth the premium you pay is debatable. It’s a little too easy to forget to use the big screen in daily life.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Photograph: Simon Hill
Folding phones have been around for years, but they still feel a bit gimmicky. For folks who think they’re a tough sell when they can get both a higher-spec flagship phone and a tablet for the price, it’s worth laying hands on one to get a feel for the experience. Foldables may not be an inevitable next step for phones, but there’s a reason they’ve carved out a niche.
The 11 Pro Fold starts at $1,899; that’s $100 more than last year’s 10 Pro Fold, but it doesn’t have a storage bump to soften the blow, as the Google Pixel 11 ($899) does. It also lacks the Pro features you’ll find in the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL ($1,099 and $1,299). If you’re set on a foldable, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 and Fold8 Ultra ($1,900 and $2,100) demand consideration, and if you don’t live in the US, check out the Honor Magic V6 ($2,100). There are other options and form factors in our best folding phones, but rumors of a folding iPhone persist, so you might want to wait and see what that looks like.
