Amid growing concerns over a government-ordered Instagram censorship drive in India, political parties and leaders are now reporting restrictions on their posts, with Meta citing “legal requirements” but providing little information about the basis for the action. Content linked to the Cockroach Janta Party protests, political parties and creators has all been caught up in the restrictions.
Over the past few days, several social media posts and accounts have been geo-blocked in India. On Instagram, users’ posts are either removed citing legal requirements or restricted from being viewed in India. Several opposition organisations and leaders have also faced such restrictions, with their posts suddenly being taken down.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
On August 6, the Aam Aadmi Party, and on August 7, the Congress party’s youth wing, the Indian Youth Congress, posted on social media to say that their Instagram posts were being repeatedly removed by Meta.
Modi ji, IYC se Dar Gaye Kya…
Meta se overtime kara rahe ho…
Aur Spineless @Meta walon, Tum Platform ho Ya BJP IT CELL ki Franchise? pic.twitter.com/Y7awNsZOcF
— Indian Youth Congress (@IYC) August 6, 2026
No explanation. No accountability. Just silence.
Democracy demands transparency, not secret restrictions and automated acknowledgements.@Meta, stop hiding behind silence. Tell India why accounts are being restricted on your platforms and whose orders you are acting on.… https://t.co/50a21ApBNo pic.twitter.com/p8tIi97ynw
— AAP (@AamAadmiParty) August 6, 2026
Clicking on a removed post shows a notice stating that it has been restricted by Meta’s automated systems in India, in accordance with legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.
Opposition Leaders’ Posts Restricted Earlier as well
This is not the first time that posts by political entities have been restricted under these rules. Earlier, posts by Congress and TVK leaders related to Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay had also been removed from Instagram and Facebook, citing the same provisions.
On May 11, Goa Congress president Girish Chodankar posted on X, asking whether Prime Minister Modi was so afraid of a Congress-TVK alliance that even a video of the chief minister’s swearing-in ceremony was being blocked. Similarly, TVK leader Aravind shared a screenshot on social media showing that his Facebook post related to Tamil Nadu chief minister Vijay had been removed.
Shame on you @narendramodi 🤦 pic.twitter.com/ujHKwW8VfI
— Aravind TVK (@Aravind8282) May 11, 2026
Around the same time, Meta blocked a reel featuring Rahul Gandhi and C Joseph Vijay, citing the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules. Following widespread criticism, Meta restored the reel.
The Union ministry of electronics and information technology said at the time that the action was the result of an internal error by Meta and had nothing to do with the ministry.
More recently, Meta itself restricted a video of Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressing students for a few hours. Meta later apologised, calling it a technical glitch. However, the incident too lacked transparency, as Meta did not publicly explain the nature of the technical glitch that had led to the restriction.
What is the Legal Provision?
The legal framework behind these restrictions is Section 79(3)(b) of India’s Information Technology Act. The provision was originally intended to determine when platforms could lose their “safe harbour” protection, or immunity from liability.
Put simply, if online platforms and social media intermediaries fail to expeditiously remove material flagged by the government after receiving notice, they may lose their legal immunity for third-party user content. This could make the social media intermediary directly liable for the material.
However, digital rights activists argue that the government is using this provision as the legal basis for a content-blocking mechanism while bypassing Section 69A, which involves greater procedural safeguards and requires written and reasoned orders.
Lack of Transparency
A serious flaw in this process is the lack of transparency. When the government sends a request flagging a post, users are not told who made the complaint or on what basis the order was issued. Instead, they see a generic notice stating that the content has been restricted in accordance with legal requirements.
Users are neither provided a copy of the order nor a case number. They are also not told which official or authority sent the takedown request.
ALSO READ: Content creators decry Instagram censorship, call restrictions a ‘digital emergency’
An even bigger problem is that ordinary users have no concrete and reliable mechanism to challenge such action. Digital rights organisations such as SFLC and IFF have been assisting some users, but the large-scale removal of posts has exposed the absence of an effective redressal mechanism.
At its core, the mechanism is unbalanced. Content is removed first, without users being given a clear reason or an opportunity to be heard. The entire burden of seeking an explanation or having the post restored is then placed on the user.
According to a recent report by The Indian Express, the government issued around 195,000 blocking orders between March and July 2026. Of these, nearly 100,000 were sent to Instagram and around 80,000 to Facebook. In addition, around 15,000 blocking orders were sent to YouTube.
A senior government official told The Indian Express that a significant share of the blocking orders — particularly those involving Instagram — were issued during a period when protests were gathering momentum.
The report also stated that Meta has integrated its API (Application Programming Interface) with the Sahyog portal. As a result, content marked on the system under government directions can be removed from Meta’s platforms automatically, without separate human review by the company. This automation leaves Meta with no meaningful opportunity to independently review or object to the directions before acting on them.
On August 20, the Press Information Bureau (PIB), the government’s nodal agency, shared details about the matter. It said that the Sahyog portal’s API was integrated in 2025 at the request of Meta, Facebook and Instagram’s parent company. This enables state governments and central ministries to notify IT intermediaries about allegedly unlawful content.
According to the PIB, around 298,000 URLs were sent for takedown between March and July 2026. Of these, 244,000 URLs, or 82%, were sent by state governments. This included 51,000 URLs sent by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) in connection with cyber, infrastructure and stock-investment scams.
How does Meta’s ‘Automated System’ Actually Work?
The most confusing and opaque aspect of this entire process is Meta’s “automated system”. Notices on restricted posts state that Meta acted under an automated system, but users are not told what criteria this system uses.
Does it automatically restrict content flagged through the Sahyog portal? Or does it operate on the basis of certain keywords, images, non-compliance with AI-labelling requirements, or other factors? There is little transparency around these questions.
During the recent students’ protests in Delhi against alleged irregularities in NEET-UG, reels posted by journalists, media outlets and student activists showing police action were also restricted. Posts by creators producing content related to the CJP protests were subsequently restricted as well. Alt News has published detailed reports on both instances.
More recently, an Alt News post that mentioned “Burhan Wani” was repeatedly removed by Instagram. In another instance, an Alt News fact-check was restricted for using the word “Khalistani”. we later discovered that searches on Instagram with ‘Burhan Wani’ or ‘Monu Manesar’ do not yield any result. We wrote to Meta asking whether there is a list of words that are not allowed on the platform or whether there is a government order to that effect, but we are yet to receive a response.

Nearly seven years ago, the Tamil Nadu government, in a historic move, banned sex-reassignment surgeries on intersex infants and children, with the aim of protecting their bodily autonomy. Doctors and activists, however, say the State, like the rest of the country, has a long way to go in improving its genetic infrastructure, which they argue would help with the diagnosis and understanding of variations in sex development in intersex children.
Sex-reassignment surgeries, or “genital-normalising” surgeries, are invasive, irreversible, and often unnecessary procedures that alter the ambiguous genital anatomy of infants with intersex traits or differences of sex development (DSD) to fit a binary male/female appearance. In 2019, following a Madras High Court ruling, the government issued a G.O. banning such surgeries unless the situation was life-threatening. It also mandated a panel comprising a paediatric surgeon/urologist, endocrinologist, social worker/psychologist/intersex activist, and a government representative to determine whether the situation was life-threatening and whether such a surgery was warranted.
What happens at hospitals
There are several different types of DSD; while some may be apparent at birth, others may manifest only later, particularly around puberty. “Some DSDs do require further genetic investigations at birth. Therefore, there is a need for better genetic testing facilities,” explained M. Kathirvel, a clinical geneticist at Apollo Hospitals, Chennai.
One important test that needs to be performed in children born with intersex traits, is karyotyping. This is a test that examines the size, shape, and number of chromosomes in a sample of cells. It is essentially a preliminary confirmatory test that gives an overall picture and analysis of the infant’s chromosomes and can show patterns that are not clear from looking at its genital anatomy. However, even this is not available at present, in most government hospitals in T.N., and has to be outsourced to private labs.
What’s missing
A senior doctor from the Government Rajaji Hospital in Madurai, who works with intersex infants, told The Hindu that the hospital sees about one to two cases of children born with intersex traits every month. Surgical corrections are performed only in cases where they are absolutely required, such as in congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) – some forms of which may cause an overproduction of male sex hormones (testosterone in a female), leading to dangerous levels of salt and fluid loss in the newborn.
However, he pointed out that better karyotyping and genetic testing facilities would greatly improve diagnostic and management outcomes (that include confirmation of XX/XY/mixed-type sex), and avoid inadvertent/irreversible gonad removal surgery for intersex children. Out of the 38 medical college hospitals in Tamil Nadu, only one – Institute of Child Health, Egmore, in Chennai, – has a dedicated genetic department, he said. “Before we can even get into complex genetic testing, we do not even have basic karyotyping testing facilities. We currently outsource it to private labs,” said the doctor.
Beyond karyotyping, examinations such as next-generation sequencing (NGS) tests, to better understand such outcomes would also help, added Mr. Kathirvel.
Infrastructure needs
Along with the equipment for the tests, the government also needs to invest in human resources, experts pointed out. There are not enough qualified personnel to perform either basic karyotyping tests or complex genetic tests. A genetic test, when outsourced to private labs, can cost about ₹8,000 to ₹10,000, and the karyotype between ₹1,500 to ₹2,500, the senior doctor added.
Dr. Kathirvel said the State needed to strengthen ICH, Egmore, which is is already a designated Centre of Excellence for Rare Diseases, and set up at least two additional centres of excellence for genetics in Tamil Nadu, particularly with comprehensive in-house genomic testing facilities, including NGS, which would benefit both DSD and other rare-disease diagnoses.
Investing in government infrastructure for genetic testing could go a long way towards helping parents and families who currently have to rely on expensive, private tests. It could also help with research into chromosomal disorders and rare diseases, as well as with counselling for expectant parents, noted experts.
What next?
“Without clinical geneticists as core members of every multi-disciplinary DSD team, accurate subtype identification, cancer-risk assessment, and fertility counselling remain incomplete,” noted Gopi Shankar Madurai, intersex activist and special monitor for SOGIESC Rights at the National Human Rights Commission of India.
“DSD diagnosis fundamentally relies on karyotyping, targeted gene panels, hormone-response assays and imaging. International protocols consistently require this expertise,” Gopi said, further calling for a national-level, affirmative medical protocol for intersex people that is evidence-based and rights-respecting.

Chinese artist jailed over satirical Mao sculptures, say rights groups
- Published
A Chinese artist known for his satirical sculptures of Mao Zedong has been handed a maximum three-year jail term for "slandering China's heroes", according to rights groups.
A court in Hebei province had ruled on Tuesday that Gao Zhen's work "infringes upon the hero's reputation and harms public interest".
Among the 70-year-old's most famous pieces, produced with his brother Gao Qiang, is a sculpture comprising a squad of Mao-like figures holding Jesus Christ at gunpoint.
Gao has been in detention for the past two years, and the UN and many rights groups have called for him to be released. Amnesty International has called his sentencing an "assault" on artistic freedom.
Gao had moved to the US in 2022 but was arrested at his studio on the outskirts of Beijing during a visit in August 2024.
Authorities seized his artworks and barred his wife and seven-year-old son from leaving China.
China watchers have said that Gao Zhen's arrest shows how the Chinese Communist Party is becoming increasingly extreme in both grasp and reach – including by policing its citizens transnationally and retroactively.
He was charged under a law that came into force in March 2018, which bans the defamation of historical figures associated with the party.
The Gao brothers' Execution of Christ sculpture was exhibited in 2009, as were two other sculptures cited in the case.
They are Mao's Guilt, a life-sized replica of the leader kneeling in a pose of solemn contrition; and Miss Mao which depicts him with large breasts and a long, Pinocchio-style nose.
Gao's case was heard in a one-day, closed-door trial earlier this year, which received limited coverage in China.
He plans to appeal the conviction, Amnesty International said on Tuesday.
If the verdict is upheld, Gao would be due to complete his sentence in August 2027 as it would take into account the two years that he has already spent in detention.
"No artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history," Amnesty International's China Director Sarah Brooks said on Tuesday.
"This trial demonstrates how broadly worded and politically motivated laws are used – and worse, in this case, used retroactively – to silence artists, activists and other individuals who dare to express views that differ from those of the Chinese government," she said.
"The case against [Gao Zhen] raises particular concerns with regard to the retroactive application of criminal law, the use of criminal sanctions to punish artistic expression, and the impact on his family," the UN's Human Rights Office told AFP news agency.
Earlier this year, his brother Gao Qiang told the BBC that the trial's "message is clear".
"Even if a work was made 15 years ago, it can still be turned into a crime if today's political climate changes," he said.

Vieira named new Senegal head coach
- Published
Former Arsenal and France captain Patrick Vieira has been appointed as the new head coach of the Senegal men's national team.
The 50‑year‑old replaces Pape Thiaw, who was sacked in the wake of the country's last‑32 exit at the 2026 Fifa World Cup.
Born in Senegal's capital Dakar, Vieira will now manage the country of his birth, having moved to France aged eight before later winning over 100 caps for Les Bleus and lifting the World Cup in 1998 and the European Championship in 2000.
Senegal's football federation (FSF) said the appointment reflects its "desire to strengthen its high-level technical staff" and is "perfectly aligned" with the nation's sporting ambitions.
Details of Vieria's contract and his starting date in the role are still being discussed.
His first matches in charge of the Teranga Lions are expected to come next month in qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon).
Vieira joins the West Africans after he left his role as Genoa head coach by mutual consent last November, with the team bottom of Serie A.
He won eight and drew nine of his 26 games during the 2024-25 season to guide the Italian club to safety and a 13th-place finish.
However, he left the club after managing just two wins in 25-26, with both of those victories coming in the Coppa Italia.
During his playing career, midfielder Vieira won three Premier League titles and four FA Cups at Arsenal, as well as silverware with AC Milan, Inter Milan and Manchester City.
He retired in 2011 and became the manager of New York City in 2016 before returning to Europe with Nice and leading them to seventh in Ligue 1 in his first season.
Vieira was sacked in December 2020 and became Crystal Palace manager the following year, guiding the Eagles to 12th in the Premier League and the FA Cup semi-finals in 2021-22.

US removes Syria from list of state sponsors of terrorism
- Published
The US has removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism after 47 years, lifting what it said was the "final major barriers" for private sector investment in the country and its reintegration into the global economy.
US Secretary Of State Marco Rubio said the move was in recognition of the Syrian government's positive actions to fully distance itself from acts of international terrorism.
The Trump administration has embraced Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former militant who once had an American bounty on his head as the leader of an al-Qaeda off-shoot.
His Islamist group, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), was also removed from the US list of global terrorist organisations.
HTS, formerly known as al-Nusra Front, was al-Qaeda's affiliate in Syria until Sharaa severed ties with the jihadist network in 2016.
In late 2024, HTS led the rebel offensive that overthrew former president Bashar al-Assad and it dominates Sharaa's transitional administration.
The US hopes to bring Syria into its orbit rather than that of Russia or China. But the risks remain significant, with Syria still far from secure and lacking representative government. It is also at the centre of growing tensions between its neighbours Israel and Turkey.
Rubio said Monday's move, which had been initially flagged in July, would give the Syrians "a path to prosperity".
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "Today's action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability."
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani greeted the news as a "historic step", according to state-run news agency SANA.
"We will continue working to remove the effects of isolation and create an environment based on transparency, mutual interests and respect," he said.
Last year, the US also revoked the designation of HTS as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation and removed Sharaa from its list of Specially Designated Global Terrorists.
Syria's removal from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism - where it had been since 1979 - leaves just three remaining: Cuba, North Korea and Iran.
The listing carries financial sanctions, restrictions on US foreign aid and defence exports and sales and can also penalise people and other countries that trade with the sanctioned state.

India didn't target Pakistan's Kirana Hills; loitering munition hit it inadvertently: Ex-CDS Anil Chauhan
Ex-CDS Gen Anil Chauhan says Indian loitering munition likely hit Kirana Hills after failing to find a radar target near Sargodha within its loiter time.
Former Chief of Defence Staff General Anil Chauhan on Tuesday said that India did not target Pakistan's Kirana Hills nuclear facility during last year's Operation Sindoor, but an Indian loitering ammunition inadvertently hit it.
Chauhan explained that a lot of loitering munitions were sent at Sargodha, which is just 10 km north of Kirana Hills. He said one of those munitions must have come and hit the Kirana Hills nuclear facility after not finding a target.
"Before those strikes, we had sent a lot of loiter ammunition at Sargodha, and Kirana Hills is 10 km north of Sargodha. So the loiter ammunition was looking for radars, which were in and around Sargodha, and it has got a lifetime. It will loiter for about two hours, and if it doesn't find a target, it will come and hit somewhere. It must have come and hit one of those hills,'' General Chauhan was quoted by ANI as saying.
The Kirana Hills is a vast rocky mountain range and a designated area under the Pakistan ministry of defence in Sargodha district. Locally referred to as the “Black Mountains” due to its brownish terrain, it stretches between the township of Rabwah and the city of Sargodha.
Former Director General of Air Operations, Air Marshal AK Bharti, had said on May 12 last year that the Indian armed forces did not target the nuclear facility at Kirana Hills in Pakistan.
Responding to a query during a press conference at the time, Bharti said, “Thank you for telling us that Kirana Hills houses some nuclear installation. We did not know about it. And we have not hit Kirana Hills, whatever is there.”
What happened?
India had launched Operation Sindoor on May 7 2025, in response to the deadly terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir's Pahalgam region on April 22, that left 26 people dead. The operation, launched by the tri-services, targeted terror infrastructure located in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK). Over 100 terrorists were killed in these strikes, according to the government.
In the following days, the Indian armed forces hit back at Pakistan's attempted retaliatory strikes. On May 10, the Pakistani army reached out to its Indian counterpart, leading to a ceasefire understanding between the two neighbours.
Immediately after the operation, as well, heavy speculations and social media chatter had claimed that India had struck the Mushaf Airbase in Sargodha, reportedly linked to underground nuclear storage beneath the Kirana Hills. The Air Force denied targeting the facility, both then and now.

What Is the Best Google Workspace Plan?
Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.

You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.
Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.

Zambia courts sealed off as election petition deadline looms
- Published
Court premises in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, and elsewhere have been shut as the deadline for filing a petition against the outcome of the recent presidential election approaches.
An unusual police presence has been reported at some courts, which have been taped off to prevent access.
Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile said he would challenge the election result, citing irregularities, after coming second with a 38% share of the vote. Incumbent Hakainde Hichilema won a second term with 60%.
Mundubile is in hiding over alleged threats made against him, amid a post-election period marked by controversy, including the shooting dead of an opposition figure and the arrest of others.
Monday is the last day on which petition against the presidential election result can be filed. Such a petition could potentially affect the inauguration of Hichilema, which is scheduled for 1 September.
On Monday, lawyers who arrived at the courts were being asked to depart.
One lawyer told the BBC that three armed men approached his vehicle, identified themselves, and instructed him to leave the area.
The courts that have been sealed off include the High Court in Lusaka, the Supreme Court, which also houses the Constitutional Court, and several local courts.
It is unclear when the premises will reopen. The BBC has contacted the Zambian police and the judiciary for comment.
Local media cite a directive by a judiciary administrative official telling all staff not to report to work following the closure of courts for "security reasons".
The memo, which has also been shared online by some opposition figures, does not give details of the security situation.
Some commentators have raised concerns over the closure while questioning the independence of the judiciary.
A prominent voice for the opposition, Emmanuel Mwamba, alleged the action was aimed at preventing Mundubile from filing his presidential election petition.
Despite the court closure, preparations for Hichilema's inauguration appear to be continuing.
The youth and sport ministry has issued a media invitation for journalists to accompany a cabinet official on an inspection of arrangements at National Heroes Stadium, where the ceremony is expected to take place.
Mundubile last week rejected the presidential election results and said he planned to challenge the outcome through the courts.
He remains in a secure location under the protection of what his campaign describes as an "international human rights body".
He went into hiding after the arrests of opposition figures and the death of former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya during a raid by security officers, in what officials described as an exchange of fire in a security operation in the capital.
The arrests as well as the death of Kafwaya prompted calls from rights groups and the Law Association of Zambia for an independent investigations.
Amnesty International described the Kafwaya's killing as "deeply alarming" and called for prompt, thorough and impartial investigations. The lawyers' association similarly expressed "grave concern" and demanded investigation.
The election day, 13 August, was described by regional and international observers as largely peaceful, but they raised concerns about late electoral reforms, media freedom and access to the media in the run-up to the poll.
The EU observation mission said restrictions on the opposition may have contributed to an "uneven contest".
On vote tallying, the mission described a heavy military presence as intimidating and said it had received reports of attacks on some tallying centres.
It said staff in many centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced, and cited weak verification between digital entries and paper records. It added that returning officers frequently paused proceedings while awaiting instructions from headquarters.
The EU mission also called for "maximal transparency" over the poll outcome, noting that the electoral commission did not publish separate polling-station results

New Tata boss to face formidable challenges
- Published
The shock resignation of Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran earlier this month has left corporate India's top job vacant. But finding his successor will be no easy task for the country's most revered conglomerate, whose sprawling $300bn empire spans Jaguar Land Rover and Air India as well as manufacturing iPhones for Apple.
Chandrasekaran resigned amid a deadlock over his reappointment and a widening rift with Tata Trusts - the charity arm which owns controlling shares of the unlisted commercial holding company.
The disagreements are said to have centred over a public listing of Tata Sons as well as capital allocation for the group's various new unlisted businesses, including semiconductors, e-commerce and aviation, all of which are bleeding money.
The group has been in the middle of the largest ever capital investment cycle, with tens of billions of dollars being deployed on everything from building India's first chip fabrication plant to manufacturing EV batteries and turning around Air India, which the Tatas bought from the government in 2022.
The new person at the helm will need to have an ability to assess and absorb the risks that have come with this breakneck expansion as well as rise up to numerous other challenges, Hetal Dalal from Institutional Investor Advisor Services (IiAS), a governance advisory firm, told the BBC.
"It is an incredibly difficult role not just for the individual who will get it but also for the selection committee to find someone. It requires a multitude of skillsets and experience from managing the Tata Trusts to the Tata Sons board, understanding various new businesses and being able to also have strong relationships with regulators and the government," Dalal said.
"There aren't many people running such large, diversified conglomerates. And will they leave their current roles to join the Tata Group?"
The complexity of the role has risen in recent years as the "collective losses of the new businesses are more than the cashflow generated by older companies like TCS, the group's software arm whose business model has been challenged by AI”, Nirmalya Kumar, who previously headed strategy at Tata Sons, told the BBC.
TCS has been the group's cash cow, contributing to some 85% of cash flows, but is no longer the pillar of support it once was.
According to Dalal, even though losses at privately held companies have mounted, the performance of publicly traded, CEO-run Tata companies has been strong.
The group has a good bench strength of internal candidates who could throw their hats in the ring. Yet, finding a candidate who's a straight "plug and play fit" will be difficult, she says.
"I think any person who comes in will have a set of skills and experience, but must be also groomed for the role."
Kumar, on the other hand, isn't convinced the internal names doing the rounds will fit the bill.
"The people internally are good executors of existing business models. Companies like Tata Steel and Tata Motors are almost running on auto-pilot with a CEO in charge. The new chairman will have to understand new business models of the four unlisted businesses that are losing money," he said.
For investors, the resignation is likely to usher in a period of prolonged uncertainty.
New leadership will bring a change in strategic direction at the group in terms of how a new chairman approaches the ambitious expansion Chandrasekharan undertook, say experts.
"Some of the bleeding businesses will need a strategic plan to be made profitable. [The new person] will need to decide whether to scale back or exit some investments," says Dalal.
Kumar says they will also need to communicate a clear plan to the market on how much further investment is needed and when a break-even is expected on these ambitious bets.
But most importantly, he adds, the focus will have to be on "driving alignment between the Trusts [the dominant shareholder] and Tata Sons".
The group's most successful run was under JRD Tata and Ratan Tata, when the relationship between the biggest shareholder and the operating company was frictionless as they were at the helm of both entities.
It broke down under Cyrus Mistry when there was a separation of the roles. Chandrasekharan's exit is the second instance where the chairman has resigned because of the rocky relationship with the Trusts.
The fact that the principal shareholder was not aligned on business strategy was perhaps a fundamental problem in the relationship breaking down, Mukund Rajan, former brand custodian at Tata Sons, told, external India Today news channel.
"You cannot have companies being run where the majority shareholder is either feeling ignored or not aligned with the way the company will be run going forward," Rajan said.
Repairing this relationship will have to be a key priority for whoever is next in the driving seat.
For now, the ongoing turmoil has dented the group's brand image, say experts.
Clear communication has been a major challenge with the Tatas, which does not bode well for the public markets, according to Dalal. While the holding company can argue that it is not publicly traded, what happens there has a direct impact on shareholders of the listed Tata universe, she adds.
"The priority should not be the volume of communication but about reducing uncertainty," Minari Shah, a communications advisor who previously worked with Tata Motors, told the BBC.
"That means demonstrating that governance mechanisms are working, reassuring stakeholders that business continuity is unaffected and providing clarity around the process for leadership transition. It is okay not to have all the answers immediately, as long as stakeholders have confidence that the disagreeing parties are in dialogue."
As of now, nearly two weeks after Chandrasekharan's resignation there have been no detailed public statements on either a succession roadmap, or the way ahead from either Tata Sons or Tata Trusts.
The former's annual general meeting also had to be adjourned because of a lack of quorum, leaving several governance and succession related decisions under a cloud at exactly the moment when shareholders of India's most iconic company will be looking for the greatest clarity.

Shopify merchants often rely on multiple applications to manage workflows ranging from loyalty programmes to GST reconciliation. The application remains private to the merchant’s store, while the merchant retains ownership of the underlying code. "A small number of mental health cases were treated with no loss of life," acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said in a statement last week.
Experts say that while the physical circumstances are difficult, a lack of careful and consistent messaging from leadership at the highest levels also contributed to the crews' mental distress.
The USS Lincoln is like a small city, according to Armen Kurdian, a retired U.S. Navy captain who served aboard the aircraft carrier in 2005. The labor aboard the carrier, he says, can be uniquely physical and difficult.
" It takes a toll on your body," says Kurdian. "The plane captains are out there on the flight deck — you know, these 18-, 19-, 20-year-olds lugging these 100-pound chains on their backs in 120-degree weather."
He describes dehydration and exhaustion as pilots have to take off and land on the carriers, sometimes at night and in bad weather, and "then just being mentally prepared to go fly because lives are at stake."
In the off-hours, Kurdian says there is little to no privacy, with people sleeping in crowded quarters.
While difficult, these conditions can be bearable, he adds. But experts say once uncertainty is thrown into this equation, it can push people to their mental brink.
Jack Stuster is a retired behavioral scientist who spent decades studying human performance.
"In conditions of isolation and confinement," says Stuster, "one of the worst things that you could do to the person is to tell them they're gonna come home at a certain time, and then you say, 'No. It's gonna be delayed.'"
Return is overdue
The Abraham Lincoln's deployment was originally scheduled to end in May.
In addition to the Navy, Stuster worked with NASA and scientists operating in small groups in places like Greenland, where return flights home were often canceled at the very last moment — even after their would-be passengers had dragged their duffle bags right up to the flight line.
" People have described to me going out there for the third time … only to be told that it wasn't gonna happen," says Stuster, which caused them "to break down in tears."
Then there's the issue of duration. A three-month deployment is ideal, says Stuster, or even six. At nine months, he says, things start to become untenable.
Dr. Phillip Hunt was, for years, a Navy physician who deployed on several submarine missions. His background is in emergency medicine, but Hunt says that in the Navy, much of what he treated was mental health. " I was kind of the father confessor, psychologist, what have you," says Hunt.
With a crew of 5,000 people on a ship, Hunt says it's inevitable that some people will struggle with mental health — even in the best of deployment conditions. "You'd have guys getting anxious. You'd have guys getting depressed."
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says reports of poor conditions aboard the Lincoln are overstated. President Trump recently called the deployment "not nearly long enough."
Hunt says a lack of certainty or reassurance from leadership at the highest levels can trickle down to impact everyone's mental well-being. "Denial of this unit's deteriorating operational conditions is highly detrimental to the crew's morale," says Hunt. "The result can include anger, anxiety, or eventually mental exhaustion and depression."
Hunt says he blames leadership at the highest levels for the lack of recognition of this hardship.
" I just, I feel so badly for that crew. It's just tragic," says Hunt. "Just thinking about them almost brings me to tears."
If you or someone you know is struggling with their mental health, please call or text the number 9-8-8 to connect with a counselor.

Fashionistas of a certain age no doubt remember the late designer Stephen Sprouse, who gave Blondie’s Debbie Harry her distinctive Bowery punk style. Sprouse’s first collections in the mid-1980s made a major splash, melding graffiti prints, a playful ’60s aesthetic, and bright Day-Glo colors that won admirers such as Andy Warhol.
Several examples of Sprouse’s work are preserved in the textiles collection of the Indianapolis Museum of Art at Newfields, where conservationists are trying to learn more about the phosphorescent and fluorescent pigments the designer used in his creations in order to keep the colors from dulling over time. They described recent advances in that research at a meeting of the American Chemical Society (ACS) held this week in Chicago.
Scientists began describing minerals that glowed in the dark as phosphors in the Middle Ages. Typically such materials take on a charge when exposed to light, storing the absorbed energy and releasing it gradually as re-emitted light. Henri Becquerel discovered radioactive decay in 1896 because of his work with phosphorescent uranium salts: He left the salts in a closed drawer with photographic plates, which fogged up even without a light source. DayGlo paints and similar materials exploit the related phenomenon of fluorescence. DayGlo pigments fluoresce in daylight by essentially converting UV light into visible light to produce brighter, more vibrant colors.
Sprouse is not the only one to find inspiration in DayGlo and similar phosphorescent and fluorescent materials. All glow-in-the-dark toys, stickers, paint, coatings in fluorescent lamps, cathode-ray tube TVs, and some clock dials rely on phosphorescence. (By contrast, glow sticks rely on a chemiluminescent process.) They’re also commonly used for traffic signage and on safety gear.
DayGlo pigments were used extensively during World War II to make fluorescent fabric panels for US ground troops, while DayGlo’s black light paints were used on Navy aircraft carriers to enable planes to land at night. And artists have used both phosphorescent and fluorescence materials extensively from the mid-20th century on, most notably for psychedelic art and Sprouse’s designs.

Remember the original Quest headset that Meta (then Oculus) trumpeted back in 2019? Meta seems to hope you don’t, since the company officially stopped supporting the wireless VR headset in 2023 to focus on the more popular Quests 2 and 3. However, tinkerers haven’t abandoned the hardware and recently released a new root-access exploit and bootloader that gives “developers and enthusiasts full control over Quest 1 hardware.”
The QuestStack project integrates previously known vulnerabilities in the Quest’s Android fastboot process into a privilege escalation chain that leads easily to full root access on the device. The bootloading process is now streamlined enough that it can be completed without any downloads through a web interface after connecting the headset to a PC.
With this exploit, the original Quest hardware can now be officially divorced from any reliance on Meta’s servers or services to be useful. That means enterprising Quest owners should be able to sideload apps without needing to register for a Meta Developer account and activating Developer Mode through Meta’s mobile app. It also means users should be able to go through the initial setup and login steps for a fresh Quest headset even if and when Meta decides to shut down the servers that currently support this process.

Swami Ramdev has recently been in the news following a public war of words with BJP MP Kangana Ranaut. The dispute began after Ranaut referred to Gen Z as “Generation Gutter”, drawing criticism from Ramdev. He questioned her remarks and commented on her past, prompting Ranaut to hit back and accuse him of making personal comments about her. On 23 August 2026, Ramdev said he did not want to escalate the matter or comment further on Ranaut (here, here, and here).
Amid this, a purported Navbharat Times (NBT) news graphic is being widely shared on social media (here, here, and here), allegedly showing a statement by Swami Ramdev praising the Congress party. The graphic quotes Ramdev as saying, “Congress, no matter how powerful it was, was not a dictator. It controlled inflation and unemployment. Our country’s journalists have tarnished Congress’s image. I too had a significant role in that. Please forgive me.” Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: A Navbharat Times (NBT) news graphic quotes Swami Ramdev praising the Congress party and apologising for previously tarnishing the party’s image.
Fact: There is no evidence that Swami Ramdev made the alleged statement, and no such report was published by Navbharat Times (NBT). Navbharat Times has clarified that the viral graphic is fake and that the statement attributed to him is fabricated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether Swami Ramdev made such a statement, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords. However, we found no credible reports or reliable sources confirming that he made these remarks. Had he actually made such a statement, it would likely have received widespread media coverage. However, we found no such reports.
We then reviewed Swami Ramdev’s official social media handles (here, here, and here), but found no record of him making the alleged statement.
We also reviewed the official website and social media handles (here, here, and here) of Navbharat Times, whose watermark appears on the viral graphic. However, we found no report or post carrying the alleged quote.
We found posts featuring statements by Swami Ramdev on NBT’s platforms (here, here, and here). The viral postcard appears to have been created by editing one of these original postcards. It appears that the text in this section has been edited and replaced. The comparison can be seen below.
On 21 August 2026, Navbharat Times (NBT) refuted the viral claim in a post on X (archived), stating that several fake posts using NBT’s name had been circulating on social media in recent days to spread misleading and false information. NBT urged users to rely only on its official social media handles and platforms for authentic news and information.
To sum up, this viral NBT graphic alleging that Swami Ramdev praised the Congress party and apologised for previously tarnishing its image is fake.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is no longer just a problem of hospital-acquired or health care-associated infections. Clinicians in Keralam are worried that the resistance profile of primary antibiotics used to treat even acute diarrhoeal diseases like Shigellosis is going up, which has important implications for antibiotic use in the State.
Data from Keralam’s KARS-NET (Kerala Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network), one of the strongest AMR surveillance systems in the country and which has been tracking the AMR profile of Shigellosis since 2023, says that the resistance profile of primary antibiotics used to treat the infection is growing.
Increased resistance
Ciprofloxacin, which continues to be included in national guidelines for treatment of Shigella dysentery and which used to be an important treatment option for bacterial dysentery, has a resistance profile of 96% and can no longer be relied upon for empirical treatment of Shigellosis.
What is worrying is that pathogenic resistance to the next available drug, Ceftriaxone, a third-generation Cephalosporin class antibiotic, has also gone up to 36% as per KARS-Net data.
“Till now, community-acquired AMR had not been a problem in the State. If you, as a citizen, have never been worried about AMR, you should be now, because it is showing up right at your doorstep. Our arsenal of effective and affordable antibiotics for common infections in the community is shrinking,” points out R. Aravind, head of infectious diseases, Government Medical College, Thiruvananthapuram, who is also the convener of KARS-Net.
Most acute diarrhoeal diseases are self-limiting and do not really require treatment with antibiotics. Shigellosis, too, is largely self-resolving with proper rehydration but in vulnerable populations (children below five years and the elderly), the infection can lead to severe dehydration, sepsis and neurological complications, requiring the use of antibiotics.
Shigella is primarily an enteric/community pathogen, which spreads from person to person through contaminated food and water and is thus a sentinel organism for detecting what is happening to AMR in the community.
“Clinicians have been using Ceftriaxone for treating Shigellosis in patients who get admitted to hospital. But the clinical implication of growing resistance of Shigella to this drug is immense. For Shigellosis patients with severe dysentery going into septic shock and multiorgan failure, it is absolutely important that the correct antibiotic is administered within an hour and that it is 100% sensitive. This means that for such serious patients, we can no longer depend on Ceftriaxone and have to go for high-end drugs like Meropenem which belongs to the Carbapenem class, widely considered the last-resort antibiotics,” explains Dr. Aravind.
Major outbreak
Shigellosis is reported sporadically from all districts in Keralam every year. But the State reported one of the major outbreaks ever in June this year, when 225 cases and six deaths were reported from Kozhikode, Malappuram and Wayanad districts.
The fact that loss of lives was unusually high this year should be read alongside the information about the rising AMR profile of Shigellosis, clinicians warn, even when there is no exact data to say that AMR led to the death of patients.
Emergence, a decade ago
Keralam documented multidrug-resistant Shigella and ESBL-producing strains more than a decade ago, signalling the emergence of Ceftriaxone resistance. ESBL-producing strains are bacteria that release Extended Spectrum Beta Lactamases enzymes, which can break down important third-generation antibiotics, rendering them ineffective.
The 2018 study published by clinicians in Government Medical College, Alappuzha, which studied the antibiotic susceptibility pattern of Shigella isolates (2011-2016) had reported that 91.6% of the isolates were multi-drug resistant and that eight of the isolates were resistant to Ceftriaxone/Cefotaxime. It had also reported that five isolates produced ESBL enzymes, making third-generation Cephalosporins less effective. This was one of the first studies from Keralam that had given a clear indication that AMR was no longer confined to just the older drugs.
What it means for patients
Rising drug resistance means more treatment failures, longer hospital stays, greater use of high-end antibiotics and increased health-care costs, apart from the threat that more drug-resistant pathogens might emerge in the community.
“Most cases of acute diarrhoea do not require antibiotics. But even when antibiotics are genuinely indicated, particularly for severe bacillary dysentery caused by Shigella, our treatment options are steadily narrowing. This is certainly a wake-up call for everyone that we need to be very careful about using antibiotics,” a senior health official points out.

The Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), the market of the Busan International Film Festival, will present InnoAsia 2026, its program built around the intersection of film and emerging technology.
This year’s participants include Amazon Web Services (AWS), Kling AI, Google DeepMind and Alibaba Group, alongside a range of other technology and content companies and startups. The program is built around a vision of cinema and technology developing side by side, with a scope that runs from brand-film partnerships to the fast-growing microdrama business.
ACFM and global marketing agency Innocean will co-host Cinema by Brand 2026, a new competition with the Producers Guild of Korea handling selection and production oversight. The platform links brand clients with filmmakers around the world to turn advertising messages into standalone films with real narrative ambition, rather than conventional commercials. This year’s contest calls for 20-minute short films built around Hanwha Group’s “Space Solar Power.” First-round picks arrive in early September, followed by final pitching later that month, with winners named during ACFM. Selected teams get production funding and will see their films shown to audiences in Korea and abroad. A market session will dig into what branded content means for the business and how the initiative came together, with participation expected from Hanwha, Innocean and the selected directors.
Popular on Variety
Beyond brands and filmmakers, InnoAsia is deepening ties with technology firms and international markets. This year’s AI-driven tech participants include AWS, Google DeepMind, BytePlus, Alibaba Cloud, Netflix’s VFX studio Eyeline Studios, MegazoneCloud, OPIM Digital, the Korean Film Archive’s VFX trading platform i.AM, Kling AI and Inshorts.
On the content-production side, France’s Atlas V joins Korea’s Mateo AI Studio, MBC C&I, Climax Studio, For Entertainment, K-Dragon and MooAm, while microdrama platforms Mango TV, FlickReels and Vigloo round out the roster. Kling AI will co-host two sessions with ACFM, New Cinematic Possibilities: Reimagining Filmmaking with Kling AI and a networking reception tied to production needs across Asia. AWS and MegazoneCloud will launch new AWS Awards linked to startup pitching, with winners chosen through a proof-of-concept process and awarded AWS cloud vouchers. On the international side, EFM-linked startup Lux AI, which builds intelligent lighting tools for virtual production, will travel to Busan along with Tanja Meissner, director of Berlinale Pro and EFM. Through a partnership with TAICCA School under the Taiwan Creative Content Agency, VFX-efficiency startup imCore will also take part.
Seven Korean startups were chosen through an open call run with the Busan Center for Creative Economy & Innovation and AWS, together spanning the full content pipeline. On the development and production side, Lumicraft’s AI casting tool Castlink pairs actor discovery with contracting and settlement, while Reproduction’s Pre-Flow handles screenplay analysis and production data sharing. For localization, Voithru’s Totus offers AI dubbing across 29 languages, and XL8 brings both MediaCAT and EventCAT for video localization and real-time interpretation. On the exhibition side, Digion Cinema will show off an online cinema platform and AR smart glasses built for film viewing. MyStarChain will present its blockchain voting platform MyStarPick, and HiStranger will introduce Insight Flow, a tool that reads biosignals to gauge audience emotional response.
InnoAsia 2026 will run several programs across three tracks: technology proof-of-concept and investment, creators and production, and industry and policy. The InnoAsia Startup Demo Jam sits at the center of the first track, with nine companies, drawn from the open call and international partner recommendations, pitching AI, virtual production and digital-asset technologies to investors and buyers. The InnoAsia WIP Showcase will preview AI-based features, animation, series and interactive projects from directors including Pierre Zandrowicz, Mark Wachholz and Kang Yunsung, paired with a colloquium on AI production pipelines.
A Cinematic AI conference will spotlight Google DeepMind’s AI animation work and an AI film from director Darren Aronofsky, both previously featured at Cannes Next, and will examine AI filmmaking ecosystems with input from Alibaba Cloud and Kling AI. AI Creators Camp offers hands-on workshops led by VFX supervisors from major studios and creators who have won at AI film festivals. On the policy side, a panel titled Microdrama – Data, AI, Formats and Audiences: China and Beyond brings together executives from Mango TV, FlickReels and Vigloo to discuss the $18 billion shortdrama market, while Next Foundation gathers voices from technology, policy and academia, including the National IT Industry Promotion Agency, to weigh questions around independent AI foundation models, AI assets, and IP and copyright in an era of AI transformation.
	InnoAsia 2026 will run Oct. 10-13, at Exhibition Center 2, BEXCO in Busan, alongside the 31st Busan International Film Festival, which runs Oct. 6-15, and the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market, held Oct. 10-13.

A Reverse Ellis Island
A city at the southern tip of Mexico has become the place where migrants’ dreams go to die.
Julio Borrell knew he was being deported, but after 47 hours on a bus rattling through Mexico, he still had no idea where the United States was sending him. Through the window, he saw the cities give way to sprawling banana plantations and coffee farms. The passengers were still wearing whatever clothes they’d had on when they were detained by ICE: shirts splattered with paint from their most recent job, pajama pants, landscaping-company uniforms, bathing suits. Borrell had lived in Miami for 46 years. Now he watched as the bus passed a sign for the Guatemala border and then pulled over on the side of the road.
“Where are we?” Borrell asked.
“Tapachula,” a Mexican immigration agent answered.
Borrell hadn’t heard of it. Neither had anyone else on the bus. The deportees weren’t from here. They weren’t even from Mexico. They were Cuban, Venezuelan, Nicaraguan, and Haitian—many of them elderly, some stripped of their green card after spending most of their life in the United States. The Trump administration, unable or unwilling to send them to their home country, had bused them 2,000 miles, from the U.S. border to a small city where they don’t have legal status. It’s a practice that started last year without any announcement and has quietly grown since then. “Why the hell did they bring us here?” Borrell, who migrated to Miami from Havana in 1980, asked me while I was in Tapachula this month.
By the time we met, Borrell, a tall, sinewy 72-year-old with a shock of gray hair, had been in Tapachula for about six months, trying to make enough money fixing tires to rent a studio apartment. He knew that a handful of other Cuban deportees had been flown even farther away, to African nations such as Eswatini and South Sudan. But it was Tapachula that had become a mass waiting area for those rebuffed by U.S. immigration policy, out of sight of lawyers and human-rights defenders. This is now where the largest concentration of deportees is dropped in Mexico, and where most migrants traveling through Latin America en route to the U.S. are halted. Donald Trump can claim that the border is “closed” because it has effectively been relocated to Tapachula. The city looks and feels the way towns in northern Mexico along the U.S. border once did—a dumping ground for those expelled from the United States and a gathering place for those snagged on their way north.
Mexican agents pull migrants out of commercial buses and cars on the freeway leaving the city, making sure the deportees don’t attempt to return to the United States. Another set of agents waits for the next busload of Cubans, Venezuelans, and Haitians to arrive so they can be processed. It’s what experts call externalization: the outsourcing of migration management to other countries.
Borrell told me that he’d come to the United States when he was 26 as part of the Mariel boatlift, the mass exodus of Cubans who traveled on crowded boats to Miami in 1980. He had seven American children, 11 grandchildren, and a great-grandchild. He had run a mechanic shop and renewed his visa each time it neared expiration. He could feel his body breaking down after years of physical labor and had been looking forward to retirement and more time with his family in South Florida.
Then, last December, he went to his scheduled immigration check-in, as he had done dozens of times before. This time, he was detained by ICE agents. They sent Borrell to Florida’s Alligator Alcatraz for four months and then to Eloy Detention Center, in Arizona. From there, he was put on a bus for the U.S.-Mexico border and then another, bound for Tapachula. He walked on the side of the road for an hour before borrowing a cellphone to call his family back in Miami. “I’m in some place called Tapachula, Chiapas,” he told his daughter.
Borrell, like thousands of other non-Mexicans deported here, arrived without clear legal status and with nowhere to stay. Many deportees sleep on the street for their first few nights. Mexico denies that it is facilitating deportations from the United States to Tapachula, even though more than a dozen migrants described to me the cooperation between U.S. and Mexican immigration agents in their expulsions. According to data from the Mexican Institute for Migration, 12,977 non-Mexicans were deported to Mexico from January 2025 to March 2026, largely to southern Mexico. They joined the tens of thousands of other migrants from all over the world who have been stranded in Tapachula during their journey to the United States, after being blocked by Mexican immigration agents from moving farther north. The mix of nationalities here has prompted officials at the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration to begin informally referring to the city as TapaYork—a kind of reverse Ellis Island. There are roughly 350,000 permanent residents of Tapachula and approximately 60,000 migrants living here. Some have tried to flee Tapachula multiple times, only to be deported back over and over again after being caught by Mexican agents.
U.S. officials have consistently said that their goal is “zero border crossings”—a more absolutist project than Trump articulated during his first term, when it was easier for migrants to advance beyond Tapachula. This month, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed that his department was accomplishing that goal. (Crossings are indeed way down, but they’re not at zero.) In meetings with their Mexican counterparts, U.S. officials continue to ask for more stringent immigration enforcement and accommodation for long-distance deportations, according to Mexican officials. The Mexicans, who fear unilateral U.S. military action, have generally complied. The Cubans, Venezuelans, and Haitians who are expelled here in buses that typically arrive a few times a week are evidence of Mexico’s acquiescence. In addition to the buses filled with foreigners, Tapachula’s tiny airport sometimes receives as many as five flights of Mexican deportees a day. (There have been more than 196 so far this year.) Most of the Mexicans arriving by plane head straight to the local bus station and return to their home state or to the border again. Some are minors and need to wait for their parents to pick them up.
In his first weeks here, Borrell, disoriented, was walking to an ATM to see whether he could withdraw cash when he saw a face he recognized. It was a Cuban friend from Miami, who ran a tile business.
“What are you doing here, man?” Borrell asked.
His friend, who had moved to the U.S. from Cuba when he was 6 and held a green card, had also been deported by bus. Borrell told him what he has said many times since: “We’ve got to get out of here. I’m not going to die in Tapachula.”
From his small stand selling bread in downtown Tapachula, Mervil Wisdael, 43, sees the groups of deportees arrive a few times a week. “They’re lost,” he told me. “They’re just dragging their feet. They don’t even know where they are.”
Wisdael, from Port-au-Prince, is part of a different population of migrants here, one that intended to pass through on the way to the United States. Tapachula has historically been a way station for migrants traveling north, including those who navigated the jungle of Panama’s Darién Gap before continuing to Mexico. I spent a week in Tapachula in 2018, when a caravan of migrants amassed there on their way north, early in Trump’s first term. Migrants slept in the central plaza, in the bus station, in rented rooms and shelters. It quickly became a media spectacle. Trump claimed that the group leaving Tapachula, which included many young Central American families, was full of criminals. He demanded that Mexico intercept them. A few days later, I walked with the migrants to the edge of the town, where Mexican immigration authorities had blocked the road. Hundreds of people were detained. Taking a break, one officer said to me, “We’re doing what your president asked.”
Since then, the Mexican government has again and again bent to the will of the U.S. government on immigration enforcement. It signed off on the “Remain in Mexico” policy in 2019, which forced asylum seekers to wait for their immigration appointments from Mexico’s northern border rather than from within the United States. Under the Joe Biden–era CBP One program, it agreed to host asylum seekers even farther south, including in Tapachula. Then, during Trump’s second term, Mexico agreed to mass deportations to the city. Mexican officials told me that the main consideration for the Americans was Tapachula’s distance from the U.S. border and the way agents could create a choke hold on the only highway leaving the city. I came back to Tapachula to see how that series of capitulations had changed the city, a gritty commercial hub surrounded by miles of farmland, where near-daily afternoon storms briefly break the tropical heat.
Read: A planeload of informants
Wisdael had planned to make his way to the U.S. to reunite with his family and apply for asylum. But by the time he arrived in Tapachula, six years ago, Mexico was no longer allowing migrants to transit through the country without a humanitarian visa or refugee status, which could take months or years to get. He stayed until he got his papers, and then he waited longer to see whether it might get easier to cross the U.S. border. Many other Haitians stayed too. Roughly 10 percent of the city’s public-school students are now from Haiti. Each of its three semiprofessional basketball teams has Haitian players. The city’s market is peppered with stalls selling Haitian food. Employees of the municipal immigration office have taught themselves Creole.
Wisdael has been in Tapachula longer than most of his countrymen. He speaks fluent Spanish. He met a Guatemalan woman, Ericka Leonardo, while working on a construction crew there. She was walking down the street.
“You’re pretty,” he said.
“I’ve never dated a Black guy,” she said.
“Maybe you should try,” he said.
They’re now married and live together in Tapachula. She works at an arcade around the corner from his bread stall. They’ve become informal sources of information about Mexico’s archaic immigration system. Wisdael explains to newly arrived Haitians that they need to line up at Mexico’s refugee office every 15 days so that a bureaucrat can sign a document proving that they have not absconded from Tapachula. After 30 or 40 or 50 signatures—anywhere from one to two years—most Haitians will have refugee status in Mexico. “They don’t want to wait that long. No one wants to wait that long here,” he said.
But Wisdael knows that it’s not a good time to attempt to cross the U.S. border. Most people don’t even get that far. Haitians without Mexican papers are typically caught by Mexican immigration agents at a checkpoint just north of Tapachula. The city once felt like a stepping stone. Now it feels like a dead end.
Almost every immigrant community in Tapachula has its own Wisdael—someone who has been around long enough to explain the rules to the newly arrived. Aside from the Cubans and Venezuelans, there are thousands of Central Americans, along with smaller groups of Congolese, Senegalese, Bangladeshis, and Nepalese. There’s a Cameroonian bar and a Ghanaian restaurant within walking distance of the 19th-century colonial church in the city center. The man guarding the door at one of the migrant shelters is Ukrainian. Most people have learned just enough Spanish to ask at least two questions: How long have you been here? And when are you leaving?
Before I left Tapachula, I was curious to meet the city employees running the municipal migrant-assistance center. I followed directions to a mostly abandoned covered market at the edge of town. I was sure I was lost. Then an enthusiastic 28-year-old, Kevin Figueroa, leapt out of his office holding a laptop. He had a PowerPoint presentation on migration in Tapachula. Did I want to see it?
He flipped through the slides on the large numbers of migrant arrivals here and all of the ways the city had integrated them into municipal life. I knew that there had been protests over the past few years by locals upset about the way their city was changing. In 2022, Roberto Fuentes, the city council’s general secretary, told reporters that “the city is in a state of siege, a state of chaos.” At least once, Haitian street vendors like Wisdael have been physically removed from the city center by local police.
But Figueroa assured me that Tapachulans had become accustomed to the way their city had been transformed. The economy was growing. The food was better. I partially believed him. In some ways, the city did seem to have settled into its new demographics. But there were still frequent confrontations between migrants and municipal employees—triggered, for example, by migrants using public electricity outlets to charge their phones. This month, several migrants set their mattresses on fire in the city’s migrant-detention center, leading the military to intervene. Two Venezuelans were arrested. Mexico’s immigration agency said obliquely in a press release that the protest was in response to “the dissatisfaction of a group of foreign nationals regarding their immigration process.”
What seems to bother those trapped in Tapachula most is not the way they are treated in the city, but that they are here at all, in a no-man’s-land, far from any place they ever lived. It’s an approach the Trump administration plans to expand to more remote locations. Not long after I left Tapachula, the Liberian government announced that it would accept 1,200 non-Liberian deportees from the United States. Such an announcement would, until recently, have been a radical departure from decades of immigration policy. But there has been little outcry. The U.S. has kept the desperation of deportees and asylum seekers at a great distance. Some of the Cubans I spoke with in Tapachula told me that in the next week or two, they will begin marching north in their own migrant caravan. They know their chances of getting to the border are close to zero. But they think the effort might be enough to remind Americans that they are there, waiting at the southern tip of Mexico.

GIVA has withdrawn its recent jewellery advertisement featuring Kriti Sanon following criticism and backlash on social media. The campaign, which was released around Rakshabandhan, has now been pulled down from all platforms. The jewellery brand has also issued an apology on its official Instagram handle, clarifying that hurting anyone’s sentiments was not the intention behind the campaign.
GIVA pulls down Kriti Sanon Raksha Bandhan ad after backlash; jewellery brand issues apology
In its statement, GIVA said, “We have the highest regard and deep respect for Indian culture, traditions and festivals. As a brand, we have always believed in celebrating these joyous moments with the entire family and this time we wanted to extend the love and celebration to our pets. If our recent advertisement has inadvertently hurt the sentiments of some segments of society, that was not our intent at all. Out of respect, we have withdrawn the said advertisement from all media. Wish you all the love & positivity this festive season!”
The advertisement featured Kriti Sanon tying a rakhi to her onscreen brother. For the campaign, the actor was seen wearing a white bralette-style top with a sheer matching cape and a traditional-style skirt. The styling became a point of discussion online, with several social media users questioning the choice of outfit for a festival associated with family traditions.
View this post on Instagram
 The campaign also drew criticism from Kangana Ranaut, who, without directly naming Kriti or the jewellery brand, questioned the styling and described the commercial as ‘creepy’.
Kriti subsequently responded to the criticism and defended her choice of attire. Addressing the broader conversation around women and clothing, she wrote, “Also, when will we stop telling women what to wear?? Ethnic fashion has evolved over the years, but still a woman's respect for her culture is measured with just her clothes!! Culture & Traditions are in her heart, not in her neckline!”
The controversy also saw Kriti’s sister Nupur Sanon extend her support to the actor. Nupur had earlier taken to Instagram Stories and questioned the criticism directed at her sister’s outfit.
With GIVA now withdrawing the campaign and issuing an apology, the advertisement has become the centre of a wider conversation around fashion, cultural traditions and the expectations placed on women’s clothing during festive occasions.

Taylor Swift shared a touching tribute to the late Dolly Parton after the iconic singer-songwriter’s death on Tuesday.
“A world without Dolly doesn’t feel possible, real, or right,” it reads. “But because of the eternally generous way she spent her time on this earth and the countless lives she changed for the better, her legacy will be an everlasting one.
“She was truly the gift that kept on giving. Dolly gave us someone to look up to while encouraging us to be who we are as individuals. Somehow she was able to give us her lessons about the world gently and honestly, simultaneously, and oftentimes hilariously. She managed to give the world the ultimate mystery and fantasy in some corners of her life, but to give full transparency in the ways that counted. Somehow she was true grace and true grit, all in one dazzling person. She possessed the softest heart when it came to the struggles of others, and a backbone of steel to defend her own self worth as an artist.
