“Delhi has registered more than 1,700 cases of swine flu this year,” Health Department officials said on Friday (August 21, 2026), as the national capital sees a surge in seasonal influenza cases during monsoon.
On the day, Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh and representatives of the Health Department are scheduled to meet Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda and senior officials from the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to review the swine flu situation in the capital.
"A report is being prepared to assess the number of cases and the overall situation. Everything is under control. There is no need for general panic. All government hospitals have been directed to ensure adequate treatment facilities," Mr. Singh told PTI.
The Minister said the government is closely monitoring the situation and has directed all government hospitals to ensure adequate treatment facilities are available.
“Healthcare institutions and officials concerned have been told to keep a close watch on infection patterns, affected areas and potential hotspots,” the Minister said, adding that separate wards are being set up for swine flu patients.
Doctors in Delhi said they are seeing a noticeable surge in number of patients with influenza and influenza-like symptoms, though most cases are mild to moderate.
Dr. Rishikesh Desai, consultant physician in the department of internal medicine at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, said the hospital is witnessing a rise in seasonal influenza cases. "Most healthy individuals recover well, but influenza can become serious in older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with chronic diseases," he said.
Dr. Neha Rastogi Panda, senior consultant in the department of infectious diseases at Fortis Hospital, Gurugram, also recounted a similar situation. "There has been a sudden increase in patients with influenza and influenza-like illnesses," she said. "Most patients have mild to moderate illness and recover well with appropriate supportive care, so there is no reason to panic." Rastogi further said doctors were seeing more prolonged cough and greater intensity of fever this season, possibly due to reactive inflammation of the lungs due to air pollution, particularly from particulate pollutants.
According to medical practitioners, H1N1 infection — commonly known as swine flu — usually presents fever, cough, sore throat, headache, body aches and fatigue. Those with persistent high fever, breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion or worsening symptoms are advised to seek medical attention promptly.
"Vaccination, hand hygiene, avoiding close contact while ill and staying home during the infection period are key to limiting transmission," Dr. Desai said.

When the Indian government announced the resignation of its education minister in late July after weeks of protest, there were widespread celebrations. Students from across the country had joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party amid growing resentment over repeated examination cancellations and question paper leaks.
The pressure of exams in the country has only increased in recent years. The number of student suicides rose from 8,068 in 2014, to 14,488 in 2024 – an increase of roughly 80% – according to the Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India report released by the country’s National Crime Records Bureau. After family problems, failure in examinations has been listed as the leading cause of suicides among students.
For families who say they lost their children to education system mismanagement and examination scandals, watching the protest scenes unfold on television came with mixed feelings. Some were happy that future students may be spared the same fate; others questioned why it had taken so long.
The Guardian spoke to four families about what happened to their children and how they feel today.
Anshika Pandey, 20, Delhi
Anshika Pandey, the eldest of twin sisters and four siblings, was, her father says, the calmest, quietest and most responsible member of the family. Revision books still lie neatly stacked, bags and accreditation cards hang from the nails where they were last placed. Her ambition was to be a doctor in the community where she lived, to be able to help the “poor people in need of medical care” some day.
Pandey studied for more than 12 hours every day, worked part-time at a store for nearly six hours and slept no more than five hours each night.
This year’s national eligibility cum entrance test (Neet) to gain entrance to medical training was her third attempt at becoming a doctor. After sitting the exam on 3 May, she was hopeful. But on 12 May she learned that the exam had been leaked for the second year in a row and there would be a resit.
“Anshika was deeply hurt. She had been hoping to enter college this year and was happy with the exam she had taken. Still, after cancellation, when I tried to console her, all she lamented was how could she hope to give another good exam,” says her father, Indradhar Pandey, a cab driver in Delhi.
Anshika remained calm and performed her household duties and engaged with everyone normally. But two days later, on 14 May, when everyone had left for work and her twin sister and younger brother were napping, she hanged herself.
Anshika’s dream had been to move her family, especially her siblings, from the slum where they lived. Her younger sister, Pragati, hopes to fulfil that dream and reminisces about how the two sisters had talked about it several times.
Anshika’s sketches and positive messages and mantra chants on the walls of their home, which she wrote to motivate herself, are now the memories her family is refusing to let go of.
Sufi Shaheen, 19, Delhi
Before leaving the house on the morning of 25 October 2024, Sufi Shaheen straightened her hair and put on her favourite jeans. As she left, she asked her mother for 10 rupees (8p), unlike other days when she would ask for 100. Then she headed for her joint entrance examination (Jee) lesson.
Her mother, Sultana Khatoon, asked her why she was leaving the house on an empty stomach. Shaheen replied she would be back soon. Twenty minutes later, she jumped from the seventh floor of a tutoring centre, about a mile away from her home.
It has been almost two years since she died, but Khatoon has not recovered from that day. She is being treated for severe depression and bouts of headaches.
“She was my only daughter of the four children and more like a friend. Every time I stepped out of the house, she would help me get ready. Even though she was deeply passionate about studying and becoming an engineer, she also loved dressing up and made everyone in the house do it too,” says Khatoon, as she looks through her daughter’s school photos.
Living with her parents and three brothers on her father’s modest income as a technical engineer, Shaheen had dreamed of becoming a software engineer and “excelling even more than the boys in her community”, says her mother.
A quick learner and highly motivated, Shaheen taught herself to draw and paint, and even learned to speak Japanese and Korean. But she had been stressed for several months and feared not being able to clear her second attempt at the national engineering entrance exam in January 2025.
When India’s National Testing Agency made changes to the Jee exam syllabus, Shaheen couldn’t sleep for days. She remained stressed, cried when talking to her brother and her best friend on the phone, and wrote a note to her parents in which she apologised and asked her younger brother, Masoom, to make their dreams come true.
“Almost two years later, Masoom was ranked 188th in the whole of India in his CUET [common university entrance test]. But we do not have Shaheen to celebrate this with,” says Khatoon.
Pradeep Kumar Mahich, 22, Rajasthan
“Even God will not be able to stop me from becoming a doctor this year,” were 22-year-old Pradeep Mahich’s words to his father right after his Neet exam on 3 May. This was his fourth attempt and, most importantly, he felt confident. But the announcement of the exam paper leak and resit broke his heart.
No one in the family had ever “dreamt so big”, says Pradeep’s father, Rajesh Kumar, a farmer in Rajasthan’s Sikar district. Kumar sold a large part of his farmland and took a loan of 11 lakhs (£8,600) under the farmer’s crop loan schemes.
“Sikar, the main coaching hub for Neet, is only an hour and a half from our village. My eldest daughter, Babita, who was preparing to join the police, and my son were both studying in Sikar, renting an apartment. This was his fourth year of tutoring, and the money from selling the land and the loan was slowly being consumed. I would send monthly expenses of £250 and Pradeep’s annual tutoring fees of £4,000, asking them not to worry about money and focus on his studies,” says Kumar.
“Pradeep had told me, ‘Papa, we will do a big celebration before I go to college. And one day I’ll return to serve the people of the village,’” says Kumar.
On 15 May, as he did every day, Kumar sent milk and curd to his two children on a bus that goes to Sikar; Pradeep came to pick it up at 9.30am then went home and told his sister he would help prepare lunch. But when his sister was showering, he hanged himself. She has taken a break from her studies and returned home.
Seeing students protesting on his television screen, Kumar says he is relieved that the eduction minister has gone but says there should be a proper investigation so that “no family suffers the same fate that we did”.
S Anitha, 17, Tamil Nadu
S Anitha belonged to an underprivileged lower caste, or Dalit, community from Tamil Nadu’s Ariyalur district. Born to a daily wage labourer, her mother died when she was seven, leaving her grandparents to raise her.
As a teenager, she decided she wanted to become a doctor. “At such a tender age, she was so focused that we used to feel proud of her,” says her brother, Manirathinam. “She knew what she wanted and never distracted herself with anything else. She never asked for any clothes, jewellery or food – her focus was clear and she knew the circumstances.”
She scored a perfect 100 in physics and chemistry at school and was offered a place to study aeronautical engineering at the state’s technological institute. But when she could not even meet the cut-off marks in the Neet exam, she realised that she had been studying a different syllabus.
Tamil Nadu had already criticised the national government for imposing an all-India examination – “disrupting the federal structure” – because it had a different education system. As a result, the state was exempted from Neet in 2016, but not in 2017, the year Anitha sat the exam.
When the supreme court ruled on 22 August 2017 that admissions to medical school would be based only on the Neet exam, she lost hope. On 1 September, Anitha hanged herself in her grandparents’ home. Her suicide became the subject of a public debate and led to widespread protests across the state and even in Delhi.
Her brother took part in last month’s protests in the capital and, while happy about the Indian education minister’s resignation in July, argues that all exams should become state-run, rather than by central government, as not everyone can afford the hefty tutoring fees needed to sit the Neet exam.
He now runs a free library and education centre in Anitha’s name.

AI tools for job interview preparation can help you understand a role, research the company, prepare likely questions, practice mock interviews, and even point out where your answers fall short.

How to Use AI to Prepare for a Job Interview
Before we get to the applications, which indeed make job interview preparation an easy affair, you must understand the importance of a solid foundation to begin with. Fortunately, this groundwork only requires leveraging existing AI tools you may already be using. After getting to know the details of the job interview, mainstream AI models, such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude, and more, can be directed to put you at an advantage from the very initial phase of your preparation. Below is what you must do first.
→ Understand the Role and Generate Role-Specific Interview Questions
Most, if not all, job descriptions are little more than a pile of technical and corporate jargon, often failing to clearly state the requirements. Misaligned interview expectations may already put you in a bad spot during the interview, so you must ensure that you are well-versed with the job description. AI models can help you do so with a few prompts, but you must include a few crucial elements to get the best results. With all this, don’t forget to upload your updated resume for a tailored response.
For starters, you cannot miss out on knowing the core competencies required for the job you’re applying for. AI can help you identify the top non-negotiable technical and soft skills that the recruiter expects of you. Such attributes are often not understood by many applicants, which prevents them from brushing up on existing skills or learning the required ones. Next, your prompt must include identifying the success metrics, or the key performance indicators of the role.
Because every hiring takes place to solve a specific problem of the organization, it’s crucial to have an idea about the performance expectations the recruiter may have from you. For tech roles, it usually revolves around solving existing issues, improving existing processes, and related tasks. In contrast, non-tech roles focus on increasing client retention, establishing business relationships, and related tasks.
Lastly, you must also ask AI to groom you based on your resume. It will help you determine whether your resume aligns well with the role and whether any specific skills need to be spotlighted. AI can not only identify potential loopholes but also help you present your projects to the interviewer in the most convincing way possible. With this initial study of the role’s requirements, you can certainly answer questions and defend yourself with confidence.
→ Study About the Company
While most candidates think they know the company they’re applying to well, the truth is, not many perform a proper deep dive. It is an important part of interview preparation, as knowing the company helps you give more relevant answers instead of generic ones.
AI makes company research much easier, but don’t simply ask it to “tell me about the company.” Start with its current market position, products, competitors, recent announcements, and anything else directly relevant to the role.
Foremost, your prompt should include information about the company’s current market position. You can assist the AI model by attaching the company’s press releases, financial reports, product launch notes, public announcements, and more. Financial reports can also be used to project the company’s future trends, map future goals, and more, which are worth knowing about.
It’s also essential to understand the company’s competitors, as it can help you frame your answers to interview questions in the company’s favor. While you are unlikely to find many, you can ask the AI model to identify and propose viable solutions to the company’s publicly available problems. It can be a significant advantage when handled appropriately and also serves as a good background for obvious questions, such as “What will you bring to the table?” and “Why should we hire you?”
→ Analyze the Interviewer
If you know who will be interviewing you, publicly available professional information can help you prepare better. Their LinkedIn profile, current role, past experience, or area of expertise may give you a fair idea of which parts of your background they are more likely to focus on.
You can provide this information to an AI model and ask it to suggest questions that someone in a similar role may ask. Don’t treat those questions as predictions, though. Use them simply to broaden your preparation and identify areas you may otherwise overlook.
This information is also useful when preparing questions to ask towards the end of the interview. Relevant questions about their team, role, or experience with the company will usually come across better than generic ones.
→ Generate Behavioral, Situational, and Technical Interview Questions
A recommended way to ensure success in an interview is to prepare for the likely questions. The question set should not only include the basic ones, but also challenging ones to put you on the spot. That way, your real-world performance will be sufficient for selection. To begin with, the basics: you can ask AI models to generate common behavioral interview questions, such as “Introduce yourself” and “Why should we hire you?” “What if we don’t select you?” “What makes you fit for this role?” and the like.
The answers to the above questions will be based on your resume and cognitive ability, which is what AI models can help you with. Next, to tackle the technical questions, your prompt must instruct the AI model to fire deep-dive technical, situational, and project-based questions at you. During all this, you can rate your technical skills and promptly improve any weak areas.
Despite the discomfort, ask the AI model to generate questions from the perspective of an interviewer who is not interested in hiring you. Understand the questions, as they can prove to be great at identifying gaps in your resume, incompetencies, and more. You can also ask the AI model to question the relevance of your past experiences, push back aggressively on your answers, and more. This will only improve your chances of getting selected.
→ Practice Mock Interviews With AI Voice Mode
In case you are unaware, most mainstream AI models offer voice modes that are perfect for back-and-forth questioning, making them ideal for interview practice. It’s not surprising that merely reading the questions and thinking you can answer them won’t cut it, which is why you need a simulation of the interview. It may cause you to memorize answers instead of coming up with your own, which may result in you sounding like a teleprompter, or worse, freezing on the spot if you forget the exact answer, leaving a bad impression.
Voice mode is best used on the mobile versions of AI agents. First, you must tell the AI its persona by verbally describing it, uploading the job description, interview details, or any other supporting documents. We also recommend uploading your resume to ensure a curated interaction. Next, you must instruct it to ask all types of questions, including behavioral, technical, and situation-based.
Remember, the purpose of this mock interview is to prepare you for the worst, so take away critical lessons and improve yourself. For this, you can ask the AI model to rate your answers and provide you with detailed assessments to help you identify your weak points. Not only will it cure the interview phobia that you may have, but it will also improve your speaking skills, conversational awareness, and your ability to answer curveballs.

Useful AI Prompts for Job Interview Preparation
Mainstream AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude can be surprisingly effective for interview preparation if you give them enough context. A common approach among job seekers is to provide the actual job description and resume, then have the AI conduct the interview one question at a time instead of generating a generic list of questions. Here are a few prompts worth trying.
1. Analyze the Job Description and My Resume
I am preparing for an interview for the job below. Act as an experienced hiring manager and analyze both the job description and my resume.
Identify:
The five most important skills or requirements for this role
The parts of my resume that match them best
Important requirements where my experience looks weak or unclear
Questions an interviewer is likely to ask about those gaps
Technical or industry topics I should revise
Five achievements from my resume that I should make sure to highlight
Don’t invent experience or skills that aren’t present in my resume.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
2. Conduct a Realistic Mock Interview
Act as the hiring manager interviewing me for the role below. Use my resume and the job description as your primary context.
Conduct this like a real interview. Ask only one question at a time and wait for my complete answer before asking the next one. Ask natural follow-up questions based on what I actually say instead of following a fixed list.
Include a mix of behavioral, situational, resume-based, role-specific, and technical questions where relevant.
Do not give me hints or feedback while the interview is taking place. Once the interview is finished, score my performance on answer quality, relevance, clarity, confidence, and completeness. Then identify my five biggest weaknesses and tell me how to improve each one.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
3. Give Me a Difficult Mock Interview
Act as a skeptical interviewer who isn’t yet convinced that I am the right person for this role.
Use my resume and the job description to identify weak points, career gaps, vague achievements, missing skills, questionable claims, or areas where another candidate may be stronger.
Ask me one difficult question at a time. If my answer is vague, generic, evasive, or unsupported, push back and ask a follow-up question. Don’t compliment every answer or make the interview artificially easy.
At the end, tell me which answers could hurt my chances in the real interview and show me how I could make them stronger without exaggerating my experience.
4. Build My STAR Interview Stories
Help me prepare 5 reusable stories from my career for behavioral interview questions.
Use my resume and the experiences I provide to identify strong examples involving leadership, conflict, failure, problem-solving, teamwork, initiative, and working under pressure.
For each story, organize the answer using STAR:
Situation: What was happening?
Task: What was I responsible for?
Action: What specifically did I do?
Result: What changed because of my actions?
Keep Situation and Task brief and spend more time on Action and Result. Ask me for missing details rather than inventing them. Where possible, help me quantify the result.
Finally, tell me which common behavioral interview questions each story could answer.
Excel in Interviews With These AI Tools
AI has made preparing for job interviews a lot less daunting than it used to be. For most people, mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are already good enough for understanding a job description, researching a company, preparing likely questions, and improving answers.
Dedicated AI interview tools become useful when you want something closer to the real thing. Exponent Practice and Interviewing.io make more sense for technical candidates, Yoodli is particularly good for communication and behavioral practice, while MyInterviewAI works well for resume-based preparation. Big Interview helps with overall delivery, Huru AI makes quick job-specific practice easy, and Ophy AI covers the widest range of interview-preparation needs.
Whichever tool you choose, don’t stop after one mock interview. Upload your latest resume and the actual job description, complete a practice session, review where you struggled, and repeat it after fixing those areas. Two or three focused mock interviews will be far more useful than memorizing dozens of AI-generated answers.
Critique My Interview Answer
I will give you an interview question followed by my answer.
Evaluate the answer as a demanding hiring manager. First, tell me:
Whether I actually answered the question
What was convincing
What sounded vague or generic
Whether I gave enough evidence
Whether I spent too much time on irrelevant context
What follow-up question an interviewer would probably ask
If it is a behavioral question, also evaluate it using the STAR method.
Only after giving me this critique, provide a stronger version that retains my real experience and sounds natural when spoken aloud. Don’t turn it into a polished corporate script that nobody would actually say in an interview.
FAQs about AI Interview Tools
Can ChatGPT help me prepare for a job interview?
Yes. You can give ChatGPT your resume and job description and ask it to identify likely interview questions, evaluate your answers, conduct mock interviews, research the role, and point out gaps in your preparation. Voice mode makes the mock interview experience significantly more natural.
Are AI mock interviews actually useful?
They can be, especially when the AI asks follow-up questions and gives detailed feedback instead of simply generating a list of questions. They are particularly useful for repeated practice, although they shouldn't completely replace practice with another person when that is available.
Which AI interview tools are free?
Exponent Practice offers a limited number of free peer mock interviews, while Yoodli has a free tier. Huru AI provides free access to try its mock interviews, and Ophy AI offers free starting credits. The exact limits can change, so check each service before signing up.
What is the best AI interview tool for software engineers?
Interviewing.io and Exponent Practice are the strongest options on this list for software engineers. They focus much more heavily on coding, system design, algorithms, and other technical interview formats than general-purpose interview coaching tools.
Can I use AI during an actual job interview?
That depends entirely on the employer and interview rules. Some companies prohibit outside assistance during interviews and assessments. Unless the interviewer explicitly allows it, the safer approach is to use AI extensively during preparation and answer the actual interview questions yourself.
How many AI mock interviews should I practice?
There is no fixed number. Instead of repeating mock interviews endlessly, complete one, review the feedback, fix the weak areas, and try again. A few focused sessions with clear improvement between them are more useful than doing many interviews without reviewing your mistakes.

The Latest Empty Threat Against Iran
The Trump administration gave its own explanation for why sanctions against Tehran won’t work.
No sooner had Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the latest tool for achieving what he said would be the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran than he revealed the reason he was reluctant to use it.
Secondary sanctions—penalties on countries, individuals, or entities that do business with Iran—are ready to go, Bessent announced to reporters in the Treasury’s ornate Cash Room yesterday. But he went out of his way not to name the chief offenders that help Tehran: China and Russia. So, Bessent was asked, why threaten rather than just do it, particularly after President Trump last week warned of economic warfare “on an unprecedented scale” if Iran doesn’t surrender to U.S. demands?
“Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent responded, explaining that the administration is offering a bureaucratic grace period before the hammer falls. Secondary sanctions, he insisted, “are a very powerful tool.” Which is true. But the administration has repeatedly offered vivid explanations of what its powerful weapons can do, be they military or financial, and then declined to use them. Remember when Trump threatened to erase Iran as a civilization? The warnings may be intended to intimidate, but the lack of follow-through instead exposes just how narrow the administration’s options in Iran have become.
The possibilities for ending the war have been steadily closed off. The list of useful military targets is diminishing, and munitions stockpiles are perilously depleted, while the tools that were supposed to do what missiles could not—sanctions, blockades, financial pressure—have failed to produce the Iranian capitulation Washington promised. Iran has absorbed enormous damage, both military and economic, without surrendering its capacity to fight. And the countries that matter most to the financial-pressure campaign, including China and Russia, have shown little inclination to help Washington finish the job.
Soon after Trump took office last year, he announced that he was “restoring maximum pressure” on Iran, directing his administration to tighten sanctions and drive down Iranian oil exports. Eighteen months later, Bessent is promising what he describes as the “toughest sanctions in history.” Maximum pressure, it appears, has a sequel, much as Trump’s contention last June that Iran’s nuclear facilities had been obliterated was followed in February by a war to destroy Iran’s nuclear capabilities.
Trump, in a Truth Social post last week, hinted at what that sequel to maximum pressure would look like. “ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” he wrote, before listing oil smuggling, financial swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, and front companies that “all” need to stop “NOW.” It was the kind of warning designed to make the entire global financial system sit up straight. Then Bessent arrived at the Cash Room making equally stark threats, before pointing to a major reason why he shouldn’t follow through, assuming countries don’t voluntarily comply.
That leaves the administration in an uncomfortable position. The war has lasted far longer than Trump suggested it would, and its economic consequences are now a central issue in the midterm elections. Sanctions have inflicted economic pain on Iran for years without producing the result Washington wants. Yet China continues to buy Iranian oil, while Russia and other oil-producing countries stand to benefit from the drain of prolonged U.S. military action in Iran and from disruptions to energy exported from the Persian Gulf. “No one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions,” Bessent said when asked about China specifically.
But Beijing and Moscow might not comply with Bessent’s demands. The Russian embassy in Washington didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington told me in a written statement that “sanctions and pressure tactics do no help in resolving issues” and called on all parties to “act rationally” and to avoid doing anything “that may further escalate tensions or deal a blow to global economic growth and financial stability.” The spokesperson added that China will watch the developments and “do what is necessary to protect our legitimate rights and interests.”
The administration’s threats have yielded some results. The United Arab Emirates last week said it was stopping all trade and financial transactions with Tehran. Asked about the announcement by the UAE, Bessent suggested that the timing was no coincidence. He added that Trump was speaking with world leaders to deliver his ultimatum personally.
But although the U.S. can certainly make Iran’s relationships more expensive, it can’t wish them away. I tried to gauge how worried officials from around the world were about these threats of economic annihilation for the noncompliant. One Arab official told me they hoped “those countries”—this person, too, declined to name China or Russia—would “take this seriously.” A European official was less impressed. “We’ll see,” this person said, before quickly changing the subject to Trump’s trade wars with allies, which appears to command considerably more European attention.
Bessent may have been full of bravado. But his caution is also well-founded. Following through with the full slate of secondary sanctions against all offenders would indeed be devastating to the global economy. “These tools are so potent,” Jason Prince, a sanctions attorney at the Washington-based law firm Akin Gump who previously served as a lawyer at the Treasury Department, told me. Announcing secondary sanctions, even as a threat, is an economic gamble, Prince said, with “a chilling effect that has repercussions that reverberate well beyond Iran.”
Bessent also announced immediate sanctions on nearly 60 Iran-linked entities, people, and vessels, accusing them of having links to Iran’s nuclear and missile programs, cyber activities, and oil shipments. He added that the first major secondary sanctions against “a financial institution” are likely to come “by the end of this week.”
Prince said that the latter threat will be key for the administration’s credibility. “They have to take some sort of action, or the de-risking and the retreat by the real targets isn’t going to take place,” he told me. He said similar measures were taken against Russian banks after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. But Sberbank, the titan of Russian banking, was first placed on a less severe sanctions list—a reflection, in part, of the impact that sanctioning the bank would have globally. (Tougher sanctions on the bank were eventually imposed as Russian attacks on Ukraine continued.)
The problem here, Prince added, is that secondary sanctions make the U.S. more vulnerable when its own economy is already under pressure, with the technology, manufacturing, and financial sectors likely to bear the brunt. Oil and gasoline prices have already risen, inflation remains a problem, and voters are unhappy with a conflict they were told would make their country safer. The American public’s approval of the war with Iran has fallen to its lowest level since the first days of the conflict, with just 31 percent supporting U.S. military action against Iran, while Trump’s popularity also sits at a record low, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. With the midterms approaching, Republicans have little reason to welcome another round of economic pain, let alone the possible U.S.-induced global financial crisis that Bessent talked about.
Regional experts I spoke with see sanctions threats like this less as an escalation strategy than as the latest step in the administration’s continuing search for an exit from the war. The administration keeps reaching for a bigger threat because the last one failed to deliver a decisive victory, or even a face-saving off-ramp. Deadlines move. Threats get grace periods. “Maximum pressure” is followed by more maximum pressure. The question is no longer simply how Washington plans to force Iran to negotiate. It is how the U.S. gets out of a war in which its options seem only to shrink.
Leverage depends not just on possessing the power to punish, but on the willingness to use that power. If Washington repeatedly announces a deadline and then moves it, threatens a consequence and then delays, or unveils a weapon and immediately explains why it cannot be fully deployed, its adversaries don’t see geopolitical might—instead, they learn something about the limits of American power.
Bessent threatened a sanctions regime so severe that countries around the world would have to choose between doing business with Iran and having access to the U.S. dollar system. Bessent and Trump described the announcement as an “economic D-Day,” but that is not an apt comparison. The real D-Day, on June 6, 1944, was an actual invasion. It came without a public ultimatum or a warning to the enemy about what was coming. This operation, officially dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast,” has both put countries on notice while also delivering a message that the U.S. will go only so far.
“We believe that it is important to level-set, and give people a cure period,” Bessent told reporters. “But they should know that that will move very quickly and that we are serious,” he added. “If people do not want to meet our expectations, then we expect, and they should expect, that they will leave the dollar system.”
Even here, the administration appears to be discovering that maximum pressure is easier to announce than to impose. After all, Iran has been under U.S. sanctions for decades. Those have undoubtedly done damage to the Iranian economy but have done nothing to push Iran closer to the negotiating table in search of a lasting peace with Washington. When Iran entered into the Obama-era Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action nuclear deal, the relief it received in return came from the lifting of U.S. secondary sanctions. Prince told me that secondary sanctions could reinstate that leverage. “There’s at least that historical precedent,” he said, “that the more secondary sanctions pressure that can be applied, the more leverage the U.S. government believes it has with respect to the Iranians.”
But Steve H. Hanke, a professor of applied economics at Johns Hopkins University, told me the economic reality, to date, is that sanctions against Iran have had “a near-perfect record of failure.”
“Just look at the plethora of sanctions that have been placed on Iran since the Islamic Revolution of 1979—they have all failed to achieve their stated objectives,” Hanke, who served on President Ronald Reagan’s Council of Economic Advisers, said. “The D-Day sanctions will meet the same fate.”
The military campaign has failed to produce the quick resolution Trump once promised. Now the economic campaign is in danger of following suit, while also adding to the domestic costs of war.

NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Wednesday reiterated its plan to hold a march in Delhi on September 5, saying three of the four demands that led it to call off its protest on July 25 were still pending.In a post on X, the party said it had withdrawn the protest a month ago after receiving assurances that all four demands would be met.It said the pending demands were compensation for the families of students, withdrawal of FIRs and no action against student protesters, and an apology from the Rapid Action Force (RAF) and Delhi Police.“Everything will be remembered” the party said in its post, while referring to its archive titled “Black Monday Record”, which it said documents the crackdown on protesters, including the use of lathis, tear gas and pellet guns and alleged assaults by unbadged personnel.
CJP also said the archive records 11 unanswered questions that it has raised as part of its demand for accountability.“With each passing day, these questions become harder to ignore and the demand for answers grows stronger,” the party said.
CJP plans India Gate to Police HQ march on September 5
CJP had announced its September 5 mobilisation earlier, saying the march would begin at India Gate and proceed towards the New Delhi Police Headquarters.The organisation said the march would be led by families of deceased NEET victims and victims of alleged police brutality, with students, youth organisations and young citizens expected to join.
CJP had said the decision to resume mobilisation followed a review of the commitments it alleged were made by the government on July 25, after which it withdrew its nationwide student protest.The organisation had also alleged that the government was delaying action on its assurances, particularly on the withdrawal of FIRs against students and protesters.It referred to Supreme Court proceedings in which, according to CJP, the court on August 18 sought a list of FIRs registered across the country so that it could consider dealing with them together.The group had said it withdrew its protest in good faith after talks with Union ministers J P Nadda and Jitendra Singh on July 25. It had then said the government had accepted its demands, including compensation for families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide and withdrawal of FIRs against protesters.
The Supreme Court later directed states to release eligible students detained during the protests and barred coercive action against students for the time being.
Ranka warns of ‘Cockroaches’ ahead of September 5
Responding to Wednesday's CJP post, one of the party’s spokespersons, Ashutosh Ranka, wrote on X, “We will not hold back. You might have the govt, the country is ours. Keep your words. Accept our demands. Or this Sept 5, be ready for Cockroaches!”
CJP had described the September 5 mobilisation as a peaceful protest march and urged students, youth organisations and young citizens to gather at India Gate.The organisation had earlier led a 37-day protest at Jantar Mantar over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak, alongside activist Sonam Wangchuk's 26-day hunger strike.On July 25, CJP said it had called off the protest following talks with the government and asked protesters to return home peacefully.

Donald Trump is presiding over an unexpected clean energy boom, as rising electricity demand spurs investment in new capacity despite the US administration’s efforts to thwart a solar and wind rollout.
Clean energy additions will rise by a record 45 gigawatts this year, according to S&P Global Energy—equivalent to the average electricity demand of Turkey. The increase is roughly 25 percent higher than the record set in 2024.
The US president’s war in Iran, which has driven up global energy prices, along with surging power demand from AI data centers and developers’ rush to capitalize on expiring tax credits, are driving the cleantech boom, said analysts. Trump’s administration has also been pragmatic in the face of its energy needs.
“There was a campaign promise to go against renewables, but at the same time they’re realizing that you can’t do without it,” said Izzet Bensusan, chief executive of Captona, an energy infrastructure investment group. “I don’t see a world where power demand is flattening out.”
S&P said new solar and wind capacity will jump in 2026 by nearly a third and almost 50 percent respectively. Solar will set another record in 2027, while wind falls back before recovering.
White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers, however, touted “record-high oil and gas production” under Trump.
“The president has delivered on his promise to unleash American energy,” Rogers said. “At the same time, the administration has ended subsidies for costly and unreliable energy sources that American taxpayers were unfairly forced to fund.”
The solar and wind additions come despite Trump’s early efforts to kill an energy transition pushed by his predecessor, Joe Biden.
The Trump administration broke up Esmeralda 7 in Nevada. It would have been the largest single solar project in the US.
The president’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act also slashed tax credits for solar and wind, and his administration has interfered with routine project approvals, including for more than 150 onshore wind projects. But under the terms of the OBBBA, solar and wind developers had until July 4 to begin work on projects and until 2030 to finish them.
The deadline “prompted developers to hurry and begin construction,” said S&P Global renewables analyst John Murray.

SAN FRANCISCO – A research duo, once pitched to lead the Jeff Bezos-backed Project Prometheus, on Tuesday unveiled what they’ve built on their own: an artificial intelligence model that can take in and produce information so vast that a lone computer might not handle it.
Their company, Accelerated Understanding, says it has developed a different type of AI model that in tests handled 5 trillion pieces of data in a single prompt. That is some 5 million times the size of what Anthropic and Google’s flagship models can typically consume — like reading Tolstoy’s “War and Peace” not once but 5 million times in one sitting.
The difference is that this new system is not built for understanding language. It is built for physics, said co-founders Anima Anandkumar and Benedikt Jenik, in an exclusive interview ahead of Tuesday’s corporate launch.

Tamil Nadu will launch the ‘Chief Minister’s Elderly Health Insurance Scheme’, covering nearly 38 lakh senior citizens aged 70 and above. The scheme will provide free medical treatment, including cancer care packages, advanced cardiac surgeries, organ transplants, and high-end diagnostic services, at empanelled government and private hospitals, with no ceiling on income, Health Minister K.G. Arunraj announced in the Assembly on Monday (August 17, 2026).
The Minister made 115 announcements for the Health Department at a total estimated outlay of ₹2,997 crore. It covered areas including policy reforms, universal free health services, new posts creation, infrastructure projects, equipment and procurement, direct beneficiary programmes and digital health initiatives.
The 87-year-old Tamil Nadu Public Health Act, 1939, will be replaced with a modern, comprehensive Act to address contemporary and future health challenges. Dr. Arunraj said a new provision would make unsupervised home births outside hospitals a punishable offence. Noting that Tamil Nadu was known as the country’s health capital, he said that ‘TN Medicity’, a world class integrated medical hub comprising clinical services, research, medical tourism, and AYUSH, would be established. The government will allocate ₹10 crore for the preparation of a Detailed Project Report in the first phase.
‘Nalam 360-Annual Free Health Check-up for All’ scheme will be rolled out. Under this, everyone aged 30 and above will receive 14 basic tests annually, free of cost, across 1,257 government health facilities in the State.
This will include blood pressure, ECG, haemoglobin, complete haemogram, random blood sugar, urea, creatinine, total cholesterol, serum bilirubin, urine albumin, and VIA screening. For the first time in the State, the Health Department will introduce Home Based Diagnostic Services — sample collection and testing services — in metropolitan areas on a public-private partnership model, he said.
Policy reforms
The department will come up with a ‘Positive Health Policy’ to promote holistic health and wellbeing at the community, family, and individual levels, accompanied by the “Nalam 360” mobile application. A new legislation ‘TN Institutions of State Importance in Health Care Act’ will come up to create institutions of State importance to provide world-class medical services.
Addressing a long-standing demand, Dr. Arunraj said 2,500 permanent posts of staff nurses would be created. Existing contract nurses on consolidated pay will be absorbed into regular time-scale pay. A total of 1,695 nursing posts on consolidated pay will be created at a cost of ₹42.72 crore.
A total of 3,594 medical staff across 24 categories, including pharmacists, nursing assistants, village health nurses, and ophthalmic assistants, will be recruited through the Medical Services Recruitment Board. Additionally, the department will create 284 temporary super speciality posts across 25 specialities such as neurology, cardiology and nephrology on time-scale pay to take advanced medical care to the district-level.
These posts will be created to accommodate doctors who complete their post-graduation every year and are posted in government hospitals on bond conditions. A number of announcements for infrastructural development such as new hospital buildings and medical equipment were also made.

Xbox has a bunch of translucent green accessories for the console's 25th birthday
This includes a keyboard, earbuds, mobile controllers and more.
It's been nearly 25 years since the very first Xbox console hit store shelves. To commemorate the occasion, Microsoft just revealed a whole bunch of hardware peripherals from several different manufacturers.
Most of these gadgets have one thing in common: They're translucent green, which has become something of a short-hand when referencing the original Xbox console. This is a little bit odd, given that the console launched in black with just a green circle in the middle. The translucent stuff came later.
In any event, there are new designs of both the Razer Basilisk V3 Pro 35K mouse and the Razer BlackWidow V4 75% keyboard. These are just reskins, so the hardware remains the same. This isn't a bad thing, given that the Basilisk V3 made our list for the best gaming mouse and the BlackWidow V4 75% is a highly-regarded mechanical keyboard.
Razer is also greenifying the Hammerhead V3 X Hyperspeed earbuds. These are great little earbuds for switching between different audio sources on the fly, thanks to the company's proprietary HyperSpeed 2.4GHz streaming platform.
8BitDo is on board with a green charging dock. It's compatible with Xbox Series X/S and Xbox One controllers. GameSir has redesigned the X5 Lite mobile controller, also in translucent green. This works with both iOS and Android devices.
Finally, there are a couple of doodads here that, for whatever reason, aren't green. The Backbone Pro Xbox 25th Anniversary Edition is another mobile game controller that's available in a trio of colorways. Weirdly, there's no way to pick which color. It's some kind of mystery box situation.
Despite the name, the PowerA Xbox Sling Bag is not a carrying case for Xbox consoles and controllers. Rather, it's for Xbox-branded Ally and Ally X handheld devices. It is jet back with minor green accents, making this the only accessory that actually looks kind of like a 2001 Xbox.
All of the above items are available to preorder right now. This can be done via the Xbox store or from the actual manufacturers.
Of course, this isn't the only move Microsoft is making to celebrate the birthday of its very first gaming console. There's a, you guessed it, translucent green Xbox Series X console launching in November.

- Path of Exile 2 launches fully on December 11, 2026.

Grinding Gear Games has finally locked in a date for Path of Exile 2, as it will leave Early Access and launch as a full 1.0 release on December 11, 2026. It will be a free-to-play game, and the announcement arrived during Gamescom ONL on August 25, alongside a new trailer.
The December 11 launch will arrive almost exactly two years after Path of Exile 2 early access came out on December 6, 2024. The game has already been available on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S, giving players plenty of time to experience the campaign systems before the final version.
The Path of Exile 2 full release is built around a six-act campaign spanning 100 environments with 600 monsters and more than 100 bosses. You can choose from 12 character classes, each with unique specializations that can create their own paths in the adventure.
Creating your builds in the game is equally enormous. With 240 Skill Gems, 200 Support Gems, and a massive Passive Skill Tree consisting of 1500 skills, you will surely have a blast unlocking each node and customizing the character suited to your playstyle.

Putin issues decree opening door to state control of key sites after drone strikes
Russian President Vladimir Putin has decreed that the state can temporarily seize control of critical infrastructure facilities if private owners fail to protect them from Ukrainian drone attacks or rebuild them after the strikes
Russian President Vladimir Putin has decreed that the state can temporarily seize control of critical infrastructure facilities if private owners fail to protect them from Ukrainian drone attacks or rebuild them after the strikes.
The move came Monday amid growing economic pressure and public frustration being felt in Russia after months of escalating Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries and e-commerce hubs that have caused nationwide disruptions.
Ukraine also is reeling from relentless aerial attacks that have smashed its power grid ahead of winter and heavily damaged homes as Russia’s invasion stretches into its fifth year.
The Kremlin's exact intentions with the decree are unclear. However, it applies to various sectors, including energy infrastructure, as well as industrial, communications, transportation and logistics facilities.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that “often business owners do not pay enough attention to taking measures to ensure safety, anti-drone safety.”
Given the threat to vital economic infrastructure, “we must take measures, we must ensure our own safety,” he said.
Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said in a statement the decree doesn’t imply the nationalization of companies or a change of ownership — only “involvement of the state in the management of an enterprise to solve specific security problems.”
He added that the decree “doesn’t imply widespread use," and that "targeted, carefully considered decisions will be made at the highest level.”
Russian political analyst Abbas Gallyamov said the measure might be a “tactical” step designed to force the owners of repeatedly damaged oil refineries into making repairs.
“Given the fact that the same refinery has already been hit three to five times, it’s safe to assume that the owners are now reluctant to invest in restoring what’s been destroyed,” he said on the Telegram messaging app.
“Why spend billions if they’re going to get hit again tomorrow?” said Gallyamov, a former speechwriter for Putin.
He said the government is giving companies an ultimatum: “If you don’t finance the restoration of the refineries, we’ll take them away from you.”
In the latest attacks, Ukraine’s General Staff said Tuesday its forces struck facilities at Russia’s Afipsky oil refinery in the Krasnodar region overnight, causing a fire. Krasnodar Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev said a fire broke out at an oil refinery in the town of Afipsky.
A Ukrainian attack also damaged the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in southern Russia’s Rostov region overnight and halted operations, Rostov Gov. Yuri Slyusar said, without elaborating.
Russian businesses face fundamental economic challenges as the costly war drags on. The government has raised taxes and increased domestic borrowing to keep its budget deficit under control, and taking over major companies could potentially bring in revenue.
At the same time, seizing damaged assets could bring another financial burden. The Kremlin may intend the measure as a way to pressure companies to shoulder more responsibility for air defense, as Russia’s vast territory is hard to protect.
Russia also is offering more help for its biggest online retailer, Wildberries, and businesses selling goods through it. The company and thousands of sellers working with it have been hit hard by repeated Ukrainian strikes on warehouses. The Finance Ministry proposed Monday extending deadlines for tax and insurance payments to give Wildberries and its sellers some financial breathing space.
On Saturday, Putin told state television that Russia “must and will improve the air defense system and enhance its capabilities.”
“We need to streamline coordination between defense, law enforcement and civilian agencies at all levels, and to leverage the capabilities of state‑run enterprises and private businesses,” he said.
In May, following deep strikes that unsettled Moscow, Russian lawmakers approved a bill that allowed the Central Bank, state-controlled Sberbank and other financial services to fend off drone attacks by installing air defenses on their premises.
News outlet RBC, citing anonymous sources in and close to the Defense Ministry, reported that month that a mechanism had been established for businesses to procure weapons and equipment to protect themselves from drone attacks, something Russian officials and lawmakers have said companies should do.

Daniel Lubetzky knows firsthand that great business ideas can sound far-fetched at first.
But the "Shark Tank" investor and Kind Snacks founder says entrepreneurs should not dismiss their most outlandish ideas too soon because they're the ones that can turn into some of the most successful businesses.
"Out of those crazy things — that's when the Kind bar comes out, the Ring machine that Jamie Siminoff invented — it has to come from the thinking outside of pushing yourself," he said, citing his company's Kind snack bar and the smart-doorbell company acquired by Amazon in 2018 for about $1 billion.
The business world is littered with such examples. Airbnb cofounder and CEO Brian Chesky has said people thought it was "crazy" to imagine strangers staying in one another's homes. And Spotify founder Daniel Ek has described the company's original aim — making every song instantly and legally available — as an "impossible idea."
Ahead of the launch of his "Build or Break" podcast on September 3, Lubetzky shared with Business Insider his three-part framework for turning any business idea — no matter how bizarre — from a brainstorm into reality.
1. Be a curious creative
"When you're brainstorming, you have to only brainstorm," Lubetzky said. "You have to not allow any filters to apply because it's almost like you need to be looking for the stupidest idea."
He said founders should push beyond the obvious options and put every idea on the board, however unrealistic it may initially appear. The goal is to escape conventional thinking, because that is where original concepts can emerge.
"The crazier you go, the more you put on your board," he said. "You cannot filter anything out because you have to push yourself outside of that box for you to come up with something that nobody else has ever come up with."
2. Be a consummate critic
Then comes the critical stage.
After stepping away from the brainstorm, founders should interrogate the ideas that remain with discipline, Lubetzky said.
They should consider whether they have the necessary skills, whether customers want the product, whether the economics work, and whether competitors could do it better.
"You take a break and then you start applying all of the filters," he said. "Do I have what it takes to do this? Are these the skills that are necessary, and do I have all those skills? Is the input-to-output correlation worth it? Does the consumer really want it? Is there no other competition that can do it better?"
This stage requires founders to be tough on their own ideas.
"You have to apply 20 filters and ask really tough questions to clean up your brainstorm list and zone in on the thing that's most creative but actually you can pull it off," Lubetzky said.
3. Be a committed crusader
Finally, once an entrepreneur has subjected an idea to that "intellectual trial by fire," they need to stop second-guessing themselves and execute, Lubetzky said.
"If you still believe that your idea is worth pursuing, once you're ready, you need to switch from being a critic to being a believer," he said. "And you have to just go and execute it no matter what."
Lubetzky said the framework applies beyond startups. People can build companies, inventions, schools, or bridges between groups, he said, but they also have a choice in how they use their ideas and energy.
"All of us can be builders or destroyers," Lubetzky said. "It's up to us to decide whether we wake up in the morning and try to tear each other apart," or use those tools "to solve problems together."

The federal government is expanding a safety investigation into a number of vehicles manufactured by General Motors after receiving hundreds of reports of brake failure. The problem affects more than 1.1 million cars, including many of GM’s electric vehicles, as well as ones it has built for Honda and Acura. The problem is with the brake-by-wire system (which GM calls eBoost), which can suffer a spindle fracture while driving.
GM says that in the event of that happening, the car should still retain a number of critical safety features—antilock brakes, traction control, and stability control—at least until it comes to a complete stop, at which point they become inoperable. But NHTSA’s ODI says that it has received many reports that contradict this behavior and allege that eBoost failures are followed by an immediate loss of braking, which obviously poses a safety risk.
Indeed, NHTSA has received 227 incident reports, a number that grows to 745 once you include the hundreds of occurrences reported to GM. Twenty-two cases resulted in crashes, and while six people have been injured in five crashes, thankfully there have been no fatal incidents.
NHTSA says that the following vehicles are equipped with eBoost: “2023-2026 MY Cadillac Lyriq, Chevrolet Colorado, and GMC Canyon; 2024-2026 MY Buick Enclave, Envision; Chevrolet Blazer EV, Equinox EV, Traverse; Cruise Origin; and GMC Acadia; 2025-2026 MY Cadillac Celestiq and Optiq. ODI is also aware of 2024-2026 MY Acura ZDX and 2024-2026 MY Honda Prologue vehicles that were built with this system.”

FBI agents raided the Ibiza, Spain, vacation rental of 41-year-old James “Fergie” Chambers, a US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects worldwide, in the days following his arrest last month, the Guardian has learned.
Baltasar Garzón, a human rights lawyer representing Chambers, revealed the details in an exclusive interview. Chambers is wanted for extradition by the Trump administration for alleged financial support of Hamas, as well as other charges.
Garzón, one of Europe’s most famous human rights lawyers, characterized the case as “very strange, one of the most remarkable I’ve worked on”. He told the Guardian the indictment against Chambers was “pretty weak and diffuse”.
The case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m that he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where Chambers lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to support the Palestinian group. The exact details of the indictment against Chambers remain sealed.
Chambers, heir to one of the richest families in the US, has supported a handful of humanitarian projects in Gaza with funds totaling more than $1m, a member of his legal team said shortly after his 10 July arrest.
It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas.
Garzón spoke with the Guardian on Thursday shortly after his second visit with Chambers, now in his second month in a Spanish jail. The former judge and veteran human rights lawyer said the FBI didn’t find anything in the raid.
He also indicated that the road ahead for Chambers may be longer than what a Spanish official told the Guardian shortly after his arrest, potentially lasting months.
First, US authorities have until Wednesday – 45 days after his arrest – to submit documentation supporting the extradition petition and the underlying indictment, which remains sealed, Garzón said.
If the US doesn’t meet this deadline, the petition expires and Chambers is released. If the deadline is met, the Spanish government evaluates the paperwork over several weeks. After that, the case winds its way through various legal and government bodies. One thing being considered from the start of the process and forward is if the petition is politically motivated, which would allow the Spanish government to deny extradition.
“It’s noteworthy that humanitarian aid and defending human rights is being criminalized,” Garzón said. “It’s a case of persecution … and they’re not going to be able to find one cent directed at terrorist or violent acts.”
The Spanish lawyer’s five-decade career includes seeking the extradition from London of the former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet, as well as pursuing accountability for human rights abuses in Spain, Argentina and elsewhere.
Chambers, a self-described communist and anti-imperialist, is heir of the Cox family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications. As part of a settlement in which his family severed ties with him at the time, he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in mid-2023. Since then he has been funding an estimated 100 projects in 20 countries, his partner, Stella Schnabel, an actor and activist, said last month.
Schnabel said the funds at the center of the US charges actually went to buy the popular football club Club Africain, and to pay off debt and past-due salaries as well as rebuilding a training center and building youth football fields.
The club went on to win the Tunisian football league in May.
Chambers has been extensively profiled in US media and was interviewed on local TV news station in New Hampshire in late 2023 about a direct action against Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, staged by a group whose legal fees he paid, then called Palestine Action – a group proscribed in the UK as a “terrorist organization”.
Garzón also revealed that the US indictment was filed in New Hampshire.
Chambers’ public comments on Israel and Gaza are part of the context in which the case is unfolding, Garzón said. For example, a week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, Chambers posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/ There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/ No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/ It’s simply genocide/ Like it has been.”
He has also been a staunch critic of the US and told a reporter in 2024: “I think the most important thing for the prosperity of humanity is the destruction of the US.”
“[Chambers] is a person who is not aligned with the views of the US government,” Garzón said. “There’s a political context to all this.”
Garzón’s visit with Chambers on Thursday lasted two hours. Spain has rejected requests to release him on bail to date but the issue could be revisited if the US submits its paperwork on time and the case continues, the attorney said.
“His freedom is being denied,” Garzón said. “It’s incomprehensible to him … as a defender of human rights.”
He also said funds have been at least temporarily halted to the Sameer Project in Gaza, which helped support a bakery producing thousands of loaves of free bread daily during Israel’s ongoing siege on the territory.

Gary Sinise, the acclaimed actor most known for his roles in "Apollo 13," "Forrest Gump" and "CSI: NY," was the subject of a claim circulating in August 2026 that he takes more than 1,000 children of fallen United States service members to Walt Disney World every year, free of charge.
The claim gained traction on Reddit with over 18,000 upvotes, with one user commenting, "This guy and his foundation does more than all the other celebrities combined for our troops and their families."
A photo included with the Reddit post depicted Sinise on an airplane surrounded by families smiling and wearing Disney gear.
Every year, actor Gary Sinise takes more than 1,700 family members of fallen soldiers to Walt Disney World for free
by u/Wonderfulhumanss in BeAmazed
The claim that Sinise took more than 1,000 children of fallen service members to Disney theme parks is mostly true.
The program is called the "Snowball Express" and operates through the actor's nonprofit organization, the Gary Sinise Foundation. According to the foundation's website, its mission is to honor "defenders, veterans, first responders, their families, and those in need" by "creating and supporting unique programs designed to entertain, educate, inspire, strengthen, and build communities."
While most versions of the claim name the specific theme park as Disneyland, located in Anaheim, California, the Snowball Express actually takes its participants to Walt Disney World Resort in Orlando, Florida, each year.
Further, while costs are minimal, participating families are responsible for some expenses, such as transportation to the airport as well as parking and luggage fees. For these reasons, we've rated this claim as mostly true.
According to the Gary Sinise Foundation's webpage dedicated to the Snowball Express program, the event, held annually in December, is a "a five-day experience for 1,750+ children of the fallen and the surviving spouse/guardian. With special time to honor their fallen and a blend of fun entertainment and inspiring programs, these families can lean on their peers for support."
In addition, the foundation's official Facebook page posted a variety of photos from the Snowball Express events throughout the years of its operation.
(The Gary Sinise Foundation Facebook page)
According to the Disney Parks Blog, "the official blog for the Disneyland Resort, Walt Disney World Resort and Disney Cruise Line," the Snowball Express has origins dating back to 2003.
The Disney Parks Blog stated:
The Snowball Express has a special connection to Disney Parks. This annual healing retreat began in 2003 when U.S. Army Private First-Class Jesse Givens wrote a letter to his wife before his deployment to Iraq, which included a wish for his family to visit Disney Parks if he didn't return.
This wish was fulfilled in 2006 when his family and others of fallen soldiers visited Disneyland Resort. Gary Sinise became involved in 2007, when he and his band, the Lt. Dan Band, performed for these families.
"In 2017, the Gary Sinise Foundation took over the program, and the first retreat at Walt Disney World took place in 2018, starting an annual tradition for the families of fallen U.S. military heroes," the blog continued.
Since the Gary Sinise Foundation took over the program, "more than 17,000 children of fallen military heroes, fallen first responders and their surviving parent/guardian have participated in the healing retreat," wrote the Disney Parks Blog.
In December 2024, "the Foundation brought more than 1,700 family members from more than 90 cities around the nation and overseas, as far as Europe and Guam," they added. "During this five-day healing retreat, the families connected with each other and enjoyed the magic of Disney while honoring the legacy of their loved one's service and sacrifice."
One such memorial included a sunrise procession at Disney's Magic Kingdom in which "nearly 1,000 Disney VoluntEARS, including many cast members who are military veterans, lined the streets before 5 a.m. to stand in reverence of these military families for their sacrifices."
Most claims shared online also alleged the program was "free of charge" to the participating families. While the heaviest financial burdens of airfare, lodging, meals and theme park passes were covered, according to the foundation's FAQ page about the program, attending families are responsible for the costs related to travel to and from the airport as well as parking and luggage fees.
The organization thanked "the generosity of the American public, our partners, donors, and volunteers" for covering a bulk of the cost.
The same FAQ page said the program "serves the children (and surviving spouse or guardian) of fallen military heroes and first responders, who served on or after Sept. 11, 2001, with a service-related death occurring on or after Sept. 11, 2001."
We've reached out to the Gary Sinise Foundation for further comment on the Snowball Express and will update this article if we receive a response.

This past week, the top health story, without any doubt, is the huge crisis that is brewing out of proportions in Africa - the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. It was first announced as an outbreak on May 15, this year.As per latest data, it has reached over 5,000 cases, making this the one of the worst Ebola outbreaks in history. The outbreak has clearly outpaced response efforts.
Data from Congo’s Ministry of Health showed the outbreak had so far recorded 5,021 cases, including 2,378 deaths as of August 16, 2026, as it rages in some of the most challenging conditions imaginable fuelled by insecurity, displacement and intense population movements. It has officially infected and killed more people at a greater speed than any other outbreak in history. Starting from the first detected case, it has spread about three times faster than an outbreak from 2014 to 2016 across West Africa, which was the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record with more than 11,000 deaths.
The dire situation was underlined as World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus announced: “We must be frank: the epidemic is far from being under control.” Safety concerns have limited the response as health workers are targeted, particularly in Ituri, the province that has been hit the worst by the outbreak. Residents recently attacked a health team in the territory of Aru after a suspected case was reported there. A mob set fire to an ambulance and damaged two other vehicles, according to Michael Wani, president of the Union of Cultural Associations for the Development of Ituri.
Meanwhile, more than 16,000 doses of the new Ebola vaccine Ervebo arrived in the DRC. WHO experts still do not know whether Ervebo protects humans against the Bundibugyo strain, but early data, notably from animal trials, suggest it could offer some protection.The Ervebo vaccine “has already been used several times, and in particular on a very large scale during the 2018-2020 outbreak”, Samuel Roger Kamba, the DRC’s Minister of Health, told the press.
The other big story in India was also about an infectious disease - H1N1. As the cases continue to surge, experts assure that there is no cause for alarm yet. However they do advise that a large number of children were being affected, and that children with asthma and other chronic conditions might require special intervention.
The H1N1 virus, commonly known as swine flu, is a subtype of influenza A, and can cause respiratory illness, with symptoms including fever or chills, cough, sore throat, a runny or blocked nose, headache, tiredness, and muscle or body aches. In some cases, patients may also experience vomiting and diarrhoea. Cases have been rising in Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru and Kerala, and while there are a number of respiratory-like illnesses also about during this season, doctors have warned that early testing is key. Bindu Shajan Perappadan reports that union Health Minister J.P. Nadda reviewed the H1N1 situation, healthcare preparedness in Delhi.
With National Eye Donation Fortnight being observed across India every year from August 25 to September 8 to raise awareness about eye donation we did our bit to highlight issues relating to eye health a little ahead of schedule.
Athira Elssa Johnson writes about the Lazy eye in children, and about squints. In the former, she focuses on how many parents may miss lazy eye among their children. Often called lazy eye, amblyopia may have no obvious signs and can remain undetected during early childhood. Screening, timely treatment and sustained follow-up are important because visual development is time-sensitive. Squints are another condition that impact the development of vision, and therefore need to be addressed on time. Squint, medically known as strabismus, is a condition in which the two eyes do not align properly. It can affect children and adults and, when it develops during childhood, can interfere with the normal development of vision
In the modern age, the field of ophthalmology is among the earliest adopters of AI systems in health care, so here is an article on using AI systems in smartphones to help detect eye diseases. Kathleen Sherwin and Rishi Raj Borah make an impassioned case for more women to lead eye health care systems.

Shrabana Chatterjee writes an interesting story on a hardly-spoken about aspect- Navigating the challenges of fertility and breastfeeding after surviving cancer. This story has a positive message for women in this position - that with careful management and supervision, it can be done.
After a cancer diagnosis, women who have not yet started their families, must be given the option for fertility preservation, say doctors. Options such as embryo freezing before cancer treatment is begun may be considered under medical guidance. Other fertility preservations techniques including oocyte and ovarian-tissue cryopreservation may also be explored before treatment begins. When it comes to breastfeeding, doctors say that after surviving cancer it may pose difficulties, but it can be done under the right medical conditions and with guidance from doctors.

Nepal represents enormous potential for cricket and could be tomorrow’s Afghanistan or even New Zealand, ICC Chief Executive Sanjog Gupta said.
The ICC has pumped nearly $5 million into Nepal’s cricket development in the last two years and has awarded the country co-hosting rights for next year’s Under-19 Women’s World Cup.
Sanjog told Reuters that the Land of Himalayas has massive potential in the sport: “Not because the country is a significant commercial market, but because of their rapidly improving standards of performance and the scale of fandom the sport enjoys in the country.”
He opined that Nepal belonged to the global stage and could be the association nation to watch out for in the coming years.
“They could be tomorrow’s Afghanistan, or tomorrow’s New Zealand for that matter,” Sanjog said.
“They have developed an elite player pool which is consistently breaking through the ICC pathways and not only featuring at our marquee events, but proving that they belong on the global stage.”
The ICC official felt Nepal benefitted from a deep passionate fanbase. “Fans today are also the players of tomorrow”.
“One of my personal highlights from the T20 World Cup 2026 was the sea of red at the Wankhede (Stadium), which had turned up to support Nepal against Scotland,” Sanjog said.
Nepal beat Scotland by seven wickets to claim its first victory on that world stage since 2014, although both teams had already been eliminated.

Ads and tracking have turned TVs into privacy nightmares. Both are so widespread among smart TVs that I’ve written a guide for avoiding them. One recommendation in that guide is to use a computer monitor. But in recent years, monitors have become more capable of pushing ads and tracking users.
Without more straightforward approaches from vendors, such as easily comprehensible privacy policies and avoiding inappropriate ads, monitors are dangerously encroaching into smart-TV-like territory.
LG monitors’ McAfee ads
LG lost some trust after a recent report that some of its monitors installed McAfee pop-up ads onto connected computers. Since at least 2024, some of these displays installed an app, LG Monitor App Installer, onto connected computers under the cover of driver updates installed through Windows Update.
An LG spokesperson tells me that the point of LG Monitor App Installer is to “make related software available to help customers access monitor-specific features and functionality.” In practice, it has pushed software ads onto connected PCs.
Sure, the ads could potentially be relevant for LG monitor owners. The app has reportedly shown users occasional ads for LG software, like LG Switch and LG Dual Controller. But just because an app may be relevant doesn’t mean a monitor should force ads for it onto a connected device.
Microsoft has since forced LG to remove the McAfee ads. The clandestine manner in which LG monitors were installing ad-pushing software onto third-party devices, however, remains seriously concerning.
LG Monitor App Installer’s page on the Microsoft Store says the app can “use all system resources” and “access your Internet connection.” When outcry about the app peaked last month, LG’s broader privacy policy drew concern that LG might use the app to collect data and share it with advertisers. However, the brief privacy policy that the app’s Microsoft Store page currently links to claims that the app “and the monitor applications distributed through it do not collect, use, store, or share personal information. If future versions introduce features that involve the processing of personal information, this notice will be updated accordingly.”
