Fire at hospital nursery in Pakistan’s capital kills 14 newborns, officials say
Officials in Pakistan say a fire that erupted at a newborn nursery at a major government hospital in Pakistan’s capital has killed 14 babies
ISLAMABAD -- A fire erupted early Wednesday at a nursery for newborns at a major government hospital in Pakistan’s capital, killing 14 babies, according to hospital officials and the government.
The nursery at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences housed at least 15 newborns when the fire broke out, hospital officials said. At least one baby was rescued.
Rescue officials said the fire began at about 6:45 a.m., apparently after the compressor of an air-conditioning unit exploded inside the nursery, which is part of the hospital’s gynecology ward. Firefighters quickly responded and extinguished the blaze, and rescue teams were carrying out cooling operations at the site, local media reported.
A hospital spokesperson did not immediately respond to calls seeking comment.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and ordered an immediate investigation. A statement from his office confirmed that 14 newborns had died. “A tragedy involving children is an irreparable loss,” Sharif said.

The DJ dropped the beat and 70 women started throwing punches. By the time the first kickboxing combination was called out, Moon Bar, a Visakhapatnam club had shed its weekend persona to turn into a makeshift fitness floor, with women punching, kicking, squatting and burpee-ing their way through an hour of high-energy cardio.
There were no opponents, no rings and no gloves to take a hit. Instead, four trainers led the women through combinations designed to raise the heart rate and work the whole body, while the music kept the tempo going. It was a part workout, part social gathering and a glimpse of how women are increasingly choosing to exercise with more intensity, more variety and with strength in mind.
Hosted by The Social Wave, a women-centric community in the city, Club Cardio brought kickboxing into a club setting, combining martial arts-inspired movements with high-intensity cardio drills. The one-hour session was conducted in collaboration with Altcrew and led by four trainers.
For Komal Bagrodia Saraf, who founded The Social Wave with Preksha Dugar, the format was designed to make exercise feel less like a scheduled obligation and more like something women would actively seek out. “The idea was to turn a bar into a fitness bar,” she says. “There is a trend of Gen Z turning a bar into a Pilates bar. We wanted to bring something more intense than Zumba.”
The response also reinforced the value of a shared workout, she says. “There was some initial reluctance among a few participants, but once we made a circle and started, the music and community spirit helped. It became a community workout.”
The format was deliberately social. The 65-minute session at Moon Bar was structured to keep the pace building. After a 10-minute warm-up, the women spent the next 40 minutes learning kickboxing combinations and working dance moves into the routines. Participants worked through combinations of punches and kicks before the final 15 minutes turned into what Komal calls the “monster challenge”, featuring squats, bicep curls and burpees.
According to Komal, a sense of community may be as important to the emerging fitness format as the workout itself. The growing interest among women in strength training, boxing, running and other high-intensity forms of exercise points to a broader change in how fitness is being understood.
Fitness coach Martina Fernandes, who attended the session, sees that change in her own experience. “I have never really believed exercise has to feel like punishment,” she says. Having played sport for much of her life, Martina associates movement with “fun, competition, music, adrenaline and people”.
She usually trains alone and considers herself self-motivated, but says community workouts offer something different. “When you are laughing, sweating, listening to good music and pushing yourself alongside other people, it stops feeling like ‘I have to work out’ and starts feeling like ‘I want to be here’.”
For Martina, physical strength has little to do with a number on the weighing scale. “It means being capable,” she says. “It is being able to pick up something heavy, run, jump, play sport, carry my kids, travel, climb stairs and generally trust my body to do what I ask it to do.”
That focus on capability becomes particularly significant as women age, she adds. “I do not want to just look strong. I want to actually be strong. I am all about longevity.”
Kickboxing, she believes, also brings a psychological dimension. Learning combinations requires concentration and coordination, leaving little room for distraction. “There is something incredibly empowering about learning that your body can hit, move, react and defend itself,” she says. “You feel more confident, more alert and more connected to your body.”
For women in their 30s and 40s, she says, preserving muscle, supporting bone health, maintaining metabolic health and remaining independent become increasingly relevant. “The scale is one very small piece of the picture. Your strength, energy, performance and capability tell you much more about your fitness.”
Participant Tanya Dhawan, who had never tried kickboxing apart from some martial arts as a child, signed up because she was looking for something new to do in Vizag. The addition of a DJ was an added attraction. “Music is always part of my workouts, so combining it with a high-energy workout sounded like a lot of fun,” she says.
She had expected a conventional kickboxing class centred on technique. Instead, she found a high-intensity cardio workout driven by music and group energy. “The music, the energy of the girls and the entire crew kept the momentum going, especially when the workout got tough.”
The appeal of women-only fitness spaces, Martina says, lies partly in removing the apprehension that can accompany entering a gym or combat-sports environment. “A lot of women walk into a gym or a boxing environment worrying that everyone is watching them or judging how much they can lift,” she says. An all-women setting can make it easier to be a beginner and gradually take on greater challenges.
Community can also make consistency easier. “Motivation gets you started, but community is often what keeps you going,” Fernandes says. For women balancing careers, children and family responsibilities, she believes the expectation of seeing familiar faces can make fitness less likely to be the first commitment sacrificed.
Komal, too, sees wellness as a larger focus for The Social Wave. The group is looking at more experiences that combine activity and social interaction, including an upcoming pickleball coaching session.

Ecuador intelligence chief and five Americans killed in Kenya helicopter crash
- Published
Ecuador's intelligence chief and his wife have been killed in a helicopter that crashed at Mount Ololokwe in central Kenya.
Michele Sensi-Contugi, 44, and his wife, fashion designer Stephany Hollihan, 42, were among the group of seven people - six tourists and the pilot - killed in Samburu county at approximately 09:13 (06:13 GMT) on Wednesday.
Five of victims were Americans, a US State Department spokesperson said. The Reuters news agency reports that Hollihan also held US citizenship.
The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) said the helicopter was on a scenic flight from a wildlife conservancy in Loisaba to Ewaso Nyiro, a river that flows along several national reserves.
Samburu county is a popular tourist destination with many private wildlife conservancies and is renowned for its stunning landscape.
Images from the scene show smoke at the wooded crash site on Mount Ololokwe, as members of the Kenya Red Cross approach the still-burning wreckage.
Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa named Sensi-Contugo director of the country's Centre of Strategic Intelligence (CIES) in January 2024.
The office of the president and Ecuador's National Assembly expressed their condolences over his death and that of Hollihan.
The Italian-Ecuadorean businessman had had close links to Noboa even before he was chosen to lead the intelligence service and was considered a close ally of the president.
Shortly before being named head of the CIES, he had served for four months as a minister in his cabinet.
Noboa has declared three days of national mourning starting on Thursday.
Newspapers in Ecuador have also run obituaries of Hollihan. The Guayaquil-based designer founded Sensi Studio, a brand praised for incorporating traditional Ecuadorean elements and materials in its designs.
Lady Lori Helicopters, which operated the Eurocopter EC130 B4 aircraft, said it was "deeply saddened" by the accident.
"Our deepest sympathies are with the guests, crew, their families and loved ones, and all those affected by this tragic accident," a statement read.
According to a memo seen by the BBC's US partner CBS News, external one of the Americans killed in the crash was NBCUniversal journalist José Alberto Suárez.
In the memo, NBCUniversal called Suárez "a deeply respected leader and beloved friend and colleague.
"José was an exceptional colleague and mentor to many," the memo read.
Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte was among the Americans killed in the crash, according to local and US media.
Commenting on his death on X, US Rep Carlos Antonio Gimenez wrote: "Our prayers are with their loved ones during this incredibly difficult time. May their memories be a blessing."
The other victims have not yet been identified.
Helicopter crashes are not uncommon in Kenya.
In February, a helicopter crash in the Rift Valley county of Nandi killed six people, including a member of parliament.
In 2024, the military chief, Gen Francis Omondi Ogolla, died after an army helicopter that was carrying 11 people crashed in the west of the country, with only two survivors.
In June 2021 at least 10 soldiers were killed when their helicopter crashed while landing near the capital, Nairobi.

Tiger Woods has welcomed the PGA Tour’s decision to introduce a 32-player match-play competition as part of a revamped Tour Championship format.
PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp announced the changes on Tuesday, ahead of this week’s Tour Championship at East Lake Golf Club in Atlanta. The new format is scheduled to begin in 2028, with the top 90 players first competing in a stroke-play event to determine the 32 golfers who will progress to the opening match-play stage.
“The conclusion of the season should be worthy of the journey it takes to get there,” Woods wrote on X. “Today’s announcement is a result of the hard work and passion of our players. Excited to usher in a new era of match play on the PGA Tour.”
The current FedExCup Playoffs are held over three weeks, with fields of 70, 50 and 30 players competing in stroke-play tournaments.
Under the new structure, the opening week will consist of a group stage. The 32 qualifiers will be split into eight groups of four, with players competing in head-to-head matches. The top two golfers from each group will advance to the second week, which will be held at a different venue.
The remaining 16 players will then compete across four rounds of match play. The final two unbeaten players will face off for the Tour Championship title, with one golfer ultimately emerging as champion.
ALSO READ: Tiger Woods set for first in-court appearance since DUI charge
“From the beginning, the goal of the Future Competition Committee was to create an easier-to-follow competitive model for our fans with greater consequence and a stronger season-long narrative,” Rolapp said.
“Throughout this process, we listened carefully to our fans, players and partners. One message came through clearly: the culmination of our season should be worthy of the journey it takes to get there. The result is a season-ending structure that rewards excellence over the course of the year while building toward a reimagined Tour Championship. We are creating something different, something distinct within professional golf that can resonate far beyond it.”

US firefighters say major blaze near Reno about a quarter contained
- Published
US fire crews have reported progress in their efforts to tackle a large wildfire menacing the city of Reno, Nevada - saying the blaze is about a quarter contained.
The Hawk Fire, which began on Saturday, had spread over 15,000 acres by Monday, firefighters said.
Evacuation orders remain in place for 23,000 people, though other residents have now been allowed to return to their homes. Tens of thousands of other residents have been told to be ready to leave at any moment.
Officials are concerned that gusts of wind could drive the flames towards more homes. Unfavourable weather conditions are forecast for the next two days, meaning the fire could continue to burn during that timeframe.
No deaths have been reported, though seven people have been injured.
The fire, which was first reported on Saturday morning, spread in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains near Reno due to those same windy and unpredictable weather conditions.
The immediate "go now" evacuation zone and wider "get set" area - where people are being warned to prepare to evacuate - do not extend to the centre of Reno, but they do affect large urban areas and part of a highway.
Large air tankers and helicopters have been flying over the affected area dropping water and fire retardants.
In their update on Monday afternoon, fire officials said the blaze had been at least 27% contained.
Chief Richard Edwards, of the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District, said those injured were four civilians and three firefighters, who suffered minor burns.
Edwards added that 32 homes had been destroyed and six damaged, and that those numbers were expected to increase. Shelters have been set up in the area to take in displaced residents.
While firefighters have made progress, more than two-thirds of the fire's perimeter remains uncontained.
The fire is thought to have been caused by humans. Edwards added on Monday that investigators did not yet know if the blaze was set intentionally.
Scientists say that human-induced climate change makes the warm, dry conditions more likely that assist the rapid spread of wildfires.
Reno's average temperature has gone up by over 4C since the 1970s, faster than any other big US city, according to Climate Central.
Nevada's Governor Joe Lombardo earlier declared a state of emergency in surrounding Washoe County, and ordered the National Guard to join firefighting and law enforcement efforts.
"This is an active and rapidly evolving situation and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," he said on Saturday.
Firefighters from Australia and New Zealand have so far taken part in the containment effort – as well as crews from 15 US states.
The University of Nevada in Reno - which has its main campus in the city close to the "get set" warning area - previously said regular campus operations would continue but that it was monitoring the situation.
But one student, James Wolfgang Perez, said some teaching staff had independently decided to cancel their classes. The sight of the fire spreading in the direction of the campus on Saturday had been "apocalyptic", he told the BBC.
Justin Davis, 29, lives on Peavine Mountain, close to Reno, and similarly watched as the fire spread towards his home on Saturday and destroyed four of his vehicles.
He told the BBC he had previously bought a water truck in case a wildfire like this occurred and had used it to save his home.
"We turned on the water truck and just started spraying down the things we wanted to save," he said.
The blaze has been been named the Hawk Fire because it was first reported near the Hawk Meadow Trail, to the west of Reno.
Reno, in western Nevada, is located close to the state boundary with California and has a population of around 280,000 people.
Wildfires are common in south-western US states, including Nevada, and are becoming more severe, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Many of these fires develop in rural and less populated areas, with only a few encroaching on population centres.

'Forget about going back': 9 years on, Rohingya crisis enters dangerous phase
CHIANG MAI, Thailand — As the world's attention stays fixed on the Middle East and Ukraine, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya Muslim refugees are marking a grim anniversary largely unnoticed.
Nine years ago this week, a military crackdown in Myanmar drove them from their homes into Bangladesh, in what the United States called a "genocide."
And still they are arriving. Even as governments discuss whether those in the camps might eventually return, more Rohingya continue crossing from conflict-torn Rakhine state into southern Bangladesh.
Despite more than 1 million people languishing in sprawling camps for almost a decade, as conditions deteriorate and aid shrinks, talk of repatriation is premature, according to analysts. The more immediate challenge is stopping more people from being pushed out.
"Forget about going back right now; people are still coming in, and nobody seems to talk pragmatically about that," independent researcher Jessica Olney, who has worked with the Rohingya for a decade, told NPR.
Mass exodus
The exodus began Aug. 25, 2017, when Myanmar's military and armed Rakhine civilians burned hundreds of Rohingya villages and killed at least 6,700 people in a single month, according to Doctors Without Borders. Between 700,000 and 750,000 people crossed into Bangladesh in that wave alone.
Today, roughly 1 million live in what has become the world's largest refugee settlement, with 200,000 more elsewhere in the country. More than half are children.
Bana Rashida fled in 2017 as soldiers fired around her family. Her husband, Mohammad Yunus, broke his leg falling from a high bank during the escape. He now walks with a heavy limp and cannot work, leaving Rashida to support their five children alone.
NPR visited their shelter in Kutupalong refugee camp near Cox's Bazar in late April ahead of the anniversary. Fires had recently gutted parts of the camps; months later, monsoon downpours would trigger deadly landslides around its tarpaulin-and-bamboo shelters.
"My life is very difficult," Rashida told NPR. "Now that we don't have enough income, I can't provide for them. I want to give my children a good education, but I can't afford it."
Her hope was modest: a sewing machine and the skills to use it. Yunus has given up on returning to his farmland in Rakhine state. "Without security and international backing, we aren't able to return," he said.
No path home
That security shows little sign of arriving. Myanmar's 2021 military coup ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and plunged the country into civil war. Fighting between the ethnic Rakhine group the Arakan Army and Myanmar's junta over control of Rakhine state forced more Rohingya to flee.
The Arakan Army now controls most of Rakhine and stands accused of its own abuses against Rohingya civilians, while a junta blockade has halted food, medicine and aid, driving hunger across the territory.
Shari Nijman, a Bangladesh-based spokesperson for the U.N. refugee agency, said 154,000 more Rohingya have arrived in the camps since 2024, a flow that continues as conditions in Rakhine "remain extremely unstable."
"After nine years, it is incredibly difficult for the Rohingya to hold onto hope that this will ever end," Nijman said.
Each year that passes, commemorations grow as people "make an effort to keep Myanmar alive in them," she added.
Some children have now spent their entire lives in the camps, while young Rohingya, stuck in limbo, despair over their own future.
"Without international attention, it becomes harder for them to believe there's an end to this suffering," she said.
Fraying lifeline
Barred from legally working in Bangladesh, Rohingya depend almost entirely on humanitarian assistance. Amid competing global crises and shifting donor priorities, that safety net is fraying.
In 2023, funding shortfalls forced U.N. World Food Program rations from $12 a person per month in March to $8 by June, even as 40 percent of children under five were already chronically malnourished, according to the U.N. It was returned to $12 by 2024, but this April it was slashed once more, this time to as little as $7 for some people under a new tiered system.
As conditions deteriorate, some refugees are risking deadly 1,000-mile journeys by boat to Malaysia. Others are being drawn — sometimes forcibly — into Myanmar's civil war or toward Rohingya militant groups and criminal gangs, which rights advocates say operate with impunity.
Olney said Washington should help fund the humanitarian response, press Bangladesh to open livelihood opportunities for refugees, and get aid to Rakhine, including territory now held by the Arakan Army. The group, she said, has seen "very little international engagement" despite controlling most of Rakhine.
"Because of the lack of engagement, there's no pressure and little visibility," she said.
The Trump administration pledged $73 million in new aid for Rohingya refugees through the U.N. World Food Program in March 2025, followed by a further $60 million pledge for the Rohingya that September, amid fears that funding cuts could deepen the crisis facing the world's largest stateless population. That falls short of the $300 million the U.S. gave in 2024, amid a broader cut to U.S. foreign aid.
In May, the U.N. and the Bangladesh government launched a $710.5 million appeal to cover food, shelter, health care, education and protection services, a request already a quarter smaller than the year before. Even so, donors have covered only around 66% of it so far.
Without restored aid or the chance to work, Olney warned, refugees are increasingly pulled toward illicit economies, gambling or dangerous boat journeys to Malaysia, exposing them to greater risk of human trafficking.
"It's going to achieve a regional security crisis, which we already have, but it will get worse," she said.

A powerful typhoon headed west over the East China Sea on Wednesday (August 26, 2026) after slamming Okinawa and other remote southwestern Japanese islands, causing blackouts, flight cancellations and threatening landslips. Two people were slightly injured.
Typhoon Saudel was about 180 kilometres northwest of Okinoerabu Island, packing winds of up to 144 kph as of late Wednesday (August 25) morning as it headed toward China's eastern coast, the Japan Meteorological Agency said.
Saudel left two people with minor injuries, the Fire and Disaster Management Agency and prefectural officials said Wednesday.
A 78-year-old woman suffered a head injury when she was blown by the wind and fell to the ground outside her home in the city of Uruma on the island of Okinawa. In nearby Amamioshima island, a woman in her 70s fell from the stairs during a blackout caused by the typhoon, according to NHK public television.
Some 150 flights to and from Okinawa's Naha airport have been cancelled. The typhoon also caused power outages for more than 30,000 homes in Kagoshima prefecture, which includes the Amami area, the Kyushu Electric Power Co. said.
More than 9 inches of rain fell in the Amami region over the past 24 hours, the JMA said, predicting more rain of up to 3.9 inches in the area and up to 4.7 inches of rainfall on Okinawa through midday Thursday.
The agency issued a landslide warning for the Amami region.

New cast members announced for Heated Rivalry Season 2
Latest pair to join cast are Canadian Daniel Diemer and Welsh actor Shaheen Jafargholi
Two new cast members have been announced for Season 2 of Crave's blockbuster hockey drama Heated Rivalry.
Canadian actor Daniel Diemer, known for playing Tyson on the television show Percy Jackson and the Olympians, will star as hockey player Ryan Price.
Welsh actor Shaheen Jafargholi will play his love interest, musician Fabian Salah. Jafargholi appeared in the HBO series War.
The characters Ryan and Fabian are the protagonists of the third novel in Rachel Reid's bestselling Game Changers hockey romance series, Tough Guy.
It tells the story of pro hockey enforcer Ryan. When he's traded to the Toronto team, he's excited to experience the city's gay village. While exploring, Ryan runs into Fabian, an aspiring musician with whom he shared an almost-kiss in high school. Despite the years that have passed, their chemistry is undeniable. But a future together might mean Ryan has to give up hockey for good.
"Fabian and Ryan each bring a distinctive energy to the world Rachel Reid has created," said writer Jacob Tierney and producer Brendan Brady in a press statement.
"They are bold, complicated and deeply compelling characters, and finding actors who could really take on all of those different sides was so important to us. Daniel and Shaheen bring such confidence and emotional honesty to the roles. We can’t wait for audiences to see what they do with Fabian and Ryan and how they make these characters their own."
Season 1 of the show adapted books one and two of Reid’s series, Game Changer and Heated Rivalry.
Crave has said Season 2 of Heated Rivalry will continue to follow the story of hockey rivals-turned-lovers Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov from Reid's novel The Long Game.
Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie will reprise their starring roles in the TV adaptation.
The second season of the show will also incorporate the stories of Troy Barrett, a hockey player traded to Ilya’s new team, and Harris Dover, a social media manager, from the fifth novel of the book series, Role Model.
Crave announced Justice Smith was cast as Harris and Charlie Gillespie, star of Julie and the Phantoms, was cast as Troy.
Other new cast members include Schitt's Creek's Emily Hampshire and drag queen Priyanka.
Season 2 of Heated Rivalry will premiere in spring 2027.

Below, we look back at the celebrities we lost in 2026, listed in alphabetical order.
Scott Adams, 68
Scott Adams worked at a telephone company in the 1980s. The experience inspired his beloved comic strip, "Dilbert."
By the end of the decade, the character and his satirical office humor began appearing in comic strips.
At its peak, "Dilbert" was syndicated in over 2,000 newspapers. A cartoon series debuted in 1999, running for two seasons.
Adams gained notoriety when he began writing blog posts praising Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run. In 2023, "Dilbert" was pulled from newspapers across the US following racist comments made by Adams.
Adams died on January 13 from metastatic prostate cancer.
Brad Arnold, 47
The lead singer of 3 Doors Down, Brad Arnold launched the group into fame with the 2000 rock anthem "Kryptonite," which peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 that year.
The success led to other hits like "Loser," "Here Without You," and "When I'm Gone." Arnold's vocal range and lyrics focused on love and love lost, which fueled the group to stardom.
Arnold died on February 7 from a type of kidney cancer.
Afrika Bambaataa, 68
A hip-hop pioneer during the 1970s and 1980s, Lance Taylor, known professionally as Afrika Bambaataa, first gained attention as a DJ in the Bronx.
He signed with Tommy Boy Records in 1981 and released landmark songs like "Jazzy Sensation" and "Planet Rock." He would go on to influence the likes of Queen Latifah and A Tribe Called Quest throughout his career.
Bambaataa founded the hip-hop awareness group, Universal Zulu Nation, in the 1970s to steer kids away from gang life. Bambaataa stepped down as the head of the organization in 2016 after accusations of sexual abuse.
Bambaataa denied all claims.
He died on April 9 due to prostate cancer.
Rob Bass, 59
One of the icons responsible for bringing hip-hop to the mainstram, Rob Bass crafted the iconic track "It Takes Two" alongside DJ E-Z Rock.
The track, released in 1988, reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot Dance/Club Songs chart and later went certified platinum. In 1989, it was voted the greatest single of all time by Spin magazine.
Bass died on May 22 following cancer.
Nicholas Brendon, 54
Nicholas Brendon was a television actor, best known for playing Xander Harris in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer."
He also starred in "Criminal Minds" and "Kitchen Confidential."
Brendon died in his sleep on March 20 due to natural causes, according to his family's statement.
In 2023, Brendon suffered a heart attack and was diagnosed with a congenital heart defect. He also had cauda equina syndrome, which led to several spinal surgeries.
"While it's no secret that Nicholas had struggles in the past, he was on medications and treatment to manage his diagnosis, and he was optimistic about the future at the time of his passing," the statement to The Hollywood Reporter read. "Our family asks for privacy during this time as we grieve his loss and celebrate the life of a man who lived with intensity, imagination, and heart."
Peabo Bryson, 75
Two-time Grammy winner Peabo Bryson is best known for his classic love ballads.
Bryson began releasing music in the late 1970s, but one of his first major hits was opposite Roberta Flack on the 1983 duet, "Tonight, I Celebrate My Love." He continued hit-making a year later with the smash "If Ever You're in My Arms Again," and in 1991, he topped the R&B charts with "Can You Stop the Rain."
Bryson found global stardom with his renditions of two Disney classics. In 1991, he released the pop version of "Beauty and the Beast," alongside Céline Dion, and a year later, he duetted with Regina Belle on "A Whole New World" from the 1992 release of "Aladdin."
Bryson died on June 2. No cause was given.
James Burrows, 85
An 11-time Emmy winner and co-creator of "Cheers," director James Burrows helped shape modern TV comedy through his work on iconic sitcoms including "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "Frasier."
Known for his comedic timing and elaborate blocking, Burrows got his start directing episodes of "The Mary Tyler Moore Show." Throughout his career, he directed episodes of "Frasier" (winning an Emmy for the pilot episode), "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "The Big Bang Theory." He directed over 50 pilot episodes.
Burrows died on June 19. No cause was given.
Kyle Busch, 41
Two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion Busch was considered one of the greatest racers of all time.
Busch was hospitalized on May 21, before two upcoming races. Hours later, he was pronounced dead.
Busch died from severe pneumonia that progressed into sepsis.
Robert Carradine, 71
Robert Carradine was best known for his roles as Lizzie McGuire's dad and as the iconic geek Lewis Skolnick in the 1980s franchise "Revenge of the Nerds."
As a member of Hollywood's famed Carradine family, Robert was destined for an onscreen career.
He received one of his first screen credits starring in his brother David Carradine's popular 1970s TV series "Kung Fu" and went on to land roles in everything from Samuel Fuller's World War II classic "The Big Red One" to the "Lizzie McGuire" series.
Carradine's family shared statements with Deadline that emphasized being open about his struggles with mental illness.
"We are bereft at the loss of this beautiful soul and want to acknowledge Bobby's valiant struggle against his nearly two-decade battle with Bipolar Disorder," Carradine's family said. "We hope his journey can shine a light and encourage addressing the stigma that attaches to mental illness."
Carradine died by suicide on February 23.
If you or someone you know is experiencing depression or has had thoughts of harming themself or taking their own life, get help. In the US, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Help is also available through the Crisis Text Line — just text "HOME" to 741741. The International Association for Suicide Prevention offers resources for those outside the US.
Bud Cort, 77
Most famous for his role as Harold in the 1971 cult-classic "Harold and Maude," Bud Cort became the epitome of 1970s counterculture thanks to his baby-faced looks, wit, and sophisticated persona.
The dark comedy starred Cort as Harold, a man in his 20s who is obsessed with suicide until he meets 79-year-old eccentric Maude (Ruth Gordon).
Before that, Cort scored bit parts in Robert Altman's "M*A*S*H*" (1970) and "Brewster McCloud" (1970).
After "Harold and Maude," Cort worked steadily for the rest of his life, occasionally showing up in hit movies like Michael Mann's "Heat" (1995) and Wes Anderson's "The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou" (2004).
Cort died on February 11 following a long illness.
Eric Dane, 53
Long before becoming one of TV's most recognizable heartthrobs, Eric Dane was building his career with guest roles on series like "Saved by the Bell" and "Married… with Children."
He later gained wider attention with appearances on "Charmed" before landing his breakout role as Dr. Mark "McSteamy" Sloan on "Grey's Anatomy." He most recently starred in HBO's "Euphoria," where he played Cal Jacobs, the father of Jacob Elordi's character, Nate Jacobs.
Dane has two children with his wife, Rebecca Gayheart. In April 2025, the actor said that he was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS.
Dane died on February 19 at age 53, his publicist confirmed in a statement to Business Insider.
"He spent his final days surrounded by dear friends, his devoted wife, and his two beautiful daughters, Billie and Georgia, who were the center of his world," his publicist said.
Clive Davis, 94
A legend in the music world, Davis was responsible for elevating pop music to unthinkable heights by discovering talents like Aretha Franklin, Barry Manilow, Bruce Springsteen, Billy Joel, Whitney Houston, and Alicia Keys, to name a few.
Over his 50-year career, along with being an executive behind millions of album sales, he also won five Grammys, including two for Album of the Year ("The Bodyguard" soundtrack and "Supernatural" by Santana).
Davis died on June 22. No cause was given.
Robert Duvall, 95
Robert Duvall starred in a plethora of timeless classics, including "The Godfather," "The Godfather Part II," "Apocalypse Now," "THX 1138," "The Natural," "Days of Thunder," and "The Apostle."
Duvall will be best remembered for starring in three of director Francis Ford Coppola's iconic films: playing Tom Hagen in the first two "Godfather" movies and Lieutenant Colonel Bill Kilgore in "Apocalypse Now," in which he delivers one of the most memorable lines in movie history: "I love the smell of napalm in the morning."
Duvall was lauded for his acting talent, from not saying a word while playing Boo Radley in his first big screen role in the 1962 classic "To Kill a Mockingbird" to his portrayal of a country singer dealing with alcoholism in 1983's "Tender Mercies," which earned him an Oscar.
He died on his ranch in Virginia on February 15. No cause was given.
Brenda Fricker, 81
This Irish actress was a fixture on the stage and screen for six decades. But she's most known for showing up in the "Home Alone" sequel.
As The Pigeon Lady in 1992's "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York," Fricker has become a fixture for families during the holiday season for decades (and in 2020 became the subject of a popular meme).
But Fricker's acting talents go beyond playing a spooky wanderer of Central Park.
In 1990, she became the first Irish actress to win an Academy Award, as she was given the best supporting actress Oscar that year for her performance in "My Left Foot."
Fricker died on July 16; no cause was given.
Mark Fuhrman, 74
Fuhrman cemented his place in popular culture as one of the lead LAPD detectives on the 1995 murder case of O.J. Simpson's ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman.
Fuhrman found the famed bloody glove on the Simpson estate, and during the trial, he gained infamy when Simpson's defense team used his past racist language to discredit him as a witness.
Fuhrman retired from the LAPD after the Simpson trial and moved to Idaho, where he wrote true crime books.
Fuhrman died on May 12 of throat cancer.
Valentino Garavani, 93
For over six decades, one name has been synonymous with women's high fashion: Valentino.
The Italian designer launched his fashion business in Rome in 1960 and never looked back. Soon, every star wanted to be seen in his creations. They've been worn by icons like Elizabeth Taylor, Joan Collins, Jackie Kennedy, Princess Diana, Sharon Stone, and more.
Though Garavani retired from designing in 2008, his label is still a red carpet staple, as is his famous shade of bright red dubbed "Valentino Red."
Garavani died on January 19. No cause was given.
Donald Gibb, 71
No one defined a bully for a generation more than Gibb's hulking fraternity character Orge in the "Revenge of the Nerds" movies of the 1980s.
Since the original raunchy comedy was released in 1984, Gibb's intimidating size and loud yells of "NERDS!" have become as memorable as the pocket protectors worn by the movie's geeks.
Gibb went on to star opposite Jean-Claude Van Damme in his classic 1988 action movie "Bloodsport." He also landed guest star roles through his career on shows like "Quantum Leap," Magnum P.I.," "MacGyver," "Night Court," and "Cheers."
Gibb died on May 12 following health complications.
Glen Hansard, 56
Irish singer-songwriter Hansard was the frontman of the rock band The Frames and one-half of the band The Swell Season. But he was perhaps best known for writing and starring in the hit 2007 indie film "Once," in which he and his Swell Season bandmate Markéta Irglová play two struggling musicians who fall in love. The duo won an Oscar for best original song for the film's standout track, "Falling Slowly."
Hansard also embarked on a solo career; his 2015 album, "Didn't He Ramble," was nominated for a Grammy for best folk album.
Hansard died on July 29 in a motorcycle crash in Dublin.
Anthony Head, 72
Rising up through the UK stage scene in the 1980s, Head found fame when he was cast as Rupert Giles, who became a father figure to Sarah Michelle Gellar's Buffy Summers in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer."
Most recently, he played the bitter former owner of AFC Richmond on "Ted Lasso."
Head's death was announced by his family on June 5. They stated the cause was "complications due to pneumonia."
David Hockney, 88
British painter David Hockney was renowned for his striking portraits and figurative pop art. Many of his best-known paintings, including 1966's "The Splash" and 1972's "Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)," were inspired by the bright colors and sun-dappled pools of Los Angeles.
Hockney moved to Los Angeles in the late '60s, and his work became synonymous with the warmth and leisure of Southern California. He was also one of the few popular artists at the time to depict openly gay scenes, and Hockney was outspoken about anti-gay censorship.
Throughout his career, Hockney split time between California, England, and France. He died at his home in London on June 12 at age 88, his publicist confirmed to The New York Times. No cause of death was given.
Jesse Jackson, 84
The Rev. Jesse Jackson was a leader of the Civil Rights Movement, a minister, and an activist icon who twice ran for president.
Born on October 8, 1941, in Greenville, South Carolina, Jackson experienced Jim Crow segregation on public buses and at school firsthand. It would shape the rest of his life.
His fight for civil rights began in the 1960s, when he helped organize protests and demonstrations across the US and worked closely alongside civil rights icon Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.
His decadeslong career as a leading civil rights activist included support for modern national movements, such as the push for voting rights, the fight against racism, and a higher minimum wage.
Jackson ran for president twice, both times as a democrat. He placed third for the party's nomination in 1984 and second in 1988. This marked the most successful presidential runs of any Black candidate prior to Barack Obama.
Jackson announced in 2017 that he'd been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. In November 2025, Jackson was treated in a Chicago hospital after complications from progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), a rare neurodegenerative condition.
Jackson died on February 17.
Patrick Muldoon, 57
In the 1990s, you couldn't escape the piercing eyes of Patrick Muldoon.
He played Austin Reed on "Days of Our Lives" for most of the decade, and when he wasn't on the soap, he was over on "Melrose Place" playing the villain role of Richard Hart.
If being on two iconic shows wasn't enough, he also showed up on "Saved by the Bell" and had a role in the cult classic movie "Starship Troopers."
Muldoon died on April 19 after a heart attack.
Sam Neill, 78
With a career spanning more than five decades and including countless memorable performances in movies and television, Sam Neill was one of the most versatile actors of his generation,
The New Zealand actor starred opposite Nicole Kidman in the 1989 thriller "Dead Calm," played the loyal first officer opposite Sean Connery in 1990's "The Hunt for Red October," played the lead in John Carpenter's 1994 horror "In the Mouth of Madness," and most recently starred in the hit series "Peaky Blinders."
But Neill will be best known for playing the brave and all-dinosaur-knowing Dr. Alan Grant in the "Jurassic Park" franchise.
Neill died on July 13; no cause was given. Neill was battling a rare and aggressive form of blood cancer, but was cancer-free at the time of his death, according to a post on his Instagram account announcing his passing.
Tom Noonan, 74
Standing at a towering 6' 5", Tom Noonan was born to play the bad guy. And he did just that, starring as the villain in movies like "Manhunter," "RoboCop 2," and "Last Action Hero."
But this actor had more to show off. He showcased his comedy chops as Rodney Dangerfield's degenerate gambling friend in the 1983 comedy "Easy Money," and set up the heist for Robert De Niro in Michael Mann's 1995 classic "Heat."
His knack for storytelling also translated behind the camera. Noonan wrote, directed, and starred in the drama "What Happened Was," which won the grand prize at the 1994 Sundance Film Festival.
Noonan died on February 14; no cause was given.
Chuck Norris, 86
Few action stars have Chuck Norris' credentials.
Before he ever stepped in front of a camera, he was a martial arts champion and a black belt in Karate, judo, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, Taekwondo, and Tang Soo Do.
His talents would become known the world over in 1972, when he faced off against Bruce Lee in "The Way of the Dragon."
Through the 1980s, Norris became one of the biggest action stars in the world thanks to movies like "A Force of One," "The Octagon," and the "Delta Force" and "Missing in Action" franchises.
In the 1990s, he took over the small screen, playing the lead in the "Walker, Texas Ranger" TV show, which aired in over 100 countries during its run from 1993 to 2001.
Norris was hospitalized on March 19 in Hawaii and died the following day, according to his family. No cause was given.
Catherine O'Hara, 71
O'Hara, who was best known for her roles in "Beetlejuice" and "Home Alone," got her start in the Canadian comedy scene, appearing in the now-legendary cast of "SCTV."
It would mark the beginning of a fruitful partnership with fellow actor Eugene Levy, who became her frequent costar and collaborator in memorable appearances in Christopher Guest films like "A Mighty Wind" and "Best in Show" and television series like "Schitt's Creek," which earned her an Emmy Award for outstanding lead actress in 2020.
O'Hara's representation confirmed her death to Business Insider on January 30. Los Angeles County Department of Public Health confirmed in a death certificate viewed by People that O'Hara died of a pulmonary embolism, with rectal cancer listed as an underlying cause.
Hayden Panettiere, 36
Panettiere began acting as a child, landing one of her earliest major roles as Sarah Roberts on the ABC soap opera "One Life to Live," on which she appeared from 1994 to 1997.
As her career progressed, she became best known for portraying Claire Bennet on "Heroes" and Juliette Barnes on "Nashville."
Over the years, Panettiere had spoken openly about her struggles with alcoholism and postpartum depression. She detailed those experiences in her memoir, "This Is Me: A Reckoning," which was released in May.
Her representative confirmed to Business Insider on August 17 that Panettiere had died at 36 but did not disclose a cause of death.
Dolly Parton, 80
Parton released her debut album, "Hello, I'm Dolly," in 1967 and went on to pen country hits like "I Will Always Love You" and "Jolene," both of which were released as singles in 1974.
In addition to her music, Parton was beloved for her flamboyant style and her philanthropy. She founded the Dollywood Foundation in 1988, a charitable organization focused on education and community initiatives in her home state of Tennessee. She continued to fund scholarship programs and donate to hospitals, public health initiatives, and disaster relief programs throughout her life.
Parton is known as the best-selling female country music artist of all time. She was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1999, the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2001, and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.
Parton's 49th and final solo studio album, "Rockstar," was released in 2023. The tracklist included both original material and covers of classic rock songs, featuring an array of guests like Paul McCartney, Ringo Starr, Sting, Joan Jett, and Parton's goddaughter, Miley Cyrus.
News broke on August 25 that Parton died following unspecified health issues. She was 80.
Vincent Pastore, 80
This character actor found fame appearing in a string of mob movies in the 1990s, like "Goodfellas," "Carlito's Way," and "Men of Respect." But Pastore truly became a star when he was cast in the hit HBO series "The Sopranos."
As Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero, Pastore was part of the main cast for the first two seasons of the show, playing Tony Soprano's mob enforcer-turned-FBI informant. Bonpensiero's shocking death was one of the most famous in the show's history and proved that no one was safe from getting whacked.
Pastore died on August 1. No cause was given.
Valerie Perrine, 82
Perrine found herself cast alongside the biggest stars of the 1970s.
She played the love interest opposite Jeff Bridges in 1973's "The Last American Hero" and Robert Redford in 1979's "The Electric Horseman." She earned an Oscar nomination for starring alongside Dustin Hoffman in 1974's "Lenny."
For most, she'll be remembered best for sharing the screen with Gene Hackman as the secretary to his evil Lex Luthor in 1978's "Superman." She also starred in the sequel. As Ms. Teschmacher, her loyalty to Luthor is questioned when she rescues Superman (Christopher Reeve) after he's chained with Kryptonite.
Perrine died in her home in Beverly Hills on March 23. She was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2015.
Sonny Rollins, 95
One of the most influential jazz musicians in history, Rollins recorded more than 60 albums over his seven-decade career.
His live album, "A Night at the Village Vanguard," is considered one of the greatest jazz albums ever made.
Rollins died on May 25; no cause was given.
Neil Sedaka, 86
Sedaka is responsible for some of the biggest pop songs of the 1960s and 1970s.
The Brooklyn native wrote over 500 songs, including classic hits like "Laughter in the Rain," "Breaking Up Is Hard to Do," "Bad Blood" and the Captain & Tennille song, "Love Will Keep Us Together."
Sedaka died on February 27; no cause was given.
Gene Shalit, 100
Before there was Rotten Tomatoes or even Siskel & Ebert, movie lovers got their recommendations from Gene Shalit.
The iconic movie critic could be seen sporting his signature look of glasses, bushy hair, and big mustache as a staple on the "Today" show from 1973 to 2010. If he wasn't interviewing the biggest movie stars, he was reviewing movies with incredible puns ("'Ishtar' is Ish-terrible.")
His larger-than-life presence left a mark on pop culture: he was parodied as a Muppet and on countless episodes of "SCTV" and "Saturday Night Live."
Shalit died on June 12; no cause was given.
Kiki Shepard, 74
In her 15-year tenure as a co-host on "Showtime at the Apollo," Kiki Shepard was considered royalty at Harlem's famed Apollo Theater.
Known in the building as "Apollo Queen of Fashion" thanks to her dazzling outfits, Shepherd was a fixture on the show from 1987 to 2002.
Throughout her career, Shepard also appeared on TV shows like "Baywatch," "A Different World," "NYPD Blue," and "Grey's Anatomy."
Shepard died on March 16 after suffering a heart attack.
Béla Tarr, 70
Hungarian filmmaker Béla Tarr became a legend in the arthouse world for his unflinching work featuring several-minute-long takes.
With movies like "Family Nest" (1979) and "The Turin Horse" (2011), Tarr showcased his slow cinema style while focusing on marginalized characters living bleak lives. Tarr pushed the envelope with his style when he made "Sátántangó" in 1994, which had a run time of 450 minutes.
His work influenced several arthouse filmmakers, including Jim Jarmusch and Gus Van Sant's "Death Trilogy" ("Gerry," "Elephant," and "Last Days").
Tarr died on January 6 following a battle with a "long and serious illness."
James Tolkan, 94
You might not recognize the name, but if you're a movie fan, you know the face.
Tolkan's tough-guy persona made a mark on movie history in films like "Top Gun" and the "Back to the Future" franchise.
In "Top Gun," he played Commander Tom "Stinger" Jardian, who famously gives Tom Cruise's character a tongue lashing, saying, "Your ego is writing checks your body can't cash."
In "Back to the Future" and its sequels, he played Principal Strickland, who had zero tolerance for "slackers."
Other credits include "Serpico," "WarGames," "Masters of the Universe," and "Dick Tracy."
Tolkan died on March 26; no cause was given.
Ted Turner, 87
Ted Turner changed the television landscape thanks to his maverick maneuvers to harness the 24-hour news cycle.
After taking over his father's advertising company in the 1960s at the age of 24, Turner embarked on a path to change the media landscape by buying up radio and TV stations around the South. He even bought sports teams including the Atlanta Braves MLB team and the Atlanta Hawks NBA team.
All of that programming would eventually become part of TBS, a "super station" that showed old movies, reruns, and Braves and Hawks games.
Turner then set his sights on the news. He founded CNN, the first 24-hour news channel, in June of 1980.
Over the decades, Turner gained celebrity status, particularly after marrying with Jane Fonda, a union that lasted from 1991 to 2001. In 1991, he was named Time's "Man of the Year." He sold his networks to Time Warner for $7.5 billion in 1996.
Turner died on May 6; no cause was given.
Bonnie Tyler, 75
Welsh singer Bonnie Tyler became one of the biggest artists of the 1980s thanks to her legendary power ballads.
Tyler was behind hits like "Total Eclipse of the Heart" and "Holding Out for a Hero," which was also featured on the 1984 "Footloose" soundtrack. Both songs were chart-toppers that have since become two of the best-selling singles of all time.
Over her career, Tyler was nominated for three Grammys and was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE) by Queen Elizabeth II in 2022.
Tyler died on July 8 in Portugal, where she was being treated for an illness, according to a statement posted on her social media.
James Van Der Beek, 48
Van Der Beek was beloved all over the world for his role as the titular teen Dawson Leery on the WB series "Dawson's Creek."
The series, which ran from 1998 to 2002, turned Van Der Beek into a star and a teen heartthrob. While "Dawson's Creek" was still airing, he'd cement his stardom playing the lead role of high school quarterback "Mox" Moxon in the 1999 coming-of-age drama "Varsity Blues."
Van Der Beek found steady work the rest of his career in movies like "Texas Rangers" and "The Rules of Attraction, and memorably played a fictional version of himself on the TV series "Don't Trust the B---- in Apartment 23," and performed on "Dancing with the Stars" in 2019.
Van Der Beek learned he had stage 3 colon cancer in 2023, and publicly announced his diagnosis in late 2024.
Van Der Beek previously told Business Insider that the news came as a shock, given the subtleness of his symptoms and his efforts to stay as healthy as possible.
"I was doing everything," he said. "I was doing sauna, cold plunge, weightlifting, Pilates. I would dance and also do football training."
Van Der Beek died on Feb. 11.
Bob Weir, 78
Weir was one of the founding members of the Grateful Dead.
The singer-songwriter wrote and/or sang on songs like "Sugar Magnolia," "Playing in the Band," "Truckin,'" "I Need a Miracle," and "The Other One."
After the Grateful Dead disbanded in 1995, Weir went on to form several other bands, including Kingfish, Bobby and the Midnites, RatDog, The Other Ones, and, alongside John Mayer, Dead & Company.
In the summer of 2025, Weir was diagnosed with cancer.
Weir died on January 10.
Victor Willis, 74
Willis was the lead singer of the iconic disco band the Village People.
Along with being the lead vocalist and dressing as the police officer (and sometimes naval officer), Willis was also the cowriter on many of the band's hits, including "In the Navy," "Macho Man," and the song that will keep the Village People in pop culture lore until the end of time, "Y.M.C.A."
Willis left the band to embark on a solo career in 1979, then re-formed the Village People in 2017.
Willis died on June 30 following a "short but aggressive illness," according to the Village People Facebook page.
Frederick Wiseman, 96
For over five decades, Wiseman's brand of non-fiction storytelling put a spotlight on everyday people.
From high schoolers to hospital workers to Air Force cadets training for nuclear war, Wiseman's close to 50-film catalogue is an unvarnished reflection of America over the last half century.
Wiseman died on Februay 16, no cause was given.

Waymo is expanding to Germany, with service in Munich planned for 2027
The company has set up subsidiaries in several European countries this summer.
Waymo is quickly expanding to more territories and Germany is next on the list. The company is bringing its vehicles to Munich and it aims to start commercial service in the city — its first location in the European Union — by the end of 2027.
It will start deploying its robotaxis in the city, which is the third-largest in Germany, in the coming weeks to map local streets and begin testing with safety drivers behind the wheel. Waymo said it's working with local, state and federal officials to obtain the permits it needs to offer fully autonomous rides in Munich next year.
This is the second European country that Waymo is moving into. The company aims to start offering rides to the public in London as soon as next month. It's not stopping there, though. Waymo has established subsidiaries in several European nations in recent months, including France, Spain and the Netherlands. Those were all set up in June, around the same time as its German office. Waymo also confirmed to Zag Daily this month that it has registered a subsidiary in Switzerland.

Normal deliveries are declining and C-section deliveries remain high at the Government Hospital for Women and Children at Kottaparamba in Kozhikode City, Keralam.
According to the Health department, there were a total of 5,201 deliveries (2,729 normal and 2,472 C-section) in 2020-21. This number came down to 2,238 (1,387 normal and 851 C-section) in 2025-26. A large number of people from the urban areas of Kozhikode are dependant on this hospital.
The data also reveal that between 2020-21 and 2022-23, a high number of deliveries were in the C-section category. In 2020-21, of the 5,201 deliveries, 2,472 were C-section; in 2021-22, of the 3,552 deliveries, 1,841 were C-section; and in 2022-23, of the 2,205 deliveries, 1,148 were C-section.
Though there were fewer C-section deliveries between 2023-24 and 2025-26, the percentage remained higher than the ideal population-level rate, between 10% and 15%, as suggested by the World Health Organisation. It is even higher than the national average of 21.5%, claims Satheesh Parannur, chairman of the Kozhikode-based rights organisation, Pouravakasha Samrakshana Samithi, who gathered the data through a Right to Information Act (RTI) query.
Mr. Parannur says that between 2020-21 and 2023-24, the number of total deliveries came down by 61% from 5,201 to 2,019. Though this number slightly went up to 2,238 in 2025-26, it was fewer than what was reported in 2020.
The RTI data show that in-patient admission dropped from 8,315 to 4,683 between 2020-21 and 2023-24. The next year, 5,089 people were admitted. The number again dropped to 4,838 in 2025-26. Meanwhile, a high number of people are seeking outpatient (OP) treatment. In 2020-21, a total of 81,329 people sought OP treatment and in 2024-25, this went up to 1,55,257 and slightly declined to 1,50,305 in 2025-26.
Inquiry sought
Mr. Parannur claims that though a large number of people could be approaching the hospital for medical check-up and medicines, at least some are not willing to get admitted there for deliveries.
He says the Health department should conduct a detailed inquiry into the decline in the number of deliveries and IP admission.

Manga-inspired theme park to be built near Paris
- Published
Three theme parks will be built near Paris as part of a €6bn (£5.13bn) deal agreed between France and Saudi Arabia.
The new development is expected to include a manga-themed park, inspired by the popular Japanese franchise Dragon Ball Z.
French President Emmanuel Macron hailed the move as on a scale not seen "since Disneyland Paris", and added "you know my interest for manga".
An opening date for the parks - which will be built near Cergy-Pontoise - has not set by the Élysée Palace, but they will open in stages and construction is expected to take years.
The project was given the green light during a two-day state visit to France by Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
It stemmed from a previous discussion between Macron and bin Salman about their shared passion for Japanese comics, "in particular Dragon Ball Z," advisers to the president told reporters on Monday.
Macron is known to be a manga fan and earlier this year ended a press briefing with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi by doing a hand gesture from the Dragon Ball series.
The project will be led by Qiddiya Investment Company (QIC) - part of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund - which previously revealed plans in 2024 to build a Dragon Ball theme park near the country's capital, Riyadh.
According to local reports, the theme parks could be built on the site of the former Mirapolis park in Val-d'Oise, which closed 35 years ago.

Ask a sixteen-year-old about a social media ban, and you get an answer sharper than most adults arguing about bans. She says, “It doesn’t prepare us for the real world when we will have to deal with these distractions in our life”. The teenager’s response strikes at the core of the ban vs. no ban debate: the necessity to teach and develop self-regulation.
The argument for and against bans
Lawmakers banning social media are working from the angle that if we remove the option altogether, the posting, compulsive scrolling, and ensuing anxiety will go away with it. The opposing argument is that bans prevent self-regulation, built through practice with social media access readily available.
Behavioral science has a fairly precise answer for which of these arguments holds up.
The bans themselves are moving fast and in earnest around the world. Australia was the first country to impose a sweeping ban on social media outright for children under-16 in 2025. Multiple countries in the EU are attempting to follow suit. These decisions to ban social media rest on neuroscientific insights showing that the human brain’s reward circuitry matures years before the prefrontal cortex that reins it in, leaving adolescents genuinely more vulnerable to engineered design working actively to grab their attention. Lawmakers are right to take this seriously.
But are social media bans for teenagers the panacea that they are made out to be?
How social media functions
Social media platforms function like a Skinner box for the modern human: our engagement on them runs on the same reinforcement-based learning as B. F. Skinner’s animal experiments. People on social media post faster exactly when their recent rate of reward, meaning engagement, has been higher. A pattern known as the law of effect, more ‘likes’ leads to more posting. Engagement on every platform runs on an unpredictable schedule; we never know which posts are going to land. Rewards are also hyper-personalised: an unending carousel of perfectly-matched content delivered based on every prior click and scroll.
What makes matters worse is that social media’s unpredictable and personalised rewards are exactly the training that will make children persist on these platforms through the interruption that comes from a ban. When there are multiple ways to get on social media, our behavior distributes itself across those options in proportion to the corresponding rewards. Think of a building with many entrances: remove one entrance without touching the others and people will continue to be able to get in. Underlying behavior does not vanish; It simply reallocates to a different mode. If a regular account stops working, we create a bustling market for fake accounts and new platforms not covered by the bans, effectively pushing teenagers to unregulated corners of the internet.
Perhaps predictably so, Australia’s ban, sweeping on paper, is showing that an estimated 85% of children under-16 are still finding their way onto restricted platforms, through borrowed logins and fake accounts, in a recent study. Bans are leaky. Short of closing every door at once, children will simply find the ones still open. But setting up strict age verification measures can be seen as an infringement upon teenagers’ rights to a private life, one of the reasons France’s newly-enacted social media ban was recently struck down by their Constitution Council.
In any case, let’s assume we manage to pull off the most stringent enforcement of a ban. Children with support systems in place will now have time to learn skills, build hobbies, and form real relationships. What happens to the vulnerable teenagers without a supportive home environment? A ban restricts access, but it does not fix the environment around the child. For teenagers building their sense of autonomy, that restriction in itself can cause harm.
In April, a commentary drawing on a year-long international working group on digital safety noted that bans are “unlikely to be effective” because they overlook how social platforms can be redesigned to build resilience, and instead place all the onus on teenagers. A nuanced solution is one that addresses the problem from both sides.
What, then, can work?
Nobel Prize winner Richard Thaler coined the term ‘nudge’ to describe choices that reshape the environment. When workers avoided retirement plans, a nudge that automatically enrolled them in superannuation funds profoundly impacted their savings. On social media, forcing platforms to batch-deliver notifications into fixed windows instead of letting them arrive at all times, and adding friction to sharing sensitive content, and disabling autoplay and infinite-scroll by default are nudges. We mandate structural corrections on the platform side. A boost, on the other hand, gives young people the skills to manage their own actions instead of complete restriction. The option to use social media stays available. Decision rules around time on social media, and encouraging goal-setting for healthier digital habits are examples of boosts.
Which brings us back to that 16-year-old. She was right: a ban will not teach her self-regulation. But unfettered access to social media where she is left to fend for herself will not work either. What she actually needs is a nuanced alternative, one that is, unfortunately, not on offer in her school’s policy.
(Maithri Sivaraman is an assistant professor at Teachers College, Columbia University. maithri.sivaraman@tc.columbia.edu)

The Productivity Commission has condemned attacks on its integrity as “unacceptable” after its scathing assessment of Western Australia’s sweetheart GST deal as a costly mistake sparked a fierce political backlash and name-calling.
Angela Jackson, a productivity commissioner and co-author of the report, said the country’s leading independent economic advisory body welcomed criticism and comments on its work.
But Jackson said comments from Roger Cook, the Western Australian premier, lampooning the commission as “east coast clowns” and describing the report as deceitful had “crossed a line”.
Cook said in a statement: “I’m doing exactly what I’ll always do and putting WA first”, adding that “it is important we continue to present our economic arguments”.
“To the Productivity Commission it may be academic but for Western Australians it’s our lives, and I’ll fight for every dollar.”
As Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, defended the “good people” at the commission and chided the WA Labor leader for his “inappropriate” language, Jackson said “we are used to public debate”.
“In fact, we welcome it at the Productivity Commission, it’s why we have interim reports,” she told ABC radio before a meeting of national cabinet on Wednesday afternoon.
“We are aiming, of course, to inform public policy debate, which can often get heated. Our view is that a line was crossed in terms of the nature of those comments from the Western Australian premier.”
Jackson linked the tone of the criticism and the language used “to attack our integrity” with “something that more broadly we are seeing in public debate internationally”.
“We want to call this out as being unacceptable.”
When asked about Cook’s sledge, Chalmers told journalists on Wednesday: “I don’t believe that is appropriate.”
“I think you can disagree with the conclusions of the Productivity Commission without denigrating them. I think it’s important that even when those conclusions are contested, as they often will be, that we continue to respect the people of the PC and the really important work that they do.”
The commission was asked to review the 2018 legislation put in place under the Morrison government.
That deal fundamentally changed the way the commonwealth distributed the GST pool between the states and territories.
The commission’s interim report found that the 2018 legislation had achieved none of its objectives, made the system less fair and had funnelled an extra $23bn in taxpayer money to the nation’s richest state.
The interim recommendation to reverse the deal was backed by all other states and territories, but was immediately declared dead in the water by Anthony Albanese.
“What I believe is, very clearly, there will be no change to WA GST arrangements whilst I’m prime minister,” Albanese said on Monday.
Jackson said Albanese’s comments were “disappointing at this point in the process”.
The PC will now do further consultation before a final report due by the end of this year.
“It’s important for us to indicate that that process will not be influenced by the prime minister’s comments, that we are above politics,” Jackson said.
“And that’s a very important position that we hold within the public policy landscape in Australia.”
Independent MP Allegra Spender said it was “frustrating” that Albanese had effectively ruled out any changes to WA’s GST deal before the independent inquiry had run its course.
“When Roger Cook calls highly qualified and capable public servants ‘clowns’ he is seeking to disparage people tasked with giving government frank advice,” Spender said.
“You may disagree with their views, but this kind of language directed at public servants is simply unacceptable from major public figures.”
She added that it was also “disappointing to hear the federal resources minister [Madeleine King] describe these comments as ‘fair enough’ on radio yesterday”.
On Wednesday, the industry and science minister, Tim Ayres, said there were “strong views” about the GST issue in WA, and a “colourful contest” about the issue when asked about Cook’s comments.
“The Productivity Commission has important work to do for Australia, and we’re not a government that gets reports that contest our view and has a glass jaw about that,” Ayres told the ABC.
Ayres claimed WA was a state with “particular needs” and defended Albanese ruling out any GST changes even before the PC’s final report.
“[Albanese] gets Western Australia, understands what Western Australians need and the contribution that they make. And everything he’s done has been completely consistent with that view and it should have surprised nobody.”
Cook’s office has been approached for comment.

'101-year-old great-grandmother' arrested for selling cannabis in Nigeria
- Published
An elderly woman, who the authorities say is 101, has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly selling cannabis, in a case that has drawn widespread attention.
Esther Ogunmabo, described as a great-grandmother, was apprehended on Saturday in Ogun state, in the south-west of the country, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) announced.
Femi Babafemi, the agency's media director, said the centenarian was found with "retail sachets of skunk, a strain of cannabis weighing 90 grams, which she claims she sells to locals".
The NDLEA said the suspect told investigators that she turned to the illicit drug trade after her provisions shop was destroyed by fire. She has been released on bail.
According to the Ndlea, one of her daughters, who lives in Lagos, allegedly arranged for the supply of the substance to her every four days. Ogunmabo is accused of then selling it on in smaller quantities to customers in her community.
Ndlea chief executive Mohamed Marwa directed that the suspect be granted bail and given counselling because of her advanced age.
Ogunmabo’s bail status means she could still be charged for criminal activity.
Her daughter has also been arrested.
Ogunmabo’s arrest came as the Ndlea also reported significant drug seizures along Nigeria's maritime routes.
In Akwa Ibom state, operatives acting on credible intelligence intercepted a wooden boat on the high seas last Friday, which was heading to Cameroon, and arrested three people on board.
More than 42kg of narcotics were recovered from the suspects.
In what the agency described as a milestone, the Ndlea also recorded its first-ever seizure of illicit drugs shipped from Thailand.

Suwadi can barely see five metres in front of him when he steps outside his home in Indonesian Borneo.
Each breath, he says, feels “like smoking a cigarette”.
It has been like this for weeks in Kalimantan, the Indonesian side of Borneo island, where fires have raged across tens of thousands of acres of land, including ancient rainforest, triggering a trans-boundary haze now threatening Malaysia and Singapore.
In West Kalimantan there has been a spike in emergency room visits, with about 5,000 people arriving with respiratory symptoms each week since July, compared with 500 per week in the first half of the year, health ministry data shows.
Children continue to go to school and adults to work, but many are suffering from the unhealthy effects of breathing in thick smoke, constantly. “What about babies, the elderly, and pregnant women who are exposed to this?” asks Suwadi.
Some classes have been suspended, with parents urging schools to switch to online learning.
Fires each year in Kalimantan are often blamed on “slash and burn” techniques used to clear land for plantations that produce palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer.
Authorities say this year’s “super” El Niño may be intensifying the blazes, with the weather phenomenon expected to peak in September.
Experts have warned the worst could be yet to come as the dry season continues into October, and the rains that could extinguish the fires look unlikely before November.
The haze is fast becoming a regional issue, with Malaysia and Brunei agreeing to raise it at Asean as thick smoke from forest and peatland fires drifts across the border.
On Tuesday, the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, was the most polluted city on earth, followed by Jakarta, according to air quality monitoring company IQAir. Almost 600 schools in the Malaysian state of Sarawak on Borneo island closed due to hot and dry conditions. Singapore went on alert.
On social media, Indonesians have tried to draw attention to the issue – highlighting the huge blazes in Kalimantan, and also in Sumatra, West Papua, and in Lombok where a fire destroyed a traditional Sade village over the weekend.
Forestry ministry data shows that nearly 94,000 hectares (232,000 acres) have burned nationwide this July alone.
On Monday, the Indonesian president, Prabowo Subianto, ordered authorities to revoke the business permits of corporations suspected of directing the land clearing, state news agency Antara reported. Indonesian police arrested 72 people suspected of starting fires in Borneo and Sumatra, with most accused of deliberately burning land to clear areas for plantations.
The response comes as regional experts fear this could be another devastating fire year, with many of Indonesia’s most severe blazes occurring during El Niño cycles. In 2015, another El Niño year, more than 6m acres were burned, with trans-boundary haze again plaguing neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore.
During a recent visit to the region, Prabowo promised government resources to contain the fires, including helicopters and water pumps.
But some Indonesians have expressed frustration at what they see as government inaction against the companies allegedly involved.
Indonesia’s unique rainforests are home to peatland ecosystems, which should be naturally resilient to fire when water tables remain high.
However, drainage networks built to clear land for pulp and oil palm plantations have robbed the soil of its natural capacity to retain water, experts say.
Fires on degraded peatlands are more difficult to control because they burn deep underground, says Justin Sentian, a professor in climate change at Universiti Malaysia Sabahand. And they produce thick, acrid smoke.
“If authorities only act after hotspots appear, they will forever be playing catch-up,” says Sentian. “True prevention must address the soil itself by halting the conversion of peatlands and actively restoring degraded areas.”
On Monday another fire broke out near the factory where Suwadi works in Kalimantan. With houses burning and smoke everywhere, Suwadi says he is afraid for the future of the region.
“The fire is getting dangerously close to homes,” he says, “People are [in] panic now.”
