90,000 forced to flee as raging Reno wildfire tears through neighborhoods
Crews have started to contain a wildfire in the Sierra Nevada foothills near Reno, Nevada
Firefighters are gaining ground on a fast-moving wildfire near Reno, Nevada, after flames destroyed more than 30 homes and forced tens of thousands of residents to evacuate or prepare to flee.
The Hawk Fire was 27% contained Monday after holding at roughly 23 square miles following a dangerous surge over the weekend, officials said.
“We are making progress,” U.S. Forest Service District Ranger Matt Zumstein said.
Evacuation orders and warnings remained in place for about 63,000 residents, down from more than 90,000 at the height of the fire. Officials warned that shifting winds could still send flames through dry vegetation toward residential neighborhoods.
At least 32 homes have been destroyed and six damaged, though authorities expect those numbers to rise as assessment teams reach more burned areas. Seven people — three first responders and four civilians — have been injured.
Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve described the speed and intensity of the flames as unlike anything she had witnessed.
“It lit up these areas like nothing I’ve seen before,” she said. “It took your breath away, in the worst way.”
The fire began Saturday near the California border before exploding in size Sunday. Nevada's governor declared a state of emergency and deployed the National Guard to assist with aerial firefighting operations and secure evacuated neighborhoods northwest of downtown Reno.
Schools across Washoe County were closed Monday to keep roads clear for emergency crews.
Some residents have grown frustrated over restrictions preventing them from returning home, but Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam warned that conditions remain dangerous.
“It just takes that little breeze and one ember,” he said.
Officials said the Hawk Fire is the third major wildfire north of Reno in two weeks. All three were caused by human activity, though authorities have not determined whether the Hawk Fire was started accidentally or deliberately.
The disaster has also complicated preparations for Burning Man, which is scheduled to begin Sunday in the Black Rock Desert. Many festivalgoers traditionally travel through Reno on their way to the event.
Burning Man organizers urged visitors not to take hotel rooms or other resources needed by people displaced by the fire.
“Treat our neighbors, first responders, hospitality workers and everyone affected by this emergency with patience and care,” organizers said.
For some residents, the devastation has been painfully familiar.
Crystal Hallock, 53, lost her home to fire for the second time in less than a decade. An electrical fire destroyed her previous home in 2018, and she moved into the rebuilt property the following year.
Hallock fled Saturday with her children, grandchildren and pets as smoke and flames approached. Her ex-husband remained behind trying to protect the property and her vintage Cadillac with a garden hose.
As conditions deteriorated, Hallock pleaded with him over the phone to leave.
“He was saying he can’t breathe, it’s so dark I can’t see, and I’m screaming at him, ‘Leave the car, just leave it,’” she recalled.
The call suddenly went dead.
About 30 minutes later, he called again. He had escaped — and managed to save the Cadillac.
“I’m truly blessed because I have a place to stay with my animals and my grandkids,” Hallock said. “We were all able to get out safely.”
Others had little time to gather their possessions.
“Honestly, I thought it was like in a movie,” said Ruby Delatorre, who returned from a concert to find her neighborhood under evacuation orders.
Another resident, Jon Hanbury, was still waiting Monday to learn whether his home had survived.
“The flames were pretty close to my house, and the smoke was really thick,” he said from a temporary shelter at Reno's convention center.
Despite improving containment, the danger is not over. Warm, dry and breezy weather is expected across western Nevada, with critical fire conditions possible later this week.
The Hawk Fire comes during a punishing wildfire season across the West. More than 50,000 wildfires have been recorded nationwide this year, the highest number at this point in a decade, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

In Summary
- The iQOO Z11 is the latest device in iQOO’s mid-segment Z series.
- The phone comes with a curved display, a sleek design, and specs and features that make it a solid mid-segmenter.
- At its starting price of Rs 34,999, the iQOO Z11 is a great option for those who want a phone that is capable of handling most tasks and has flaunt value too.
iQOO’s latest mid-segmenter sports sleek curves of the display sort, packs in decent, entertainment-friendly specs, manages to squeeze a big battery into a slim frame, and tops it all with a generous serving of AI. But will all this be enough for the iQOO Z11 to click with its target audience in a time of rising prices and declining specs? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
iQOO Z11 looks and appearance: Curved display and a Pixel-like camera bar
The iQOO Z11 is a tall, slim phone that will turn heads with its appearance. It sports a curved display in front and also has curved sides, while on the back is a camera bar that reminds us of the Google Pixel. It is a tall phone at 164.4 mm, although it is very slim at just 7.99 mm, and surprisingly light for its size at just 199 grams – that’s taller, and yet lighter and slimmer than the iPhone 17 Pro Max. The front is smooth glass while the back and sides are made of polycarbonate, but they can be easily mistaken for metal or glass. The camera bar on the back is made of aluminum, which gives the phone a very premium feel. It comes with IP68/69 dust and water resistance, so it can easily survive a fall in the water, and has a very reassuringly solid feel to it.
The iQOO Z11 comes in Celestial Blue and Aurora Green shades. Both have a subtly shiny look that shimmers and changes shades in the light, and also have matte finishes that do not smudge or stain easily. We got the Aurora Green shade. This phone has flaunt value without being loud – the curved display and the camera bar give it slim and tall Pixel vibes, which is not a bad thing at all.
iQOO Z11 Spec Sheet and Hardware: Solidly upper mid-segment
The iQOO Z11 comes with a 6.83-inch AMOLED display with a resolution of 2800 x 1260 and a refresh rate of 144 Hz, which is rare at this price point. Sound is handled by a pair of stereo speakers. The phone is the first in the Indian market to be powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 7500 Ultra processor, which is supposed to be a steady performer with some gaming ability as well. This is paired with RAM and storage variants of 6 GB/ 128 GB, 8 GB/ 128 GB, 8 GB/ 256 GB, and 12 GB/ 256 GB. The RAM is LPDDR4X, while the storage is UFS 3.1, which are, like the processor, not top of the line, but actually very capable. The camera bar on the back has a 50-megapixel main Sony IMX882 sensor with OIS, accompanied by an 8-megapixel ultrawide, while selfie and video call duties are handled by a 32-megapixel front-facing camera. In spite of being very slim, the iQOO Z11 comes with a large 7025 mAh battery with support for 44W charging, and a 44W charger in the box.
The iQOO Z11 runs on OriginOS 6 on top of Android 16 and comes with an assurance of three years of Android upgrades and five years of security patches. Once again, that’s par for the course for the segment. The phone also comes with not only a number of AI tools (apart from Google’s standard Gemini suite), but also with unlimited AI credits for AI captions and AI creations using iQOO’s tools, basically allowing consumers to use them without restrictions, which is rare to see at this price.
iQOO Z11 cameras: Colorfully pleasant mostly
Photography on the iQOO Z11 is largely a single-camera show – something that is beginning to become the rule in this price segment. The 50-megapixel main camera takes very pleasant snaps with ample detail. Purists might feel that the images come with slightly saturated colors, but mainstream users are unlikely to complain. Even low-light and night photography is impressively colorful. We would suggest shooting videos in the daylight, though, as low-light videos are not the best.
The front camera takes good selfies, with plenty of beautification and skin smoothing by default, although these can be toned down. The ultrawide camera is basically good for a different perspective, but its quality is not the greatest. Portraits are impressive, but lossless zoom is limited to 2x, while digital zoom goes up to 10x. There are plenty of shooting and editing options to let one do more with images, but this is a phone for casual point-and-shooters rather than enthusiasts.
iQOO Z11 performance: Doing it all well, instead of doing a few things brilliantly
The iQOO Z11 is one of the rare phones out there that does many things well. The combination of that large display and very good stereo speakers makes it a great phone for viewing content, whether it is viewing shows and films, reels, or just browsing the Web. The 7050 mAh battery comfortably keeps going for a day and a half of normal use, and the 44W charger gets the phone from empty to full in about 70-75 minutes, with half an hour generally being enough to take the phone up to 50 percent (which is enough to see off a day of use).
The Dimensity 7500 Ultra sails through routine tasks effortlessly, and we were able to switch between 6-10 apps quite easily without any lag. While the phone is not a gaming beast, we were able to play titles like Call of Duty and Asphalt after a few minor tweaks, and even Genshin Impact (with graphics toned down) ran well on the phone. The display and speakers again play key roles here. The phone never heated up excessively either, no matter what we burdened it with.
iQOO Z11 Software and UI: Unlimited AI
OriginOS 6 runs smoothly on the iQOO Z11, and there are plenty of AI tools to play around with. AI Creation is a powerful writing tool, and AI Transcript Assist works perfectly for those who love to have written records of meetings, classes, or lectures (do double-check names, though). There are also tools for AI translation, summaries, and more. They all work very smoothly indeed (though you need to log in to an iQOO account and have an Internet connection for most), with many coming with unlimited usage – something college-goers and AI addicts on a tight budget will appreciate. Of course, one also gets Google’s AI tools such as Gemini and Circle to Search.
While there is some bloatware (most of which can be uninstalled), there are a number of handy utilities and features too, including iQOO DocMaster, which lets one work with multiple document formats, the Dynamic Island-like Origin Island, and the ability to easily share information with not just Android but also iOS devices. The software seems to be a little overwhelming, but is extremely useful once one gets the hang of it. And works smoothly most of the time.
iQOO Z11 Review Verdict: Great for those who want a do-it-all, which also looks good
The iQOO Z11 is available in the following RAM and storage configurations at these prices:
6 GB/ 128 GB: Rs 34,999
8 GB/ 128 GB: Rs 39,999
8 GB/ 256 GB: Rs 44,999
12 GB/ 256 GB: Rs 49,999
Given the trend of insanely high prices, these are extremely competitive. In fact, although some might frown at the relatively modest RAM in the base 6 GB/ 128 GB model, the fact that it is priced below Rs 35,000 could tempt many users. Even at its higher price points, its combination of design, specs, and performance makes it very good value for money at a time when prices are increasing dramatically.
It is this unique cocktail of features that lets the iQOO Z11 hold its own against some very tough competition. The Moto Edge 70 Pro has a more powerful processor and cameras with a higher megapixel count but loses out in the looks department and has a smaller battery. The Redmi Turbo 5 brings a quirky design and a powerful chip to the table but has a smaller display. Another contender is the OnePlus Nord CE6, which comes with a huge battery and a good processor, but loses out in the camera and design stakes.
This tick-all-boxes versatility sums up the iQOO Z11. It may not be the very best in any performance category, but there is actually very little that it cannot do. Want a quick gaming session? It will handle it. Want to check or post on social media? It will handle it. Want to binge-watch shows? It has got your back. Want to send images and videos to your iPhone-carrying friends? It can do that too. Want to get notes and summaries? Its AI will chip in, but it does the job.
The iQOO Z11 is very much a generalist, rather than a specialist in any field. It is a masterly jack of all trades. And a very good-looking one too. One of the best all-rounders you can get for under Rs 40,000 right now.

- Smooth performance
- Very good stereo speakers
- Lots of AI features (some with unlimited usage)
- Good main camera
- IP68/69 rating
- Ordinary ultrawide camera
- Bloatware in OS
- Competition has faster chips and memory

Rumours swirled after a Vietnamese teen was run over - then came a stunning admission
- Published
Until recently, there would have been little to distinguish Vietnam's so-called Justice Tree from the hundreds of others lining the streets of Hanoi. Then the bouquets started piling up.
It was here that former politician Nguyen Sy Cuong was driving his BMW in May last year when he veered into the opposite lane and smashed into a motorbike carrying a father and his teenage daughter.
The father, Do Viet Hung, suffered a broken leg but survived. The daughter, 18-year-old Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy, died in hospital 10 days after the collision which severed her right leg.
Fifteen months later, her death, and the silence surrounding it, has become a lightning rod for discontent among Vietnam's youth.
In early August, a legion of anonymous social media users started publishing millions of posts with the hashtags #NguyenSyCuong and #BMW across Facebook, Instagram, Threads and X. The users identified themselves as Gen Z – and they demanded accountability.
Initial discussions circled around whether the former politician was in fact the one who had caused the accident, and why authorities had only released sparse information.
Some pointed to reports that the driver of the BMW had the initials NSC and was born in 1961, leading to speculation that he was a former member of parliament. Others claimed the incident had been swept under the rug due to the influence of powerful figures. Many reported that their posts had been deleted by social media platforms at the request of the Vietnamese government – providing screenshots of notifications as evidence. These claims could not be independently verified.
Expressions of outrage and calls for a proper investigation grew in number, volume and force.
Meanwhile, masked flower bearers started to appear, gravitating towards the scene of the incident and laying vibrant bouquets at the base of what has now been dubbed the Justice Tree. Police quickly arrived to get rid of the flowers, prompting mourners to create a virtual equivalent of the tree online - where hundreds of thousands of people have since sent tributes and paid respects.
Pressurised by more than a year's worth of growing suspicion and a rush of online attention, the issue had become too big to ignore.
Then, last Monday, the government made an extraordinary admission.
State broadcaster Vietnam Television (VTV) televised an official statement from authorities, confirming what had happened on the day of the incident. Former National Assembly deputy Nguyen Sy Cuong was indeed driving his car down Nguyen Huy Tu Street on 30 May, 2025, when his vehicle suddenly swerved across the road and into an oncoming motorcycle.
VTV cited police and prosecution sources who said that because Nguyen Sy Cuong "sincerely confessed and actively and fully remedied the consequences of his actions", Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's family had submitted a petition to exempt him from prosecution. The report did not specify what form this remedy took, but Nguyen Sy Cuong was cleared of all criminal liability.
While such a decision is lawful under Vietnam's legislation, lawyers have questioned whether the criminal proceedings were conducted in accordance with due process – or conducted at all. Social media users were quick to highlight his political connections and call for a more thorough investigation.
Such online pressure had yielded results in the past.
In March this year, a 66-year-old man driving under the influence of alcohol in Hanoi collided with seven other cars and three motorcycles in a chain-reaction crash that killed one woman and seriously injured two others.
In the wake of that incident, it emerged that the driver, Nguyen Van Sau, was a retired police colonel who had previously served as deputy director of a department under the Ministry of Public Security. Fearing that the driver was not being held culpable, the victim's family appealed for help. Social media users in turn amplified the issue, and after three months Nguyen Van Sau was charged with "violating regulations on participation in road traffic".

  - Published23 January
- British teen dies in reported Vietnam motorbike fall 
  - Published8 April
Many now feel that a similar groundswell may be the only way to deliver justice for the teenager who died last year. But their efforts have been met with friction.
Do Viet Hung, the teenager's father, appeared in VTV's broadcast to thank internet users for their sympathy, but said the family was satisfied with the investigation's findings, and asked people to leave them alone. Notably, he also warned people "not to be drawn into the influence of reactionary elements".
Also appearing in the broadcast was a senior police official, who suggested that people were leveraging the incident to stoke dissent.
The Ministry of Public Security had "uncovered highly dangerous plots and intentions by hostile forces, reactionaries and bad actors to incite unrest and cause disorder", the official said.
"The ministry advises the public, especially young people, to remain fully alert and highly vigilant."
Similar rebukes have also started emerging on social media, with some claiming that conspiratorial forces were manipulating young people in Vietnam to stoke political discontent, manipulate public opinion online and rally people in real life ahead of the country's national holiday on 2 September.
Others have accused Gen Z Vietnamese of plotting a "colour revolution" – a term used to refer to mostly nonviolent protest movements that use specific colours or flowers as their symbol.
This is a familiar line of critique from Vietnamese authorities, who have previously labelled people's grievances or resentments as being untrue, unreasonable, or stemming from information fabricated by some "anti-government" or "reactionary" organisation.
Many in this case have said such accusations are baseless, insisting they are simply seeking justice for the victim of a fatal traffic accident. But the growing outrage has inevitably become a flashpoint amid broader, simmering grievances felt by Vietnam's youth.
Despite the Vietnamese government's tightening control over people's online freedom of expression – through measures ranging from intimidation and fines to criminal prosecution – public opinion in some corners has started to swerve against the Communist Party line.
On platforms such as Threads and Reddit, where anonymity is more normalised, many young people have expressed discontent towards various social issues: from the expansion of police power and land reclamation projects to exam cheating scandals and stricter regulation of online communication.
Such grievances echo those condemned by other Gen Z-led movements across the broader Asia region.
In countries like Bangladesh, India and Nepal, youth-led anti-government uprisings have over the past 12 months rallied immense support against the various pressure points of corruption, nepotism, economic inequality and democratic backsliding. Unofficially dubbed "the Asian Spring", the expanding influence of these movements has spread from Iran, Mongolia and the Maldives to the Philippines and Timor-Leste.
But protests in Vietnam have rarely, if ever, reached such fierce extremes. Vietnamese authorities have historically proven effective at detecting and stifling dissent before it boils over into action. Virtual places of mourning, anonymous social media posts, and online protests seem to be the most strident action many civilians here can afford to take.

Chinese teens are turning to mind-numbing drugs to 'run away from reality'
- Published
At 14, *Xiaomei, a high-performing student from a coastal province in China, decided to overdose on cough medication.
She wanted to impress an older boy who told her it would help her relax. The tablets were usually only available with a doctor's prescription, but she managed to buy them online.
At first she found that they made her a bit dizzy. But she was soon hooked to the slightly numb sensation, which, to her, felt like a brief respite from the pressure of looming exams. When taken in large doses, the drug can cause serious side effects, including hallucinations and impaired coordination.
Eventually she tried other medication recommended to her on chat groups. Some were for pain or epileptic seizures. Sometimes she would take five tablets. Other times she would try more than 10 to feel the effects of different drugs.
For two years, she took large quantities of various prescription drugs. None of them were prescribed to her or anyone in her family. She bought them all on the internet.
"When I felt too much pressure from my studies, or I didn't do well at exams, or even when I quarrelled with my parents, I would take these drugs," she told the BBC. "I was running away from reality."
The BBC has heard similar stories from dozens of Chinese teenagers in chat rooms across various social media platforms. Nearly every one of them seemed to be escaping the same thing: pressure. They were doing that by chasing what is being described as a "pharmaceutical high".
One girl shared a voice note after taking large doses of a neuropathic pain drug. Her words were slurred and hard to comprehend: "I feel my body doesn't belong to me. I'm so dizzy."
“Just sleep," comes the advice. "You will be fine tomorrow."
One boy offered to use his father's old prescription to fake a new one for the same drug.
Some offered tips: "If you want to hallucinate, you can just buy... it's not been controlled yet," says one user, suggesting a drug used by people with Parkinson's to control tremors. In excessive doses it can cause confusion or even delirium.
"Which keyword should I use to search for it on online platforms," another user asks.
It is hard to gauge the scale of the problem, as there are few official figures.
But it is serious enough that the government launched a nationwide crackdown two years ago against the cough suppressant Xiaomei started using, classifying it as a psychotropic drug which would only be available to patients with a doctor's prescription. That made it much harder for young people to buy online.
Then in April this year, authorities noticed that young people had switched to another drug and imposed tighter controls on how it is prescribed and dispensed at chemists. Still the BBC was offered the drug in an online chat room for as little as 10 Chinese yuan ($1.5; £1.09) per gram.
"Non-regulated substances are easy to acquire and even when one drug is controlled by the authorities, young people quickly find alternatives," says a 2025 paper written for the Crime Prevention Institute at the Ministry of Justice.
In some cases the BBC found that teens online were using different names for drugs to avoid detection, which the 2025 study also noted.
There is growing evidence that young people across the world are turning to prescription medication to fight off pressures and anxiety.
So easy access to cheap prescription drugs in China is perhaps not that surprising given that it produces the vast majority of the world's pharmaceutical ingredients.
When Xiaomei wanted to buy the cough suppressant, it just took a few clicks for an entire box of the medication to be delivered at her door, she says. "You could simply enter your ID number on shopping platforms and buy it directly."
The ID, which is a national identity number, includes her age but she says she was still sold the drug, no questions asked. It was also cheap - often 50 tablets cost less than a dollar.
On paper, China is winning the war on illegal drugs. Official data for 2025 shows a dramatic fall - 41% - in newly identified drug users under the age of 35.
However authorities have had to acknowledge that the misuse of prescription drugs is becoming a widespread problem. It has been especially surging among minors, China's National Narcotics Control Commission warned in a recent report.
Xiaomei says that a lot of students in her elite chemistry class were discussing ways to overdose on prescription drugs to avoid feeling like "complete losers".
"It is just so hard to pass exams and to stay in elite classes. In our school, the elite classes operate on an elimination system; if your academic scores drop, you get kicked out of the class. When you fail, you feel like failures, believing you have no chance in life."
Part of the pressure comes from parents who also see their child as their only hope for the future, says renowned Chinese sociologist and director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, Xiang Biao.
Because of the one-child policy which ended in 2016 after decades, many families only have one child, Biao adds, who shoulders all their expectations.
"What makes Chinese teens different is their isolating environment. They spend at least nine or 10 hours in school. They have very few chances to develop social relationships, very few opportunities to witness what life is really like."
More worrying, he sees a link between prescription drug abuse and an increase in self-harm. The BBC noticed, for instance, that in many of the chat rooms, young people would encourage one another to cut themselves "to feel something".
As an extremely competitive high school entrance exam drew close, Xiaomei tried a different drug, searching for ways to numb the anxiety.
"But my memory deteriorated rapidly," she says. "I couldn't remember anything clearly, and I lived in a constant daze."
The drug is usually prescribed to help control epileptic seizures and it works as neuropathic pain medication. When Xiaomei explained the side effects in one of her chat groups, they suggested another drug, which is given as pain relief. She says it gave her some release but she soon needed higher doses.
Months before sitting the important exam, she went too far.
She'd taken 50 tablets and started to panic. "I was afraid something serious might happen, but I didn't want to have my stomach pumped so I wanted to wait before telling my parents."
But she became so unwell that she had to confess.
Her parents decided to listen to what they saw as their daughter's cry for help.
"They mostly expressed how heartbreaking it was for them to see me like that. They didn't scold or criticise me. Their approach was gentle."
For her, this has made all the difference.
"Many children receive lots of attention but the type of attention they want is to be asked how they feel. Do they feel lonely or stressed? Often in China parents brush that away and say you just have to be stronger," Biao says.
"There's a very loud alarm being sounded out across Chinese society. Adults have to examine how to be responsible for a teenager. Having an open conversation as a family - that is probably the most rewarding part of life."
And that is where the real battle lies, according to experts. Rather than playing whack-a-mole trying to suppress online sales of prescription drugs, the government should focus on what may well be a mental health crisis, they say.
In 2023, a study for China's Mental Health Blue Book found that nearly 95 million people suffer from depression and more than 30% were under 18 years old.
The Chinese government has recognised the need for mental health support for teens. Those plans include counselling rooms in every school, psychiatric services in at least one hospital in every county and more mental health professionals. The aim is to build a nationwide system of psychological support and crisis intervention by 2030.
So far they have been quite successful. According to the State Council, 92% of primary schools and 95% of junior middle schools now have a counsellor. Many major cities, including Beijing, have started to incorporate mental health into the curriculum.
However, there is still a major shortage of medical psychiatrists specialising in children and adolescents.
A 2020 study published in British medical journal The Lancet claimed there were only 500 qualified child psychiatrists in the country, and many of them were based in major cities such as Beijing and Shanghai.
This is a huge challenge in a country that has undergone three decades of unprecedented social and economic change.
The China Xiaomei's parents grew up in is very different from the future she is facing. Her parents followed a script set by the Communist Party: work hard and you will be rewarded. Now, even if young adults pass with high grades and get a university degree, a bright future is not guaranteed.
Following gruelling pandemic restrictions, the Chinese economy has struggled to bounce back. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find a job and families are spending less.
"People have become more pessimistic in general," Biao admits. And the anxiety extends to adults, he adds.
"I think parents feel confused and anxious because they see a problem in their children, but they don't see an alternative. If my child has a problem, it's the end of the world. If my child doesn't do well in school, it's the end of the world. If my child doesn't speak to me, it's the end of the world. I think we should pay more attention to parents as well as children."
Fortunately Xiaomei and her parents have managed to find a way to cross this bridge.
"In the past, my parents didn't really understand me and would say some pretty harsh things. I felt like I had no help and was truly on my own," she says.
But that changed when she was rushed to hospital after the overdose. They started listening to her and talking to her, and "knowing that there was someone standing by my side made me feel really good", she says. It even helped her perform well in the entrance exam she had been dreading for so long.
"I am lucky to have their support," she adds.
Not everyone finds such support though, and that's where *Lu Jingchan hopes he can help.
The 22-year-old spent years battling depression. He found it hard to beat the euphoria that came from taking prescription drugs, and overdosed more than four times in four years.
"The drugs drove me to the brink of madness. You risk sinking into an abyss of addiction, destroying your health," he says.
He has now quit all prescription medication, and spends his time on social media urging others not to start. And he has this advice for young people battling the pressures he once did.
"I hope you can face life head-on, without needing medicines to numb yourselves. If you are overdosing, I want to give you the courage to stop. I believe your lives will improve. I believe you will all find happiness."
*Names have been changed to protect their identity

The Union Health Ministry has proposed amendments to the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, to promote ease of doing business. The amendments seek to simplify regulatory requirements, standardise testing fees and facilitate faster market access for eligible medical devices.
The Centre has eased regulatory requirements for medical device manufacturers by removing the need for a separate licence for outsourced sterilisation and expanding the list of countries and regulatory jurisdictions whose approvals can facilitate waiver of clinical investigation requirements in India, a release issued by the Ministry said on Monday (August 24, 2026).
Under the proposed amendment to Rule 44, manufacturers that outsource sterilisation of their medical devices to a facility holding a valid licence under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, will no longer have to obtain a separate loan licence for the sterilisation activity.
Earlier, manufacturers had to secure a separate loan licence even when the outsourced sterilisation facility itself held a valid licence. The government said removing the duplication would reduce paperwork, administrative burden and compliance costs, particularly for manufacturers without their own sterilisation facilities.
However, a traceability requirement has been retained. Manufacturers will have to mention the licence number of the sterilisation facility on the medical device label. A six-month transition period has been provided to allow companies to modify labels, packaging and related processes.
The government said the change was intended to balance regulatory oversight with ease of doing business by retaining traceability while simplifying the licensing framework.
In another change, the amendment to Rule 63 includes the European Union (EU) among the stringent regulatory jurisdictions recognised for waiving clinical investigation requirements for medical devices that do not have predicate devices in India.
The provision already recognises the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and Japan. With the EU now included, medical devices approved in the EU that meet the eligibility conditions can benefit from the waiver provisions in India.
The move is expected to reduce regulatory timelines for eligible importers and manufacturers and facilitate quicker availability of newer medical technologies to Indian patients.
The amendments follow stakeholder consultations and are part of the government’s broader effort to streamline the regulatory framework for medical devices while maintaining standards for their quality, safety and performance.
The changes are also expected to promote greater international regulatory convergence and improve the competitiveness of India’s medical device industry, the government said.

Ex-cricket captains urge 'proper medical care' for Imran Khan
- Published
A group of former cricket captains, including Indian batting legend Sunil Gavaskar and one of England's longest-serving skippers Sir Alastair Cook, have called on Pakistan to ensure its ex-PM Imran Khan be given proper care while in custody.
The cricketer-turned-politician has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges which he denies.
In a letter to Pakistan's current leader Shehbaz Sharif, the 21 former skippers aired concern that Khan, 73, was allowed "only a few hours" at a hospital last week where he was examined by a state-appointed team.
Khan's party has also filed a contempt petition against the government for not giving him access to his own doctors, as ordered by the top court.
The former cricket captains laid out three demands in their letter, the first of which is that Khan be assessed by a medical board directed by Pakistan's Supreme Court – which would include his personal physicians – particularly on the reported loss of vision in his right eye.
They also urged authorities to allow weekly visits by Khan's family, as ordered by the court, "without interruptions or administrative delays".
Finally, they asked that any treatment recommended by the medical board be "provided without delay".
"Imran Khan is 73 years old and has now spent more than three years in custody," read the letter initiated by former Australian captain Greg Chappell.
"Whatever the legal and political arguments surrounding his case, the basic decency of ensuring a court-ordered medical process is actually completed is not, in our view, a controversial request."
Among the other signatories were England's Michael Atherton, Michael Brearley, Nasser Hussain, Andrew Strauss and David Gower, India's Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar, and Australia's Belinda Clark, Adam Gilchrist, Steve Waugh and Kim Hughes.
Fourteen of the former skippers had also supported an earlier appeal for "humane treatment and proper medical care" for Khan which was submitted in February.
Khan's lawyer claimed at the time that his client had 15% vision left in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
The signatories of both letters had described themselves as "former colleagues and rivals who share a bond forged on the cricket field", adding that the bond "transcends the borders and disputes that too often divide countries".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.
He was imprisoned in August 2023 and has faced charges in more than 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, all of which he and his party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf say are politically motivated.
His jailing sparked large-scale protests by supporters, which were met with a crackdown by authorities.
Pakistan's Supreme Court had on Tuesday directed the government to transfer Khan to a private hospital to be examined by physicians.
He was instead seen by doctors at a government-run hospital in Islamabad, who deemed him "medically fit", before he was moved back to prison.

Celtic deficiencies laid bare on another night of Champions League pain
- Published
When Callum McGregor eviscerated his own team-mates in the wake of Celtic's stupefying Champions League collapse against LASK, he delivered their one coherent moment of a spineless night.
In branding his fellow players "passive" and "scared" and in then sending a telling shot across their bows - "now we'll see what people are made of" - it is hard to recall him being so full of fury after a European game.
And there are plenty to choose from, plenty of dark nights, plenty of embarrassment, plenty of soul-searching over many years.
For close to a decade he has been Celtic's best player, a near ever-present. That longevity has brought him many trophies, but he's been around for many mortifications, too.
Where losing a 4-0 advantage ranks in the pantheon of Celtic failures is a moot point. What is unarguable is that it was a total capitulation, a feeble collapse in the face of LASK's physicality and desire and belief.
The Celtic captain called his players "scared" when winning 4-0. No media hatchet man could come up with a more damaging word to describe what happened out there.
McGregor has been through the European mill.
He was there last season when Celtic's fecklessness saw them go goalless for 210 minutes against the popgun boys of Kairat Almaty before failing to score from three of their five penalties in the shootout.
He was there for the 7-1 against Borussia Dortmund and the 6-0 against Atletico Madrid.
He's a survivor of the Champions League play-off exit to Midtjylland and the pair of 4-1 losses to Sparta Prague in the Europa League.
He was around for earlier Champions League play-off exits against Ferencvaros, AEK Athens and Cluj.
He's a veteran of the 7-1 loss to PSG and the 7-0 loss to Barcelona. He wears the scars as much as he holds the medals.
It is difficult, though, to recall him being as seething as he was on Tuesday night.
He wasn't ranting - that is not his style. He spoke calmly which lent his words more power.
He was raging in his own way. Raging at another exit, raging that when the chips were down too many of his fellow players panicked and allowed themselves to be overrun, raging at professional pride being trampled underfoot for all to see.
'Rabbits in headlights don't look as lost as Celtic did'
It was McGregor who opened the scoring on the night, a deflected shot and a 4-0 lead on aggregate.
LASK had started well but that goal looked to all the world like a kick to their solar plexus. They had chances in Glasgow and they had chances in the opening minutes in Linz - and they were 4-0 down!
How many punches can one team take before they lose their fight? Many, as it turned out.
Celtic were obliging, of course. Painfully so. We trumpeted their classy goals and their adventurous play a week ago and wrongly assumed that they had gumption to go with it. Big mistake.
When Benjamin Nygren's ridiculously loose pass led directly to LASK's equaliser on the night, the first signs of a wobble were visible.
Thirty two minutes had been played and Celtic did not look wholly comfortable at 4-1 on aggregate. Mad, but true.
When they conceded again three minutes into the second half, there were a few jelly legs on show. Auston Trusty was culpable this time. Brushed off the ball. Swatted and 4-2 now.
Trusty was poor, not the only one, but a point of real weakness that LASK went for.
Ten minutes after the hosts scored their second, they scored their third. Too many parts of the Celtic team were in full fright mode now. The slow death was picking up pace.
Camilo Duran, the hero of the first leg, was reduced to a non-event. Kasper Hogh worked hard but with no impact. Passes went astray. Celtic were directionless. Everything fell apart.
Rabbits in headlights do not tend to look as lost as Celtic did when the pressure really hit.
If McGregor was trying to put out fires in his own team he was failing. He could not cut through the tension.
Martin O'Neill looked on like a man 10 years older than his true age. This was a shocking night for him. One of his worst in football, he said later. He took responsibility, but he cannot be alone in that.
He emptied his bench in a desperate attempt to stem the flow, but his substitutions, five in 12 befuddled minutes, had zero impact.
Celtic did not have a shot on target in the second half of normal time nor in extra-time. They only existed as a man hanging off a cliff edge exists. There was only one way this was going to end.
LASK's fourth goal might have come in the 90th minute but it was deserved.
By that point they'd had 33 shots on Celtic's goal (they finished on 40) to go with the 20 from last week. It was a rout.
Cameron Carter-Vickers was hobbling about on one leg. Hogh much the same. Forward came the waves and Celtic tried to hold them back with a back four of Anthony Ralston, Dane Murray, Trusty and Liam Scales.
The fifth goal was a mercy, and another Celtic player doing the wrong thing at the wrong time in the wrong place. For Nygren and Trusty read Luke McCowan. Hapless and helpless - and out of the Champions League.
'Celtic ambition will be questioned again'
The night meandered to its conclusion. LASK missed a penalty for 6-1 before Miguel Freckleton, recently of St Mirren, slalomed his way into the Celtic box and threatened, for a second, to score.
All credit to Freckleton and his new beginning in Austria, but in flashes he was made to look like a serious player in his few minutes on the pitch. When that kind of things happens it tells a story.
Celtic were beyond disarray by then. Spooked, over-powered, out-fought, out-played. The smooth-running killers of last week in Glasgow was an optical illusion that hid psychological deficiencies.
Nobody could have predicted that they would fall in such a heap at 4-0, but they did.
Celtic, quite obviously, need a back-up left-back to Kieran Tierney and they don't have one.
They absolutely need, and this is no secret, a physical presence in the middle of the pitch, a player of stature in every sense of the word, a guy who would not be bullied as Celtic were bullied in Austria. They don't have one of those either.
They have done good deals but not enough of them. They're in net profit in their transfer business this summer.
The A-word - ambition - is going to get another airing. When you finish a £40m match with a back four of Ralston, Murray, Trusty and Scales then, as a club, you have not done your work properly. Nobody did on the night, on the field and off.
All those other defeats were incredibly costly in a financial but also in a self-worth sense.
They hoped they'd left the Champions League drawing board behind, but they're right back where they were when Kairat and Midtjylland and Ferencvaros and Cluj and AEK were the ones inflicting the pain.
Incredibly, another name has to get added to the list.

India’s captain Salima Tete also stressed the league’s role in widening the national talent pool.
“We have many players from HIL in the Indian team. They get a chance to be selected for the national camp, which is an important opportunity for them,” she said.
“This is just the beginning for us, and there is much more to achieve. For that, HIL is a must so that our talent pool is broadened and the girls get good exposure to handling the pressure of international hockey.”
Sakshi Rana, one of the players to have benefited from the league, said playing alongside experienced stars helped her overcome pressure.
“HIL has given me confidence, which was very useful in this tournament. It is about handling pressure. We have played alongside many veteran players like World Cup topscorer Yibbi Jansen and learnt a lot,” she said.
Navneet Kaur said sharing the dressing room with international stars had removed the fear and hesitation among younger Indian players.
“We have been playing HIL for the last two years and gained confidence from that. We have played with some of the biggest names in international hockey, and after sharing the dressing room with them, the fear and hesitation was gone,” she said.
“That gave us self-belief. We often discuss that they are like us and we can beat them because we have played with them.” Navneet also urged the teams and corporate houses to support the league at a time when its future is under a cloud.

“We have heard that a few teams are pulling out of the Women’s HIL, but at a time when our performance graph is going up, we want to request them to support us. It will be a big setback for women’s hockey and the future crop of players,” she said.
For the Indian players the women’s league is not merely a commercial venture but an important pathway for developing the next generation. Ishika, Sakshi, Shilpi Dabas, and Lalthanluangi are the players who are in the World Cup squad due to their powerful performances in HIL.
With India producing its strongest World Cup campaign in decades, the players believe this is precisely the time to strengthen, rather than discontinue, the competition that has helped them take the next step.
“I request the Sports Ministry and Hockey India to save this league. I also request the corporate sector, which invests huge money in cricket, to support women’s hockey.
“Our league does not require that much money. It is not about money; we need exposure. The Women's Hockey League should survive. We will do even better in the future,” said Navneet, who was player of the tournament last season with the Delhi team.
The inaugural season featured four teams -- Delhi SG Pipers, JSW Soorma Hockey Club, Shrachi Rarh Bengal Tigers and Odisha Warriors. The Warriors were later terminated over non-payment of player dues and franchise fees, with Ranchi Royals replacing them in the second season.
The Ranchi franchise has also since been terminated, with Indian players still awaiting payments.
Last season’s finalist, the Shrachi Rarh Bengal Tigers, is also contemplating withdrawal, citing financial pressure.
Franchise sources said the league is currently not commercially viable. The cost of running both a men’s and a women’s HIL team is estimated at around ₹10-12 crore, including an administrative fee of around ₹1 crore. The franchise fee of ₹2.5 crore has, however, been removed for the third season for the women’s team.

Rejoice, coffee lovers - Pumpkin Spice Latte season is officially brewing at Starbucks once again.
Starbucks 2026 Fall Menu out
The coffee giant as confirmed that its signature Pumpkin Spice Latte (PSL) will return to menus from 25 August, joined by an expanded selection of seasonal drinks and a handful of new additions.
Customers will once again be able to order the Pumpkin Spice Latte hot, iced, or blended.
Other familiar pumpkin drinks are also making a comeback, including the Pumpkin Cream Cold Brew, Iced Pumpkin Cream Chai, and Pumpkin Spice Frappuccino.
This year's menu, however, goes beyond the usual autumn favourites.
Starbucks is introducing the Iced Pumpkin Cream Shaken Espresso, Pumpkin Spice Chai and Iced Pumpkin Cream Matcha, expanding its pumpkin-inspired range across coffee, chai, and matcha drinks.
Pecan is also back on the menu, with Pecan Cortado, Iced Pecan Crunch Latte, and Pecan Crunch Latte returning for the season.
Another notable edition is the banana bread range. The new Iced Banana Bread Latte and Iced Banana Bread Chai bring the flavour of the popular baked treat into Starbucks' seasonal drinks menu.
The chain has also introduced the Chaider, a cider-inspired take on chai designed to offer another autumnal flavour profile.
Seasonal food is part of the launch as well. The menu will include a Chicken Bacon Protein Pocket, Hedgehog Cake Pop, and the returning Pumpkin Cream Cheese Muffin.
The fall menu arrives as the Pumpkin Spice Latte continues to be one of Starbucks' most recognisable seasonal products, with its annual return marking the beginning of the autumn drinks season for many customers.
With new flavours joining long-standing favourites this year, Starbucks' 2026 fall offering combines the familiar appeal of pumpkin spice with newer experiments centred on pecan, banana bread, and chai.

CIA director John Ratcliffe meets with Russian officials in Moscow, reports say
No immediate comment from the CIA or Kremlin
CIA director John Ratcliffe travelled to Moscow on Tuesday for meetings with Russian officials, U.S. media outlets reported, citing unnamed sources.
It would be the first known visit to the Russian capital by a U.S. spy chief since Ratcliffe's predecessor, William Burns, held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in November 2021. About three months after that meeting, Putin launched Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
CBS News and Axios reported the visit by Ratcliffe, U.S. President Donald Trump's CIA chief, who served as director of national intelligence in Trump's first term. The outlets did not say whom he was meeting or what the talks are expected to cover. ABC News, CNN and the Wall Street Journal also reported the meeting taking place.
The CIA declined to comment, and the Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The U.S. last week asked Ukraine not to launch airstrikes around Moscow, St. Petersburg and some northern territories of Russia between Monday and Wednesday of this week because a plane carrying a senior U.S. official would be flying to the Russian capital, said a source familiar with the matter.
The source declined to provide further information. The Financial Times first reported the U.S. message to Ukraine.
On Monday, the U.S. warned countries to cut business ties with Iran or face secondary sanctions, a move aimed at stepping up economic pressure in order to settle the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran launched in February.
No U.S. ambassador to Russia
The U.S. has no ambassador to Russia, which maintains a close strategic partnership with Iran involving extensive military, economic and diplomatic ties.
Tehran supplied Moscow with drones for its war against Ukraine.
In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of supplying its version of those drones to Iran.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment reported by Reuters in April said that Russia has aided Iran with satellite imagery for use in targeting U.S. facilities in the Middle East.
Moscow denies providing such assistance and has said it is ready to help resolve the U.S.-Iran conflict.

In a significant step to safeguard the health and safety of young children, the government has imposed restrictions on the manufacture, sale and distribution of all fixed dose combinations containing Chlorpheniramine Maleate and Phenylephrine Hydrochloride, mandating a clear warning that these medicines shall not be used in children below four years of age.
Earlier, vide a notification dated April 15, 2025, the government had restricted certain fixed dose combinations (FDCs) containing the two chemical compounds, subject to the same age-specific warning.
The latest notification extends this requirement to all formulations containing these two ingredients.
The decision followed recommendations by an expert committee and the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB).
The government noted that the use of such combinations may pose risks to children below four years of age and that safer alternatives are available.
Manufacturers have been directed to clearly display the warning – “Fixed Dose Combination shall not be used in children below four years of age – on the label, package insert and promotional literature associated with these formulations.
The notification has been issued under Section 26A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and is effective from the date of its publication in the official gazette.

Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Tuesday (August 25, 2026) said India’s security policy must be framed keeping in view emerging global challenges, including geopolitical instability, energy and resource insecurity, supply chain disruptions, rising radicalisation and cyber misinformation campaigns, while urging security agencies to anticipate threats before they become major crises.
Mr. Shah said he had visited all land-border States over the past eight months and shared with them a document outlining a four-pronged border security strategy. Stating that the government aimed to make the country “infiltrator-free” in a short period, he said illegal immigrants posed threats to national security, the economy and demographic balance. “This country is not a dharamshala and only citizens of the country have the right to live here,” he said.
Addressing the valedictory session of the Intelligence Bureau’s National Security Strategy Conference (NSSC), Mr. Shah said the forum should study trends over the next 15-20 years and identify potential security challenges and strategies to counter them. “We have to identify challenges in advance and destroy them before they become major problems,” he said, calling for the creation of an ecosystem capable of delivering a secure, infiltrator-free and narcotics-free India.
Linking national security with the government’s long-term development agenda, Mr. Shah said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s goal of making India a developed nation by 2047 could only be achieved with strong internal security. “If we want to become number one in every field, internal security will have to be strengthened further,” he said.
The Home Minister said previous governments had failed to anticipate problems such as narcotics trafficking, Left-wing extremism and unrest in the Northeast before they became acute, forcing the country to deal with their consequences for decades. He said the government had succeeded in overcoming challenges posed by the three major internal security hotspots, crediting State police forces, Central agencies and the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) for the achievement.
New criminal laws
Mr. Shah said the three new criminal laws would be implemented fully within a year. According to him, their implementation would enable criminal cases to be disposed of up to the Supreme Court level within three years and increase conviction rates by 25%.
On counter-terrorism, the Home Minister called for taking the anti-terror framework “Prahar” from a policy document to everyday practice and urged agencies to dismantle “360-degree terrorist networks”. He cited the coordinated nationwide action against the Popular Front of India (PFI) and its subsequent ban as an example of effective Centre-State coordination.
Mr. Shah also asked State police forces to implement the Narcotics Control Vision Document 2026-2029 and work on the three pillars of “Detect, Disrupt and Destroy” to achieve the goal of a drug-free India. He said the fight against narcotics could be won only through coordinated action by the Union government and all State governments.
Highlighting the role of technology in policing, Mr. Shah said integrated databases linking CCTNS, ICJS, NatGrid and NAFIS had been created. He urged young officers to use artificial intelligence for data integration, analysis and identifying criminal modus operandi to generate actionable intelligence and prevent future threats.
The Home Minister further said the government had strengthened mechanisms against fugitive offenders and that around 274 fugitives had been brought back to India from abroad between 2019 and 2026. He urged all States to work towards ensuring that offenders hiding overseas were brought within the ambit of Indian law.

The United States sent 20 deportees to Liberia, who arrived on Thursday as part of 1,200 migrants that the African country will receive under a new deal.
The deportees arrived at the Roberts international airport outside Monrovia. The Liberia-US agreement is among the largest third-country deportations driven by the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigration.
The 1,200 deportees will include African nationals and also nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean, according to Liberian information minister Jerolinmek Piah.
During a briefing on Tuesday, Liberian justice minister Natu Oswald Tweh said that the majority of the deportees had committed migration-related violations and offenses, and that they could seek asylum in the West African country if they wished.
Under a series of often-secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to nearly two dozen countries that aren’t their own, advocates say, with about 10 of them in Africa.
Immigration lawyers have said the Trump administration uses deportations to third countries as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum-seekers back to their home countries.
In many cases, migrants are deported to countries they’ve never been to or where they face safety risks and are left with little choice other than to return to the home countries they were fleeing from.

5 killed, 20 injured as bus rams iron rod-laden truck in Telangana
Five people were killed and around 20 injured after a private bus carrying 42 passengers rammed an iron-rod-laden container on the Hyderabad–Vijayawada highway in Telangana's Suryapet district.
Five people were killed and around 20 others sustained serious injuries after a private travel bus rammed into an iron-rod-laden container from behind in Telangana’s Suryapet district on Wednesday.
The accident occurred at around 4.30 am on the Hyderabad–Vijayawada National Highway when the private bus, carrying 42 passengers, was travelling from Hyderabad to Eluru in Andhra Pradesh. According to police, the bus rammed the truck from the rear.
The impact caused the iron rods loaded on the container to pierce into the bus, worsening the severity of the accident. Several passengers became trapped inside the mangled bus and cried for help.
Police carried out a rescue operation for more than an hour to pull the injured and trapped passengers out of the bus. The injured were shifted to nearby hospitals for treatment.
The accident caused a major traffic jam on the Hyderabad–Vijayawada National Highway.
Based on a preliminary investigation, police said the truck is suspected to have already hit a road divider before the bus collided with it from behind. Further investigation is underway, police added.
Telangana Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy expressed condolences over the deaths in the accident and conveyed his sympathies to the bereaved families.
He directed the Chief Secretary to take necessary measures to provide advanced medical care to those injured, an official release said.

Mondelez India Foods, maker of Bournvita and Cadbury products, has withdrawn health and nutrient-comparison claims flagged by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), along with related advertisements from e-commerce platforms, as the regulator steps up action against misleading food claims.
The action is part of a wider drive in which FSSAI has issued more than 150 notices to food companies over misleading advertisements, false claims and labelling violations. Nestlé India, PepsiCo, Coca-Cola India, Abbott India, Red Bull India, Danone India, Monster Energy India, Ferrero India and Kenvue are among companies named by the regulator.
Bournvita had come under scrutiny in 2023 over its sugar content and nutritional claims, particularly its marketing to children.
The latest corrective-action drive has also prompted Amway India to remove “100%” from its “100% Pure Coconut Oil” packaging and promotional material and drop the “Energy Drink” descriptor from its caffeinated XS range. Keralam-based Juza Foods has agreed to withdraw claims including “boost immunity”, “support stronger bones” and comparative calcium claims from its baby-food products.
The action follows FSSAI’s May 2025 advisory asking food businesses to discontinue the use of “100%” on labels, packaging and promotional material, arguing that the term could imply absolute purity or superiority.
The FSSAI has also widened enforcement to e-commerce platforms and food-service establishments, issuing 12 notices to e-commerce companies and more than 30 to food-service establishments, including major restaurant chains.
The regulator’s latest action underlines its focus on ensuring that food claims are substantiated and do not mislead consumers. The challenge, however, will be to ensure sustained compliance after companies withdraw or modify the claims.

The effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison. Unfolding in observational vignettes, Pankaj Johar and Sunaina Kapoor’s thought-provoking documentary centres on Vidya Mutth, a prestigious Hindu school in the holy city of Varanasi, India, where sectarian beliefs are drilled into its students, all in the name of cultural preservation.
The film opens with controversial speeches made by the school’s spiritual leader, Guru Avimuktesh, who advocates the abolition of religious freedom, and for Indian Muslims to either convert to Hinduism or leave for Pakistan. A prominent Hindu figure with a large following, he personally oversees the entrance exam, a sequence captured in dynamic handheld shots. While boys take the test, their parents look on with apprehension and anxiety; to be accepted would be an honour, not only for their child but for the whole family.
For those who do get in to Vidya Mutth, what follows is far from a glorious, enlightening experience. Focusing on two new entrants called Satyarth and Hari, the film documents their daily routines, which largely revolve around Sanskrit classes. The learning of this ancient script, supposedly to maintain a linguistic tradition, is actually in service of religious dogmatism; in between classes, Guru Avimuktesh continues to preach Islamophobic and casteist ideas, packaged as fact.
Moreover, though fanatically strict on its Hindu teachings, the school pays little attention to the mental and physical wellbeing of the pupils. Scenes of the school’s lavish celebration of its leader’s birthday are intercut with the students’ ramshackle living quarters. Even more shocking than this are the changes we observe in the boys over the course of mere months. Once a fresh-faced youth with a gentle demeanour, Hari soon starts to parrot the guru’s intolerant ideology with terrifying conviction. Laying bare the mechanism of indoctrination, Johar and Kapoor’s film sounds an urgent alarm for a new generation growing up under the spell of extremism.

When the NFL season kicks off next month, millions of Americans will gather around their televisions to watch athletes of comic book proportions crash into each other at breathtaking speeds. Inevitably, those players’ heads will smash into each other, leaving them dazed on the field. And according to a major new study, these repeated head-on collisions may eventually lead to a degenerative brain disease for many — if not most — of the players long after they’ve left the field.
Football is dangerous. Parents are finally steering their kids away from it.
A new study found at least one in four former NFL players had CTE at their time of death.
For years now, America has been reckoning with the tension between its love for football and the growing evidence of its dangers. Those concerns can be boiled down to three letters: CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, which is the progressive brain disease that can lead to dementia, depression, suicide, and other serious mental health problems.
One major question over the past 20 years has been: Exactly how often does playing football lead to CTE? What are the risks for peewee players versus pros? How quickly does the brain deteriorate once the disease takes hold? And new research, published this week in the British Medical Journal, has provided us with some staggering answers. After analyzing the death records for hundreds of former NFL players, the co-authors concluded that at least 25 percent of the former players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE at the time of their death.
And the actual prevalence could be much higher, but more players’ brains would have to be given over to scientists for a CTE assessment for us to know for sure. Because among the 338 players whose brains were donated and studied, the CTE rate was an astonishing 93 percent. The question is, according to the researchers: Is that percentage skewed because the players exhibiting CTE symptoms were more likely to offer up their brain for research? Or, as the authors suggest is possible, is the real CTE rate closer to 90 percent? Only further research will be able to tell us, but even the latest estimate — one in four — is cause for concern.
It’s a stark reminder of football’s risks, delivered right on the cusp of a new season for pro, college, and high school teams around the country. And according to the Aspen Institute’s annual State of Play report, there are signs that the game’s future may actually be at risk.
More and more American parents are steering their kids away from tackle football. How long can an elite league like the NFL last when the pool of players is getting smaller and smaller — at the same time the scientific evidence of its dangers is becoming clearer and clearer?
The youth football pipeline is drying up
Despite the latest research, the NFL is going to be fine in the short term. Professional football is the biggest TV show in the country: Last year, 83 of the top 100 rated TV shows were NFL games, up from 72 in 2024. The next Super Bowl will almost certainly attract more than 100 million viewers and end up the single most-watched TV program in the US for the whole year. Football is one thing that transcends politics in an increasingly polarized America.
But with each new piece of evidence about the physical and mental costs of playing football, football’s long-term dominance looks less and less certain. Already, if you dig into the trend lines for youth participation, they reveal a real threat to the sport’s future.
Let’s start with the good news for football enthusiasts: Flag football has become more and more popular among kids, supported by investments and promotion by the NFL itself and expert consensus that it’s much safer than tackle, especially when it comes to head injuries. According to the Aspen Institute’s State of Play survey, flag football participation among kids ages 6 to 12 grew by 13.6 percent from 2019 to 2024, while tackle football play dropped 7 percent among the same age group over that time.
But it’s participation among the next age group that may be most revealing. According to the Aspen Institute, tackle football participation rates among Americans ages 13 to 17 — the prime age for middle school and high school teams — decreased 9 percent from 2019 to 2024. It has even fallen behind tennis among the teenage cohort. Many of the tweens who play flag football may never strap on a helmet to play tackle.
Even if fewer kids play tackle football year over year, the sport may still subsist on its promises of upward mobility for people who come from poorer backgrounds. With the recent introduction of compensation for college players, elite athletes can make millions of dollars in income before they even reach the NFL. It may be no surprise, then, that the young people still playing tackle football are more likely to be lower-income and live in conservative states.
Another study found that Black and Hispanic parents, who on average earn less money than their white counterparts, are more likely to see football as a path to college scholarship or even a professional career; the Washington Post reported in 2023 that the proportion of white players at the college level is falling while the percentage of Black players is rising. Football players are often thought of as modern gladiators: participants disproportionately from lower classes aspiring to riches and glory in a violent game for the viewing pleasure of the general public. That’s becoming more and more true as we learn more about its dangers.
As the annual hoopla around the NFL kickoff makes clear, football’s cultural dominance remains unrivaled among professional sports. But this new study has left even me, a lifelong football fan, wondering how much longer it can, and should, last.

From former 'street kid' key to South Africa's police corruption inquiry
- Published
The name of controversial businessman Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala has haunted the proceedings of South Africa's major inquiry into alleged police corruption.
The 49-year-old has been accused of supplying generous gifts - including 20 impalas, the weight-loss drug Ozempic and personal loans - to help him buy influence and get police contracts.
In police custody for more than a year in connection with a separate case, Matlala is giving his side of the story before retired Constitutional Court judge Mbuyiseli Madlanga and his panel after an earlier hearing last month was aborted.
The revelations at the Madlanga Commission, in progress for 10 months, have gripped South Africans and they are eager to hear how Matlala responds.
Dressed in a Fendi shirt and Gucci glasses, Matlala did give evidence at a parallel corruption inquiry in parliament last November.
He said he did not know senior police officers and politicians personally and denied corruption allegations though he admitted to having made donations for activities related to the African National Congress (ANC), the main party in the coalition government.
But he has not yet been asked to address the wider allegations made at the Madlanga Commission or the accusation that he was part of a drug trafficking cartel, allegedly known as the Big Five.
Matlala may now be a central figure, but he only came to public prominence three years ago when his name was mentioned in news reports around alleged tender irregularities at a state hospital - though he said he had nothing to do with the tender.
What little is known about his early life is based on what he told parliament last year.
He was born in 1976, when South Africa was still run by a white-minority government, and grew up in a township east of the capital, Pretoria.
He told lawmakers that he was for a time raised by a single mother, who he said then "disappeared on me".
"I had to raise myself. I was actually a street kid," he told lawmakers.
He eventually reunited with his mother in 2002, when she was terminally ill.
After she died, Matlala learned that she had been sexually assaulted, which he said was because of her albinism. Myths surround the condition include people believing that having sex with a woman with the condition would cure the men of illness.
After leaving school, he said he started an informal business to make ends meet, which led to various brushes with the law.
In 2001, he was convicted and served time in prison for the possession of stolen goods.
Over the years, he would be arrested for a string of crimes, including house robberies, a cash-in-transit heist and assault. He denied involvement in them all and was either acquitted or had the charges withdrawn against him.
He told the parliamentary committee that his nickname "Cat" was not, as some had suggested, down to his "nine lives" and ability to survive trouble, but because of his large family - he has nine children with his wife.
But things caught up with him in May 2025 when he was arrested and charged with attempted murder, which he denies. His wife is accused of the same crime and also denies the charge. Unlike her husband, she has been granted bail.
He was later charged with corruption over allegations in relation to providing health services to the police - and last month pleaded guilty as part of a deal with the prosecution but has since withdrawn the plea as the agreement has fallen apart.
He told the parliamentary inquiry last year that he turned his life around in 2017, when he registered his first formal business to provide security services.
Matlala said he later expanded his services into healthcare, and this led to him scoring lucrative contracts, first with a hospital and then the police, even though, as he admitted to lawmakers, he had no track record providing healthcare services.
But since last September, as witnesses gave evidence to the Madlanga Commission, allegations that Matlala had a close and corrupt relationship with senior police officers emerged in the public domain.
This included allegations that the now-suspended Police Minister Senzo Mchunu was indirectly receiving financial campaign money from Matlala to fund his "political endeavours". Mchunu denied these accusations.
Matlala has also been accused of having dealings with Mchunu's predecessor Bheki Cele.
Matlala told parliament's inquiry he had paid Cele a 500,000 rand ($31,000; £23,000) "facilitation fee", which the latter had demanded after police returned firearms seized from Matlala.
The businessman alleged that Cele also made other requests, including asking for help to purchase a home and pay for his son's studies, to which Matlala refused to accede.
Cele admitted to MPs that he had known Matlala for a couple of months and had stayed at his rented penthouse in Pretoria on two occasions but denied receiving money from Matlala.
Matlala's relationship with suspended deputy police chief Maj-Gen Shadrack Sibiya has also come under examination.
Both Matlala and Sibiya denied having a close relationship, insisting their dealings were strictly professional.
But testimony given at the Madlanga Commission painted a different picture.
It was alleged that Sibiya had received 20 impalas from Matlala around the same time Matlala was awarded the police contract. Sibiya denied this, saying he would never "receive anything from a service provider".
A witness also alleged that Matlala had bragged about his "close connections with very senior police officials", including Sibiya, following his arrest in May last year.
Matlala's alleged relationship with other senior police officers have also been brought up at the Madlanga Commission.
Brig Rachel Matjeng, who oversaw the controversial police contract awarded to Matlala, told the commission she had had an on-off romantic relationship with the businessman that included lavish romantic presents – among them shots of Ozempic.
Another senior officer, the head of the police's organised crime unit Maj-Gen Richard Shibiri, admitted to receiving a "personal loan" of $4,000 from Matlala which he repaid.
Shibiri, who oversaw anti-gang, narcotics, illegal mining investigations among others in his role, said the money was for repairs to his son's car. He denied having a close friendship with Matlala, despite speaking to him often and advising him on personal matters.
"At no stage was I aware that he was a member of any cartel or that he was a subject of any criminal investigation," he said.
Shibiri and Matjeng have since been fired from the police force.
Matlala's name was also mentioned in relation to an alleged scandal in Ekurhuleni, a local government area just east of Johannesburg.
It was alleged that while Julius Mkhwanazi was Ekurhuleni's acting police chief, he arranged for blue lights and sirens to be fitted on Matlala's personal vehicles.
Mkhwanazi, who has since been suspended, denied the allegations but did admit to receiving money from Matlala, describing him as a "blood brother" during his appearance at the Madlanga Commission.
The startling revelations that have emerged since September, when the Madlanga Commission began, have left people wondering how such things were allowed to happen.
Many South Africans, anxious to understand the mechanics of the alleged corruption, hope that Matlala has the answers as his testimony continues.

Good morning. The US supreme court has sided with Donald Trump in his effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it is unclear whether or not his administration will be able to take action before the midterm elections in November. The court’s justices voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction that a judge in Massachusetts had placed in June on an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in place, and the ruling leaves room for legal challenges.
Trump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own use of it and overwhelming evidence that the system is secure. In March he ordered the government to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters, requiring that mail-in ballots only be delivered to people on that list. Iran vowed retaliation against any country that takes part in the US-led isolation campaign.
