The Transcendence of Dolly Parton
The late singer was perhaps the only person in the United States who commanded nearly universal affection.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Dolly Parton transcended.
It almost didn’t matter what: class, gender, region, musical genre, partisanship. She transcended boundaries in all of them. During an era when politicians act like pop stars, pop stars are expected to engage in politics, and politics divide fiercely, Parton was perhaps the only person in the United States who commanded nearly universal affection. Her death today, at 80, leaves an absence that no contemporary cultural figure could dream of filling.
Parton’s origin story was, in the most literal sense, a rags-to-riches tale. She was born in a one-room cabin in the Appalachian Mountains of East Tennessee, one of 12 children of an illiterate sharecropper father. She memorialized her impoverished childhood in “Coat of Many Colors,” which tells of how her mother sewed a jacket from rags. When she wears it to school, “with patches on my britches / and holes in both my shoes,” her classmates mock and laugh at her. Rather than a hard-luck story, this is a triumph. Parton gets the last laugh: “But they didn’t understand it and I tried to make them see / That one is only poor only if they choose to be.” The song showcases one of the keys to Parton’s success: the ability to bare her soul while keeping a sense of humor and a smile.
Her rise to fame began when she was hired by the rhinestone-adorned country singer Porter Wagoner as a “girl singer” in his act. Parton quickly demonstrated that she had more than an attractive face and voice, writing a string of successful songs, such as “Jolene” and “My Tennessee Mountain Home.” One indication of her songwriting talent was that her most famous song was a bigger hit for another singer. Parton had initially hoped that Elvis Presley would record “I Will Always Love You,” but she refused his manager’s demand to give Presley songwriting credit, and she cut the song herself. It topped the country charts twice, but after Whitney Houston rerecorded the song for The Bodyguard’s soundtrack in 1992, it was a No. 1 pop hit for weeks.
Today, little separation exists between country music and the mainstream, but the genre garnered much less respect when Parton’s career began. She helped tear down old prejudices in an era when many music listeners might have professed to like “anything other than country.” Her success helped pave a path for later crossover stars such as Shania Twain and Taylor Swift. She pursued her own genre experimentation, too, collaborating with a range of artists. When she was nominated for the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, she protested that she wasn’t a rock musician and tried to withdraw from consideration. When the hall refused, she announced with appealing humility that she would earn the honor by making a rock album—her 49th and final—with guests including Joan Jett, Ringo Starr, and Paul McCartney.
Parton always maintained her connection to rural southern music. Few country stars could claim a more authentic origin. She kept her down-home accent and platinum-bouffant hairstyle, and she spoke openly about her abiding Christian faith. These traits may have allowed her to take stands that might otherwise have been controversial. (She also avoided electoral politics, and declined Presidential Medals of Freedom from both Donald Trump and Joe Biden.)
Like her predecessor Loretta Lynn, she cultivated a no-nonsense strain of feminism in her lyrics. In 1980, she starred alongside the outspoken liberals Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in the movie 9 to 5, a workplace comedy in which three women conspire to get even with their sexist-pig boss. Parton agreed to take the role if she could write the theme song, and the track has proved even more enduring than the film. “It’s a rich man’s game no matter what they call it / And you spend your life puttin’ money in his wallet,” she sang. Was this working-class grievance or progressive economics? Radical feminism or mass-market entertainment? Why not both?
Parton was beloved by the gay community, and she reciprocated that affection. She also quietly fostered change using her fortune. In 1986, she opened Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, and the theme park became the largest job provider in the area. In 1995, she launched Dolly’s Imagination Library. Starting first in her native Sevier County, and then expanding around the United States as well as in a few other countries, the program mails a book each month to children from birth to age 5, to encourage literacy and a love of reading. In 2020, she donated $1 million to help fund the development of a COVID-19 vaccine, then proudly received the shot.
In her middle age, during a perhaps less enlightened time in American society, Parton was often a punch line. Her voluptuous chest and many plastic surgeries were frequent fodder for jokes, and Parton perfected the trick of playing along with the gags while also subverting them. One of her earliest singles is titled “Dumb Blonde,” but it warns, “This dumb blonde ain’t nobody’s fool.” In a 2002 New York Times interview, she said, “Hopefully people can see beneath the hair to know there’s a brain, beneath the boobs to know there’s a heart, and behind all the other stuff to know there’s some talent.”
If that wasn’t always the case, Parton got her wish in the end. Admiration for her became an unshakable conviction across cultural lines. One sign of Parton’s status is that even Trump is on his best behavior, treating her death with a reverence he usually reserves only for his biggest public admirers, of whom she was not one. The president ordered flags flown at half-staff for a week to mark her death. It is a fitting farewell for an artist who united Americans in a way that few people ever have or will.

Karnataka minister flags proposed Bengaluru parking fee of up to ₹25,000 to CM Shivakumar, asks to reconsider
Reddy, who is also an MLA from Bengaluru, acknowledged the need to regulate roadside parking amid the city's growing vehicle population.
Karnataka Minister Ramalinga Reddy has urged Chief Minister D K Shivakumar to reconsider the proposed annual fee of ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 for roadside vehicle parking in Bengaluru, saying the charges could place an additional financial burden on middle-class and ordinary families.
In a letter dated August 24, Reddy, who is also an MLA from Bengaluru, acknowledged the need to regulate roadside parking amid the city's growing vehicle population and worsening traffic problems.
However, he said the economic condition of ordinary citizens should also be considered before introducing the proposed charges.

Rise of prices and additional parking fee: Reddy
Reddy said middle-class and ordinary families were already under financial pressure due to rising prices of essential commodities and increased expenses on cooking gas, petrol, diesel, GST and tolls.
"Imposing an additional annual parking fee of ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 merely for owning a vehicle could become another financial burden on such families," he said.
Under the draft GBA (Parking) Rules, 2026, Bengaluru residents seeking to park vehicles on public roads outside their homes may have to pay an annual residential parking fee of up to ₹25,000, depending on the vehicle type. The draft rules propose an annual residential parking permit fee of ₹15,000 for hatchbacks, ₹20,000 for sedans and ₹25,000 for sports utility vehicles.
Reddy noted that the state government had implemented various welfare guarantee schemes to improve people's living standards and provide economic support. He said care should therefore be taken to ensure that urban families were not subjected to another unavoidable financial burden.
While some residents with large plots or independent houses may be able to park their vehicles within their premises, most middle-class families live in houses with limited space or apartments and often lack adequate parking facilities, he said.

Why objection to parking fee?
Reddy welcomed the emphasis on parking arrangements under rules governing new building construction. However, he pointed out that older buildings and residential areas in Bengaluru often cannot provide parking facilities that match the city's current vehicle population.
"Many families are already managing home and vehicle loans, children's education, healthcare and other day-to-day expenses. In this context, an additional annual parking fee could put a financial burden on them," he said.
Reddy said regulating roadside parking through appropriate fees and penalties was necessary and welcomed such measures. At the same time, he urged the government to consider exemptions for ordinary families who did not regularly use their vehicles and did not have parking facilities within their buildings.
He also suggested that the government consult Bengaluru legislators, civil society organisations and concerned officials before taking a final decision on the proposed parking charges.
"It would be appropriate to take a decision after considering the public interest and the ground realities of parking in Bengaluru," Reddy said.

A video of Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi is going viral on social media (here, here, and here), allegedly showing him making controversial remarks about women and rape. In the video, he is purportedly heard saying, “Eighty per cent of rapes are caused by women. Rape happens in India, and rape does not happen in Bharat. The girl has a place; she should be in a cage; there should be control over her. She shouldn’t be working, and boys should be given full freedom.” Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Rahul Gandhi making controversial remarks about rape and women.
Fact: The video has been edited. In the original video, Rahul Gandhi was not making these statements himself; he was quoting past controversial remarks made by RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat and former Haryana Chief Minister Manohar Lal Khattar while criticising their views. The viral clip deliberately removes his attribution, making it appear as though he was expressing these views himself. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to the original video uploaded on the official YouTube channel of the Congress party on 22 August 2026. The video is from the Congress’s “Chhatraon Ki Goonj” event held in Pune on the same day. The viral clip appears at the 1:00:12 timestamp. In the original video, Rahul Gandhi refers to statements previously made by RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat and former Haryana Chief Minister Manohar Lal Khattar. Gandhi attributes to Bhagwat the statement that rape happens in “India” and not in “Bharat”, while attributing to Khattar the remark that 80% of rapes are caused by women. Gandhi then describes these remarks as reflecting a mindset that he says they are fighting.
This makes it clear that the viral video has been edited to remove the portion in which Gandhi identifies Bhagwat and Khattar as the sources of these remarks, making it appear as though he himself made the statements.
We also conducted a Google keyword search and found (here, here) that, during RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat’s visit to Silchar on 4 January 2013, he made a controversial remark about rape incidents, saying that such crimes occur more in “India” and less in “Bharat”. The statement sparked controversy at the time. Then-RSS spokesperson Ram Madhav clarified that Bhagwat was referring to Indian traditions of respecting women and saying that people who moved away from these values could become involved in criminal cases.
Similarly, in November 2018, then Haryana Chief Minister Manohar Lal Khattar made a controversial remark (here, here) about rape and molestation cases. He said that 80–90 per cent of such incidents involved people who knew each other and suggested that some cases arose after people had been in relationships for a long time.
To sum up, this viral video of Rahul Gandhi making controversial remarks about rape and women is edited.

Thousands of angry young job-seekers clashed with police in Jharkhand, one of India’s poorest states, on Monday as a weeks-long protest over alleged irregularities in recruitment drives for coveted government jobs escalated into a march on the state legislature.
Police fired water cannon and teargas and swung batons as they tried to stop flag-waving demonstrators from clambering over barricades and surging towards the assembly in Ranchi, the state capital. Some of the protesters responded by dancing and cheering as jets of water drenched the crowd.
The unrest comes just weeks after the Cockroach movement, a youth-led protest campaign – which began as an online joke and grew into a nationwide outcry over leaks in a national medical entrance examination – put the BJP-led national government under heavy pressure and led to the resignation of the education minister.
Both protesters and police officers were injured in the Jharkhand clashes, local media reported, although no official figures were released.
“The baton charge was barbaric. We were protesting peacefully, but the government used batons against us,” protester Piyush Kumar Soni told the Press Trust of India.
The demonstrators are demanding an investigation by the CBI, India’s premier investigative force, saying only an independent inquiry can get to the bottom of alleged wrongdoing in government recruitment examinations.
They accuse authorities of failing to prevent irregularities in public service exams, including test paper leaks and cheating, and say the alleged scandals have deprived young people of a fair chance.
Jharkhand has long struggled with high unemployment, making government jobs highly sought after. Competition is intense for civil service and other public sector posts, which offer job security, health and pension benefits.
Government recruitment drives routinely attract hundreds of thousands of applicants, and many young people spend years preparing for examinations. In one recent Jharkhand recruitment exercise, nearly 640,000 applications were received for 2,025 posts. In another, more than 322,000 candidates competed for 510 vacancies.
The state government, led by a regional party allied with the opposition Congress, has sought to defuse the crisis through talks. Officials say most of the protesters’ demands have been accepted and that they are open to more negotiations.
The Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, condemned the use of force. “Students have a right to peaceful protest, and only dialogue can yield solutions,” he said.
The row has already toppled senior figures. The former Jharkhand public service commission chair was arrested over alleged exam irregularities, while three commission members have resigned.
The protests underscore mounting frustration among young Indians over corruption in public examinations and recruitment systems, a shortage of good jobs and fears that opportunities are being lost to cheating and political influence. Nearly two-thirds of Indians are under 35.
Official data shows unemployment fell to 9.9% last year, but a 2026 study by Azim Premji University found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed.

When people in India are used to buying all sorts of medicines over the counter (OTC), the challenge is the enforcement of laws which make prescription mandatory, said Hyderabad-based paediatrician Sivaranjani Santosh even as she welcomed the Centre’s decision to make all syrups, including cough syrups, as prescription-only.
Why India has restricted chlorpheniramine, phenylephrine medicines for children under 4 | Explained
Many in the pharmaceutical trade as well are uncertain how effectively the new rules can be enforced among consumers accustomed to buying medicines over the counter (OTC).
On Tuesday (June 16) the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare notified amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, ending the OTC sale of syrups, including cough syrups. Following the amendment, cough lozenges, pills and tablets will continue to be available over the counter, but syrups will require a prescription.
Dr. Santosh welcomed the move, saying concerns over overdoses, incorrect dosing and indiscriminate use of cough-and-cold preparations justified tighter controls. Many formulations contain ingredients such as terbutaline, levosalbutamol, salbutamol, chlorpheniramine maleate and phenylephrine, which could add to complications if used inappropriately, she said.
ALSO WATCH Watch: Why are prescriptions now mandatory for cough syrups? | Above the Fold | 16.06.2026
Doubts over implementation were echoed by pharmacists. Uday Kumar of Mor Chemists and Druggists said consumers increasingly expected immediate relief and questioned whether a blanket prescription requirement would work in the long run. “Everyone wants to recover instantly. If they fall sick today, they want to become well tomorrow,” he said.
Mr. Kumar argued that counterfeit, adulterated and unbranded medicines posed a bigger challenge. He added that identifying genuine and fake products was difficult and laboratory testing often took months.
Neelesh Kanodia, who runs Yash Agencies, distinguished between codeine-based cough syrups and regular formulations. “I don’t think the blanket rule will continue in the long run. But restrictions on codeine-containing syrups will continue,” he said. According to Mr. Kanodia, codeine-containing cough syrups were already largely dispensed against prescriptions only, whereas commonly used formulations had traditionally been available over the counter.
Meanwhile, the Telangana Chemists and Druggists Association (TCDA) moved quickly to inform retailers about the new rules. Krishna Kumar, treasurer of the association, said broadcast messages had been sent to pharmacies across the State immediately after the notification was issued. “We also circulated those messages in Telugu so that they reach even the remote corners of the State,” he said.
Mr. Kumar said Telangana had around 39,000 pharmacies, of which nearly 18,000 were located in Hyderabad.
A Hyderabad-based pharmacist who runs a prominent store in Panjagutta and requested anonymity said implementation was likely to vary across regions. “Large and reputed pharmacies in metropolitan cities and affluent areas would comply with the rules but enforcement in smaller localities and towns could prove more difficult,” he said.
He added that consumer behaviour is a major obstacle. Patients often reuse old prescriptions instead of returning to doctors, while consultation fees, travel costs and waiting times discourage repeated visits.

Trump times his Ireland trip to coincide with major golf tournament at his own club
President Trump will stay at Doonbeg next month, just as resort hosts Irish Open
President Donald Trump has timed his upcoming trip to the Republic of Ireland to coincide with the final two days of the Irish Open.
The president will be in Ireland on September 12 and 13 and will visit the U.S. Embassy in Dublin and meet with Irish President Catherine Connolly and Taoiseach Micheal Martin, according to The New York Post, citing a White House official.
The encounter could prove tense as Connolly has previously called him “volatile”, “unpredictable” and capable of “acting like a bully.”
Perhaps of greater interest to Trump will be his stay at his own golf course, the Trump International Golf Links and Hotel, in Doonbeg, County Clare, which will see him arrive in time to catch the Open as Rory McIlroy, a personal favorite, seeks to defend his title.
Trump hosted McIlroy at the state dinner he held for King Charles III in April and took time out to praise the Masters champion’s “unconquerable courage.”
“That was very good, Rory,” he said. “Where is Rory McIlroy, can you stand up please? I don’t know if that helps them talk about how wonderful my speech is but I had to interrupt my speech because I watched that man win a tournament that was a tough… that was a tough one. Congratulations, very proud of you.”
McIlroy famously taunted Trump last September when his European side beat the U.S. team in the Ryder Cup at Bethpage Black, New York, posting a viral video in which he led his teammates in a chant of: “Are you watching, Donald Trump?”
The president has form when it comes to turning his official duties into a golfing opportunity, arranging last year’s trip to Scotland to meet with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and then-British prime minister Sir Keir Starmer so that it took place at his Turnberry course in South Ayrshire.
He also used that trip, which inspired local protests over the cost of his security requirements incurred by local taxpayers, to open a new private course in Aberdeen.
More recently, was at his club in Bedminster, New Jersey, for a weekend coinciding with the four-day LIV Golf New York tournament. His visit sparked a security scare when several planes crossing into local airspace were in violation of temporary flight restrictions, forcing fighter jets to be scrambled to escort them to safety.
The Doonbeg course was designed by another golfing great, Greg Norman, and was acquired by Trump in 2014, 12 years after its opening.
He made a memorable visit there with his sons Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump during his first term in June 2019 when the younger Trumps descended on the local pub to buy the punters a round.
Trump made a more low-key return in May 2023 when he was out of office, during which he claimed his course had “revitalized” the community and was greeted by local supporters, some of whom wore MAGA merchandise with an Irish twist in tribute.

U.S. drugmakers Merck and Moderna said Wednesday a personalized cancer treatment had shown success in reducing the recurrence of melanoma tumors in a late-stage trial hailed by experts as a "breakthrough."
The news sent shares in Moderna soaring 145% to $154 while Merck's stock was up more than 12% to $152.
The drug, called "intismeran autogene," is based on the same messenger RNA (mRNA) technology behind Covid-19 vaccines.
Researchers have for years been trying to apply mRNA treatments against cancer, but this was the first time such a drug showed positive results in a large, late-stage clinical trial.
"Today marks an extraordinary milestone for Moderna, for mRNA science and, most importantly, for patients with cancer," Moderna CEO Stephane Bancel said in a statement.
The trial lasted approximately a year and involved 1,137 patients who, following surgical removal of their cancers, were randomized into groups, with two-thirds receiving the new treatment plus pembrolizumab -- the current standard-of-care drug -- while the rest received pembrolizumab alone.
The companies said they would present their data at an upcoming international conference and begin filings with regulators for approval.
Proof of principle
Lennard Lee, an oncologist and assistant professor at the University of Oxford who was not involved in the trial, called the results "very encouraging," adding: "We should now look forward to seeing the complete data."
Oncologist Marco Gerlinger, a professor at London's Barts Cancer Institute, added that beyond being good news for patients with melanoma, it was "proof of principle that personalised cancer vaccines work."
"I think it is fair to call it a breakthrough in the development of new cancer immunotherapies," he added, while also noting the press release was short on details.
The treatment works by taking a sample of the patient's tumor and identifying its unique mutational signature, or "fingerprint," then using mRNA technology to fight it.
Messenger RNA technology uses synthetic molecular instructions encased in tiny fat bubbles that temporarily enter cells, causing them to produce targets that train the body's immune system.
The technology was first conceived decades ago but came to the fore during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Moderna and Pfizer developed vaccines that were highly effective against serious forms of the illness.
Melanoma is one of the deadliest forms of skin cancer, with more than 330,000 new cases diagnosed worldwide in 2022.
"Together with Merck, we are now studying intismeran in combination with pembrolizumab and other anti-cancer therapies, and as a monotherapy, across multiple tumor types and stages of disease, including melanoma, lung, bladder and kidney cancers," said Bancel.

Arunachal Pradesh – A Living Treasure of Biodiversity
Arunachal Pradesh is one of India’s most biologically diverse states, where forests, rivers, wetlands, mountains and communities are part of one interconnected ecological landscape. Its extraordinary range of habitats supports thousands of plant and animal species, including several rare, endemic and threatened species.
The State’s biodiversity is shaped by its remarkable variation in altitude and climate. From tropical forests in the foothills to temperate forests, alpine meadows and high-altitude ecosystems, Arunachal Pradesh offers a continuous range of habitats within a relatively compact geographical area.
With more than 80 per cent of its geographical area under forest cover, the State plays an important role in maintaining the ecological balance of the Eastern Himalayas. It is also part of the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, one of the world’s globally recognised regions of exceptional biological richness and conservation importance.
A Landscape of Remarkable Ecological Diversity
The geographical diversity of Arunachal Pradesh is reflected in its forests. Depending on altitude and climatic conditions, the State has tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, moist deciduous forests, subtropical broad-leaved forests, pine forests, temperate forests, coniferous forests, sub-alpine vegetation and alpine meadows.
This remarkable transition from the warm foothills to the high Himalayas creates habitats for species with very different ecological requirements.
The State is home to more than 5,000 species of flowering plants, around 600 species of orchids, about 75 species of rhododendrons, 45 species of bamboo, 17 species of cane and hundreds of medicinal plants. Arunachal Pradesh is particularly renowned for its orchid and rhododendron diversity.
The forests also support a remarkable variety of mammals, including the tiger, leopard, clouded leopard, snow leopard, golden cat, marbled cat, Asiatic elephant, red panda, takin, hoolock gibbon and several other rare and threatened species.
A Paradise for Birds
Arunachal Pradesh is equally celebrated for its avian diversity. Its forests and mountain ecosystems provide habitats for hundreds of bird species, making the State one of the most important birding regions in India.
The Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary in West Kameng is one of the best examples of this extraordinary richness. Located within the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, Eaglenest is home to a wide variety of hornbills, pheasants, kingfishers and other birds. The sanctuary is also known for the discovery of the Bugun liocichla, a bird named after the Bugun community that lives in the region.
Protecting Arunachal’s Wildlife
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is protected through an extensive network of national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, tiger reserves and other conservation landscapes.
The state is home to important protected areas such as Namdapha National Park and Tiger Reserve, Kamlang Tiger Reserve, Pakke Tiger Reserve, Mouling National Park, Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary, Sessa Orchid Sanctuary, Dibang Wildlife Sanctuary and Mehao Wildlife Sanctuary, among others.
These landscapes support an exceptional range of wildlife, from high-altitude species such as the snow leopard and red panda to tropical forest species including the clouded leopard, hoolock gibbon and numerous birds, reptiles and amphibians.
Recent wildlife surveys have continued to expand scientific knowledge of these ecosystems. A 2024 WWF-India survey in Arunachal’s high-altitude rangelands recorded six wild cat species, including photographic evidence of the elusive Pallas’s cat, marking the first such photographic record from the state. The survey used 136 camera traps across 83 locations, covering approximately 2,000 sq km.
The Orchids of Arunachal Pradesh
Among the many botanical treasures of the State, orchids hold a special place.
Arunachal Pradesh has one of the richest orchid assemblages in India, with hundreds of species occurring across its varied habitats. The Sessa Orchid Sanctuary in West Kameng was established in 1979 to conserve and study orchids in their natural habitats. The sanctuary has recorded a remarkable diversity of orchid species, including epiphytic and terrestrial orchids.
The Orchid Research and Development Centre at Tipi further strengthens conservation and research efforts. Its facilities include orchid species houses, natural orchidaria, a herbarium, tissue culture laboratory, museum and hardening units. These initiatives support both ex-situ conservation and the rehabilitation of orchids in their natural habitats.
Glaw Lake: Arunachal Pradesh’s First Ramsar Site
A landmark development came in August 2026, when Glaw Lake, located within the Kamlang Tiger Reserve in Lohit district, was designated as India’s 101st Ramsar Site and became Arunachal Pradesh’s first Ramsar Site.
Situated at an elevation of around 1,168 metres, Glaw Lake covers approximately 82 hectares and forms part of the catchment of the Kamlang, Lang and Lati rivers, which flow into the Lohit River. The lake is recognised by the State Forest Department as an important repository of aquatic biodiversity.
Its Ramsar designation gives international recognition to the ecological importance of the wetland and strengthens the focus on its conservation and sustainable management. The recognition is also significant for Arunachal Pradesh’s wider efforts to protect wetlands and the ecosystems and communities that depend on them.
A State Where New Discoveries Continue
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity story is still being written.
Recent scientific discoveries demonstrate how much remains to be documented within the State’s forests and mountains. The rare plant Vaccinium piliferum, a relative of the wild blueberry that had not been documented for nearly 188 years, was rediscovered in Vijoynagar in Changlang district recently.
New orchid species have also been identified in different parts of the State, while researchers have recorded new cascade frog species from Arunachal Pradesh. In 2026, scientists also identified a new butterfly species, Euthalia zubeengargi, from Basar in Leparada district.
Such discoveries are a reminder that Arunachal Pradesh is not merely a repository of known species. Its forests and mountains continue to offer opportunities for scientific research and the discovery of life forms that may not yet be fully documented.
Biodiversity and Indigenous Knowledge
For generations, the indigenous communities of Arunachal Pradesh have lived closely with their natural surroundings. Forests provide food, medicinal plants, fibres, fuel and other resources, while traditional knowledge has helped communities understand seasonal changes, plants, wildlife and sustainable use of natural resources.
Today, this relationship is increasingly important to conservation.
A recent example comes from West Kameng, where indigenous communities are sustainably harvesting Zanthoxylum, locally known as Khagi, a wild Himalayan spice. The initiative has reportedly involved around 200 families while contributing to the protection of approximately 100 square kilometres of forest and generating livelihood opportunities.
Such efforts demonstrate that conservation and livelihoods can move together when local knowledge and sustainable practices are placed at the centre of biodiversity management.
Conservation: Protecting a Living Legacy
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is a natural asset of national and global importance. At the same time, ecosystems across the world are facing growing pressures from habitat loss, climate change, pollution, invasive species and unsustainable exploitation of natural resources.
Protecting Arunachal’s biodiversity therefore requires more than creating protected areas. It calls for habitat restoration, scientific research, responsible tourism, community participation, sustainable livelihoods and greater awareness among citizens.
The State’s protected areas, community conservation initiatives, biodiversity documentation programmes and institutions dedicated to research and conservation all contribute to this larger effort.
Looking Ahead
The story of Arunachal Pradesh is inseparable from its forests, rivers, mountains and wildlife. Its biodiversity sustains ecosystems, supports livelihoods, enriches traditional knowledge and strengthens the ecological security of the Eastern Himalayas.
From the orchids of Sessa to the forests of Namdapha, from the bird-rich landscapes of Eaglenest to the wetlands of Glaw Lake, every ecosystem adds another chapter to the State’s natural heritage.
The recent recognition of Glaw Lake as a Ramsar Site is an important milestone, but it is also a reminder of the responsibility that comes with being home to such extraordinary natural wealth.
Arunachal Pradesh is a living treasury of biodiversity and conserving it is not only about protecting nature today, but ensuring that its forests continue to breathe, its rivers continue to flow, and its remarkable species continue to thrive for generations.

Water is supposed to be the simplest thing we consume. The premium bottled water industry has transformed it into something that requires a backstory.
Supermarket shelves now distinguish between glacial, iceberg, volcanic, spring, mineral, and alkaline water. Restaurants are introducing water menus, while trained water sommeliers assess bottles by their mineral composition, mouthfeel and provenance. At the extreme end of the category, Svalbarði Polar Iceberg Water sells Arctic water for as much as €100 (around $116) a bottle.
The category’s growth rests on a mixture of verifiable differences and carefully constructed associations. Water can contain different minerals. Those minerals can change how it tastes. But claims about purity, alkaline pH, and remote natural sources can also create the impression that expensive water must be healthier.
According to Michael Mascha, who founded the platform FineWaters in 2002 to train water sommeliers and drag premium bottled products out of the commodity aisle, prices often reflect remote sourcing and difficult transport rather than superior health benefits. Luxury water, he argues, is better understood as a dining experience than as a more effective source of hydration.
Does Expensive Water Hydrate You Better?
There is no established evidence that luxury water hydrates an otherwise healthy person better simply because it is more expensive or comes from a celebrated source.
“Fundamentally, true hydration is about consuming enough water throughout the day to replace daily losses rather than brand status or origin,” says Lucy Semerjian, associate professor of environmental science and technology at the University of Sharjah in the United Arab Emirates.
What matters most is drinking enough safe water to replace the fluid the body loses. Its chemical and microbial composition must also remain within safe limits.
Are the Minerals in Bottled Water Better for You?
Minerals are responsible for some of the genuine differences between waters. As water travels through soil and rock, it can absorb calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate, sodium, and other dissolved substances. Their type and concentration depend partly on the geology surrounding the source.
These minerals are already dissolved into ionized forms, meaning the gastrointestinal tract can absorb them. Mineral water can therefore contribute to a person’s calcium or magnesium intake, although its nutritional significance depends on the concentration, the quantity consumed, and the rest of that person’s diet.
The word “mineral,” however, does not tell consumers how much of any particular nutrient is present.
“People see terms like rich in minerals, high TDS numbers, or alkaline pH on a premium label and assume those are automatically markers of superior quality,” says Maria Abi Hanna, cofounder and CEO of nutrition intelligence software Food Label Maker, “when in reality none of those numbers tell you anything on their own.”
Total dissolved solids, or TDS, measures the combined concentration of dissolved substances in water. A higher number does not function as a score for safety, purity, or health. It mainly describes the water’s mineral load.
The same problem applies to alkaline water. Its higher pH is frequently positioned as a wellness advantage, but pH alone does not establish that a bottle is healthier. The stomach is already highly acidic, and the body tightly regulates the pH of the blood.
Consumers should instead look at which minerals appear on the label and in what concentrations. People limiting their sodium intake, for example, may have different priorities from someone specifically looking for a water containing calcium or magnesium.
Does Mineral Content Change How Water Tastes?
Minerals may not transform hydration, but they can transform taste.
“Some waters taste very light because they have very low mineral content,” Mascha says.
Rainwater that has had little contact with the ground may contain very few dissolved minerals. Iceberg and some glacial waters can also fall towards the low end of the TDS scale, producing a relatively light or neutral taste.
At the other end, water containing upwards of 2,000mg of mineral content can have a noticeably heavier mouthfeel and a stronger flavor. Individual minerals can introduce salty, bitter, chalky, or slightly sweet characteristics.
The differences are real. The leap from “tastes different” to “is healthier,” however, is usually where the marketing begins to outrun the evidence. Luxury water makes the most sense when treated as a taste category: something selected for a particular mineral profile, dining experience, or personal preference. The price is not a reliable shorthand for its nutritional value.
Is Glass-Bottled Water Safer Than Plastic?
The most consequential thing about a bottle of water, though, may not be the water itself.
Premium brands often use glass packaging, reinforcing the perception that the water is both luxurious and protected from the concerns surrounding plastic.
“Plastic bottles are sensitive to thermal stress, UV radiation, or extended storage times,” says Nidia Rodriguez-Sanchez, senior lecturer in physiology and nutrition at Scotland’s University of Stirling.
This is particularly relevant in hot climates. Leaving bottled water inside a vehicle or storing it for prolonged periods at high temperatures can increase the migration of substances from PET into the water. Studies have found that heat can increase the release of antimony, a substance used during PET manufacturing, although the concentrations vary by bottle, temperature, and storage time.
Glass is not an entirely plastic-free solution. A 2025 study led by France’s Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety, or ANSES, found microplastics in beverages packaged in glass.
The glass itself was not identified as the main source. Researchers traced many of the particles to the painted coating on metal bottle caps, which could become scratched as the caps rubbed together during storage.
The results also varied by beverage. Soft drinks and beer in glass bottles contained considerably more particles than the same drinks in other packaging. Water contained far fewer particles overall, although glass-bottled water averaged slightly more than water packaged in plastic or cartons.
The study does not prove that glass packaging is more dangerous than plastic. It demonstrates that changing the bottle material does not eliminate every other potential source of plastic exposure.
Mascha’s response to all this is that the anxiety is selectively applied. “Everyone talks about microplastics in water. There’s also microplastics in wine, in beer, and in Coke,” he says.

Under anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the US health department is considering changing how vaccine recommendations are categorized and described. The move creates the possibility that vaccinations currently considered “routine” or “universal” could be given new designations that sound less definitive or more conditional, such as “recommended with qualification” or recommended based on “shared clinical decision-making.”
Kennedy has made no new rules or recommendations for the categories yet. However, he laid out ideas and possibilities in a Request for Information (RFI) posted online Friday and published in the Federal Register on Monday. In the 10-page document, Kennedy poses questions about the current categories and asks the public to weigh in on ideas for how to change or replace them. The deadline to comment on the questions and ideas is September 20.
Currently, there are three categories of vaccination recommendations granted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which is informed by a panel of independent expert advisors, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). The three categories are: routine, otherwise considered universal (a recommendation that everyone should get a vaccine); risk-based recommendations (only certain groups at higher risk should get a vaccine); and recommendations based on “shared clinical decision-making,” or SCDM (a flexible but uncommon recommendation for vaccination based on the characteristics, values, and preferences of a patient and the judgment of their healthcare provider).
Before Kennedy’s oversight, the CDC and ACIP used an evidence-based decision-making framework to determine which type of recommendation to give a vaccination. There is no clear, evidence-based reason to question the current categories, nor any evidence to support changing to the new categories Kennedy proposes. In his RFI, Kennedy prefaces his efforts only by citing an executive order on vaccines that Trump signed two weeks ago that aimed to slash and overhaul federal vaccine recommendations.

For years, AI industry watchers of all stripes have been warning of a coming jobs apocalypse driven by ultra-intelligent AI systems that will be able to replicate most human tasks more cheaply. Now, newly updated research from Stanford University economists suggests AI seems to be causing significant entry-level job losses for younger workers in some fields, even as older workers appear largely unaffected so far.
The August 2026 edition of “Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence” updates and revises a paper of the same name published last year with fresh data and refined statistics. In that update, the Stanford researchers find the employment trends they identified for entry-level workers last year are persisting and expanding. Specifically, employment levels for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most “AI-exposed” occupations are now 19 percent below those of their peers in fields less exposed to AI disruption.
When crunching the numbers economy-wide, the researchers found little to no difference in relative overall employment between the jobs judged most and least affected by AI on these metrics. When separating out workers aged 22 to 25, though, the researchers found that, since 2022, employment in the top 40 percent of “AI-impacted” jobs had fallen by about 11 percent. In the 60 percent of jobs with the least AI impact, by contrast, total employment for those young workers grew by 10 percent over the same period.
Across the entire economy, relative employment effects in more heavily AI-impacted fields are relatively muted.
For entry-level workers, though, there is a large and widening gap between employment in fields that are or are not impacted by AI.Brynjolfsson et al
Across the entire economy, relative employment effects in more heavily AI-impacted fields are relatively muted.Brynjolfsson et al
For entry-level workers, though, there is a large and widening gap between employment in fields that are or are not impacted by AI.Brynjolfsson et al
Digging deeper into the data, the researchers found that this phenomenon is mainly manifesting itself through lower hiring rates for entry-level workers in AI-impacted fields, rather than increased firings or employees quitting. They also found that the labor market effects among this age group were mostly seen in lower overall employment, rather than reduced pay rates.
But not all jobs that show potential for AI “disruption” are created equal, the researchers found. In its Economic Index, Anthropic differentiates between queries related to tasks that are “automative” (i.e., fully replacing work previously done by a human) or “augmentative” (i.e., helping human workers be more effective at tasks they are still needed for). By this measure, jobs like “accountants and auditors” and “receptionists and information clerks” were among those judged most susceptible to AI automation, while jobs like “chief executive” and “registered nurse” were among those using AI augmentation most often.
Unsurprisingly, jobs where AI automation is prevalent are the ones showing the worst relative employment levels for entry-level workers these days. “The findings are consistent with automation-oriented uses of AI substituting for labor while complementary uses are associated with flat or rising employment,” the researchers write.
For 22-25 year olds, jobs where “automative” users of AI are especially prevalent show heavily declining entry level employment rates.
For 22-25 year olds, jobs where “automative” users of AI are especially prevalent show heavily declining entry level employment rates.Brynjolfsson et al
For jobs where AI is merely “augmentative,” the entry level jobs picture is much more muddled.
For jobs where AI is merely “augmentative,” the entry level jobs picture is much more muddled.Brynjolfsson et al
For 22-25 year olds, jobs where “automative” users of AI are especially prevalent show heavily declining entry level employment rates.Brynjolfsson et al
For jobs where AI is merely “augmentative,” the entry level jobs picture is much more muddled.Brynjolfsson et al
Stay in school, kids
The researchers also theorized that entry-level workers could be especially affected by AI’s impact on jobs requiring heavily “codified” knowledge—the kind of “formal, standardized, documented knowledge that can be taught through education, textbooks, or written procedures.” That would contrast with jobs where AI mainly complements an experienced worker’s more “tacit” knowledge, which is overwhelmingly “acquired through practice, mentorship, and repeated exposure to real situations,” the researchers write.
To test this hypothesis, the researchers used the required level of formal education in O*NET’s extensive occupational database as a proxy for how reliant that job is on codified knowledge. Breaking out the employment data, the researchers found that “occupations with higher codified knowledge have slower entry-level employment growth, while occupations with higher tacit knowledge have faster employment growth for mid-career and senior workers.”
At the same time, the researchers found that higher education might still serve as a buffer against the employment effects the Stanford researchers identified. As they write, occupations with a higher share of college graduates showed more “muted differences between more-exposed and less-exposed occupations” regarding AI. In jobs with few college graduates, on the other hand, “the least AI-exposed occupations [saw jobs] growing and the most exposed occupations [were] declining in employment.”
In a recent interview with The Washington Post, lead researcher Erik Brynjolfsson warns that the current trends suggest a near future in which jobs for those employed in the pre-AI era largely persist while many jobs for the incoming working-age cohort start disappearing. “The entry-level effects we’re measuring are real, persistent and widening,” he said, “and I’m more worried than I was about a labor market that keeps its overall employment level while quietly closing the on-ramp for people starting their careers.”
Kyle Orland has been the Senior Gaming Editor at Ars Technica since 2012, writing primarily about the business, tech, and culture behind video games. He has journalism and computer science degrees from University of Maryland. He once wrote a whole book about Minesweeper.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Every summer evening, Gulshan follows the same routine. She washes the floor of her one-room home several times so it cools a little for her four children to sleep on. Last summer, the family saved enough to buy a desert cooler, which uses evaporation as a cheaper alternative to air conditioning.
The family uses the appliance cautiously to save on energy costs. But even when it is on, Gulshan, who does not use a surname, has to dampeneveryone’s clothes before sleeping. The 39-year-old and her children now have rashes and one has a skin infection from the wet cloth against their skin.
This summer, Gulshan started jotting down these coping strategies in a garmi khata, or heat registry. “I feel relieved that at least somebody might read my family’s experiences,” she says.
They are one of 40 households in Sunder Nagri, a slum in north-east Delhi, documenting their experiences of surviving the city’s increasingly longer and more frequent heatwaves.
Over the last few years, cities across India have begun drawing up heat action plans – agreements formulated by a municipality or district administration on how to prepare for and respond to extreme heat.
While some incorporate data such as satellite-derived land surface temperatures to identify heat hotspots, there are still significant gaps in information on people, making it difficult to understand how heat is experienced differently across communities.
Aravind Unni, an urban planner and researcher in Delhi, says: “Experiences of heat are vastly different depending on geography, income, occupation, gender, caste, class.
“While we have some meteorological data on heat, what’s absolutely missing is people, community – what they feel, what they experience.”
Most data collated in heat planning is usually just meteorological, such as air temperatures and heatwave thresholds.. The idea for the heat diaries was to “move beyond just the numbers”, says Nibedita Saha, a Greenpeace India researcher who worked on the project.
Aakiz Farooq, a senior campaigner at the group, says the team contemplated how best to encapsulate experiences and thought: “What if they become their own storytellers, they write their own evidence, they write their own testimonies?”
Arshi, 19, who lives in one room with five other family members, is a distance-learning student at Delhi University. She also works at home making decorative tassels for trucks.
She makes about 150 rupees (£1.17) working with her mother and sister for a day. “Sometimes I go to the college library just to sit in the air-conditioned space for a while. But I have to come back home so I can help my sister and mother,” she says. These experiences are part of Arshi’s diary.
The diaries, which ask about daily routines, work, home, mood and families, are intended to serve as comprehensive journals of residents’ daily lives.
Arshi’s small brick house is extremely humid, and while the temperatures are lower after rain, the combination of heat and humidity means everyone is sweating profusely.
The ambient air temperature insideis 29.3C (85F), but with relative humidity at 84.6%, the “feels-like” temperature is 36.3C (97F).
Raja, a 21-year-old street vendor, experiences temperatures as high as 45C during peak summer months as he sells vegetables from his pushcart. The fresh produce spoils quickly, leading to losses, and he has noticed a drastic drop in numbers of people on the street, which also reduces his income.
Every night, he returns to a home with limited ventilation and no cooling source beyond a ceiling fan. As the gap between day and night temperatures narrows year after year in Delhi, people in homes such as Raja’s get no respite, even after the sun sets. “I started sleeping out on the roof in May so I could feel some air,” he says.
Workers such as Raja, Unni says, could be better protected by public policy if the state knew of their experiences at a micro-level and establish systems to provide compensation.
When Sunder Nagri’s residents set out to map heat indices within their neighbourhood, they found that some streets, including where Raja sells vegetables, reflected temperatures on the ground of more than 54C (129F). The residents are attempting to find pragmatic solutions, such as shade, water sources or increased greenery.
This summer, satellite analysis found striking differences across Delhi. For instance, an analysis by the news magazine India Today found an average land-surface temperature of nearly 44C in the south-west district of Mahipalpur, by the airport, compared with about 37C just 2 miles (3km) away in the leafy, upmarket suburb of Vasant Kunj.
Unni feels the diaries and community heat mapping can help form urban resilience policy, but says a big stumbling block is that “Indian cities do not have the administrative capacity or infrastructure to have decentralised action”.
The diaries have now been submitted to India’s National Human Rights Commission, urging it to recognise extreme heat as a human rights issue and recommend measures to protect people.
Farooq says the team also plans to share the testimonies with ministries, policymakers and MPs to push for more targeted measures to protect people from extreme heat.
He says they are also working to develop the testimonies into evidence of impacts and injuries that could be used for lawsuits to increase accountability, given the supreme court’s 2024 ruling that protection from the most adverse impacts of the climate crisis forms part of the right to life.
On 4 August, India’s government added heatwaves to the list of nationally notified disasters, allowing states to access emergency relief funds.
Unni and Farooq say it “would be ideal” if the decision meant funds could support local action guided by community participation.
Arshi also feels more hopeful after the new guidelines. “Even if the government sees something as small as our rising medical and electricity costs and tries to help with that, it would feel like a win for me. At least they would have seen what we are going through,” she says.

For decades, the average Indian man’s festive wardrobe was simple. One dependable kurta that was worn for Diwali, family functions, office celebrations and the odd festive ceremony or ritual. Throw in a jacket or a pair of mojris or traditional leather sandals, and the same outfit could feel new. This was the state of ethnic wear for men in India, till D2C brands began showing them the world beyond the once-a-year kurta purchase. With the emergence of dozens of brands, Indian men are trading jeans and polos for ethnic wear that feels comfortable, contemporary and suited to the occasion. Younger audiences are increasingly choosing lighter garments, contemporary colours, short kurtas, kurta-shirts and versatile separates for dinners, college events and casual gatherings. And the trend is prevalent across all corners of India, with each state and region having D2C brands that are carving a niche in ethnic wear. What began as brands experimenting with kurtas (inspired by Fabindia’s rise) has now become something bigger. According to Yash Sarawagi, cofounder of Kolkata-based D2C men’s ethnic wear brand Kisah, Indian men are becoming particular about how ethnic wear reflects their style, body type and occasion. “Reels, creators and marketplace listings are helping customers compare silhouettes, colours, fits and styling choices in a category where a kurta was once treated simply as a kurta.” These consumers are looking for complete, occasion-specific looks rather than individual garments, giving brands room to expand across products, price points and markets. “The opportunity, therefore, is no longer simply to sell more kurtas during more festivals, but to create new reasons for men to buy Indian wear for dinners, work events, travel, casual gatherings and celebrations,” added Kora by NM’s cofounder Nilesh Chhadva. That’s why this is the second wave in men’s ethnic wear in the D2C and new-age retail space. However, this comes with ‘conditions apply’. More occasions do not necessarily mean more annual spending. As brands expand their assortments, stores and marketing calendars, the real test will be to create incremental demand while making the economics of repeat purchases, inventory and offline retail work. From Festive Wear To Everyday Occasions Currently, for brands, the challenge is to ensure that more occasions translate into more purchases. According to Puneet Mansukhani, the global retail head of digital and technology transformation at KPMG in India, this can be addressed by creating new use cases for contemporary ethnic wear across social gatherings, travel, work and celebrations — occasions that can increase purchase frequency and expand the addressable market. The effort will, however, require changes on both the operational and marketing fronts. “Instead of making one large seasonal bet, brands need to focus on shorter merchandise cycles, smaller initial orders and faster replenishment,” said Mani Singhal, managing director and co-lead of the consumer and retail practice at Alvarez & Marsal India. Inventory allocation also needs to reflect regional differences, since the same festival does not generate equal demand across the country. Marketing faces a similar challenge. Running campaigns around 10 festivals does not automatically create 10 purchase decisions. Incremental demand is more likely to come from products designed for new use cases such as a lighter kurta for a pooja, an office Diwali collection, coordinated family looks or garments that can move between ethnic and everyday settings. The opportunity of men’s ethnic wear may be expanding, but the profitability and long-term sustainability of the businesses running these brands remain complicated. Like any other category, there is the risk of low purchase frequency, designs not working or the SKUs going out of fashion. Profitability varies sharply across segments with premiumisation underway among the established brands. Mass and mid-market products can offer greater scale and repeat potential, while premium ethnic wear brings higher ticket sizes but greater markdown risks. The segment with the highest sales volume, therefore, may not generate the best return on capital, while the highest-ticket products may not deliver the strongest store productivity. Fit adds another layer of complexity. A t-shirt can tolerate some variation in fit but a structured ‘bandhgala’, ‘sherwani’ or fitted kurta may not. Since alterations are more or less a given, brands need physical presence through dedicated experience and retail stores, expert tailors or an additional service layer, adding both cost and operational complexity. This is what sets the ethnic wear business apart from casual fashion or fast fashion, which often do not need such extras in their stores. Retail expansion and omnichannel strategy is almost inevitable for men’s ethnic wear brands moving up the fashion ladder. And as products and SKUs become more premium and of higher value, these are non-negotiables. Singhal suggested watching four indicators: falling full-price sell-through, rising inventory days or heavier end-of-season discounting, store additions outpacing like-for-like growth, and customer acquisition costs rising faster than gross profit per customer. Smaller brands can bank on marketplaces and can ride on the quick commerce bandwagon to scale up without physical presence. And where such retail presence is needed, they can also look at multibrand retail partnerships rather than dedicated stores. Shuchi Pandya, consumer investor at Fireside Ventures, added that instead of relying entirely on exclusive brand outlets, newer brands or on-the-rise labels can use multi-brand retail and franchise-operated stores to expand with less capital. Then there is the fundamental problem of repeat purchases not being very regular in this category. In many D2C categories, customer acquisition costs can be spread across several transactions a year because of the frequency of purchase. Men’s ethnic wear follows a different beat and often customers may not spend anew for every occasion. It can also help D2C men’s ethnic wear brands build product awareness and expand organised retail into underserved markets. There is always the risk that several brands end up using capital to compete for the same urban customer, Pandya said. But the opportunity is meaningful enough that new brands can make a big dent, and particularly because men’s ethnic wear remains a fragmented category. Per CRISIL, men’s ethnic wear also accounts for only around 7% of the overall menswear market. This leaves room for brands to move customers from tailoring and fragmented local retail into organised formats. Sir Nick Faldo says LIV golfers seeking a return to the DP World Tour may have to "eat a bit of humble pie" before regaining eligibility for the European-based circuit.

Deloitte just became the latest company to face the consequences of President Donald Trump's crackdown on DEI, or diversity, equity, and inclusion practices.
The Big Four professional services firm agreed to pay $21.5 million to settle allegations that it violated rules against employment discrimination in its federal contracts, the Department of Justice announced Tuesday. The agency accused Deloitte of discriminating on the basis of race and sex in its hiring and promotion practices.
Deloitte did not admit liability as part of the settlement. The company said in a statement it was "pleased to have resolved this matter to avoid the cost and distraction of protracted litigation."
The Justice Department called out DEI practices in its statement announcing the settlement.
"Government contractors cannot reward or penalize employees based on race or sex — and labeling the practice DEI does not make it lawful," Attorney General Todd Blanche said. "The Justice Department will aggressively pursue government contractors that have used taxpayer dollars to fund unlawful discrimination."
The settlement is part of the Trump administration's broader probe of DEI practices at major companies with federal contracts. Several companies have pulled back on their DEI practices in recent years following pressure from conservatives and Trump's return to office. In early 2025, Deloitte cut some of its DEI policies and told some staff to remove their pronouns from their email signatures.
In April, IBM agreed to pay $17 million to settle similar allegations of employment discrimination. IBM did not admit liability as part of the settlement.
In a separate settlement also announced Tuesday by the state of Indiana, Deloitte agreed to pay $1.2 million over allegations that it violated nondiscrimination requirements in its work with the state. Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita's office said in a statement that the settlement was "the first of its kind between a state and a government contractor."

It is the summer of salmonella, it seems. Multiple overlapping salmonella outbreaks now sprawl across at least 30 states as of late August, even as cases of prodigious-poop-causing parasite cyclospora seem to be receding. Hundreds have been sickened, and simultaneous recalls are in effect for products as diverse as eggs, granola, jalapeño peppers, greens powders, nut butters, and dog food.
Salmonella, and its attendant havoc on the GI tract, are these days a hallmark of American summer—not just in meat and eggs but, increasingly, fresh produce, as climate change brings warmer and wetter summers. Foodborne bacteria enjoy the same weather as corn and tomatoes and are happy to hitch a ride.
“When we see warmer temperatures, that is going to create conditions that are favorable for bacteria like salmonella or parasites like cyclospora to grow,” Ellen Shumaker, a food safety expert at NC State Extension, told WIRED this month.
Luckily, there's already a simple preventive technology known to be wildly effective against salmonella. It's called “cooking.” While anything above the USDA-recommended food-safe temperature of 140 degrees Fahrenheit can kill salmonella if cooked for long enough, the bacterium is dead nearly immediately above 165 degrees.
Heat is the last, best line of defense against salmonella. I'm the WIRED Reviews team's lead reviewer for cooking technology, and I consider my food thermometer the single most important food safety item in my kitchen.
And yet, while most Americans own a food thermometer, more than 70 percent don't regularly use it to assess food temp, according to a recent food safety survey. This is a statistic that would terrify my mother.
I have convinced myself that the problem is that your thermometer is terrible. A lower-cost thermometer, like this $14 quick-read thermometer my editor has in her kitchen, will give you an accurate enough internal temperature for your meat or lasagna. But it'll take as long as seven or eight seconds to get a useful ballpark reading, which can feel like a lifetime when hovering over a pan or an open oven door.
The best meat thermometer is the one you'll actually use. For more than a decade, the WIRED Reviews team has been recommending an instant-read food thermometer that costs seven or eight times the price of a “fast-read” thermometer on Amazon.
The reason is simple: speed. The above Thermapen One offers a stable digital readout of food's internal temperature within just a couple seconds. This difference is pivotal, because it means you're likely to actually use it rather than dread using it. This gives the Thermapen a much better claim to hang out in the important real estate next to the stove rather than jumbled somewhere nearby in a drawer.
What Food Temperatures Can Kill Salmonella?
If you're looking for the maximum reduction in your risk of salmonella, you need to “introduce a kill step,” said Jerold Mande, an adjunct professor of nutrition at Harvard’s School of Public Health. And in the case of bacteria, your kill step likely involves temperature.
Salmonella and other dangerous bacteria thrive, and propagate, in the temperatures between 40 degrees and 140 degrees Fahrenheit. To be safe, food must be either placed in the fridge or cooked and held at temps higher than 140 degrees.
To kill bacteria, the FDA recommends that red meat be cooked to 145 degrees or above and rested for three minutes. Eggs and ground meat should be cooked to 160 degrees Fahrenheit or higher. Poultry should be 165 degrees Fahrenheit.
Wireless Options
For stovetop purposes, an instant-read thermometer like the Thermapen One is going to have the most utility. But for oven-cooked meats, for air-fried wings, and even for thicker produce like potatoes or layered dishes like casseroles and lasagna, I tend to prefer a wireless temperature probe.
The most reliable I've used, especially if you also plan outdoor cooks in thick-walled smokers, is the Typhur Sync Gold series, which offers the best mix of easy use and admirable signal strength. In addition to being a food safety tool, the Typhur's predictive function can be a useful helper in hitting precise temp targets on long cooks, and the Sub-GHz (915 MHz) signal can travel a good ways down the block before fading.
But if you're just planning to cook indoors in a space with a good Wi-Fi signal, I've also found the TempPro TempSpike Pro ($130) to be convenient at a lower cost, with a digital temperature monitor that has a magnetic back so I can mount it on the fridge. The app's not as fancy as Typhur's, and the signal range also isn't as good if you're trying to take this outside. But the accurate ambient temperature readings are a lot more precise than the thermostat in my range oven; the internal temps are likewise reliable. But especially, the TempSpike's fridge-mounted digital temp readout makes it the probe I often reach for.
And (say it with me): The best meat probe for food safety is the one you actually use.
More Food Safety Gear
Lately, increasing reports about tomatoes and onions and jalapeños had me worried: Do I need to use a meat thermometer for veggies now?
Deaths from acute food-borne illnesses range from the hundreds to the low thousands in the US, and foodborne illnesses have declined significantly since the turn of the millennium. Compared to the long-term chronic disease risks of avoiding fresh produce and eating processed foods, the acute risk posed by your lettuce and carrots can look comparatively insignificant, Mande said.
This said, each person's risk tolerance is, well, personal. This is true especially if you're a parent, or an older or immunocompromised person. Those worried about salmonella outbreaks in the news should first consult local public health authorities to determine whether an outbreak is active in their area, Mande said.
Washing produce helps, though it's not foolproof. So does using separate cutting boards for meat and produce and avoiding cross-contamination of cooked and uncooked food. Most food safety experts tend to recommend that the best cutting board for raw meat is a less-porous, high-density cutting board like this one from Great Jones, which WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loves for its juice groove and easy portability.
I don't like piling up extra cutting boards. And so I use an ingenious, svelte, steel-reinforced dual-sided cutting board from Steelport, which has end-grain walnut on one side for veggies and a high-density, non-porous polymer on the other side for meats.

Crested ibises, a species designated as a special national natural treasure in Japan, taking to the skies over the Noto region of Ishikawa Prefecture in May marked the first release of the birds on Honshu.
The move represents a significant step in efforts to reintroduce the crested ibis to the wild after the species had become extinct in Japan. The environment ministry has revised its road map for the program and plans to fully launch initiatives aimed at establishing the birds on Honshu and expanding their habitat.
Once found across Japan
The crested ibis inhabited regions throughout Japan until the Edo Period (1603 to 1867) and is said to have been highly valued as a resource, including for use in arrow feathers.
Its population, however, plummeted during the Meiji Era (1868 to 1912) due to overhunting and environmental destruction.
In 2003, a female named Kin, who had been taken into protective care from the wild, died, marking the extinction of Japan’s native crested ibis population.
Meanwhile, wild crested ibises were rediscovered in China in 1981. After they were confirmed to be the same species as Japan’s crested ibis, a pair was presented to Japan in 1999 as a “symbol of friendship.”
Artificial breeding of the pair began at a conservation center on Sado Island in Niigata Prefecture. Sado had been the bird’s last habitat in the country, and the project aimed to reintroduce the species into the wild.
The release of crested ibises began on Sado in 2008.
By the end of 2025, a total of 530 birds had been released, and about 470 are believed to be living in the wild.
Reintroducing species that have become extinct in the wild can help increase populations and restore ecosystems. Still, such efforts may also carry risks, including the spread of infectious diseases and competition with other organisms for feeding grounds.
Although Sado Island as a whole is thought to have the capacity to support more than 1,000 crested ibises, there are concerns that rising population density in certain forests could lower survival rates and worsen crop damage, such as rice plants being trampled.
For this reason, releases will also be carried out in areas of Honshu where crested ibises are believed to have lived in the past and where environmental conditions are considered suitable.
To expand the bird’s habitat, the environment ministry in 2022 selected five areas on Honshu as candidate sites.
Following the Noto region, a release is scheduled for June 2027 in Izumo, Shimane Prefecture.
Hopes for regional revitalization
The environment ministry’s road map, revised in the fiscal year that ended in March, clearly states that, for the time being, efforts should focus on releasing crested ibises on Honshu.
The road map sets a goal of having about 50 crested ibises released on Honshu living in two or more areas by fiscal 2030, with breeding confirmed in at least one of the locations. Its ultimate aim is to increase the number of mature crested ibises living in the wild to more than 1,000.
There are also hopes that releasing crested ibises in Noto will play an important role in regional revitalization.
The birds have been positioned as a “symbol of recovery” from the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake and torrential rain disasters.
To preserve feeding grounds, the Ishikawa prefectural government has established a certification system for rice cultivation that reduces the use of pesticides and chemical fertilizers. The prefecture hopes to increase the added value of locally grown rice and expand its sales channels.
The Izumo municipal government, meanwhile, aims to create a new regional brand as “a city where both crested ibises and people thrive.” To build momentum, the city is considering measures such as designating a “Crested Ibis Day,” holding related events and introducing an ordinance.
“As population decline remains a challenge in hilly and mountainous areas, we hope (the planned release of crested ibises) will encourage people to learn more about the region, help increase visitor numbers and lead to the development of new products,” a city official said.
Beyond the reintroduction in Noto and the release planned for Izumo, efforts are underway in three other areas, including Tome, Miyagi Prefecture, to create habitats in anticipation of ibises that may settle there.

New Zealand to introduce bill for under-16s social media ban
- Published
New Zealand is to introduce a bill seeking to ban under-16s from using social media.
Under the latest proposals, platforms including TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and Facebook, will have to take steps to check users are over 16 and platforms that fail to meet their obligations could face fines of up to 10% of their global revenue.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said social media was exposing children to "harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with". But several political parties have said they will vote against the bill.
The move follows a similar ban in Australia, while countries including the UK and Greece are set to introduce restrictions next year.
Luxon said social media was affecting children's family life, mental health, sleep and education.
"We have protections to keep children safe in the real world and we need them in the virtual world too," he said.
New Zealand's government has not outlined which other "high risk" platforms could be impacted.
A statement said that under the Online Safety Bill, which is being introduced to parliament on Monday, social media companies would be required to "take reasonable steps" to check users are over the age of 16 by using methods including existing account information, facial age estimation and digital identity checks.
Platforms regularly used by children would also be required to regularly assess the risks they pose and report on how they are being identified and reduced.
No penalties are proposed for children, parents or caregivers for breaches of the ban, but fines for social media companies could be substantially higher than in Australia, where the maximum penalty is $99m (£51.7m).
