- Published
A tornado has torn through the village of Pomas in south-west France, injuring 39 people and damaging hundreds of homes.
Authorities said 15 people were taken to hospital and two were in a critical condition. One man said his pregnant wife was injured after their house collapsed on her.
More than 120 emergency workers were deployed to the village south of Carcassonne after winds reaching 117km/h (73mph) tore roofs off houses and damaged an estimated 300 homes on Monday.
"Half the village has been destroyed," said one resident called Pierre, who described the tornado as swirling like a "huge red and yellow chimney".
"There's a huge castle and a third of it is has collapsed - even though these are stones that have stood for 1,000 years," Pierre told Ici Occitanie.
The third stage of the Vuelta a España cycle race, which was taking place in the Aude area of south-western France, had to be cancelled when a hail storm forced the riders to take shelter about 15km from the finish line.
The extreme weather has left about 2,800 homes across 10 villages without electricity, according to officials.
Local sub-prefect Emmanuelle Plantier-Lemarchand told French radio that she was not aware of anyone missing. She lowered the number of victims from 41 to 39, and said 15 of them had been treated in hospital.
"I heard this massive noise... then I saw everything flying around in the air and my roof collapsed over my head," shocked resident Chantal told French radio. "I've got no house left, that's for sure... I was really scared. I thought that's it, this my final hour."
French authorities had issued an orange alert for thunderstorms in large parts of the country's south-west, which have already been hit by power outages and transport disruptions.
Eyewitness footage from the region captured the swirling vortex of the tornado looming in the horizon above houses and trees.
Images from the small village of Pomas, which was the hardest hit, showed uprooted trees, damaged cars and rubble from destroyed homes.
Meanwhile there were flight delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and north of Paris to the north, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot.
On average, France experiences several dozen tornadoes per year, according to the country's national weather service Météo-France.
It comes after Europe's summer of unprecedented heatwaves and wildfires, with France's south-west region among the worst affected with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in one of the largest forest fires since World War Two.

Trump says China is driving opposition to US data centres. These residents disagree
Community living near AI facility in Virginia reports invasive levels of noise, fumes and gas turbines – and it’s not Chinese propaganda
On the tree-lined streets of Sterling, northern Virginia, Lindsay Shaw’s home sits across from an industrial neighbour that has consumed the past several years of her life: a data centre.
When Shaw sits outside, she can hear its constant hum. At night, the security lights blaze through her window, making it harder to sleep. Gas turbines, diesel fumes, and 24/7 industrial noise have choked Shaw’s neighbourhood since the data centre moved in.
“It’s not China telling us anything. It’s not Russia telling us anything,” Shaw said. “It’s truly living next to it is what it is.”
Shaw came to this view gradually. She did not initially oppose the project. Shaw and her husband had worked in cybersecurity and understood the need for data centres to power cloud infrastructure and artificial intelligence.
Their concerns only emerged after the facility was approved, when eight gas turbines were added to power it while it awaited a connection to the electrical grid – a process that can take years. It was not until it was up and running that the constant noise, occasional smoke and nightly lights came.

The US-Canada trade war is already getting ugly.

What’s happening? Remember last week, when Trump said that the US and Canada had a trade deal in place? It turns out they do not. In addition to trade terms, the US allegedly made requests to weaken Canada’s French-language protections, which Carney said would have infringed on Canadian “sovereignty.”

On a longer timeline, the Trump administration is doing damage to the US-Canada relationship that goes far deeper than specific tariffs and will be far harder to reverse. Already, in January, Carney delivered a speech charting a plan to move past relying on the US as a global partner; Trump’s latest trade war will only accelerate that rupture.

Six months on, U.S. Navy families who evacauated Bahrain remain in limbo
NORFOLK, Va. - At a virtual town hall meeting, Navy families who abruptly evacuated from Bahrain six months ago had many questions. They said they still aren't getting enough answers.
NPR has reviewed a recording of the meeting, along with a full list of questions the families were asking Navy officials.
The families left Bahrain on short notice with few possessions shortly after the U.S.-Iran war began. Many are still living in temporary conditions, at hotels and short-term rentals, both inside the United States and in other parts of the world. About 580 people participated in the call last week, where Navy leaders tried to provide some answers but also left many unsure of what comes next.
The head of the Navy's Fifth Fleet, Vice Adm. Curt Renshaw, acknowledged the hardships brought on by the rapid evacuations and that the Navy is "making it up as we go because nothing is conceived to go on this length of time." He also went on to say, "these are complex problems and the solutions have not been exactly obvious."
When the military and the State Department ordered the evacuation of dependents on March 2, Renshaw told families the Navy expected only a brief displacement, similar to when the U.S. and Israeli forces attacked Iran's nuclear facilities in June 2025. That war lasted 12 days.
"Unfortunately, this has just stretched on and on, and has evolved into something greater and a bigger challenge," Renshaw said during the conversation. "When we talk about that challenge, we've delayed making some hard decisions because we didn't want to close the door on getting people back into Bahrain."
U.S. dependents left everything behind
The Iran war has left the Navy scrambling to figure out what to do with 1,300 dependents who left just about everything behind in Bahrain, the headquarters of the Navy's Fifth Fleet. The number doesn't include the sailors and civilian workers, who were also displaced.
One Navy spouse, who has two small children, says she is now on her eighth relocation in less than six months. Like many families, they initially went to Europe and then to various locations in the U.S. NPR is not using her name because she worries about the impact on her husband's career. Her husband is in the Navy and is still in Bahrain.
"I need to take control over my life again and not just be at the whim of the administration, and I need to make plans and move on from this," she said. "I don't want to be dragged around in this anymore. I feel like my spouse is holding up his end of the deal."
School is about to start for the couple's two children. She expects to spend more out of pocket just to stay in a single location throughout the coming school year.
"I'm all alone and in a state that doesn't really have a military presence," she said. "No one really gets what's going on or even knows where Bahrain is."
People in the community occasionally notice the higher gas prices, but otherwise the war has no real impact on them.
"It's very lonely and exhausting," she said.
Searching for a permanent solution
On Tuesday, the State Department will end the ordered departure which governs the evacuation. The Navy, Department of Defense civilians and the State Department, each have different rules that govern how families are paid while they live under mandatory evacuation orders.
"The safety and security of our personnel and their families remain the Department's top priority as we continue to assess conditions across the region," said a State Department spokesman. "Authorized departure and ordered departure cannot go past 180 days. As this deadline approaches for the U.S. Embassy in Bahrain, we are working with our post to finalize a determination of appropriate posture."
According to information relayed during the virtual town hall, the Navy wants families to pick a more permanent location, while the military decides what will eventually happen to families assigned to Bahrain. They would receive a housing allowance, similar to what other military families receive.
The spouses NPR spoke with, who also did not want to be named, said they believe the Navy has already waited too long to see if their situation would return to normal. They are also concerned that a growing number of expenses will now come out of their own pockets. Most people have not received their belongings from Bahrain. Many people have had to buy second cars and new clothing.
While the typical Navy tour lasts two to three years, some civilian employees have been in Bahrain for more than a decade. The Navy was not able to answer questions about the status of family members who don't have a U.S. visa to remain in the United States.
Vice Adm. Renshaw also acknowledged that some of the problems involve outdated regulations. The cap on rental car payments hasn't changed since the 1990s.
Naval Support Activity Bahrain is a main supply hub for the Navy, but carriers and supply ships can't currently use the base, because of risk of attack from nearby Iran, just across the Gulf.
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel who was once stationed in Bahrain, said the base looks like a piece of Southern California dropped into the Middle East.
Several families told the Navy and NPR that they wanted to return to Bahrain. But Cancian, who's now a military analyst with the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the war may have permanently changed how the U.S. operates its bases in the Middle East, including Bahrain.
"The families won't go back there, at least not for quite a while. It's just too dangerous," Cancian said.
After nearly six months of conflict, the U.S.-Iran war is now defined by an extended U.S. naval blockade, which is monopolizing two U.S. aircraft carriers. With neither side backing down, Cancian expects the conflict will drag on well past the midterm elections in November.

Nintendo reveals its latest Switch 2 bundles just ahead of the console's price increase
It's still cheaper to buy the console, Mario Kart World and three months of Switch Online access now.
Just ahead of the company increasing the price of the Switch 2, Nintendo has announced a new Nintendo Switch Sports Resort bundle for the console, as well as a revamped version of a previous Mario Kart World package. Colombian officials say criminal groups could have set Tolima forest fires
The governor of Colombia’s Tolima province says criminal groups could be behind some forest fires that have burned large areas this month
BOGOTA, Colombia -- The governor of Colombia’s Tolima province said Tuesday that criminal groups could be behind some of the forest fires that have burned almost 30,000 hectares (74,131 acres) of land this month in the country's central region.
In an interview, Gov. Adriana Matiz said there are “serious clues” that suggest saboteurs caused some of the fires, adding that she has filed a complaint with Colombia’s attorney general.
Matiz said videos filmed by locals show men on motorcycles setting fires to some areas. She said a report by a local fire department has said gasoline was used to cause one.
The governor said armed groups could be using the fires to distract law enforcement from a strategic area where criminal groups profit from gold mines.
In a message on X on Monday, President Abelardo de la Espriella expressed concern that some fires may have been caused deliberately and said he had asked law enforcement to investigate.
De la Espriella also said he had asked the governments of the United States and Chile for support to put out the fires.
Temperatures in Tolima this month have been unusually high, reaching more than 2 degrees Celsius above average in some areas, while rain has been 30% lower than usual, according to the province’s environmental agency, Cortolima.
Other areas of Colombia have experienced forest fires this month, including the provinces of Cundinamarca, Valle del Cauca, Narino and Boyaca.
In Tolima, the worst affected region, 50 homes and almost 8,000 hectares of farmland have been destroyed by the fires, according to the regional government. They have caused no deaths.
“We have people who lost all of their corn crop, or their lemons. People who have no way to feed their cattle,” Matiz said. “We are going to face a strong economic crisis that we are starting to prepare for.”

Dolly Parton once said that she always wore heels and makeup at home so she was "ambulance-ready at all times" — but the country music icon was far from flash over substance.
Parton died on Tuesday after a lifetime of philanthropy and songwriting excellence. She was 80 years old.
The singer, a self-described "professionalist," first topped the Billboard Hot 100 chart in 1981 and earned the Recording Academy's Lifetime Achievement Award in 2011. She released her 49th and final album, "Rockstar," in 2023, which debuted at No. 3 on the Billboard 200 — her highest-charting album ever.
Below are Parton's top 10 signature songs from her decadeslong career, listed below in chronological order.
"Coat of Many Colors" (1971)
"Coat of Many Colors" is the title track from Parton's eighth studio album. In a 2024 interview with The Guardian, Parton said it's the song she is proudest of writing.
"I'm proud of all of them. I think the one that's most personal to me is the lil' 'Coat of Many Colors,' because it talks about my mom, my parents, and kind of gives you an insight," Parton said. "It also covers bullying, acceptance, and all that."
"My Tennessee Mountain Home" (1972)
"My Tennessee Mountain Home" was released as a single in 1972 and served as the title track and centerpiece of Parton's 1973 album of the same name.
Written solely by Parton, the song pays tribute to her rural childhood in Tennessee. She was raised in a two-room log cabin as one of 12 siblings, although one of her brothers, Larry, died when he was a baby.
"Jolene" (1974)
"Jolene" is the title track from Parton's 13th studio album of the same name. It was released as a single in January 1984 and quickly rose to No. 1 on Billboard's Hot Country Songs chart.
Today, "Jolene" is celebrated as a country music staple. The song has been widely covered by other artists, including Olivia Newton-John, the White Stripes, and Parton's own goddaughter, Miley Cyrus, on multiple occasions.
More recently, Beyoncé put her own spin on "Jolene" for her 2024 country album "Cowboy Carter." Parton also serves as one of three narrators throughout the album, alongside Willie Nelson and Linda Martell.
"I Will Always Love You" (1974)
"I Will Always Love You" was released as the second single from "Jolene." Parton is the sole songwriter credited on the track; in fact, Parton later revealed that she wrote both of the album's hit singles on the same day.
"I Will Always Love You" was famously covered by Whitney Houston, who reimagined the song as a soaring pop power ballad. Houston's version won record of the year at the 1994 Grammy Awards and topped the Billboard Hot 100 for 14 weeks.
"A lot of people say that's Whitney's song," Parton told Katie Couric in 2016, "and I always say, 'That's fine, she can have the credit, I just want my cash.'"
"Here You Come Again" (1977)
"Here You Come Again" was Parton's biggest hit on Billboard's Hot Country Songs chart, spending five weeks at No. 1.
It was released as the lead single from Parton's album of the same name, "Here You Come Again," which was Parton's first album to be certified platinum in the US.
The album also earned Parton her first Grammy Award for best country vocal performance (female) at the 1979 ceremony.
"9 to 5" (1980)
Parton wrote and recorded "9 to 5" for the comedy film of the same name, in which she starred opposite Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda.
The crossover hit became her first No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, peaking in 1981. It also won two Grammys and was nominated for an Oscar.
"Islands in the Stream" (1983)
"Islands in the Stream" was originally written by the Bee Gees and recorded as a duet between Parton and Kenny Rogers. It was released as a single from Rogers' album "Eyes That See in the Dark."
The song became Parton's second No. 1 on the Hot 100, remaining atop the chart for two weeks.
"Wildflowers" (1987)
"Wildflowers," a solo Parton composition, was included on "Trio," her landmark collaborative album with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris.
"Trio" was the only album in Parton's discography to be nominated for album of the year at the Grammys. Although it lost to U2's "The Joshua Tree," it won the Academy of Country Music Award for album of the year in 1988.
"I know, for me, this will always stand as one of the great musical things that I've ever done in my entire life," Parton later said of the supergroup. "I've never been prouder of anything. I love these girls like sisters, but what we did as a trio, really, I think is going to stand up long after we're gone."
"Shine" (2001)
Parton's 2001 album "Little Sparrow" was dedicated to her father, who died months before its release.
The album's second track was a Dolly-fied cover of Collective Soul's alt-rock '90s hit "Shine," which earned Parton a Grammy for female country vocal performance. "Little Sparrow" was also nominated for best bluegrass album.
"Rockin' It" (2023)
Parton's final album, "Rockstar," was a mix of original material and classic rock covers. She said she was inspired by her Rock & Roll Hall of Fame nomination to craft a tribute to the genre.
"Even though I am extremely flattered and grateful to be nominated for the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, I don't feel that I have earned that right," Parton said when she tried to decline the nomination.
"I do hope that the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame will understand and be willing to consider me again — if I'm ever worthy," she continued. "This has, however, inspired me to put out a hopefully great rock 'n' roll album at some point in the future, which I have always wanted to do!"
Despite her statement, Parton was inducted later that year and debuted a new song, "Rockin' It," at the induction ceremony. The live recording was later included on the deluxe version of "Rockstar."
"I've been rockin', rockin', rockin' since the day I was born," Parton sings in the chorus. "I'll be rockin' 'til the day I'm gone."

Gray and white matter might both work together to support cognitive health among older adults in India and health of the brain's white matter wiring may help soften the cognitive effects of gray matter loss, a study has revealed.
"Gray matter and superficial white matter are physically close and may play different roles: gray matter processes information, while superficial white matter helps nearby brain regions communicate," first author Yingxu Liu, a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Southern California's school of medicine, said.
"Our findings suggest that cognitive health depends not only on how much gray matter is preserved, but also on the condition of the wiring that connects it," Liu said.
The study, published in Alzheimer's and Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, analysed brain scans and cognitive assessments from 459 community-dwelling adults aged 60 and older across India. Data for the analysis came from the Harmonised Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia for the Longitudinal Aging Study in India, or 'LASI-DAD'.
The study is among the first to examine the brain's superficial white matter in a community-based population from a low- and middle-income country, they added.
An advanced form of diffusion MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) was used to assess neurite density -- the small projections that allow nerve cells to send and receive signals -- and the amount of freely moving water around them.
Participants also completed tests of language, memory, executive function and visuospatial ability.
A lower neurite density or more free water can indicate a tissue disruption associated with processes such as loss of myelin, inflammation, or swelling, the researchers said.
A healthier superficial white matter was most consistently associated with stronger language skills, with clearest links appearing in frontotemporal areas involved in recognising words, speaking fluently, and holding language information in mind.
Further, decrease in gray matter remained the strongest overall predictors of cognition.
However, the relationship between gray matter and cognitive performance was found to depend in part on superficial white matter -- when this local wiring showed poorer integrity, gray matter loss was seen more strongly tied to worse language performance and cognitive impairment.
When superficial white matter was healthier, the associations were found to be weaker.
"The findings point to superficial white matter as a possible source of resilience," senior author Leon Aksman, assistant professor of research neurology at the University of Southern California, said.
"Two people with a similar degree of gray matter loss may not experience the same cognitive effects if the local connections surrounding that gray matter differ in health. Following participants over time will be essential to test whether preserving these connections can help maintain cognition," Aksman said.

Topline
Trump-backed wealth fund executive and former state Senator Mike Mazzei won the GOP’s nomination for the Oklahoma gubernatorial race on Tuesday, after winning a runoff against state Attorney General Gentner Drummond, who the president had labeled as a “fake Republican.”
Key Facts
The race was called by the Associated Press at 11 p.m. ET with nearly all ballots counted, and Mazzei secured 50.3% of the vote, scoring a narrow win against Drummond, who got 49.7%.
Both candidates advanced to the runoff after neither secured an outright majority to win the primary election in June—where Drummond topped the field with 26.25% of the vote while Mazzei got 25.97%.
Mazzei will now take on Democratic candidate Cyndi Munson in November and is a heavy favorite to win in the red state, which Trump carried by more than 34 points in 2024.
In a statement on X, Mazzei thanked the voters, said he is honored to be the GOP nominee, and touted his plans to reclaim “Oklahoma’s potential.”
Mazzei currently serves as the chair and CEO of the Tulsa-based wealth management fund Trinity Strategic Wealth.
Trump acknowledged Mazzei’s win with a graphic posted on Truth Social touting his endorsement of the candidate.
What Had Trump Said About The Race?
In a post endorsing Mazzei on Monday, Trump attacked Drummond, calling him a “FAKE Republican, who donated to SLEEPY Joe Biden.” The comment was a reference to a $1,000 contribution made in 2020 to Biden, which Drummond previously claimed was made by his wife but was later refunded. Trump also attacked Drummond’s opposition to a $4 billion aluminum smelting plant in Tulsa, which is supported by Mazzei. As attorney general, Drummond has filed an injunction against the plant to allow the state to study its environmental impact. Trump blasted Drummond for wanting to “dethrone” the “magnificent, job producing, desperately needed, and brand new, Aluminum Plant.”
tangent
Mazzei previously was an Oklahoma State senator from 2004 to 2016 and later served as the state’s Secretary of Budget. Aside from Trump, he also secured an endorsement from the state’s term-limited Governor Kevin Stitt—who has also been the subject of the president’s attacks. Earlier this year, Trump attacked Stitt, calling him a “mediocre (at best!) RINO,” meaning Republican in name only, after the two clashed earlier this year over the White House’s handling of the annual gathering of the governors of all states in Washington.

Families with teenagers in education know the private, hidden pain of exam season. But this year, what might have been a summer of quiet family anxiety has erupted in several countries into public unrest.
Exam-related turmoil has led to mass student protests in Mexico after nearly 60,000 university applicants were forced to resit tests amid suspected cheating, while Portugal’s disastrous attempt to digitise school exam marking sparked the country’s worst education crisis in decades.
By far the largest and most ground-shaking incident was in India, however, where an exam paper leak affected millions of students and was linked to more than a dozen students taking their own lives. The scandal forced the education minister to resign, and challenged the government’s hold over its 1.4 billion citizens.
Why does this exam season seem to be particularly tense and volatile? Experts say the growth of AI cheating and attempts by academic institutions to digitise examinations are at the heart of the issue. When coupled with the high stakes of good grades in an increasingly precarious global economy, the result can be explosive.
“It would seem that exams are getting more fraught on a global scale,” said Dr Sarah Eaton of the Werklund School of Education at the University of Calgary. “The pressure on young people has absolutely changed.
“We’ve seen the economic situation change around the world in the last decade. And the results of one examination determining a person’s entire future really creates untenable pressure on young people,” said Eaton, a leading expert on academic ethics. “This is a tragedy when young people are dying by suicide because of an examination outcome.”
When a single test can determine a young person’s entire future, cheating is no longer just about individuals but becomes a systematic issue, said Eaton. This is compounded when illicit commercial industries, known as the “education mafia”, exploit student desperation by stealing and then selling exam papers, something that has become widespread in India and elsewhere.
Students from across India joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party, a youth-led protest campaign that began as an online satirical joke and grew into a nationwide outcry that poses an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government.
“When you get large-scale fraud combined with systemic failure, there’s almost a guarantee of a breakdown of public trust,” said Eaton. “And once that trust is broken, it’s almost impossible to regain. I can’t imagine how India is going to deal with this, just given the levels of corruption and fraud that we’ve seen.”
In Portugal, the national fallout from a failed push by its education minister, Fernando Alexandre, to fully digitise the exam marking process has landed the government in a crisis. Parents, teachers, and students have been protesting, demanding Alexandre’s resignation after his policy resulted in serious marking errors.
Similar demonstrations took place in Mexico. The National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam), the country’s most prestigious university, announced that due to abnormally high marks in entrance exam results, which raised suspicions of widespread cheating, approximately 58,000 students would have to retake the exam.
Schools worldwide are rushing to deal with AI use by students, either through bans or teaching AI literacy and ethics to pupils. Denmark announced this month that from the new term, teenagers would have to make a verbal defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating.
Eaton has implemented similar reforms in her class. “AI can generate a perfect essay in seconds. So an essay is no longer a viable way to demonstrate students’ learning,” she said. “We should let it die with dignity and find other ways to assess student learning.”
In Eaton’s view, cheating is a “human problem” and so grading and assessing student learning has historically also been a human responsibility, which she said cannot easily be off-loaded to the latest tech.
But what institutions around the world have been doing instead, she said, is hoping technology can be easily and cheaply used to prevent cheating en masse.
Dr Thomas Lancaster, a computer scientist at Imperial College London who researches the educational use of generative AI, has studied how cheating has gone hi-tech. It is no longer about sneaking notes written on a sleeve, he said, but sophisticated communication.
Lancaster says students have always cheated but it has become far easier, with pupils using earpieces or miniature cameras, and increasingly, communicating with friends or family with access to internet searches.
“I think the number of notes you sneak in, they’re only useful if they’re the right notes and if you can interpret them very quickly,” he said.
“But with any kind of communication technology, you can have that expertise waiting outside for you in a human form. They either know the answers; they’ve got the expertise; or they can look them up online. You can go further than that now and have access to AI to communicate directly during the exam as well,” he added. “It’s spy technology, really.”
Rather than individual student misconduct, Eaton said the failure to properly train educators was forcing students to spend valuable time trying to navigate through these “broken” systems rather than focusing on learning.
“This idea of these mass examinations happening at scale, it sort of dehumanises the learning process and the assessment process,” she said.
This, she said, “sort of perpetuates this idea that examinations are the most important thing for students. I think we’ve lost the thread. Learning should be the most important thing for students.”

Becerra, running for governor of California, faces a health insurance problem
By the time Democrat Xavier Becerra left Washington, D.C., more Americans than ever had health insurance, owing partly to his work over the years to pass, defend, and expand the Affordable Care Act.
It's an achievement the former congressman and U.S. secretary of Health and Human Services often touts as he campaigns for California governor against Republican Steve Hilton, a former Fox News commentator.
But should Becerra cruise to victory in November, as polling suggests, he will face what may be the steepest decline in health insurance coverage in a generation, one that will land especially hard in his home state.
Federal cuts mean more people uninsured
By 2030, the number of uninsured Californians under 65 is expected to nearly double from 2.4 million to 4.6 million as recently enacted state and federal cuts to Medicaid and ACA marketplaces begin to roll back historic gains in health coverage, according to a May analysis by the University of California, Berkeley Labor Center. The anticipated rise in the uninsured population could have broad implications for hospital systems, insurers, and the economy.
In February, Miranda Dietz, the labor center's healthcare program director, told legislators the changes could end up costing California about 200,000 jobs, mostly in the healthcare industry.
Hospital executives have begun reporting more unpaid medical bills, and experts warn health plans will raise premiums further as they're left with enrollees who are, on average, sicker and more expensive to cover.
"It's triage," said Jessica Altman, executive director of Covered California, the nation's largest state-run health insurance marketplace. "That's what the next governor is walking into."
California achieved one of the most dramatic drops in its uninsured population in the nation, largely credited to the state's robust adoption of the ACA. If tapped to lead the wealthy, progressive state, Becerra would wrestle with how uninsured Californians get care and who pays as the Trump administration shrinks a federal safety net he once oversaw.
Becerra has some experience pushing back against Washington, D.C. As California attorney general, he successfully defended many provisions of the Affordable Care Act, including access to birth control.
Becerra said he would issue an executive order to keep those affected by federal cuts insured. But he has not detailed how the state would backfill as much as $30 billion in federal funding California stands to lose annually.
At a policy forum hosted by Politico this month, Becerra promised Californians would not lose health coverage despite federal cutbacks, saying he would push the industry to eliminate waste from "attorneys, accountants, pencil pushers" that cost consumers billions.
"I'm going to ask them to help me extract some of that waste and put it into healthcare, which helps us cover the cost of keeping Californians insured," he said.
His opponent, Hilton, is trying to appeal to voters opposed to President Donald Trump, despite receiving the president's endorsement, and has stumped on cutting off coverage for Californians without legal status, which is paid for with state funds. Hilton has vowed to use those savings to issue state income tax breaks, calling it an immediate antidote to high costs.
"We all understand that the healthcare system is a mess and needs major reform," Hilton said in an interview. "The quickest thing we can do on healthcare costs is actually to tax people less."
Left behind?
In 2010, Becerra was part of U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's leadership team and helped whip up votes to pass the law. He also had a hand in crafting it, though his attempt to include a government-backed coverage option failed.
A decade later, when lawmakers considered him for the nation's top healthcare job, Becerra said his primary mission would be to carry out President Biden's vision to expand access and cut costs under the Affordable Care Act.
Before the ACA, some 50 million Americans — roughly 1 in 6 — were uninsured. Within a few years of the law's passage in 2010, its expansion of Medicaid eligibility and financial aid to lower-income marketplace enrollees helped slash the U.S. uninsured rate by nearly half.
Millions more gained coverage during the COVID-19 pandemic after Becerra implemented a freeze on Medicaid disenrollment and administered generous but temporary tax credits that put the cost of Obamacare plans within reach for more people.
As Biden's health secretary, Becerra launched aggressive public awareness campaigns, loosened enrollment rules, and distributed hundreds of millions in grants to pay consumer assistants, also known as healthcare navigators, to help enrollees wade through paperwork.
"One of the common things we would hear from him as a leader was, 'Who's being left behind?'" said Benjamin Sommers, a Harvard health policy professor who was a deputy assistant secretary under Becerra.
Under Biden and Becerra, the percentage of people with health insurance reached a historic high of 92%, or 310 million Americans having health coverage in 2024.
Republican response
But conservatives said those policies inflated enrollment by attracting fraudulent and wasteful coverage. In response, the second Trump administration has tightened enrollment windows and toughened income reporting.
"It's simple and easy to say, well, the numbers are up so the program must be working," said Edmund Haislmaier, a senior research fellow at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank. "My argument would be that's the wrong metric."
Last summer, the GOP-led Congress passed Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Republicans argued preserves Medicaid for those who need it most while rooting out fraud and waste. Altogether, the law is expected to cut Medicaid spending by $900 billion-plus over a decade.
Congress also allowed enhanced premium tax credits for Obamacare plans to expire last year, spiking premium payments for middle-income Americans and driving down enrollment by nearly 3 million this year.
"We are now witnessing almost a wholesale reversal of pretty much all those policies" that helped cover millions more Americans, said Sabrina Corlette, co-director of the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.
For Eric Maciel, the $800 cost of a Covered California plan is too much. To avoid injury, the 28-year-old stays home more and rarely plays pickup soccer at the park — the other players, he added, can get pretty rough.
"That's another car note," Maciel said. "I'd be left with nothing."
Health economists say Maciel is the type of customer insurers need to stabilize their risk pools: young, healthy, and less costly.
Hilton criticized state leaders for passing a revised provider tax he asserts will send premiums soaring and said he wants to inject more competition into California's health insurance market — but he offered no specific ideas.
Playing defense
Higher-than-expected state costs coupled with federal cuts have prompted California to retreat on healthcare coverage. Federal funds account for one-third of the state's budget and more than 60% of spending by Medi-Cal, the state's Medicaid program.
Gov. Gavin Newsom has frozen enrollment for immigrants without legal status, enacted monthly premiums for some, and plans to only temporarily backfill federal assistance for legal immigrants and refugees.
Newsom and Democratic lawmakers agreed to delay some cuts until July 2027, leaving the next governor to weigh further rollbacks against increased taxes. Becerra, a California native born to Mexican immigrants, opposes what's known as the billionaire tax, on November's ballot. This month, he said he supported legislative efforts to penalize large corporations whose workers rely on Medi-Cal, arguing that taxpayers are subsidizing employers' low wages and paltry benefits.
County governments, which are legally required to provide healthcare to uninsured residents too poor to afford care, are lobbying lawmakers for funding to treat what they describe as a fresh deluge of patients who need free care.
"It's a pretty big cliff if all this stuff goes into effect," said Dietz, the labor center's healthcare program director. And there's a choice whether to make it less bad and maintain coverage for folks."

Bangladesh could consider joining the Mecca pact, a mutual defence agreement signed this month between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, a minister said, a move that could complicate its foreign relations, particularly with neighbouring India.
Ties have been strained as Bangladesh accused Indian border forces of forcibly pushing in people while it seeks extradition of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who has lived in exile in India since her ouster in a protest movement in August 2024.
"If there is a security arrangement among Islamic nations in the Middle East, it is not unusual for us to consider participating. It is being viewed positively," said junior foreign minister Humayun Kabir.
"They are inviting the leadership of Bangladesh, particularly Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, to come and participate," he told reporters on Monday.
A source in the Bangladesh foreign ministry told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had invited Dhaka to join the pact, but did not say when the invitation was made. The source sought anonymity as he was not authorised to speak to media.
The three Sunni Muslim-majority countries signed the agreement, modelled on NATO's collective-defence principle, in the Saudi holy city of Mecca this month.
They pledged that an armed attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all, amid heightened tension in the regional conflagration that has brought Iranian missile fire across the Middle East.
Bangladesh, like Turkey, is a secular republic, although more than 90% of its population identifies as Sunni Muslim.
Asked for comment on the minister's remarks, the embassies of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in the South Asian country did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia was open to expansion.
Analysts say joining a military alliance would test Bangladesh's long-standing foreign policy of avoiding rival geopolitical camps to help it attract investment, expand exports and maintain economic ties with competing powers.
The economy relies on exports of readymade garments, most of which go to Britain, the European Union and the United States, while remittances from millions of workers abroad, mainly in the Middle East, are a major source of foreign exchange.
Formal alliance membership could complicate Bangladesh's ties not just with India, but also China, Iran, Japan, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Russia, the United Arab Emirates and the United States, said geopolitical analyst Kollol Kibria.
"These relationships would not automatically break, but once Bangladesh joins a military bloc, the question of which side Bangladesh is on becomes much harder to avoid," Kibria said.
The invitation comes at a delicate moment in Bangladesh's relations with India under Rahman's six-month-old government, despite efforts by both to ensure cordial ties.
The prime minister has yet to decide whether to visit India, Rahman's spokesperson said this month, as Dhaka awaits New Delhi's response to its extradition request for Hasina.
Dhaka has previously called for a "propitious environment" for such a visit after Hasina spoke to journalists in New Delhi this month, a move criticised by Bangladesh.
India's foreign ministry spokesperson on the Mecca pact said it was closely following developments in West Asia.
Analysts said New Delhi was unlikely to welcome Bangladesh's membership of a security alliance that includes arch foe Pakistan, although Dhaka would ultimately need to weigh the broader economic and strategic consequences of such a move.
The perception of alignment could create risks for Bangladesh's export-driven economy, reliant on stable commercial and diplomatic ties with a wide range of partners, said Asif Shahan, a development studies professor at Dhaka University.
"If Bangladesh joins this alliance, several countries, including India, will not be pleased," Shahan added. “However, that should not be the basis of Bangladesh's decision.”

Three years ago, Andrew Stockwell had his hiring routine down to a science.
As head of people for the software-buying company Vendr, Stockwell posted a listing, waited a few days, and then reviewed a few dozen applications—up to 100, if he was lucky. Recruiters identified other potential candidates, adding a few more applicants to the mix. Stockwell read résumés, conducted interviews, and passed along sterling candidates to hiring managers.
“It was really about finding that great talent, sussing out that talent, speaking with that talent, and identifying the best possible people,” Stockwell tells WIRED.
Sometime in the last year or so, Stockwell says, everything changed. The process started off the same way, but within a day or two, Stockwell wasn’t looking at 100 candidates. Instead, he was flooded with hundreds of applications. Sometimes, the incoming topped a thousand. A good chunk were “total bogus,” Stockwell says—fake candidates. Many more appeared to have been written using artificial intelligence, stretching the truth and making it difficult to distinguish one applicant from another. The sheer quantity was overwhelming. Stockwell says he found himself “paying my talent-acquisition professionals—who are high-paid, high-quality individuals—just to look through applications all day long.”
Stockwell is one of many recruitment professionals who believe looking for a job is fundamentally broken. In 2026, job hunting has become as easy as online shopping: AI can crank out tailored résumés and cover letters in seconds. Browser extensions can autofill applications, no human necessary. LinkedIn serves users dozens of jobs a day, many with the option to apply with “just a few clicks.”
“A year ago, every recruiter would tell me: We want to make it as easy as possible to apply for jobs,” offering candidates a “seamless experience,” Ophir Samson, the head of voice AI for Greenhouse, tells WIRED. Samson joined the recruiting platform earlier this year, when it acquired his startup, which used AI to conduct job interviews. “What they got was 2,000 applicants in 24 hours for a job. That is a shitty experience for everyone.”
Good applicants can’t stand out, while bad candidates slip through the cracks. Recruiters, Samson says, face the tortuous task of judging thousands of candidates, every single day. Instead of taking the time to search LinkedIn for dream employees, they spend hours in applicant tracking systems, tweaking filters to try to determine whose applications are worth a 30-second skim.
Now, recruiters are telling Samson, “actually, we kind of want friction,” he says. “The friction is good. We want to make it harder.”
The desire to remove pain points in the application process makes sense: If the highest number of qualified candidates apply for a role, it stands to reason that a company can maximize the chances of finding the best possible fit. So for years, recruiters have posted on job boards and LinkedIn; they signed up for LinkedIn’s “Easy Apply” feature; they promised candidates a “one-click” application process. Post-pandemic, recruiters’ efforts to simplify the process went into superdrive, as employers struggled to fill open roles.
“Everyone was job hopping, because you literally could have three offers in an afternoon,” Jane Curran, the chief transformation officer at real estate giant JLL, tells WIRED. Now, “it is the polar opposite.”
Openings peaked at a record 12.3 million in March 2022, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, followed by two years of decline. Since mid-2024, openings have hovered at around 7 million, give or take 500,000.
But as the number of job openings contracted, the barriers to entry for applying declined even further. AI—which entered the mainstream in late 2022 with the public release of ChatGPT—allows applicants to rewrite résumés and track new postings almost instantaneously. Companies like JobAssist, Sonara, and Ladder’s Apply4Me promise applicants that their technology will handle all the busy work of applying for jobs, by submitting “10x as many applications with less effort than one manual application.” If you wanted to, you could apply for dozens of jobs a day.
This formula has led to ballooning candidate pools and laborious hiring processes. LinkedIn tells WIRED that submissions per applicant on the platform are up 46 percent compared to February 2020. Since the launch of ChatGPT, applications are up 22 percent. The explosive number of applications led to LinkedIn adding limits to cut back on automated and low-quality applications. This month, the platform is rolling out a feature that informs (seemingly) underqualified applicants that they probably aren’t a good fit for a role, and suggests other jobs.
“We're currently in a place where employers are complaining that they can't find good people, and people are complaining that they can't find jobs,” Tessa White, a former HR executive, tells WIRED.
White worked in HR for two decades before leaving corporate America in 2018. During the pandemic, she began posting on TikTok, where she has built a following of 800,000 by sharing advice and commentary on the job market. She believes the current situation is unworkable, and is a result of recruiters’ quest for speed and ease. “Every time we seem to strive for efficiency, we seem to give up quality,” she says.
Recruiters know they have a problem. Sure, an avalanche of résumés is welcome for some roles, such as skilled trades workers, where employer demand consistently exceeds employee supply. But for the typical unemployed white-collar knowledge worker, JLL’s Curran says, there “is not enough churn, not enough jobs coming into the market.” That means recruiters in these industries face a barrage of résumés every time they post a new role.
Many recruiters are turning to AI tools themselves, hoping to wrangle the sea of applications into something more manageable. Companies have used automated applicant tracking systems to screen résumés for at least a decade; now, many are using agents to conduct first-round interviews with candidates.
“We frequently hear from recruiters: They have 1,000 applications, but they know that only 30 of them are serious,” Greenhouse’s Samson says. An AI interview can sort the unserious from the serious, he says, offering recruiters context beyond a résumé.
While Samson says that these AI interviews are not friction for friction’s sake, they have the added bonus of weeding out bots and halfhearted candidates. Curran says she expects some companies to turn to knock-out questions that cut down the application pool via strict criteria. Others might add skills testing earlier in the process.
But White isn’t convinced these changes fix the underlying problem—that the frictionless résumé drop has rendered the first round of the application process essentially worthless. “Employers are having such a hard time hiring people with the current antiquated process,” White says. “Even AI and applicant tracking systems, which sound so high-tech, are an antiquated way to look at people and skill sets.” AI simply does not have the capabilities, she says, to accurately judge someone’s potential.
“I definitely think recruiting and the way we do it is due for a massive overhaul,” White says. “And I don't even know that I have the right answers.”
The deluge of applications has increased recruiters’ reliance on referrals and internal hires. While these human-to-human connections have always been important, today, some see them as the only ways to circumvent the glut of applications. Stockwell believes this benefits people whose backgrounds align with existing employees’, which isn’t conducive to a diverse workforce. “The whole thing is a big mess,” he says.
Stockwell is now dealing with the mess from the other side of the application portal. In February, he left Vendr, and is now on the job hunt. He treats the search like a job, “pounding the pavement” and attending in-person networking events. He knows that without a personal connection the chance of actually getting an interview is close to zilch. When he applies to jobs online, he estimates it only leads to a phone interview less than 2 percent of the time.
“I'm biased, of course, about my own capabilities,” Stockwell says. “But companies are missing out on fantastic talent.”

Referring to former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee interacting with her supporters through social media, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday (August 24, 2026) suggested that his predecessor remains active on Facebook and said that he will ensure that she does not hit the streets.
“Remain active on facebook. You will not have to go out on the streets anymore. I will also make arrangements so that you cannot go out on the streets,” the Chief Minister said, while addressing a press conference at the State Secretariat.
ALSO WATCH TMC in crisis: Mamta Banerjee’s leadership questioned as MLAs break away | The Hindu explains
Ms. Banerjee, who only a few hours ago reiterated that she will not be pushed into a political sanyas, described the remark as a threat.
“A NEW LOW in Indian politics! @SuvenduWB, while seated in a government office, has brazenly THREATENED me, publicly declaring that he will ensure I cannot even leave my home. I call upon the Hon’ble President of India, the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India, and the people of India: Is this the India envisioned by our Constitution?” the Trinamool Congress chairperson wrote on X in a late evening post. A number of leaders of the Trinamool Congress joined Ms. Banerjee in taking on the Chief Minister.
After the defeat in the West Bengal Assembly polls 2026, Ms. Banerjee, who made her political mark as a ‘street-fighter ’, has not hit the streets often. On a few occasions she tried to do so the response has been tepid.
Mr. Adhikari cited the two instances of Baruipur, where a minor was raped and killed, and Halisahar, where a Trinamool supporter was killed in police custody and said that she failed at both the occasions.
However, the remark to keep the Trinamool Congress chairperson confined to social media has larger ramifications. Despite her party facing the biggest existential crisis – with majority of MPs and MLAs switching sides and warming up to the BJP, Mamata Banerjee remains the only leader to take on the might of the BJP which has 207 MLAs in a 294 member house.
Over the past few years, the politics in West Bengal has been hinged on a contest between an ageing leader who wants to pass over the baton to her nephew and one of her closest aides turned rival. Suvendu Adhikari has defeated Mamata Banerjee directly in an electoral contest on two occasions — in Nandigram in the 2021 Assembly polls by a margin of 1956 votes and in 2026 at Bhabanipur by a margin of 15,065 votes. The 2026 Assembly polls might not be the end of political rivalry, and people of West Bengal may continue to see the two political personalities taking on each other.
There is an enthusiasm among the BJP leadership after coming to power, but the Suvendu Adhikari government is caught in the same policy trap of giving cash doles which had been a hallmark of the Trinamool Congress regime.
With women protesting the denial of cash incentives under Annapurna Bhandar scheme as promised by the BJP during the election campaign, Mamata Banerjee sees it as an opportunity to revive both her credibility and her party.
There is also unease among the leaders who left Mamata Banerjee to warm up to the BJP, particularly those who are from the minority community, and that can be a silver lining for the Trinamool Congress chairperson. For Suvendu Adhikari, the challenge is how long can they keep the former Chief Minister confined to her residence and social media.

A rumor that Yellowstone National Park rangers warned the public that ravens at the park had learned how to open car doors spread online in August 2026.
For example, the Facebook page Casper Planet posted shared the claim (archived) on Aug. 24:
Yellowstone Rangers Warn Visitors After Ravens Learn to Open Vehicle Doors
Yellowstone officials are warning visitors to secure and lock vehicle doors after ravens reportedly learned how to open several different types of vehicles and push button hatch backs.
Rangers say the birds have mostly taken snacks and small objects, although one visitor reported returning to find a raven sitting inside the car on the steering wheel.
Park officials recommend locking cars whenever possible and absolutely do not recommend attempting to negotiate with the ravens.
Variations of the rumor also spread on LinkedIn. Some users seemed to interpret the rumor that rangers issued a warning about ravens as true, and Snopes readers contacted us in search of more information.
To investigate the rumor's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Bing and Yahoo. If Yellowstone rangers had really released such a statement, these searches would have uncovered such evidence.
That was not the case. We did not find any credible reporting about ravens unlocking car doors at Yellowstone National Park. Rather, the Facebook post above primarily appeared as the top result.
We identified the rumor's original source: satirical social media account Casper Planet, which describes its output as "Snews that doesn't matter."
In addition to a location tag on "Satire Street," its Facebook bio reads (archived):
Delivering the Snews that doesn't matter directly to your Snews feed. Did we say this is satire? Well it is, names/locations are made up
We reached out to the page owner for comment in January 2026 regarding another claim about AI-generated images of massive snow bank on Wyoming's Devils Tower. The account's administrator, Justin Hathaway, told Snopes over the phone: "I just love doing this satire stuff, it's such an outlet for me." He continued: "Another reason is people don't really read things fully anymore, and it's a good way to educate people on reading stories fully if they sound somewhat unbelievable."
In sum, while ravens are notoriously intelligent and several species do live in Yellowstone National Park, there is no evidence that park rangers released any kind of public statement regarding ravens opening car doors.
Other Casper Planet posts Snopes has debunked include a claim that a Wyoming mountain collapsed and another that a man received a DUI while riding a bear.
Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Next to perhaps its lineup of kids programming, when the average person thinks of PBS, they likely think of the network’s impressive lineup of documentary series, including Frontline, American Experience and Nova.
Raney Aronson-Rath is the editor-in-chief overseeing GBH’s documentary programming, which includes American Experience, Frontline and Nova. She is also an Oscar-winning producer and has been executive producer and editor-in-chief of Frontline for the past decade.
American Experience recently announced several new projects, including the three-part documentary series Lindbergh, which premieres in May 2027.  Ken Burns will be the executive producer of the project, teaming up with acclaimed director/writer Stephen Ives. 
The other major documentary coming from American Experience is a four-part series The Bureau: A Secret History of the FBI, directed by Sharon Grimberg and Sarah Colt, “charting the rise, weaponization, and survival of the nation’s most powerful law enforcement agency.”
I recently spoke with Aronson-Rath about those projects, as well as what to expect from Frontline and NOVA. We all discussed the impact the federal funding cuts had on the shows and how she has learned to lean into the new digital audience for the shows.
The interview has been lightly edited for clarity:
Let’s start with the big part of your job. You’ve been an EP at Frontline for more than a decade. Now you’re overseeing three shows, and how does that change your day-to-day workflow? I mean, obviously, it’s more complicated, but the shows are also very different and I suspect require very different approaches.
Raney Aronson-Rath: Yeah. It's definitely different. I think it's actually been an intellectual reorganizing moment for me.
So to think about it, I do oversee Frontline. Still. I’m the executive producer and editor-in-chief.
I’m very passionate about current affairs and investigative journalism. But I think when Susan Goldberg asked me to take on the other shows, I started to think about the importance to our democracy of factual, science-based information and fact-based history. And so intellectually, I was sparked and inspired.
And I think that's really where I've taken the three factual shows: to think about how can we think together? How do we dream together? How do we think about big areas of intellectual pursuits for us that Americans in the global community really need to know and work together collaboratively? That's where I get excited. So it is more work. But the other thing I need to say is we have really talented teams at NOVA and American Experience and Frontline.
So it's not just me doing everything. We have incredible filmmakers and collaborators and contributors. And so together, we're really working across the three shows.
That’s really intellectually very exciting to think about how all these different ideas can fit together. Now, how in the weeds do you want to get with any particular episode?
I mean, obviously, as you said, there’s a whole crew. They’re doing it regardless of whether you’re there. But how close attention are you paying to this is what the episode looks like, this is how the reporting out across the episode?
Raney Aronson-Rath: So for Frontline, I'm very involved. I'm very much in the edit room because I am its editor-in-chief. And I'm very hands-on with the films.
I'm involved with the commissioning. I'm involved with who's going to be on camera. And I have a very strong senior team at Frontline as well.
At NOVA, I'm much more involved from an exec level. So I'm weighing in on the cuts. I'm talking to them about their ideas.
But we have very talented executive producers at NOVA. And then at American Experience, I’m very involved with thinking through what are the big tentpole editorial projects. So we're doing Charles Lindbergh, as you know, and we're doing a big film about the FBI. Those are ideas that I'm really deeply involved with.
On the digital side, we have a great digital team. So with American Experience and Frontline, I'm very editorially involved. But with NOVA, I'm involved more at a studio exec level.
I love the show, and I’m very helpful. I give notes. But we have really excellent people running NOVA.
One of the things that struck me is that I've watched these programs forever. For American Experience, you're talking about typically topics that aren't going to change. Ten years from now, you look at an American Experience documentary, and it's probably not going to be that different fact-wise.
 
The Historical Challenges Of Documentary Making  
 
But with NOVA, science changes all the time. With Frontline, it could be a very topical story that three years from now seems like ancient history. So given how important the digital side is, given the importance of things like Passport, how do you balance that thing of “We want to do something topical, but we don’t want to just burn through show after show that won't have any value in two years?”
Raney Aronson-Rath: I think I ask a question over each of the different fact-based strands. So I’ll start with Frontline. For Frontline, we are current affairs.
But what I’m always trying to think about, and why our films do have staying power, is I’m thinking about what absolutely needs to be told right now as a record. I very much have a this-will-be-here-for-the-long-term mindset. And the reason for that is because, as you know, Frontline's a big streamer now.
We're on YouTube. And so we're there in perpetuity. We're there for the long haul.
Let’s take 20 Days in Mariupol as a great example. That is the only record of what actually happened in Mariupol in Ukraine that was captured and filmed. So now it's 2026.
Is that still relevant? I would argue absolutely, right? So Frontline is not a news show. We’re not breaking news all the time. But we're telling investigations that really have credible records that will be there for the long haul.
For American Experience, interestingly, I'm taking a different approach. I'm thinking about what is the history that needs to be told right now that we need to know currently.
So it's almost like the inverse. What do you and I need to know right now about our democracy, about our global community, about what's happening today? And what's the history that we can tell that will help you understand today? And that has to do with things like the FBI. Very helpful to understand the history of the FBI today.
It's very important for us to understand our future through a historical lens. And with NOVA, you're absolutely right. Science is evolving all the time.
That's why that show is so exciting. They tend to take on topics that have staying power as well, so that we can think about it with a long tail in mind. That's where we're different from a breaking-news ecosystem here.
We're thinking longer term. We're thinking about what is the value proposition for somebody who watches this month, next month? I mean, I've been educated by the stream environment, right? Sometimes people find us on YouTube two years later, and you see millions of people surrounding a documentary two years later because something in it is capturing them. So that's just also who I am as a person.
You know, I'm a books person. I'm a documentary person. And I love a narrative.
I love stories. I love stories that can live with us forever.
How does that digital long tail impact the production of these shows? Where you have the opportunity of deciding, “Look, don’t just discard that footage because it doesn’t fit in the completed thing. We can use it elsewhere.”
We can pop that on YouTube. We can do a short and put it on TikTok. For example, how does that change your production flow for Frontline, which you’re probably the most intimately involved with?
Raney Aronson-Rath: So one of the big changes for Frontline has been that we started to share our underlying interviews. We did that as an act of transparency. I did that as a trust-building exercise to bolster our democracy. It was a high-minded idea.
However, what we found is millions of people love to watch the uncut, unedited versions of interviews. And that's just like, who knew about that community? Then we have the micro shorts that we're really all pushing into so aggressively.
So basically, everything that you film is now important. Everything that you film actually needs to be archived, has to be shared. And it just is amazing how much you can get out of a single documentary process now across social, across digital, across text.
So it’s actually an exciting time for filmmakers. Who are really used to gathering materials and making a bespoke version of what they've gathered, fact-based and fair, but they've really spent a lot of time in the edit room making it that story. That was a little disruptive for my filmmaking team at Frontline, but I would say most everyone has embraced it because they see the upside. We're reaching a younger generation.
We're reaching millions of new people. We're now 60% global at Frontline, which is amazing. And that's because of our reach across the YouTube landscape with all these new properties in addition to our films.
 
How The Digital Audience Is Different From The One For Linear TV
 
As this digital stuff has rolled out over the last few years, is there something that surprised you - where you found yourself thinking, “I can't believe that the viewers like this or this was something that they resonated with?”
Raney Aronson-Rath: I have two teenagers, mind you, so I’m educated by my own teens, right? I was so surprised that long-form documentary films were actually the biggest achievers in the YouTube landscape. And I share this often because what we see is our long-form, most serious work, the serious work about Mohammed bin Salman and MBS, the serious work about the platforms like Facebook or Amazon. When you see that work do so well, it is so encouraging.
Our average watch time is 22 minutes. That means people, younger generations, are coming to watch these really serious films that really contend with nuance and fairness. And there are facts throughout the whole thing.
We're not dumbing it down for YouTube at all. That's been so surprising. And inspiring.
And it’s why I still do what I do. And I feel like the future is bright because I feel as if younger people are hungry for this type of authentic, fact-based work, then we’re going to be okay. We're going to be okay if they're curious still about this type of work.
I really feel it. The other surprising thing for me is our global community. I am so surprised that people all across the globe now are hungry to watch us in real time and share us in places like the Philippines and India and South America.
I'm very proud of that. And so we're leaning much more into international storytelling. And I'm talking to American Experience and NOVA about this almost every day.
They're kind of tired of me saying it. But there's a whole world out there for our incredibly well-told documentaries to reach people outside of our borders. And what could be better than to have a global community seeing the same thing, understanding the same facts, not having an ahistoric telling of something, understanding how stories can be told from a nonpartisan point of view and still be true.
That's really, really why I wake up every morning feeling like I'm doing something good here with this work. 
 
The Impact Of Federal Funding Cuts On PBS Documentaries
 
You’re talking a lot about the future. And I’m just curious if you can talk a little bit about the impact the rescission cuts have had. Because I know earlier in the year, they were talking about, well, there may not be any new American Experience episodes at all this year. And I’m glad to see that that's not the case, but obviously it's had an impact.
Raney Aronson-Rath: Well, I think the system's determination is nothing short of amazing.
And we have seen a huge uptick in people supporting us, and foundations coming forward and individuals who really care about having this type of media, having this forum—the forum's historical, current, and science, all in the public interest. Because remember, we're in front of the paywall. This is really important to have this work for the public still.
And we are all across stations in America. So we've seen this at all levels. Station giving has increased.
We’ve seen it across the foundations, saying, “Hey, public media matters. We have your backs.”
And I think we've seen it in the giving that goes to the shows directly. I think the question for us now is how do we think smartly going into the future together about sustaining our system? Public media matters. We need to have some media that doesn't have commercial interests, that doesn't have people leaning into it, that doesn't have pressures from the corporate world.
And so we're actually really inspired right now as a system. And I think for us, it's just being really smart.
So one of the things that we did do, and this took a lot of huge effort, you mentioned it in the beginning, is think about how do we work across the strands in a way and be less siloed? How do we think about our resources differently and really think smartly and strategically about how we can create enough funding for the actual work, but not all of the redundancies of some of the collecting that we were doing?
And I think that's been a really important thing in the factual unit of science, history, and current affairs. Us thinking together as a collective team—we're just thinking together, we're stronger together. And so that's the upside.
The challenge, of course, is that the money was rescinded. CPB (Corporation for Public Broadcasting), unfortunately, is a thing of the past. But we have so many supporters coming forward.
One of the things I think that maybe is underappreciated is that PBS is a great distribution system for documentaries. As you know, there's a lot of documentaries made that no one ever sees because, you know, they can't get it into a theater or not enough theaters, or they can't get it onto a streamer that's big enough. And you have that ability to do something and push it out in front of all these eyeballs.
Raney Aronson-Rath: We do have a huge audience, and that audience is growing. That's the thing that I would say about the PBS audience across the country and the globe: we're only growing. And that's because partly we're really leaning into the digital strategy of making sure everyone can see our work.
I think it’s also the stories that we tell. What we do is so unique now in the media ecosystem.
If you think about Frontline and NOVA and American Experience, there's not a lot of competition out there, which is also challenging, obviously. But I do think you're right that it's really hard to get some of this really thoughtful work onto commercial platforms. And that's where we come in.
You know, some people say we’re earnest. I would say it's thoughtful and it's nuanced and it's fair. Those are the words I use.
Because I see the reach of our work. We're not just over here in a corner with our little silo of an audience.
We’re actually massive. Frontline has a billion views right now on YouTube. So we're big because of that effort that we make to be fair, to be fact-based, to be trusted.
And I think that's going to be our actual secret sauce into the future.
So you’re the MrBeast of documentaries.
Raney Aronson-Rath: So we are. We absolutely are. In fact, I have a son, and he really is the one who showed me first MrBeast and the YouTube environment. He is now an older teen.
He's now 20, as a matter of fact. And he started to show me this ecosystem of how these influencers were growing. And this is about eight years ago.
And I really started to look at YouTube with that in mind. And he convinced me at the time, when he was 14, that there was a place for serious documentaries on YouTube. He was sure of it because he saw how people were talking about real issues.
And he’s now impressed with our numbers. The whole way through these eight years, Rick, he’s laughing at my numbers. He’s like, “Oh, my God, that's terrible.”
But now finally, he’s like, “OK, Mom, you’ve arrived.” And having your teenage son say that to you, it says a lot because he really was ahead of this with me on YouTube.
 
The Next Digital Frontiers For Storytelling
 
There are so many new platforms, new places for eyeballs to see your programming. Where do you see the next frontier?
Raney Aronson-Rath: I definitely think that we're seeing platforms overall really prioritizing video and a bit longer-form video. So we're seeing great success on platforms like Instagram, TikTok, and others.
We’re reaching all sorts of new people on those platforms. I think for history in particular. It's extraordinary to see *American Experience's reach now that we really shifted their priority to being digital first and to see the hunger for history on these actual platforms is nothing short of inspiring if you think about it.
And the reason I want us to be there is because this is where younger people are getting their news, where they're getting their information. And so I've always believed that we needed to have our work where people were watching. You know, I believe that so much because I do have children and I wanted us to be in their consideration set.
I wanted them to stumble across our work and say, oh, is that right? Is that true? And to think harder, right? So what it means for us is that we have to create more video, more stories, tell more stories, and do it in the native format.
You can’t just take a film and put it on TikTok. You have to think about, how do people watch - what do they consume there? What are they looking at there? And then figure out how to adapt. And that adaptation has been at the heart of the reinvention that we're all undertaking right now in public media.
Well, let me wrap it up with this question, sort of Frontline-specific. Obviously, when you’re laying out what program you’re going to do, what story you’re going to tell, there are budget issues, there’s all different kinds of things to consider. If someone gave you an unlimited amount of money and said, “Do the story that you can't tell for whatever reason now,” is there a story or two that you just think, you know, I'd love to do it, but it'd be a hundred-million-dollar project and no one would ever pay for it?
Raney Aronson-Rath: I love that question. Thank you for asking. That's the best question anyone's ever asked me.
So first of all, there’s no story, Rick, and I say this earnestly, that I feel we should tell that we’re not telling right now. I have the privilege of funding that allows me to tell the most important stories. That said, because I am ambitious, what I really love to do is I would love to take Frontline, the documentary series and expand it.
I would love to create a shorter-form series that was original investigations, more in the sort of 15-to-20-minute range. And I would love to do that all the time. So right now we’re at 20 films a year.
I would love to double it and be able to tell stories in a shorter length as well because we see our average watch time is about 22 minutes on streaming. And I think that a lot of the stories that we could tell globally could be shorter too, and that we could do more, and that's what I really want to do. I want to do more.
I want to hire more journalists. Journalists all across the country and the globe are losing their jobs. And I want to hire the best of them and put them to work. And I want to put them to work globally.
So that would be the other thing I would do is I would have Frontline Global, which is just literally having reporters all over the world reporting for us, which we do now, but we do for a documentary. So that's my dream, you know, everybody has a dream and I'm working towards it.
